title: Mesh Inference: A Formal Model of Collective Intelligence Without a Center
summary: We present a formal model of mesh inference: how a population of independent agents, each holding private state and exchanging only admitted, typed observations, derives a conclusion none of them holds alone, with no central coordinator and no agent exposed. No agent shares weights, gradients, or hidden state, and the agents may span different teams, networks, and organizations. Motivated by the observation that asking a model is energy-minimizing inference, we model the mesh as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally. We show that a single admission/emission policy governs three properties. First, mesh inference converges to a unique answer for any admission, symmetric or not, because the coupling is always an M-matrix. Second, it is identification-complete: it derives the centralized optimum exactly when the contributing views are carrier-connected. Third, it is observation-only: no node transmits its internals, and confidentiality is the dual of identification. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime every derived answer is determined, hence equal to the centralized optimum, at O(diam^2) latency, the measured price of removing the center. One such derivation is one turn of a center-free learning loop, which we formalize as architecture rather than prove. The open problem we state is when asking improves the collective rather than corrupting it: whether the non-linear closure derives an upgraded answer or a confident error. To our knowledge, this is the first formal model of mesh inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a formal model for mesh inference, where decentralized agents with private states reach a shared conclusion through typed observations without sharing weights, gradients, or hidden states. The model is framed as coupled free energy minimization, proving convergence, identification-completeness, and observation-only confidentiality with content-addressed lineage as the sole side-channel.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by the observation that model inference is energy-minimizing. The authors seek to formalize how decentralized, heterogeneous agents across different organizations can collaboratively derive a conclusion without any central coordinator and without exposing internal model states — addressing practical needs for privacy-preserving, cross-organizational inference.
AI.method: The authors model mesh inference as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally. The coupling is characterized as an M-matrix, guaranteeing unique convergence. They define three properties governed by a single admission/emission policy: (1) convergence to a unique answer under any admission structure, (2) identification-completeness (exact centralized optimum when views are carrier-connected), and (3) observation-only confidentiality. They analyze the linear-Gaussian regime and formalize a center-free learning loop architecturally.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Mesh inference always converges to a unique answer because the coupling is an M-matrix. (2) It is identification-complete: it recovers the centralized optimum exactly under carrier-connected views. (3) It is observation-only: no node transmits internals; confidentiality is the dual of identification, with content-addressed lineage as the only global side-channel. (4) In the linear-Gaussian regime, every derived answer is determined and equals the centralized optimum, with O(diam²) latency — the measured cost of decentralization.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents the first formal model of mesh inference, establishing convergence, completeness, and confidentiality guarantees. The authors leave an open problem: determining when non-linear mesh inference improves collective knowledge versus producing confident errors. The center-free learning loop is formalized architecturally rather than proven.

title: SIGMA: Skill-Incidence Graphs for Compositional Multi-Agent Design
summary: Existing graph-based multi-agent system (MAS) designers mainly improve collaboration by optimizing communication topologies over predefined agents, roles, or groups. However, because each node remains a closed-set entity, these methods struggle to generalize to tasks that require unseen combinations of capabilities. We propose SIGMA, a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills. Given a task and a skill library, SIGMA predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, composes agent node embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology over the constructed agents. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to the relevant assigned capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational. Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance and improves over CARD, the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline, by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points, respectively. It also shows stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points. These results suggest that compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design beyond communication topology optimization. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SIGMA-2338/.

AI.tldr: SIGMA is a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills, composing agent embeddings from a skill library and decoding communication topologies dynamically, outperforming topology-only baselines on reasoning and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based MAS methods treat agents as closed-set entities with predefined roles, limiting generalization to tasks requiring novel combinations of capabilities. There is a need for compositional agent construction that goes beyond mere topology optimization.
AI.method: SIGMA predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix from a skill library conditioned on the task, composes agent node embeddings by aggregating selected skill embeddings, and decodes a communication topology over the constructed agents. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to relevant assigned capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational.
AI.result: Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance. It improves over CARD (the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline) by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points across the three LLMs. It also demonstrates stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points.
AI.conclusion: Compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design, orthogonal to communication topology optimization. SIGMA's skill-incidence approach provides a more generalizable framework for building adaptive multi-agent systems.

title: Blame is easier than praise: Measuring off-ball defensive performance in football
summary: The defensive performance of football players is commonly measured through a limited number of actions like tackles and interceptions while their continuous impact through positional behaviour has hardly been studied before. We formulate this problem as an attribution over multi-agent spatiotemporal trajectories without player-level ground truth labels, where event-level changes of expected threat are distributed among individuals. We propose a framework that performs this attribution using player involvement scores calculated from defensive pressure areas (DPAs). By computing role-conditioned baselines within automatically detected team structures, we can determine each defender's expected responsibility for threat created through arbitrary passes. The validity and robustness of this approach are evaluated on a uniquely extensive cross-gender and cross-competition data set, including positional and event data from 64 matches of the men's World Cup, 116 matches of the women's German Bundesliga and 336 matches of the men's German 3. Liga. In the absence of a ground truth, we propose an evaluation protocol that combines multiple relatively weak proxies into robust summary scores. We find a validity score that is improved by around 1 standard deviation compared to the best action-based metric and demonstrate that many popular measures show limited validity. The "blame" for conceding high-value actions shows especially strong correlations with external ratings and market values, making it the first published metric in football to reliably measure positioning errors. All code underlying this work is publicly available to support reproducibility and further research.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for attributing defensive responsibility in football by analyzing continuous positional behavior through Defensive Pressure Areas (DPAs), rather than relying solely on discrete actions like tackles. It introduces role-conditioned baselines within automatically detected team structures to quantify each defender's expected responsibility for conceded threats, and validates the approach on a large cross-gender, cross-competition dataset, showing significant improvements over traditional action-based metrics.
AI.motivation: Traditional defensive metrics in football (tackles, interceptions) capture only discrete actions and fail to measure the continuous positional impact of defenders. There is no established method to attribute "blame" for conceded threats across multiple players using spatiotemporal trajectory data, especially without ground truth labels.
AI.method: The authors formulate defensive attribution as distributing event-level changes in expected threat among players. They introduce Defensive Pressure Areas (DPAs) to compute player involvement scores. Role-conditioned baselines are derived from automatically detected team formations/structures, enabling calculation of each defender's expected responsibility for allowing high-threat passes. An evaluation protocol combining multiple weak proxies into robust summary scores is proposed due to the absence of ground truth.
AI.result: The proposed validity score improves by approximately 1 standard deviation over the best action-based metric. Many popular existing measures show limited validity. The "blame" metric for conceding high-value actions correlates strongly with external ratings and market values, making it the first published metric to reliably measure defensive positioning errors in football.
AI.conclusion: Continuous positional analysis via DPAs and role-conditioned baselines provides a substantially more valid and robust measure of defensive performance than traditional action-based metrics. The framework reliably captures positioning errors and represents a significant advance in football analytics, with all code publicly released for reproducibility.

title: MonaVec: A Training-Free Embedded Vector Search Kernel for Edge and Offline AI Systems
comment: 27 pages, 11 figures. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/mona-hq/monavec (PyPI: monavec; crates.io: monavec-core). Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20559587
summary:
We present MonaVec, a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel for edge and offline AI -- settings where server infrastructure, network connectivity, and training data are all unavailable. Existing vector-search systems assume a persistent server, gigabytes of RAM, or a training pass over the corpus; MonaVec instead targets the deployment profile of SQLite: one file, one function call, runs anywhere. Its quantization core is training-free by default and data-oblivious: a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions any input distribution toward N(0,1), so precomputed Lloyd-Max tables quantize to 4 bits (8x smaller) with no learned codebook and no data pass. The index persists as a single .mvec file whose embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed makes results reproducible across architectures and byte-identical within a build -- a determinism guarantee that parallel-build graph libraries cannot offer.
  On semantic embeddings (AG News, 45K x 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce reaches 0.960 Recall@10 in 27 MB -- leading float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall -- while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism. A single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends the same data-oblivious pipeline to magnitude-sensitive L2 data, and optional IvfFlat and HNSW backends carry it to million-vector corpora.
  MonaVec is implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar). It targets on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval -- the niche SQLite occupies for relational data: one file, one call, runs anywhere.

AI.tldr: MonaVec is a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel (like SQLite for vectors) that uses a training-free, data-oblivious quantization method (Randomized Hadamard Transform + Lloyd-Max) to compress embeddings to 4 bits with no codebook learning, packaged as a single-file pure Rust library with reproducible, byte-identical results.
AI.motivation: Existing vector-search systems require server infrastructure, significant RAM, or a training pass over the corpus. There is no equivalent of SQLite for vector search — a simple, embedded, single-file solution that runs anywhere offline. MonaVec fills this gap for edge AI, offline agents, and embedded retrieval where no server, network, or training data is available.
AI.method: The core innovation is a training-free quantization pipeline: (1) A Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions arbitrary input distributions toward N(0,1), making the data distribution predictable without scanning the corpus; (2) Precomputed Lloyd-Max tables then quantize to 4 bits (8× compression) with no learned codebook. The index persists as a single .mvec file with an embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed for cross-architecture reproducibility. An optional fit() pass extends this to L2-sensitive data via global standardization. Backends include BruteForce, IvfFlat, and HNSW for scaling to million-vector corpora. Implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar).
AI.result: On AG News (45K × 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce achieves 0.960 Recall@10 in just 27 MB, outperforming float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall, while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism.
AI.conclusion: MonaVec successfully brings SQLite-like deployment simplicity to vector search: one file, one function call, runs anywhere — targeting the underserved niche of on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval with deterministic, training-free 4-bit quantization that matches or exceeds the recall of heavier server-oriented alternatives.

title: Human-like autonomy emerges from self-play and a pinch of human data
summary: Self-play reinforcement learning has recently emerged as a way to train driving policies without any human data. It uses cheap, large-scale simulations to substitute expensive, large-scale human driving demonstrations. A key limitation of this approach is that policies trained through pure self-play can learn effective but alien driving conventions incompatible with people. Previous works attempt to mitigate such behavioral misalignments through extensive reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive. Instead of completely discarding human demonstrations, our method treats them as a regularization objective on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. Like the spice in a good stew, we find that a little human data goes a long way: our method uses only 30 minutes of human demonstrations, 2500x fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches. Resulting policies coordinate with held-out human trajectories and complete training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. Videos and full source code are available at https://spiced-self-play.com/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a self-play RL approach that uses a minimal amount of human demonstrations (30 minutes) as a regularization objective, rather than for imitation, achieving human-compatible driving policies with dramatically less data than pure imitation learning methods.
AI.motivation: Pure self-play RL for autonomous driving produces policies that succeed but develop "alien" driving conventions incompatible with human behavior. Prior mitigation strategies (reward engineering, domain randomization) are brittle and labor-intensive. The key insight is that completely discarding human data is unnecessary — a small amount can effectively regularize self-play toward human-compatible behavior.
AI.method: The method adds human trajectory data as a regularization objective atop a minimal safe goal-reaching reward in a self-play RL framework. Crucially, only 30 minutes of human driving demonstrations are used — 2,500× fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches — treating human data as a behavioral spice rather than the main ingredient.
AI.result: The resulting policies coordinate successfully with held-out human trajectories, demonstrating human-compatible driving behavior. Training completes in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU, making the approach computationally accessible.
AI.conclusion: A small amount of human demonstration data (30 minutes) is sufficient to regularize self-play RL toward human-compatible driving policies, avoiding the labor-intensive reward engineering and domain randomization required by pure self-play approaches while being far more data-efficient than imitation learning.

title: VCG: A Multimodal Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Video Feeds under Extreme Cold-Start Conditions
summary: The digital commerce landscape is shifting from static, search-driven catalogs to dynamic, immersive video feeds. This transition introduces an ``extreme cold-start'' problem: unlike traditional items, new short-form videos lack the dense interaction history required for collaborative filtering. Furthermore, immersive feeds introduce strong position and duration biases that distort standard engagement signals. In this paper, we demonstrate the Video Candidate Generation (VCG) system, a scalable multimodal retrieval engine designed to solve these challenges in a large-scale e-commerce environment. By leveraging a domain-adapted vision-language model (based on CLIP), we map users and videos into a shared semantic space, enabling zero-shot retrieval based on visual content rather than behavioral history. We detail the system's architecture and present a rigorous evaluation comparing generative (LLM) vs. discriminative (CLIP) embeddings. Our results show that while generative models excel at attribute prediction, they suffer from embedding space collapse in retrieval tasks. Online A/B testing demonstrates that VCG effectively mitigates engagement biases, yielding a 50\% uplift in deep video completion. To showcase the system's capabilities, we present an interactive demonstration featuring three bi-directional retrieval scenarios: Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search.

AI.tldr: A scalable multimodal retrieval system (VCG) using domain-adapted CLIP embeddings solves the extreme cold-start problem for short-form video recommendations in e-commerce, outperforming LLM-based embeddings and achieving a 50% uplift in deep video completion via online A/B testing.
AI.motivation: The shift from static search-driven catalogs to dynamic immersive video feeds creates an "extreme cold-start" problem where new short-form videos lack interaction history for collaborative filtering. Additionally, immersive feeds introduce strong position and duration biases that distort standard engagement signals, necessitating a fundamentally different retrieval approach.
AI.method: The VCG system employs a domain-adapted vision-language model based on CLIP to map users and videos into a shared semantic space, enabling zero-shot retrieval from visual content without behavioral history. The authors compare generative (LLM) vs. discriminative (CLIP) embeddings and evaluate via online A/B testing and three bi-directional retrieval demonstrations: Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search.
AI.result: Discriminative CLIP embeddings outperform generative LLM embeddings for retrieval tasks, as LLMs suffer from embedding space collapse despite excelling at attribute prediction. Online A/B testing shows VCG effectively mitigates engagement biases and yields a 50% uplift in deep video completion.
AI.conclusion: Domain-adapted discriminative vision-language embeddings (CLIP-based) are superior to generative LLM embeddings for cold-start video retrieval in e-commerce. The VCG system demonstrably reduces engagement bias and significantly improves user engagement metrics in production.

title: Secure Coding Drift in LLM-Assisted Post-Quantum Cryptography Development: A Gamified Fix
comment: Accepted for 2026 SIGIR Workshop on Vulnerabilities in Generative Systems for Information Retrieval track
summary: The transition to Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) introduces considerable implementation complexity, requiring strict adherence to constant-time execution, side channel resistance, and precise parametrisation. Simultaneously, large language models (LLMs) are heavily embedded in software development workflows, including cryptographic engineering. While LLMs improve productivity, evidence shows that they frequently generate insecure or suboptimal code, particularly in security critical domains. This paper introduces Secure Coding Drift in PQC, a novel socio technical vulnerability model capturing the gradual degradation of secure coding practices due to sustained reliance on LLM-generated code. Unlike prior work that focuses on static vulnerabilities, we conceptualise security risk as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon rising from human AI interaction. To mitigate this, we propose a gamified, LLM augmented secure coding framework that embeds adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into development workflows. Our approach reframes LLMs from passive assistants into active security co-pilots, contributing toward safer PQC implementation in AI mediated environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "Secure Coding Drift in PQC," a socio-technical vulnerability model describing how sustained reliance on LLM-generated code gradually degrades secure coding practices in Post-Quantum Cryptography implementations. The authors propose a gamified, LLM-augmented framework with adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring to mitigate this drift.
AI.motivation: PQC transitions demand rigorous constant-time execution, side-channel resistance, and precise parameterization. Simultaneously, LLMs are increasingly used in cryptographic engineering despite evidence they generate insecure code. The authors identify a gap: prior work examines static vulnerabilities, but no model captures the longitudinal, behavioural degradation of secure coding practices arising from sustained human-AI interaction.
AI.method: The paper conceptualizes "Secure Coding Drift in PQC" as a novel socio-technical vulnerability model grounded in longitudinal behavioural analysis of human-LLM interaction patterns. To counter this drift, the authors propose a gamified, LLM-augmented secure coding framework integrating three components: (1) adversarial evaluation of generated code, (2) behavioural feedback mechanisms targeting developer practices, and (3) security scoring embedded directly into development workflows.
AI.result: The abstract does not provide quantitative empirical results. The primary contribution is conceptual — the Secure Coding Drift model itself and the architectural design of the proposed mitigation framework. The paper positions LLMs as reframed from passive assistants into active security co-pilots.
AI.conclusion: Sustained reliance on LLMs in PQC development creates a gradual, longitudinal security risk that static vulnerability analysis fails to capture. Embedding adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into LLM-augmented workflows can transform LLMs into active security co-pilots, contributing to safer PQC implementations in AI-mediated environments.

title: LLM-Mediated Human-AI Interaction in Search and Rescue: Impact of Expertise on Attentional Allocation
summary: Human-AI teaming (HAT) increasingly involves AI systems that provide real-time, context-aware guidance in complex tasks. While such systems can improve performance, their effectiveness depends on how they shape human cognition and behavior. In particular, AI assistance can introduce cognitive demands and influence attention, planning, and interaction with the task environment, with effects that can vary across levels of expertise. This work investigates these mechanisms in a simulated search and rescue (SAR) environment. We compare human performance under two LLM (Large Language Model)-guided conditions and a no-LLM baseline, and analyze interaction at multiple levels, including task performance, eye-tracking measures, and planning behavior. Eye tracking provides fine-grained insight into attention allocation and interaction with AI guidance, while behavioral measures capture how users structure and adapt their decisions over time. Results indicate that LLM guidance enhanced task efficiency (higher rewards and victims-per-step) but did not increase total victims saved. Eye-tracking data revealed an attention-guidance trade-off, with visual resources shifting to the chat interface alongside increased pupil size variability. Expertise moderated this effect: novices exhibited passive AI reliance, whereas experts maintained a "verification loop" through persistent environmental scanning. These findings suggest that LLM-mediated teaming efficacy depends on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth to maintain situational awareness.

AI.tldr: In a simulated search-and-rescue task, LLM guidance improved task efficiency but not total victims saved. Eye-tracking revealed an attention-guidance trade-off (shifted gaze to chat, increased pupil variability), with novices showing passive reliance and experts maintaining verification-based environmental scanning.
AI.motivation: Human-AI teaming systems increasingly provide real-time, context-aware guidance, but their effectiveness depends on how they shape human cognition, attention, and behavior — effects that may differ by expertise level. Understanding these cognitive mechanisms is critical for designing effective AI-assisted decision support.
AI.method: A controlled experiment in a simulated search-and-rescue (SAR) environment comparing three conditions: two LLM-guided conditions and a no-LLM baseline. Multi-level analysis included task performance metrics (rewards, victims-per-step, total victims saved), eye-tracking measures (gaze allocation, pupil size variability), and behavioral planning data, with expertise as a moderating variable.
AI.result: LLM guidance improved efficiency metrics (higher rewards, higher victims-per-step) but did not significantly increase total victims saved. Eye-tracking showed an attention-guidance trade-off: visual attention shifted toward the chat interface, accompanied by increased pupil size variability (indicating cognitive load). Expertise moderated these effects: novices displayed passive AI reliance, while experts maintained a "verification loop" — persistently scanning the environment to cross-check AI guidance against ground truth.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated teaming efficacy hinges on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with the task environment to preserve situational awareness. Passive reliance (common among novices) undermines this, while expert verification behaviors sustain it. Design should encourage verification and mitigate attention competition from AI interfaces.

title: Supporting Design Decisions in Rule-Based Model Transformations
summary: Model Driven Engineering relies on model transformations to automate the derivation of target models or source code from source models. However, the design decisions that govern how source elements are mapped to target artifacts typically remain embedded in the transformation source code, limiting flexibility, reusability, and traceability. This paper proposes an approach to explicitly model and manage design decisions in rule-based model transformations. Design decisions are separated from transformation implementation through three mechanisms. First, a decision model captures design decisions and their options independently of any source modeling language for a given transformation domain. Second, a binding model connects these decisions to specific metamodel concepts in a given source modeling language, enabling reuse of the same design knowledge across transformations from similar languages. Third, a configuration model records the specific option chosen for each applicable source model element, with defaults pre-selected automatically. During execution, variability points in transformation rules are resolved dynamically according to configured choices. A trace model records which rules and options were applied to produce each target element. We establish a formal mathematical framework that defines the core concepts of variability-based transformations and proves key properties of the resulting transformations. The formal concepts are realized in a practical architecture of four interconnected artifact models. We demonstrate practical feasibility by extending an existing embedded domain-specific language for model-driven engineering with variability support and illustrate the approach with a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes explicitly modeling design decisions in rule-based model transformations by separating them from implementation via decision, binding, and configuration models. A formal mathematical framework defines variability-based transformations, and a practical architecture demonstrates feasibility through an ER-to-Relational example.
AI.motivation: Design decisions in model transformations are typically hard-coded in transformation source code, which limits flexibility (cannot easily change mapping choices), reusability (decisions tied to specific languages), and traceability (no record of which decisions produced which outputs). The authors aim to externalize these decisions to address all three limitations.
AI.method: The approach uses four interconnected models: (1) a decision model capturing design decisions and options independently of any source metamodel; (2) a binding model linking decisions to specific metamodel concepts, enabling cross-language reuse; (3) a configuration model recording chosen options per source element with automatic defaults; and (4) a trace model linking target elements to the rules and options applied. A formal mathematical framework defines the core concepts and proves key properties. The approach is realized in an extended embedded DSL for MDE.
AI.result: The formal framework proves key properties of variability-based transformations. The practical architecture demonstrates that decision models can be separated from transformation logic. The approach is validated through a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example implemented in an extended embedded DSL.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling design decisions through decision, binding, configuration, and trace models successfully decouples transformation logic from mapping choices, improving flexibility, reusability, and traceability in rule-based model transformations. The formal foundation ensures correctness, and the practical implementation confirms feasibility.

title: Exposing the Unsaid: Visualizing Hidden LLM Bias through Stochastic Path Aggregation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit representational and syntactic biases that are difficult to evaluate due to the stochastic nature of text generation. Standard auditing methods rely on a single output inspection or static automated metrics. These approaches obscure the underlying probability distributions and fail to capture biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. This paper introduces TreeTracer, a visual analytics tool designed to evaluate LLM bias through aggregated comparison. Using a systematic perturbation analysis pipeline, the tool replaces ontology-defined terms in each input prompt, aggregates hundreds of stochastic generations into a syntax-aligned hierarchical structure, and then performs classification-aware node merging with an auxiliary language model. The resulting structure is visualized through a custom Sankey diagram. By juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees, the workspace enables direct comparison between semantic contexts and supports systematic bias detection. Because any visualization reflects only a subset of the model's learned behavior, the system further applies contrastive inference to compute and directly display counterfactual token probabilities across contexts, reducing the risk of misinterpreting the presence of bias. We validate the workspace through case studies comparing an unaligned baseline model GPT-2 XL against the constitutionally aligned Apertus models. The visual aggregation successfully exposes hidden representational harms, such as counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization of individuals. A preliminary user study confirms that the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and effectively supports analysts in detecting systemic biases.

AI.tldr: TreeTracer is a visual analytics tool that aggregates hundreds of LLM stochastic outputs into syntax-aligned hierarchical Sankey diagrams for systematic bias comparison. By perturbing ontology-defined terms and merging classification-aware nodes, it surfaces hidden representational biases (e.g., pronoun suppression) and uses contrastive inference to display counterfactual token probabilities, validated through case studies on GPT-2 XL vs. aligned models.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM bias auditing relies on single-output inspection or static automated metrics, which obscure underlying probability distributions and miss biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. There is a need for methods that expose the full stochastic behavior of LLMs to enable systematic, comparative bias detection.
AI.method: TreeTracer employs a systematic perturbation analysis pipeline: (1) ontology-defined terms in prompts are systematically replaced; (2) hundreds of stochastic generations per prompt are aggregated into a syntax-aligned hierarchical structure; (3) classification-aware node merging is performed using an auxiliary language model; (4) results are visualized as custom Sankey diagrams juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees for direct semantic context comparison; (5) contrastive inference computes and displays counterfactual token probabilities across contexts to reduce misinterpretation risk.
AI.result: Case studies comparing unaligned GPT-2 XL against constitutionally aligned Apertus models showed that TreeTracer successfully exposes hidden representational harms, including counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization of individuals. A preliminary user study confirmed the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and supports analysts in detecting systemic biases.
AI.conclusion: Aggregated comparative visualization with contrastive inference provides a more reliable and interpretable approach to LLM bias auditing than single-output inspection. TreeTracer demonstrates that exposing probability distributions across semantic contexts enables detection of subtle, systemic representational harms that would otherwise remain hidden.

title: Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. To be published in the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Agentic Services which is part of the IEEE Conference on Web Services
summary: Autonomous agentic AI systems driven by Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new class of security, privacy, and compliance challenges: an agent that can invoke tools, manipulate data, install software, and coordinate with peer agents across organizational boundaries must be constrained not just by authentication and access control, but by the full structure of enterprise governance. This includes specifying what agents are permitted and prohibited from doing, what they areobliged to do after certain actions (e.g., notify the CISO), under what conditions a standing obligation may be waived, and which rules take precedence when policies conflict. This governance problem exceeds what current policy engines provide. Systems such as XACML, Rego, and Cedar address only the permit/prohibit subset of this governance structure. They do not provide obligation lifecycle management, meta-policy conflict resolution, dispensations that waive obligations in specific circumstances, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies commonly found in applications such as healthcare, cybersecurity, or data privacy. We propose AgenticRei, which realizes key governance requirements such as obligations, dispensations, policy conflict resolutions, and reasoning over policies, as well as the basic permit/prohibit constraints. We use a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed as OWL (Web Ontology Language) and evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages. We show through examples that deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production engines. Our approach composes naturally with industry-standard frameworks like A2AS.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven autonomous agents introduce governance challenges beyond authentication/access control, requiring policies that handle obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, and domain reasoning. The authors propose AgenticRei, a deontic policy framework built on Rei and OWL, evaluated by an external logic engine, that captures governance constraints inexpressible in current production engines like XACML, Rego, or Cedar, and integrates with industry standards like A2AS.
AI.motivation: Current policy engines (XACML, Rego, Cedar) only address permit/prohibit decisions. LLM-driven autonomous agents—capable of invoking tools, manipulating data, installing software, and coordinating across organizational boundaries—require richer governance: obligation lifecycle management (e.g., notify the CISO after certain actions), dispensations waiving obligations conditionally, meta-policy conflict resolution when rules clash, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies. No existing production system provides this full governance structure.
AI.method: AgenticRei uses a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed in OWL (Web Ontology Language). Policies are evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine operating entirely outside the LLM, governing both tool invocations and agent-to-agent messages. The approach composes with industry frameworks like A2AS and supports permit/prohibit, obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning.
AI.result: Through examples, the authors demonstrate that deontic policies in AgenticRei can capture security and privacy governance constraints that are largely inexpressible in current production policy engines. The pipeline successfully governs both internal tool invocations and inter-agent communication.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous agentic AI demands a deontic governance model encompassing obligations, dispensations, and conflict resolution—not merely permit/prohibit decisions. AgenticRei provides this by combining OWL-based deontic policy expression with an external runtime logic engine, bridging a critical gap between current enterprise policy infrastructure and the governance needs of LLM-driven agent systems.

title: Computational Identifiability
summary: Identification conditions describe the computability of a target query or parameter of interest as a function of the type and amount of information available. In causal identification, this information is often expressed in the form of a causal graph, and data are observed or collected for some subset of variables in the graph. Target queries may be for a single effect alone or for a class of effects in a given model. The derivation of an identification algorithm then defines mathematically the process by which the desired causal effect(s) can be uniquely determined, theoretically, in expectation. Identifiability in expectation, or 'theoretical identifiability,' generally assumes asymptotic properties, infinite data, or other mathematically idealized conditions. In this paper, we explore a fundamental distinction between this theoretical, idealized notion of identifiability and a proposed alternative that is computation-bound. The framework we propose - 'computational identifiability' - is to instead define a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator. If this process finds an estimator empirically, within a desired error tolerance, then identifiability is satisfied, conditional on the specified assumptions of the search (i.e., a prior distribution over the parameters) and conditional on the search procedure itself. Through several experiments, we demonstrate how this framework allows us to answer fine-grained, practical identification questions, such as identification with small finite samples, with ambiguous graphical criteria, with mixed observational-interventional data, and across counterfactual data and estimands. Code is available at https://github.com/lbynum/metadentify.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "computational identifiability," a finite-sample, computation-bound alternative to classical theoretical (asymptotic) identifiability in causal inference. It defines identifiability as the success of a finite computational search for an empirical estimator within a tolerance, conditional on search priors and procedure.
AI.motivation: Classical identifiability in causal inference relies on idealized, asymptotic conditions (infinite data, perfect graph specification). This fails to address practical challenges: small samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, mixed data types, and counterfactual estimands. The authors seek a practically meaningful, computation-grounded notion of identifiability.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework where a finite computational search procedure attempts to find an empirical estimator for a target causal query. If the search succeeds within a specified error tolerance, identifiability is declared satisfied—conditional on the search procedure and a prior distribution over parameters. The framework is validated through experiments spanning small-sample settings, ambiguous graph criteria, mixed observational-interventional data, and counterfactual estimands.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that computational identifiability can resolve fine-grained, practical identification questions that classical asymptotic identifiability cannot, including identification with small finite samples, under ambiguous graphical criteria, with mixed data types, and across counterfactual settings.
AI.conclusion: Computational identifiability offers a pragmatic, computation-bound complement to theoretical identifiability, enabling identification judgments under realistic finite-sample and structurally ambiguous conditions. The framework broadens the scope of answerable causal questions in practice.

title: Token Factory: Efficiently Integrating Diverse Signals into Large Recommendation Models
summary: Large Recommendation Models (LRMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in industry-scale recommendation tasks. However, holistically integrating traditional signals into these transformer-based architectures effectively and efficiently remains a major challenge. Conventional approaches that "textualize" these signals directly or create discrete item representations often lead to excessively long prompts, substantial memory footprints, and high computational overhead. To overcome these limitations, we propose "Token Factory", a framework designed to transform traditional signals into "soft tokens" that can be directly processed by LRMs. This approach enables efficient integration and compression of heterogeneous input features, preventing prompt length explosion while enhancing model performance. We detail the architecture of Token Factory and present experimental results validating its effectiveness in a production-scale recommendation environment.

AI.tldr: Token Factory converts traditional recommendation signals into "soft tokens" for efficient integration with Large Recommendation Models, preventing prompt length explosion while improving performance.
AI.motivation: Large Recommendation Models (LRMs) show promise in industry-scale tasks, but integrating traditional signals into transformer architectures via textualization or discrete representations causes excessively long prompts, large memory footprints, and high computational overhead. A more efficient integration method is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose "Token Factory," a framework that transforms traditional recommendation signals into compact "soft tokens" directly processable by LRMs. This enables heterogeneous input feature integration and compression without inflating prompt length. The paper details the architecture and validates it in a production-scale recommendation environment.
AI.result: Experimental results in a production-scale recommendation setting demonstrate the effectiveness of Token Factory. The approach successfully integrates heterogeneous features while maintaining efficiency and enhancing model performance compared to conventional methods.
AI.conclusion: Token Factory provides an effective and efficient solution for integrating traditional signals into LRMs, overcoming the limitations of textualization and discrete representation approaches. It enables practical deployment of LRMs in industry-scale recommendation systems.

title: FloatDoor: Platform-Triggered Backdoors in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in sensitive settings such as software engineering, where their outputs directly shape downstream artifacts. Recent work has shown that an identical model can produce measurably different outputs depending on the deployment platform, a consequence of non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. We study the security implications of this platform-dependent variability and uncover a novel attack surface on LLM deployments. We introduce FloatDoor, the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack against generative LLMs. The compromised model exhibits adversary-chosen behavior when served on a target platform and is otherwise benign. FloatDoor is realized through two lightweight LoRA adapters, one that amplifies inter-platform numerical divergence and one that binds the resulting platform signature to a malicious downstream task, while leaving aggregate model utility largely intact. FloatDoor exploits a pronounced time-of-check, time-of-use gap between model auditing and serving. We demonstrate FloatDoor on Qwen3-4B across a broad range of deployment targets, including NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. As a final case study, we show that FloatDoor reliably induces exploitable code vulnerabilities on a chosen target platform. Our results establish a new class of attacks on LLM deployments and underscore the pressing need for trusted model supply chains in sensitive, LLM-powered applications.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FloatDoor, the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack against LLMs. It exploits floating-point non-associativity and divergent kernel implementations across hardware platforms to make a model behave maliciously only on a specific target platform (e.g., NVIDIA GPU vs. Google TPU), while appearing benign elsewhere. The attack uses two lightweight LoRA adapters and demonstrates reliable induction of code vulnerabilities on chosen platforms.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in sensitive domains like software engineering, where outputs directly affect downstream artifacts. Recent findings show that identical models produce measurably different outputs on different hardware platforms due to floating-point arithmetic. The authors investigate whether this variability can be weaponized to create a security threat, exploiting the time-of-check, time-of-use gap between model auditing and serving.
AI.method: FloatDoor uses two LoRA adapters: (1) an amplification adapter that magnifies inter-platform numerical divergence to create a robust platform signature, and (2) a binding adapter that ties this platform signature to a malicious downstream task. The model is trained so that the malicious behavior triggers only when the amplified numerical signature matches the target platform's floating-point characteristics, while aggregate utility remains largely intact on non-target platforms.
AI.result: The attack was demonstrated on Qwen3-4B across diverse hardware targets: NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. FloatDoor reliably induced exploitable code vulnerabilities on the chosen target platform while maintaining benign behavior on others. The attack preserves aggregate model utility, making it stealthy and difficult to detect during auditing.
AI.conclusion: FloatDoor establishes a new class of attacks on LLM deployments, highlighting that platform-dependent numerical variability is a viable attack vector. The results underscore the pressing need for trusted model supply chains and platform-aware security auditing in sensitive, LLM-powered applications.

title: Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations
comment: Pre-Print of a paper to be published at the International Computing Education Research (ICER) conference 2026
summary:
Program visualizations are widely used to support novice programmers, yet students often ignore or resist well-designed visual scaffolds. Research on multiple external representations (MERs) offers cognitive design principles for coordinating views, but less is known about what shapes learners' engagement with available representations.
  We conducted a within-subjects study with 19 undergraduates who had completed CS1 and CS2. Students completed think-aloud tasks, reflective interviews, and webcam-based gaze tracking while using a multi-representational probe with synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views, and Python Tutor, across scope, while loops, and linked lists.
  Gaze analysis showed that students spent nearly half their time focused on code despite available visual scaffolds. Students without prior experience anchored even more heavily in code and engaged minimally with metaphor views. Interviews identified three factors shaping selective engagement: agency, as students sought control over cognitive effort rather than simply having it reduced; representational fit, as identical designs differed in whether they felt helpful or overwhelming; and legitimacy, as some students avoided metaphorical scaffolds they perceived as childish or insufficiently rigorous for university-level work.
  These findings suggest that multi-representational tools in computing education require attention to affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical considerations include positioning visualizations as verification instruments, offering toggleable abstraction levels, and framing tools to signal disciplinary legitimacy. More broadly, the themes help explain why cognitively sound visualization tools may fail to engage the students they are designed to help.

AI.tldr: A study of 19 post-CS2 undergraduates using gaze tracking and interviews found that students spent ~50% of time on code despite available visual scaffolds. Three factors shaped selective engagement: agency (seeking control over cognitive effort), representational fit (same design perceived differently), and legitimacy (rejecting "childish" metaphors). Results argue for considering affective/social factors alongside cognitive design in computing education tools.
AI.motivation: Program visualizations are widely deployed to support novice programmers, yet students often ignore or resist even well-designed visual scaffolds. While research on multiple external representations (MERs) provides cognitive design principles for coordinating views, the field lacks understanding of what actually shapes learners' selective engagement with available representations. This gap motivates an empirical investigation into the behavioral and psychological factors driving students' attention and resistance.
AI.method: A within-subjects study with 19 undergraduate students who had completed CS1 and CS2. Participants completed think-aloud tasks and reflective interviews while using two tools: (1) a multi-representational probe featuring synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views, and (2) Python Tutor. Tasks covered scope, while loops, and linked lists. Webcam-based gaze tracking captured real-time attentional allocation across representations.
AI.result: Gaze analysis revealed students spent nearly 50% of their time on code, despite available visual scaffolds. Students without prior experience anchored even more heavily in code and engaged minimally with metaphor views. Three qualitative themes emerged from interviews: (1) agency — students wanted control over cognitive effort rather than mere reduction; (2) representational fit — identical visual designs were perceived as helpful by some and overwhelming by others; (3) legitimacy — some students avoided metaphorical scaffolds they viewed as childish or insufficiently rigorous for university-level work.
AI.conclusion: Multi-representational tools in computing education must address affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical recommendations include positioning visualizations as verification instruments, offering toggleable abstraction levels, and framing tools to signal disciplinary legitimacy. These themes help explain why cognitively sound visualization tools may fail to engage their intended users.

title: AgentArmor: A Framework, Evaluation, \& Mitigation of Coding Agent Failures
summary: Software engineering and deployment are increasingly being delegated to AI coding agents. The scale of their adoption is surfacing rare, but highly destructive, failure modes. In this paper, we study these failure modes as stemming from three distinct mechanisms: underspecification, where default model behavior is unsafe; capability errors, where the safe action is available but the model does not adhere to it due to bias or capability limitations; and agent harness errors, where the model fails to execute the safe action through the harness. We evaluate these across 8 different evaluations, each inspired by real-life deployment failures, totaling 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. Based on this evaluation, we propose AgentArmor, an agent harness modification, to mitigate these errors. By adding an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a ``3 strikes'' policy, deterministic guardrails, and tools for the agent to edit its own context, we show that AgentArmor is safer across a statistically significant number of samples. Thus, we suggest concrete mitigations for current coding agents and a design philosophy for future agent harness features.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies three failure mechanisms in AI coding agents—underspecification, capability errors, and agent harness errors—evaluates them across 8 evaluations with 20 coding environments, and proposes AgentArmor, a harness modification combining extended prompts, a command classifier, a "3 strikes" policy, deterministic guardrails, and self-editing tools, demonstrating statistically significant safety improvements.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents are increasingly deployed for software engineering tasks, rare but highly destructive failure modes are emerging. These failures are not well-characterized, and existing agent harnesses lack systematic mitigations. The authors aim to taxonomize these failures and propose concrete, implementable safeguards.
AI.method: The authors decompose failure modes into three mechanisms: (1) underspecification (default model behavior is unsafe), (2) capability errors (safe actions exist but are not selected), and (3) agent harness errors (safe actions fail to execute through the harness). They construct 8 evaluations inspired by real-world deployment failures, spanning 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. AgentArmor is then proposed with five components: an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a "3 strikes" policy, deterministic guardrails, and tools enabling the agent to edit its own context. Safety is evaluated statistically across samples.
AI.result: AgentArmor demonstrates statistically significant safety improvements across the evaluated scenarios. The taxonomy of failure modes (underspecification, capability errors, harness errors) proves effective for diagnosing and addressing agent failures.
AI.conclusion: Concrete, harness-level mitigations like AgentArmor can substantially reduce destructive failure modes in AI coding agents. The authors recommend adopting these mitigations in current systems and using the three-mechanism taxonomy as a design philosophy for future agent harness development.

title: Ensembles of Large Language Models for Identifying EQ-5D Studies in PubMed Based on Their Abstracts
summary: The rapid increase in scientific publications leads to the fact that manual study screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) is increasingly resource consuming, inefficient, and inconsistent. Classifying studies that clearly report health-related quality-of-life results, such as EQ-5D data, requires a high level of clinical interpretation and poses challenges for human reviewers. This study investigates the use of Google's Gemini and Gemma large language models (LLMs) in automating EQ-5D detection in the PubMed biomedical database based only on published abstracts. A multi-phase framework is proposed that integrates few-shot prompting, weight ensembling aggregation, and a soft stacking meta-classifier. Nine LLMs are evaluated on a dataset of PubMed studies manually labeled by two experts regarding EQ-5D reporting. The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b obtained a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, exceeding individually attained results. The ensembling of top-performing models improved the balance between precision and recall compared to individual models, while the soft stacking approach provided greater reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis shows that the probability results from the models are important in guiding the final predictions. The findings suggest that an ensemble-based LLM setup is a reliable and scalable approach for automating screening in biomedical research.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an ensemble-based LLM framework using Google's Gemini and Gemma models to automate the detection of EQ-5D health-related quality-of-life reporting in PubMed abstracts, achieving a 0.74 weighted F1-score through few-shot prompting, weight ensembling, and soft stacking.
AI.motivation: Manual study screening in systematic literature reviews is increasingly resource-intensive, inefficient, and inconsistent due to the rapid growth of scientific publications. Detecting studies reporting EQ-5D data requires high-level clinical interpretation, making it a challenging classification task for human reviewers that could benefit from automation.
AI.method: A multi-phase framework integrating (1) few-shot prompting of nine Google Gemini and Gemma LLMs on PubMed abstracts, (2) weight ensembling aggregation combining top-performing models (gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, gemma-3-27b), and (3) a soft stacking meta-classifier for final prediction. The dataset was manually dual-labeled by two experts.
AI.result: The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b achieved a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, outperforming all individual models. The ensemble improved precision-recall balance, while soft stacking enhanced reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis confirmed that model probability outputs were key drivers of final predictions.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based LLM approaches represent a reliable and scalable solution for automating biomedical literature screening, with superior performance and interpretability compared to single-model configurations.

title: Measuring Curriculum Alignment across Topical Coverage, Competency, and Cognitive Depth: A Longitudinal Framework Applied to CS2013 and CS2023
summary: Undergraduate computer science is governed by international curricular guidelines revised about once a decade, yet programs lack a reliable, reproducible way to measure how completely they cover the current guidelines and how that coverage shifts when the guidelines are restructured. We address this with a human-in-the-loop pipeline that measures a program's coverage of an external body of knowledge, applied longitudinally to one accredited BSc in Computer Science against Computer Science Curricula 2013 (CS2013) and 2023 (CS2023). The pipeline represents the program and each guideline as structured corpora, generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches by semantic retrieval, and confirms them through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition. Of seven benchmarked retrievers, a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble was strongest, and a reputed long-context model underperformed a small sentence model, so retriever choice must be measured. Both maps were validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's kappa 0.64 for CS2023, 0.69 for CS2013). The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units, near-constant across a decade. Extending the same retrieve-then-confirm design to competency articulation and cognitive depth shows that the program articulates the competency for ~88% of covered units under each guideline, yet delivers it at the recommended depth for 76% of present units under CS2023 against 95% under CS2013, a gap reflecting the newer guideline's raised expectations, not the program. The longitudinal comparison separates persistent structural gaps (parallel and distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, systems fundamentals), uncovered against both guidelines and ABET, from differences that reflect the standard's evolution. The instrument is reusable and available from the authors on request.

AI.tldr: A reusable human-in-the-loop pipeline measures a CS program's coverage of curricular guidelines, applied longitudinally against CS2013 and CS2023. Coverage remained ~50% across a decade, but the program meets recommended cognitive depth for only 76% of covered units under CS2023 vs. 95% under CS2013, reflecting raised expectations in the newer standard.
AI.motivation: Undergraduate CS programs lack a reliable, reproducible instrument to measure how completely they cover international curricular guidelines (CS2013, CS2023) and how coverage shifts when guidelines are restructured. Existing approaches are ad hoc and not systematically validated.
AI.method: The authors build a retrieve-then-confirm pipeline: (1) represent both the program curriculum and guideline knowledge units as structured corpora; (2) generate candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches via semantic retrieval (benchmarking 7 retrievers and selecting a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble); (3) confirm matches through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition; (4) validate with an independent second rater (Cohen's κ = 0.64–0.69); (5) extend the design to competency articulation and cognitive depth analysis.
AI.result: The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units — near-constant coverage across a decade. Competency is articulated for ~88% of covered units under both guidelines. However, recommended cognitive depth is met for 76% of covered units under CS2023 vs. 95% under CS2013, revealing raised expectations in the newer standard. Persistent structural gaps were identified in parallel/distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, and systems fundamentals. Notably, a small sentence model outperformed a long-context model in retrieval.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides a validated, reusable instrument for longitudinal curriculum-to-standard mapping. The observed decline in cognitive-depth match (95% → 76%) reflects evolution of the guideline, not program degradation. Identifying persistent vs. standard-driven gaps helps programs make targeted, evidence-based curricular decisions.

title: When to Trust, How to Distill: Multi-Foundation Model Guidance for Lightweight, Robust Scientific Time Series Forecasting
comment: KDD 2026, paper decision: Accepted, track: AI for Science. total 12 pages including references and appendix
summary: The deployment of Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) in physical sciences is hindered by a critical trade-off: while these models encode rich, universal temporal dynamics, they suffer from severe distributional misalignment when applied zero-shot to specific scientific domains, and their computational cost prohibits deployment in edge-computing sensor networks. We address a fundamental challenge: How can we extract latent structural knowledge from misaligned foundation models (FM) to train lightweight, specialized forecasters? We propose Gated Uncertainty-Aware Routing for Distillation (Guard), a novel framework that reframes multiteacher distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that acts as a "circuit-breaker," automatically attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from domain reality. We evaluate our proposed lightweight framework on four climate-critical domains: meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids. Our method significantly reduces RMSE relative to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline, successfully distilling knowledge from pretrained FMs (teachers) even when they exhibit suboptimal zero-shot accuracy due to distribution shift between the original and target data domains. We demonstrate that these domain-misaligned teachers can still serve as critical correctives, outperforming the globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. Ultimately, this enables high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/RupasreeDey/GUARD-KDD2026.

AI.tldr: GUARD proposes a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework that uses a Contextual Router and Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism to extract useful structural knowledge from domain-misaligned Time-Series Foundation Models, enabling lightweight, high-precision forecasters for resource-constrained edge deployment in physical sciences.
AI.motivation: Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) capture rich universal temporal dynamics but suffer from severe distributional misalignment in specific scientific domains and are computationally prohibitive for edge-computing sensor networks. The core challenge is extracting latent structural knowledge from misaligned foundation models to train lightweight, specialized forecasters suitable for edge deployment.
AI.method: GUARD (Gated Uncertainty-Aware Routing for Distillation) frames multi-teacher distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher per instance based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse FMs; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that functions as a circuit-breaker, automatically attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from the target domain reality.
AI.result: GUARD significantly reduces RMSE compared to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline. Domain-misaligned teachers serve as critical correctives, outperforming globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. The approach was validated across four climate-critical domains: meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that even domain-misaligned foundation models contain extractable structural knowledge that can be effectively distilled into lightweight student models, enabling high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment.

title: Before the Pull Request: Mining Multi-Agent Coordination
comment: 9 pages, 2 tables. LNCS format. Code, dataset, and mining toolkit: https://github.com/neul-labs/grite
summary: Autonomous coding agents now open millions of pull requests, yet large-scale studies find their PRs are produced faster but accepted less often - a coordination and trust gap that pull-request-level telemetry cannot explain. We argue the missing signal lives before the PR, in how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work. We study this process through grite, our open-source coordination substrate that needs no central server and stores its records inside git itself, so its append-only, signed event log captures the coordination process directly. We show that (i) this shared substrate reduces duplicate and conflicting work at bounded overhead - the share of work that merely re-does a teammate's task falls from 78% to 0% while useful throughput more than triples; (ii) every agent's copy of the log converges to the same state with no write silently dropped, where a file-based tracker loses concurrent writes; and (iii) the log is a mineable artefact from which concrete failure modes - conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close - are automatically recoverable with provenance, several invisible in pull-request history. We release the dataset, harness, and mining toolkit.

AI.tldr: Autonomous coding agents face a coordination gap where pre-PR collisions over shared work go undetected. The authors propose Grite, a serverless coordination substrate that logs events inside git itself, demonstrating it eliminates duplicate work (78% → 0%), prevents lost concurrent writes, and enables automatic recovery from failure modes invisible in PR history.
AI.motivation: Large-scale studies show autonomous coding agents produce pull requests faster but suffer lower acceptance rates — a coordination and trust gap unexplained by PR-level telemetry. The authors argue the missing signal originates before the PR, in how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work.
AI.method: The authors developed Grite, an open-source coordination substrate requiring no central server. It stores append-only, signed event logs directly inside git repositories, capturing the full coordination process. The system was evaluated along three axes: (i) reduction of duplicate/conflicting work via shared substrate, (ii) log convergence guarantees compared to file-based trackers, and (iii) mineability of the log to automatically recover failure modes (conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close) with provenance.
AI.result: (i) Duplicate work — tasks that merely re-do a teammate's work — dropped from 78% to 0%, while useful throughput more than tripled. (ii) Every agent's log copy converges to identical state with no silently dropped writes, unlike file-based trackers that lose concurrent writes. (iii) Concrete failure modes are automatically recoverable with provenance from the log, several of which are invisible in pull-request history.
AI.conclusion: Pre-PR coordination, captured via git-native append-only logs, closes a critical observability gap for multi-agent coding systems. The dataset, harness, and mining toolkit are publicly released.

title: SAFE-Cascade: Cost-Adaptive Vision-Language Routing for Chart Question Answering
comment: Demo paper submitted at CIKM 2026. 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are powerful for chart question answering, but invoking a VLM for every query can be unnecessarily expensive when many questions are answerable from OCR text and lightweight language reasoning. We demonstrate SAFE-Cascade, an interactive system for cost-adaptive chart question answering. Given a chart image and a natural-language question, SAFE-Cascade first extracts chart text with OCR, obtains a provisional answer from a text-only language model, and then uses a learned router to decide whether to accept the text answer or escalate to a VLM. The demo exposes this decision process to users: OCR evidence, text-only answer, routing probability, escalation decision, final answer, estimated cost, and estimated latency are shown side by side. SAFE-Cascade is designed as a transparent interface for understanding when visual grounding is actually needed. Users can upload or select charts, ask questions, inspect the evidence used by each pathway, compare text-only and VLM answers, and adjust the escalation threshold to explore the accuracy-cost frontier. The system is implemented with Azure Document Intelligence for OCR, gpt-5-mini as the text-only model, gemini-2.5-flash-image as the VLM, and a Random Forest router trained on inference-time features. On a held-out ChartQA test split of 375 examples from a 2,500-example experiment, SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% unified accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, compared with 67.7% accuracy and 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The observed +1.4 percentage-point difference is statistically uncertain, so we interpret SAFE-Cascade as matching full-VLM performance while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%. The demonstration shows how selective modality routing can make multimodal knowledge systems more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware.

AI.tldr: SAFE-Cascade is a cost-adaptive chart QA system that uses a learned router to decide whether a text-only LLM answer suffices or a VLM must be invoked, achieving comparable accuracy to full-VLM baselines while reducing VLM calls by ~27% and cost by ~9%.
AI.motivation: Invoking expensive VLMs for every chart question is wasteful when many questions can be answered from OCR-extracted text and lightweight language reasoning alone. The authors aim to reduce cost while maintaining accuracy, and to make the routing decision transparent and tunable for users.
AI.method: SAFE-Cascade extracts chart text via Azure Document Intelligence OCR, generates a provisional answer using gpt-5-mini (text-only LLM), then employs a Random Forest router trained on inference-time features to decide whether to accept the text answer or escalate to gemini-2.5-flash-image (VLM). Users can adjust the escalation threshold to explore the accuracy-cost trade-off.
AI.result: On a held-out ChartQA split of 375 examples, SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation vs. 67.7% accuracy with 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The +1.4pp difference is not statistically significant, so performance is interpreted as matching the baseline while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%.
AI.conclusion: Selective modality routing via SAFE-Cascade demonstrates that multimodal systems can be made more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware without sacrificing accuracy — matching full-VLM performance while meaningfully reducing inference cost.

title: G-Lox: Group-Adaptive, Privacy-Preserving Bridge Distribution with Two-Party Computation
summary:
We present G-Lox (group-adaptive Lox), a bridge-distribution system that preserves Lox-style distributor blindness while enabling hidden, stateful group-level adaptation. G-Lox places adaptive assignment logic behind a two-server privacy wall, so no single server learns group identifiers or group-to-bridge assignments. Private state access and state-dependent updates use two-server DPF/FSS protocols and secure two-party computation, supporting blockage reporting, transport-aware reassignment, and privacy-preserving group splitting.
  We evaluate G-Lox through system measurements and policy simulation. In our C++/EMP implementation over real TCP sockets, private state access has low client-visible overhead: across state sizes up to 2^16, communication remains in the low-KiB range per iteration. At M=1024, the client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in about 0.25 s. Simulations with group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration show that G-Lox improves robustness over Lox- and rBridge-like baselines among systems that maintain broad issuance.

AI.tldr: G-Lox extends the Lox anonymous bridge-distribution system with group-adaptive assignment, using two-server DPF/FSS and secure two-party computation to hide group identities and assignment logic while enabling stateful, group-level adaptation against blocking and Sybil attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing anonymous bridge-distribution systems like Lox provide distributor blindness but lack group-level adaptation. Bridge distributors need to adapt assignments based on group-specific blocking patterns and Sybil enumeration without learning which users belong to which groups, creating a tension between privacy and robustness.
AI.method: G-Lox introduces a two-server privacy wall partitioning adaptive assignment logic. It employs distributed point functions (DPF), function secret sharing (FSS), and secure two-party computation (2PC) for private state access and state-dependent updates. Key mechanisms include private blockage reporting, transport-aware reassignment, and privacy-preserving group splitting. The system is implemented in C++ using the EMP toolkit, evaluated over real TCP sockets.
AI.result: Private state access imposes low client-visible overhead: with state sizes up to 2^16, communication stays in low-KiB range per iteration. At M=1024, the client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in approximately 0.25 seconds. Simulations demonstrate that G-Lox achieves superior robustness over Lox-like and rBridge-like baselines under group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration, while maintaining broad issuance.
AI.conclusion: G-Lox successfully reconciles distributor blindness with stateful group-level adaptation, delivering practical performance and improved censorship resistance against targeted blocking attacks.

title: Building Drift: Documenting On-Site Construction Adaptations Across Material Lifecycles
summary:
