In a circular economy for construction, reclaimed materials carry prior lives of use and go on to have post-lives in future buildings. Yet working with such materials introduces unpredictability that requires on-site improvisation, making their reuse challenging to document and scale across building lifetimes. Without documentation, the on-site adaptations that make construction with reclaimed materials possible leave collaborators, evaluators, and inheritors without the information they need to continue, assess, and reuse materials. We call the collective deviation of the physical state from the digital model through these adaptations "building drift." Through a case study, ReShelter, a reclaimed timber pavilion constructed in the forest, we develop a taxonomy for building drift that characterizes the collective deviation across building lifetimes: Tending the Site, Foraging for Fit, Interpreting the Material, Marking Measurements, and Coordinating Across Communities.
  To put our taxonomy for building drift into practice, we present Pentimento, a documentation tool that leverages video documentation and 3D Gaussian Splatting to spatially, temporally, and semantically represent on-site adaptations in relation to the designed model. Pentimento enables each stakeholder to navigate material histories in ways that reduce barriers to material reuse. Together, these contributions open pathways towards computational tools that support the on-site improvisation essential to construction with reclaimed materials, enabling more sustainable cycles of recovery, repair, and reuse.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "building drift" — the cumulative deviation between a building's physical state and its digital model due to on-site improvisation when using reclaimed materials — and presents a taxonomy of its forms alongside Pentimento, a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based documentation tool that spatially, temporally, and semantically captures these adaptations to support circular construction.
AI.motivation: Reclaimed materials carry prior histories and introduce unpredictability requiring on-site improvisation. These adaptations are rarely documented, leaving future collaborators, evaluators, and inheritors without critical information needed to continue, assess, and reuse materials across building lifetimes. This documentation gap bottlenecks the scaling of circular construction practices.
AI.method: The authors conduct a case study of ReShelter, a reclaimed timber pavilion built in a forest, to develop a taxonomy of building drift with five categories: Tending the Site, Foraging for Fit, Interpreting the Material, Marking Measurements, and Coordinating Across Communities. They then design and present Pentimento, a documentation tool combining video documentation with 3D Gaussian Splatting to capture on-site adaptations spatially, temporally, and semantically relative to the original digital model.
AI.result: The taxonomy systematically characterizes how building drift manifests across building lifetimes, and Pentimento demonstrates a practical approach for enabling stakeholders to navigate material histories, reducing barriers to reuse.
AI.conclusion: Computational tools that explicitly support on-site improvisation are essential for scaling construction with reclaimed materials. By documenting building drift, such tools can enable more sustainable cycles of recovery, repair, and reuse within a circular economy.

title: DynAMO:Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration via Topological Multi-Agent Scheduling
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables, 4 algorithms. Evaluated on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark. Code: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO
summary:
While LLM-powered agents offer end-to-end automation for industrial asset lifecycles, real-world Industry 4.0 deployment is hindered by latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks. We present DynAMO (Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration), a deployment-ready engine using a Plan-then-Execute architecture to generate verifiable workflow graphs. DynAMO supports both SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency). By dynamically identifying independent tasks, DynAMO preserves structural correctness and safety while significantly improving efficiency through controlled reasoning overlap.
  Across six controlled experiments on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark, DynAMO demonstrates substantial performance and robustness gains. Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6x over sequential orchestration, rising to 1.8x on highly parallelizable workflows. After instrumenting external tool calls with realistic latencies, a latency decomposition shows that LLM reasoning and orchestration still account for more than 90% of execution time, identifying model inference as the primary system bottleneck. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by approximately 30%, and DynAMO maintains correct functional behaviour (task completion, agent sequencing, and output quality) while exhibiting graceful degradation under controlled fault injection. Reproducibility analysis further confirms stable execution under repeated runs, with parallel scheduling reducing latency variance. These findings establish DynAMO as a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines. Code is available at: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO

AI.tldr: DynAMO is a deployment-ready multi-agent orchestration engine for Industry 4.0 that uses a Plan-then-Execute architecture with verifiable workflow graphs. It supports both sequential and parallel execution, achieving 1.6–1.8× latency reduction while maintaining safety and correctness under fault conditions.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered agents for industrial automation face three critical deployment barriers: high end-to-end latency, instability under concurrent execution, and safety risks in real-world Industry 4.0 settings. Existing approaches lack a practical orchestration framework that balances efficiency gains with verifiable correctness.
AI.method: DynAMO employs a Plan-then-Execute architecture that generates verifiable workflow graphs. It supports two execution modes: SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency via dynamic identification of independent tasks). The system incorporates structured context pruning to reduce inference latency and is evaluated on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark across six controlled experiments, including controlled fault injection and reproducibility analysis.
AI.result: Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6× (up to 1.8× on highly parallelizable workflows). LLM reasoning and orchestration account for >90% of execution time. Structured context pruning yields ~30% inference latency reduction. Under fault injection, DynAMO exhibits graceful degradation with correct functional behavior. Reproducibility analysis confirms stable execution with reduced latency variance under parallel scheduling.
AI.conclusion: DynAMO provides a practical, scalable, and safety-aware blueprint for deploying LLM-based agents in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines, demonstrating that dependency-aware concurrency can significantly improve latency without sacrificing correctness or robustness.

title: Disentangling Linguistic Relatedness from Task Alignment in Cross-Lingual Transfer
summary: We study cross-lingual transfer by fine-tuning seven large language models (4B--671B parameters) on Arabic and evaluating zero-shot reading comprehension on Semitic languages and non-Semitic controls. Across dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, we find no evidence of Semitic-specific transfer: models with weak baselines improve dramatically across all languages, while strong-baseline models show only marginal gains regardless of language family. A chain-of-thought ablation reinforces this finding -- the same models that benefit most from fine-tuning benefit equally from inference-time reasoning, suggesting both mechanisms address task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual knowledge transfer.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs on Arabic yields zero-shot reading comprehension improvements across all languages, not just Semitic ones. Gains depend on baseline model strength, not language family, suggesting fine-tuning addresses task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual transfer of linguistic knowledge.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether fine-tuning on a Semitic language (Arabic) produces language-family-specific cross-lingual transfer to other Semitic languages, or whether observed improvements reflect a more general mechanism like task-format alignment.
AI.method: Seven LLMs (4B–671B parameters, spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures) were fine-tuned on Arabic reading comprehension. Zero-shot evaluation was conducted on both Semitic languages and non-Semitic control languages. A chain-of-thought ablation compared inference-time reasoning effects against fine-tuning effects.
AI.result: No evidence of Semitic-specific transfer was found. Weak-baseline models improved dramatically across all languages; strong-baseline models showed only marginal gains regardless of language family. The chain-of-thought ablation showed the same models benefiting most from fine-tuning also benefited equally from inference-time reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Both fine-tuning and chain-of-thought reasoning address task-format alignment rather than enabling genuine cross-lingual knowledge transfer. Language-family-specific transfer does not occur under this paradigm.

title: Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized language modeling through autoregressive generation, enabling strong performance across a wide range of tasks. Recently, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as an alternative paradigm that generates text through iterative denoising rather than next-token prediction, allowing parallel refinement of entire sequences. While numerous diffusion-based architectures have been proposed, differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters make it difficult to compare their capabilities and understand the trade-offs they offer. In this work, we present a systematic experimental analysis of modern DLMs. Specifically, we evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving, while explicitly considering both generation quality and computational efficiency. Beyond downstream evaluation, we analyze the impact of key inference-time factors, including denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies, and complement large-scale experiments with controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets. We show that the behavior of DLMs is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. Overall, our study provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic experimental comparison of eight state-of-the-art Diffusion Language Models across eight benchmarks, analyzing performance vs. efficiency trade-offs and the impact of inference-time design choices like denoising steps, context length, and parallel unmasking strategies.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of diverse DLM architectures with inconsistent evaluation protocols makes meaningful comparison difficult. The authors aim to provide a standardized, comprehensive benchmark to clarify the capabilities, limitations, and trade-offs inherent in diffusion-based language modeling versus autoregressive LLMs.
AI.method: Evaluation of eight SOTA DLMs on eight benchmarks (reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, structured problem solving). Controlled experiments include identical-condition training of smaller models. Systematic ablation of inference-time factors: denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies. Both generation quality and computational efficiency are measured.
AI.result: DLM behavior is heavily influenced by generation-time design choices, creating distinct performance-efficiency trade-off curves. No single DLM architecture dominates across all tasks. Inference budget and hyperparameter configurations significantly modulate downstream performance relative to autoregressive baselines.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion Language Models represent a viable but nuanced alternative to autoregressive LLMs, with their practical utility depending critically on task alignment and inference-time configuration. The paper provides actionable guidance for DLM deployment and highlights directions for improving diffusion-based text generation.

title: Closing the Social-Semantic Gap: SPSD for Edge-Based Prompt Compression in Cloud LLM Inference
summary: The prefill stage of Large Language Model (LLM) inference is a growing contributor to cloud-scale energy cost. Many consumer-support and conversational prompts contain social scaffolding: politeness markers, apologetic preamble, repetition, and rapport-building language that is important for human communication but carries low marginal information for machine reasoning. We call this discrepancy the Social-Semantic Gap. We present SPSD (Sentiment Preserving Semantic Distillation), an edge-based pipeline that compresses user prompts using a 4-bit quantised Small Language Model before transmission to a cloud-deployed LLM. Evaluation on a 248-prompt corpus using Gemma-2-2B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) as the SLM and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the cloud evaluation model yields a mean input token saving of 99.9 tokens per distilled call, with all 146 distilled calls yielding positive savings. Response quality, assessed by blind LLM-as-judge scoring across 121 pairs, is non-inferior to the raw path within a pre-specified 1-point margin on a 15-point rubric; the judge awarded 43 percent ties, 28 percent distilled wins, and 29 percent raw wins. Cosine similarity is mixed: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1 percent of pairs above the 0.70 reference threshold. Safety-critical domains are conservatively routed to passthrough via rule-based gates. Per-call net energy saving is estimated at 70-270 uWh under stated assumptions. SPSD shows that on-device prompt distillation can reduce cloud LLM input-token cost while preserving response quality within a practical non-inferiority margin.

AI.tldr: SPSD is an edge-based prompt distillation pipeline that compresses user prompts using a quantized Small Language Model before sending them to cloud LLMs, achieving ~100 token savings per call while maintaining response quality within a non-inferiority margin.
AI.motivation: User prompts in consumer-facing LLM applications contain substantial "social scaffolding" (politeness markers, apologies, repetition, rapport-building language) that is important for human interaction but carries low marginal information for machine reasoning — termed the Social-Semantic Gap. This redundant content contributes unnecessarily to cloud-scale inference energy costs during the prefill stage.
AI.method: SPSD deploys a 4-bit quantized Gemma-2-2B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) SLM on edge devices that performs sentiment-preserving semantic distillation — compressing verbose prompts into concise equivalents while preserving core semantic intent. The distilled prompt is transmitted to a cloud LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for inference. Safety-critical domains are routed to passthrough via rule-based gates. Evaluation uses a 248-prompt corpus with blind LLM-as-judge scoring on a 15-point rubric across 121 response pairs.
AI.result: Mean input token savings of 99.9 tokens per distilled call; all 146 distilled calls yielded positive savings. LLM-as-judge scoring: 43% ties, 28% distilled wins, 29% raw wins — demonstrating non-inferiority within a 1-point margin on the 15-point rubric. Cosine similarity: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1% of pairs above the 0.70 threshold. Per-call net energy saving estimated at 70–270 μWh.
AI.conclusion: On-device prompt distillation via a quantized SLM can significantly reduce cloud LLM input-token costs while preserving response quality within a practical non-inferiority margin, offering a viable edge-cloud optimization strategy for LLM inference.

title: Exit-and-Join Dynamics for Decentralized Coalition Formation
summary: This paper studies coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process driven by unilateral exit-and-join decisions. Agents evaluate local moves using the Aumann-Dreze value, so payoffs are computed within the agent's current coalition rather than through a globally negotiated coalition structure. The resulting model links cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior: a terminal partition is precisely a coalition structure with no admissible, individually profitable exit-and-join deviation. We establish equilibrium characterizations, identify conditions under which the dynamics admit scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations, and analyze how switching and acceptance costs shape local stability. Numerical experiments test finite-time stabilization, cost sensitivity, and a special convex-game benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper models coalition formation as a decentralized process where agents unilaterally exit and join coalitions based on Aumann-Drèze value payoffs, linking cooperative allocation with noncooperative best-response dynamics. It characterizes equilibria, identifies Lyapunov/potential representations, analyzes cost effects on stability, and supports findings with numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between cooperative payoff allocation and noncooperative coalition formation dynamics by studying how decentralized, self-interested exit-and-join decisions lead to stable coalition structures, without requiring global negotiation.
AI.method: Models coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical system where agents make unilateral exit-and-join moves based on the Aumann-Drèze value (payoff computed within the current coalition). Characterizes terminal partitions as structures with no admissible profitable deviations. Analyzes the dynamics using Lyapunov functions and exact-potential representations, and incorporates switching and acceptance costs. Numerical experiments test finite-time stabilization, cost sensitivity, and a convex-game benchmark.
AI.result: Establishes equilibrium characterizations for the dynamical process. Identifies conditions under which the dynamics admit scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations, enabling convergence guarantees. Demonstrates how switching and acceptance costs shape local stability. Numerical experiments confirm finite-time stabilization, explore cost sensitivity, and validate results on a convex-game benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The Aumann-Drèze value provides a viable local payoff metric for decentralized coalition dynamics, with equilibrium structures corresponding to no-deviation states. Potential and Lyapunov structures yield convergence, while adjustment costs affect stability. The framework offers a tractable link between cooperative and noncooperative coalition theory.

title: Closing the Calibration Gap in Semantic Caching
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures. Source code: https://github.com/aditeyabaral/calibration-gap-semantic-caching ; Models and Datasets: https://huggingface.co/redis
summary: Semantic caching cuts LLM inference costs by serving a cached response to semantically similar queries. Standard practice evaluates these systems using PR-AUC, a metric that only measures how well scores rank and ignores whether they are usable at a fixed threshold. We show this mismatch leads to systematically poor deployment choices, as models with the highest PR-AUC are often the worst in operation. We introduce Precision-Cache Hit Ratio (P-CHR) AUC, a cache-aware metric that measures precision across cache utilization levels, and Calibration Retention Rate (CRR), which captures how much offline ranking quality survives at deployment. We decompose the operational gap between offline and deployed quality into a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component fixed by the dataset's positive rate. Our experiments show that the calibration gap is governed by the training objective rather than data scale, and post-hoc calibration only partially closes it. Ultimately, model selection for semantic caching is a calibration problem, not a ranking one, and measuring it is the first step to closing the gap.

AI.tldr: Semantic caching evaluation relies on PR-AUC, which fails to predict deployed performance. The authors introduce P-CHR AUC and CRR to measure calibration across cache utilization, decompose the offline-deployment gap into calibration and structural components, and demonstrate that model selection for semantic caching is fundamentally a calibration problem, not a ranking one.
AI.motivation: Standard semantic caching evaluation uses PR-AUC, a ranking-only metric that ignores score usability at fixed thresholds. This causes systematically poor deployment choices: models with the best PR-AUC often perform worst in production. The paper aims to quantify and close this operational gap between offline evaluation and deployed quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce two new metrics: (1) Precision-Cache Hit Ratio (P-CHR) AUC, which measures precision across varying cache utilization levels, and (2) Calibration Retention Rate (CRR), which quantifies how much offline ranking quality survives at deployment. They decompose the offline-to-deployed quality gap into a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component determined by the dataset's positive rate. Experiments analyze how training objectives and data scale affect the calibration gap, including post-hoc calibration attempts.
AI.result: Experiments reveal that the calibration gap is primarily governed by the training objective, not data scale. Post-hoc calibration only partially closes the gap. Models with the highest PR-AUC frequently underperform in operational settings, confirming the metric's inadequacy for deployment decisions.
AI.conclusion: Model selection for semantic caching is fundamentally a calibration problem rather than a ranking problem. Proper measurement using cache-aware, calibration-sensitive metrics is the essential first step toward closing the operational gap between offline evaluation and real-world deployment.

title: PUFFERDOS: Efficient and Effective Attack String Generation for Regular Expression Denial of Service Vulnerabilities
summary: ReDoS attacks constitute a critical class of resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities. In such attacks, adversaries exploit the pathological worst-case execution behavior of regular expression (regex) engines to induce highly asymmetric computational workloads, ultimately exhausting system resources and degrading service availability. To protect systems against ReDoS attacks, numerous detection techniques have been proposed that simulate the attack process by generating attack strings to proactively exploit ReDoS vulnerabilities at the early development stage and facilitate remediation. Existing techniques broadly fall into two classes: static analyses that search for pathological regex structures, and dynamic exploration methods that synthesize candidate attack strings. However, the generated attack strings are often impractical for real-world exploitation because they usually assume unrealistic input-length budgets and do not validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the attack at the program level. Therefore, many generated strings fail to trigger vulnerable regexes when applied to real-world programs, further limiting the practical utility. To address these shortcomings, we introduce an effective and efficient attack string generator, PUFFERDOS, designed to synthesize attack inputs that are both feasible within realistic length budgets and validated at the program level, enabling effective exploitation of ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs. Specifically, we first define three vulnerable patterns based on our observation and formal verification. According to the patterns, PUFFERDOS conducts a synthesis technique to generate attack strings, and then refines and validates the strings with ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution to guarantee real-world exploitability.

AI.tldr: PUFFERDOS is a tool that synthesizes realistic, program-level validated attack strings for exploiting ReDoS (Regular Expression Denial of Service) vulnerabilities, addressing limitations of prior approaches that produce impractical strings with unrealistic input-length assumptions.
AI.motivation: Existing ReDoS detection techniques generate attack strings that are often impractical for real-world exploitation because they assume unrealistic input-length budgets and lack program-level validation of attack effectiveness and efficiency. This limits their practical utility in actually triggering vulnerable regexes in real programs.
AI.method: PUFFERDOS defines three vulnerable regex patterns based on observation and formal verification. It then synthesizes attack strings according to these patterns and refines/validates them using ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution to ensure real-world exploitability within realistic length budgets.
AI.result: The paper presents PUFFERDOS as an effective and efficient attack string generator capable of producing feasible, program-level validated attack inputs that successfully trigger ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs.
AI.conclusion: By combining pattern-based synthesis with compositional concolic execution, PUFFERDOS bridges the gap between theoretical ReDoS detection and practical exploitation, generating attack strings that are both length-feasible and validated at the program level for real-world effectiveness.

title: Syndesmoscope: The Power of Invariant Plots\\Linked to Traditional Network Views
summary: Traditional network representations, such as node-link views and adjacency matrices, can show dramatically different visual patterns, depending on the underlying layout or seriation algorithm. In contrast, invariant plots consistently surface the same visual pattern for the same input topology; yet researchers have underexplored them and have not integrated them into visualization systems. We present Syndesmoscope, an interactive system for network exploration that juxtaposes multiple views of the same network. Panes show a familiar a force-directed view alongside three panes with interpretable geometric layouts based on graph-theoretic properties: dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, and spectral bisection. As a secondary contribution, we introduce kSnakes, a new invariant plot based on density decomposition. Syndesmoscope supports two key interactions: leapfrogging, or linked highlighting between different and interpretable visual patterns; and hopscotching, or hop-based traversal that extends data selections through the underlying topology. Through usage scenarios across a corpus of 72 diverse networks, we demonstrate how these interactions reveal network patterns inaccessible through any single view alone. Live demo available at https://syndesmoscope.vercel.app/.

AI.tldr: Syndesmoscope is an interactive network exploration system that juxtaposes force-directed layouts with three invariant geometric layouts (dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, spectral bisection) plus a novel kSnakes density-based invariant plot, enabling linked highlighting (leapfrogging) and topology-based selection extension (hopscotching) to reveal patterns invisible in any single view.
AI.motivation: Traditional network visualizations (node-link, adjacency matrices) produce inconsistent visual patterns depending on layout/seriation algorithms. Invariant plots yield consistent patterns for the same topology but remain underexplored and unintegrated into practical visualization systems. The authors aim to bridge this gap by building a system that combines multiple invariant views with traditional layouts to unlock richer network exploration.
AI.method: The authors built Syndesmoscope, a multi-pane interactive system. One pane shows a force-directed layout; three panes show invariant geometric layouts based on graph-theoretic properties (dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, spectral bisection). A secondary contribution is kSnakes, a new invariant plot using density decomposition. Two interaction techniques are introduced: (1) leapfrogging — linked cross-view highlighting connecting different interpretable visual patterns; (2) hopscotching — hop-based traversal extending selections through the underlying topology. The system was evaluated through usage scenarios on a corpus of 72 diverse networks.
AI.result: Through usage scenarios across 72 diverse networks, the authors demonstrated that the combination of leapfrogging and hopscotching interactions across multiple invariant and traditional views reveals network patterns that are inaccessible through any single view alone. A live demo was deployed.
AI.conclusion: Invariant plots provide consistent, topology-grounded visual representations that complement traditional network views. When integrated into an interactive system like Syndesmoscope with cross-view linking and topology-based traversal, they enable analysts to surface structural patterns that would otherwise remain hidden, advocating for broader adoption of invariant visualizations in network analysis tools.

title: Bistable by Construction: Wall-Clock-Calibrated State Monitors Have No Moment-Detection Regime at Agent Cadence
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Sequel to arXiv:2606.04296. Pre-registered; falsification clauses honored (H5 unsupported; H7 strict band 16/20) repo:https://github.com/2025eb1100268-tech/intervention-timing-saturation-trap
summary: Runtime monitors for autonomous agents commonly threshold an accumulated internal state - a behavioural baseline, a drift statistic, or, in our prior work, a modelled affective state. We previously reported a State Saturation Trap: threshold-on-state triggers over a continuous affect engine become near-constant alarms on SWE-bench debugging agents (Modgil 2026). A post-release audit found the engine received dt=0 between actions, so its exponential decay never operated: the published trap is a pure-accumulator result. We correct the record (erratum, v2) and treat the flaw as an experiment. The key variable it exposes is whether a monitor's dynamics are calibrated in sample time (per observation, as in CUSUM) or wall-clock time (half-lives in seconds, as in affect models and EMA baselines). On fixed-rate streams these coincide; on agent streams, where inter-action time varies by orders of magnitude, they do not. A pre-registered sweep over uniform intervals (dt in {0..600}s) on 20 trajectories shows the wall-clock level trigger has two regimes: at dt<=1s a constant alarm (20/20; median 18 firings); at dt>=60s silent. Every critical dt lies in (1,30]s. Real agent runs measure latency at median 1.53s (p90 2.33s); real coding cadence sits inside the trap regime, vindicating the empirical finding under a corrected mechanism. The structure is a property of the calibration class, not the engine: a minimal wall-clock accumulator over the raw error stream reproduces the same cliff, while a sample-time CUSUM over the identical stream is exactly dt-invariant (20/20). A rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires 0-3 times per trajectory in every condition. We conclude that wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime in which they act as moment detectors on agent streams; transition detection escapes the trap at every cadence, but does not recover human intervention timing.

AI.tldr: A prior paper's "State Saturation Trap" was found to be a pure-accumulator artifact caused by dt=0 between agent actions. The corrected experiment reveals a fundamental property: wall-clock-calibrated monitors (exponential decay, EMA) exhibit a critical cliff regime on variable-rate agent streams, while sample-time monitors (CUSUM) are dt-invariant. Rising-edge triggers with hysteresis avoid the trap entirely.
AI.motivation: To correct a published error (erratum, v2) and investigate whether the State Saturation Trap is a genuine phenomenon of wall-clock-calibrated monitors on agent streams with variable inter-action timing, versus an artifact of the specific affect engine implementation.
AI.method: Pre-registered sweep over uniform dt intervals (0–600s) on 20 SWE-bench trajectories. Three monitor classes compared: (1) wall-clock leaky accumulator over raw error stream, (2) sample-time CUSUM over identical stream, (3) rising-edge trigger with hysteresis. Real agent latency measured (median 1.53s, p90 2.33s).
AI.result: Wall-clock threshold-on-state triggers exhibit two regimes: dt ≤ 1s → constant alarms (20/20, median 18 firings); dt ≥ 60s → silent. All critical dt lie in (1,30]s — precisely where real agent coding cadence falls. A minimal wall-clock accumulator reproduces the same cliff. Sample-time CUSUM is exactly dt-invariant (20/20 across all dt). Rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires only 0–3 times per trajectory across all conditions.
AI.conclusion: Wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime where they function as moment detectors on variable-rate agent streams. Transition detection (rising-edge with hysteresis) escapes the trap at every cadence but cannot recover human intervention timing.

title: How LLMs Fail and Generalize in RTL Coding for Hardware Design?
summary: Translating sequential programming priors into the parallel temporal logic of hardware design remains a crucial bottleneck for large language models(LLM). To investigate this, we introduce a new error taxonomy grounded in problem solvability, inspired by cognitive theory. Our taxonomy categorizes failures into syntactic, semantic, solvable functional, and unsolvable functional types. Evaluations reveal a strict empirical ceiling on the VerilogEval benchmark, as frontier models plateau at a 90.8% initial pass rate. These plateaus are defined by unsolvable functional errors, exposing persistent knowledge gaps immune to test time compute scaling. Furthermore, we expose a striking surface convergence gap: optimization readily eliminates syntax errors but concurrently exacerbates deeper functional failures. Our findings demonstrate that alignment techniques merely teach models to compile. While repeated sampling strategies can patch solvable errors, register-transfer level(RTL) coding capacity remains strictly bounded by pretraining knowledge. Addressing challenges in the current LLM based hardware generation pipeline requires more studies in model reasoning rather than alignment interventions.

AI.tldr: Frontier LLMs plateau at ~90.8% on VerilogEval due to unsolvable functional errors rooted in pretraining knowledge gaps. Optimization eliminates syntax errors but worsens deeper functional failures, revealing that alignment only teaches models to compile—true RTL coding capacity is bounded by pretraining and requires reasoning-focused advances.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to translate sequential programming knowledge into the parallel temporal logic of hardware design. The authors aim to systematically characterize why frontier models hit a performance ceiling on VerilogEval and to understand whether test-time compute scaling or alignment techniques can overcome these limits.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel error taxonomy grounded in problem solvability (inspired by cognitive theory), categorizing failures into: syntactic errors, semantic errors, solvable functional errors, and unsolvable functional errors. They evaluate frontier LLMs on the VerilogEval benchmark, analyzing pass rates, error-type distributions, and the effects of repeated sampling and alignment-based optimization.
AI.result: Frontier models plateau at a 90.8% initial pass rate on VerilogEval. Unsolvable functional errors define this ceiling and are immune to test-time compute scaling. A "surface convergence gap" emerges: optimization removes syntax errors but exacerbates deeper functional failures. Repeated sampling can patch solvable errors, but RTL coding capacity remains strictly bounded by pretraining knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Alignment techniques merely teach models to compile rather than to reason correctly about hardware design. Overcoming the current LLM-based hardware generation bottleneck requires advances in model reasoning rather than further alignment interventions or test-time scaling strategies.

title: Hidden Anchors in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
summary: Multi-agent LLM deliberation, where agents exchange and revise answers over several rounds, is increasingly used to improve reasoning and accuracy, yet how and why it works is rarely modelled. Such deliberation mirrors how humans reach decisions. As social animals we are pulled both by the group, the herd effect that classical opinion-dynamics models such as DeGroot and Friedkin--Johnsen capture, and by our own internal belief, which they do not. We model multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system in which each agent carries a hidden internal belief, its anchor, that continually pulls its opinion regardless of its neighbours. We show this anchor can be recovered from the deliberation alone, and that it explains a behaviour classical consensus rules forbid: an agent's confidence in the correct answer can climb past where any agent started, escaping the space (convexhull) formed by the initial beliefs. Checking whether the recovered anchor also predicts held-out runs (generalizes) gives a simple test for when a model is truly driven bysuch an anchor. Across three open-weight model families this is a spectrum, not all-or-nothing. All anchors' influence are about equally strongly, but they differ in where the anchor sits, and only when it sits far from the initial opinions does deliberation escape the hull and need the full closed-loop model.

AI.tldr: The paper models multi-agent LLM deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent has a hidden internal belief ("anchor") that continually pulls its opinion. This anchor can be recovered from deliberation data and explains how agents can exceed initial confidence bounds (escape the convex hull). A generalization test reveals anchor-driven behavior exists on a spectrum across model families, with hull-escaping deliberation occurring only when the anchor sits far from initial opinions.
AI.motivation: Current understanding of multi-agent LLM deliberation lacks formal modeling of the underlying mechanism. While deliberation improves reasoning and accuracy, existing opinion-dynamics models (DeGroot, Friedkin-Johnsen) capture group conformity (herd effect) but fail to account for each agent's persistent internal belief. The authors aim to fill this gap by modeling the interplay between social influence and intrinsic conviction.
AI.method: The authors formalize multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent possesses a hidden, static "anchor" representing its internal belief. This anchor exerts a continuous pull on the agent's expressed opinion, independent of neighbor influence. The anchor is recovered from deliberation trajectories alone. A generalization test checks whether the recovered anchor predicts held-out deliberation runs. The model is evaluated across three open-weight LLM families.
AI.result: The anchor can be successfully recovered from deliberation data. It explains a phenomenon forbidden by classical consensus models: agent confidence can surpass any initial belief, escaping the convex hull of starting opinions. Anchor-driven behavior is not binary but exists on a spectrum across model families. All anchors exert roughly equal influence strength, but their spatial positioning differs. Only when the anchor is positioned far from initial opinions does deliberation escape the hull, requiring the full closed-loop model.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM deliberation is governed by a recoverable internal anchor mechanism that operates on a spectrum rather than as a discrete property. The closed-loop anchor model successfully captures deliberation dynamics that classical opinion-dynamics models cannot, particularly the hull-escaping phenomenon, providing both a diagnostic tool and a theoretical framework for understanding when and why deliberation improves LLM reasoning.

title: Performance Analysis and Optimization of 3D Generative Diffusion Models across GPU Architectures
summary: Diffusion models have become essential for high-fidelity 3D MRI synthesis, yet their deployment remains constrained by substantial GPU resource demands arising from hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample and a highly heterogeneous kernel behavior. This paper performs a comprehensive performance analysis of the state-of-the-art medical diffusion model, Med-DDPM, across three generations of NVIDIA architectures to study kernel-level runtime breakdowns, instruction-mix characteristics, memory system utilization, warp-level activities, and profiler priority-score estimates. We show that training is overwhelmingly dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels, with inefficiencies arising from memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and limited Tensor Core utilization. Guided by these insights, we evaluate two architecture-aware optimizations TF32 Tensor Core activation and a 3D channels-last layout and demonstrate that they reduce SM cycles by up to 100x, cut dynamic instructions by 100x, raise Tensor Core utilization from 1.45 to 9.98x, and increase IPC by 7% on A100, all without degrading synthesis quality.

AI.tldr: A performance analysis of the Med-DDPM diffusion model across three NVIDIA GPU generations reveals training is dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels, with inefficiencies in memory access and Tensor Core usage. Two architecture-aware optimizations (TF32 Tensor Core activation and 3D channels-last layout) yield up to 100x reduction in SM cycles and dynamic instructions, with Tensor Core utilization improving from 1.45× to 9.98×.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models for 3D MRI synthesis are high-quality but GPU-intensive, requiring hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample with heterogeneous kernel behavior. Understanding and mitigating these computational bottlenecks is critical for practical deployment in medical imaging.
AI.method: The authors perform a comprehensive kernel-level performance analysis of Med-DDPM across three NVIDIA GPU architectures (spanning multiple generations). They examine runtime breakdowns, instruction-mix characteristics, memory system utilization, warp-level activities, and profiler priority-score estimates. Based on these insights, they evaluate two architecture-aware optimizations: (1) TF32 Tensor Core activation and (2) a 3D channels-last memory layout.
AI.result: Training is overwhelmingly dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels. Key inefficiencies stem from poor memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and limited Tensor Core utilization. The proposed optimizations reduce SM cycles by up to 100×, cut dynamic instructions by 100×, boost Tensor Core utilization from 1.45× to 9.98×, and increase IPC by 7% on the A100, all without degrading synthesis quality.
AI.conclusion: Architecture-aware optimizations—specifically TF32 Tensor Core activation and 3D channels-last layout—can dramatically improve the efficiency of medical diffusion models on modern GPUs without compromising output fidelity, making high-quality 3D MRI synthesis more practically deployable.

title: Library-Aware Doubles and Iterative Repair for Large Language Model-Generated Unit Tests in OpenSIL Firmware
summary: Validating changes in low-level C firmware is expensive because unit tests (UTs) are fragile under strict build constraints, where missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently prevent compilation and linking. This study introduces an automated UT authoring workflow for the Open-Source Silicon Initialization Library (openSIL) firmware codebase maintained by Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) that reduces manual effort through a large language model (LLM) guided multi-agent pipeline. The workflow combines automated generation of test scaffolds, library-aware creation or reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes, and an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop driven by build logs and line-coverage feedback. We evaluate the approach using compilation success, repair iterations, dispatch success, and line coverage, with time, cost, and token usage as secondary measures. Across 76 functions under test, the workflow generated compilable UTs for 73 functions. In a configuration without line coverage guidance or retrieval augmentation, mean line coverage reached 73.9%. On a 48-function subset evaluated under both configurations, mean line coverage reached 98.8% with line-coverage guidance alone and reached 94.7% when combined with vector-database retrieval. Results show that automated generation-and-repair pipelines can substantially improve UT creation efficiency and coverage for constrained firmware environments while reducing manual debugging effort.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM pipeline automates unit test generation for AMD's openSIL firmware, using iterative compile-dispatch repair loops to achieve compilation for 73/76 functions and up to 98.8% line coverage with coverage-guided feedback.
AI.motivation: Validating low-level C firmware changes is expensive because traditional unit tests (UTs) are fragile under strict build constraints — missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently prevent compilation and linking. Manual effort to create and maintain UTs in such constrained environments is prohibitively high.
AI.method: The authors propose an automated UT authoring workflow using an LLM-guided multi-agent pipeline. It consists of three core components: (1) automated generation of test scaffolds, (2) library-aware creation or reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes, and (3) an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop driven by build logs and line-coverage feedback. Two configurations are compared: with line-coverage guidance alone and with additional vector-database retrieval augmentation.
AI.result: Across 76 functions under test, compilable UTs were generated for 73 (96%). Without coverage guidance or retrieval, mean line coverage was 73.9%. On a 48-function subset, mean line coverage reached 98.8% with coverage guidance alone and 94.7% when combined with vector-database retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Automated generation-and-repair pipelines can substantially improve UT creation efficiency and line coverage for constrained firmware environments while reducing manual debugging effort. Coverage-guided feedback proves particularly effective, though retrieval augmentation may introduce trade-offs.

title: Stellar: Scalable Multimodal Document Retrieval for Natural Language Queries
summary: Multimodal document retrieval--selecting the most relevant multimodal document from a large corpus to answer a natural language query--plays an essential role in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. State-of-the-art methods represent each document and query with multiple token-level embeddings and use late interaction to achieve high effectiveness. However, such multi-vector representations incur substantial memory overhead during retrieval, leading to poor scalability and hindering real-world deployment. In this paper, we present Stellar, a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that stores token-level document embeddings on disk and loads only a small set of candidate embeddings into memory for late interaction. Stellar comprises two key components: (i) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF), which fine-tunes a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a sparse encoder to produce high-quality lexical representations, enabling efficient and effective document filtering to significantly reduce the candidate set; (ii) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI), which designs an on-disk token embedding storage layout guided by a balanced clustering algorithm, and dynamically loads only the necessary token embeddings into memory using a simple yet effective cost model. Extensive experiments on four real-world benchmarks and a newly presented large-scale dataset demonstrate that Stellar reduces memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods without compromising retrieval effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Stellar is a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that reduces memory overhead by storing token embeddings on disk and selectively loading only necessary candidates via lexical filtering and a disk-backed late interaction mechanism, achieving 1-2 orders of magnitude reduction in memory and latency without sacrificing retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Multi-vector (token-level) late interaction methods achieve high retrieval effectiveness for multimodal document retrieval in RAG systems, but suffer from substantial memory overhead that hinders scalability and real-world deployment.
AI.method: Stellar has two components: (1) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF), which fine-tunes an MLLM as a sparse encoder to generate high-quality lexical representations for efficient document filtering; (2) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI), which uses a balanced clustering algorithm to design an on-disk token embedding layout and a cost model to dynamically load only necessary token embeddings into memory.
AI.result: Experiments on four real-world benchmarks and a newly introduced large-scale dataset show that Stellar reduces memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods, while maintaining retrieval effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Stellar enables practical deployment of high-quality multi-vector multimodal document retrieval at scale by decoupling storage from memory via intelligent on-disk embedding management and effective candidate pre-filtering.

title: A Layered Security Framework Against Prompt Injection in RAG-Based Chatbots
comment: Submitted in ICCK Transactions on Information Security and Cryptography
summary: Prompt injection is ranked as the most critical vulnerability in large language model (LLM) deployments by the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, yet existing defenses operate at isolated pipeline stages and remain incomplete. Input filters cannot inspect retrieved documents, while output monitors cannot prevent malicious payloads from reaching the model. Consequently, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbots remain vulnerable to indirect injection, where a poisoned knowledge-base document compromises every user whose query retrieves it. We present a three-layer framework that intercepts both direct and indirect prompt injection throughout the inference pipeline. Layer 1 screens user input using a rule-based pattern library and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier. Layer 2 enforces a provenance-based instruction hierarchy during context assembly, preventing retrieved content from overriding operator policy. Layer 3 audits model output using a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector before delivery. A continuous audit loop aggregates structured logs and supports retraining to adapt the classifier to emerging attack patterns. The framework is model-agnostic and deploys as middleware without modifying the underlying LLM. Evaluation on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B shows that the framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 71.4\% to 11.3\%, outperforming the best single-layer baseline by 27.3 percentage points and a published guardrail system by 23.8 percentage points, while maintaining a 4.8\% false positive rate and a median latency overhead of 61.2 ms. Ablation studies confirm that all three layers provide complementary protection and that their combined effect exceeds the sum of individual contributions.

AI.tldr: A three-layer middleware framework for defending against direct and indirect prompt injection attacks in RAG-based LLM applications, achieving significant ASR reduction (71.4% → 11.3%) with low latency overhead across multiple LLMs.
AI.motivation: Prompt injection is the top LLM vulnerability per OWASP, but existing defenses are isolated, incomplete, and fail to address indirect injection in RAG pipelines where poisoned knowledge-base documents can compromise all downstream users.
AI.method: A three-layer inference pipeline defense: (1) input screening via rule-based patterns and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier; (2) provenance-based instruction hierarchy during context assembly to prevent retrieved content from overriding operator policy; (3) output auditing with a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector. A continuous audit loop aggregates logs for classifier retraining. Deployed as model-agnostic middleware.
AI.result: Evaluated on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B. Attack Success Rate reduced from 71.4% to 11.3%, outperforming best single-layer baseline by 27.3 pp and a published guardrail system by 23.8 pp, with 4.8% FPR and 61.2 ms median latency overhead. Ablations confirm all three layers provide complementary, super-additive protection.
AI.conclusion: The three-layer framework provides robust, complementary defense against both direct and indirect prompt injection in RAG systems without requiring LLM modification, combining to produce a synergistic effect greater than the sum of individual layers.

title: Vibe Coding for Visualization Implementation: An Empirical Study of Practices and Challenges
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Short paper under review
summary: Data visualization is essential for data analysis and communication, yet creating expressive visualizations remains labor-intensive. Recent AI-driven ``vibe coding'' tools enable users to generate visualizations through natural language interaction, lowering the barrier to entry. However, visualization implementation requires precise alignment between user intent and visual representation, which may differ from general software development practices. We present an empirical study with 16 participants of varying expertise to examine how users employ vibe coding tools for visualization implementation. Participants completed two visualization tasks and a semi-structured interview. Our findings characterize the diverse practices users adopt across prompting, evaluation, and iteration, and surface the challenges they encounter throughout the process.

AI.tldr: An empirical study with 16 participants examining how users with varying expertise employ AI-driven "vibe coding" tools for visualization implementation, characterizing prompting, evaluation, and iteration practices and the challenges encountered.
AI.motivation: Data visualization creation remains labor-intensive despite its importance. While AI-driven natural language tools lower barriers, visualization implementation demands precise alignment between user intent and visual representation — a requirement that may diverge from general software development. Understanding how users actually employ these tools is critical yet underexplored.
AI.method: An empirical user study with 16 participants of varying expertise levels. Participants completed two visualization implementation tasks using vibe coding tools, followed by semi-structured interviews to capture their practices and challenges.
AI.result: The study characterizes diverse user practices across three key phases: prompting strategies, evaluation behaviors, and iteration patterns. It also surfaces specific challenges users face throughout the visualization implementation process when using vibe coding tools.
AI.conclusion: Vibe coding tools show promise for democratizing visualization creation, but the mismatch between natural language expression and precise visual specification creates distinct challenges that differ from general-purpose code generation. The findings provide empirical grounding for improving future visualization-oriented AI tools.

title: Interpretable and Verifiable Hardware Generation with LLM-Driven Stepwise Refinement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in software development. However, they are susceptible to hallucinations, meaning that they can introduce subtle semantic and logical errors. Due to the high stakes in chip design and manufacturing, hardware engineers are still reluctant to rely on LLMs for register-transfer level (RTL) generation. In this paper, we propose a hardware generation framework that combines the creativity and broad knowledge of LLMs with the explainability and mathematical rigor of formal methods. Specifically, we devise a set of transformation rules that cover various design decisions and hardware features. By iteratively applying these rules, an LLM agent can convert a design specification into an RTL program with guaranteed correctness. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the framework.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hardware generation framework that integrates LLMs with formal methods to produce correct-by-construction RTL designs, addressing LLM hallucination risks through iterative application of transformation rules.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel in software development but suffer from hallucinations that introduce semantic/logical errors. The high stakes of chip design mean hardware engineers cannot trust LLMs for RTL generation without correctness guarantees, creating a gap between LLM capability and practical adoption in hardware design.
AI.method: The authors devise a framework combining LLM creativity with formal methods. A set of transformation rules covering design decisions and hardware features is created. An LLM agent iteratively applies these rules to convert a design specification into an RTL program, with formal guarantees ensuring correctness at each step.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate both the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework for RTL generation.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with formal methods via rule-based iterative transformation is a viable approach for generating trustworthy RTL designs, potentially bridging the trust gap that currently limits LLM adoption in hardware design.

title: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence
summary: We present a preview version of DeepSeek-V4 series, including two strong Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models -- DeepSeek-V4-Pro with 1.6T parameters (49B activated) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash with 284B parameters (13B activated) -- both supporting a context length of one million tokens. DeepSeek-V4 series incorporate several key upgrades in architecture and optimization: (1) a hybrid attention architecture that combines Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) to improve long-context efficiency; (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) that enhance conventional residual connections; (3) and the Muon optimizer for faster convergence and greater training stability. We pre-train both models on more than 32T diverse and high-quality tokens, followed by a comprehensive post-training pipeline that unlocks and further enhances their capabilities. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max, the maximum reasoning effort mode of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, redefines the state-of-the-art for open models, outperforming its predecessors in core tasks. Meanwhile, DeepSeek-V4 series are highly efficient in long-context scenarios. In the one-million-token context setting, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of KV cache compared with DeepSeek-V3.2. This enables us to routinely support one-million-token contexts, thereby making long-horizon tasks and further test-time scaling more feasible. The model checkpoints are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.

AI.tldr: DeepSeek-V4 introduces two MoE models (Pro: 1.6T/49B activated; Flash: 284B/13B activated) with 1M-token context, featuring hybrid attention (CSA+HCA), manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC), and Muon optimizer. Trained on 32T+ tokens, the Pro-Max variant sets new open-model SOTA, achieving dramatic long-context efficiency (27% FLOPs, 10% KV cache vs. V3.2).
AI.motivation: To advance open-source language models by improving long-context efficiency, training stability, and convergence speed, while pushing the performance frontier beyond predecessors like DeepSeek-V3.2, especially for long-horizon tasks and test-time scaling.
AI.method: The series employs: (1) a hybrid attention architecture combining Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) for long-context efficiency; (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) to enhance residual connections; (3) the Muon optimizer for faster convergence and stability. Both models are pre-trained on 32T+ diverse, high-quality tokens followed by a comprehensive post-training pipeline. A maximum reasoning effort mode (Pro-Max) is introduced for the Pro variant.
AI.result: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max achieves state-of-the-art results for open models, outperforming predecessors on core tasks. In 1M-token contexts, DeepSeek-V4-Pro uses only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of KV cache compared to DeepSeek-V3.2, enabling routine support for million-token contexts.
AI.conclusion: DeepSeek-V4 represents a significant leap in open-source LLMs, combining architectural innovations (hybrid attention, mHC, Muon) with massive-scale training to deliver both superior performance and unprecedented long-context efficiency, making long-horizon reasoning and test-time scaling practically feasible.

title: DeXposure-Claw: An Agentic System for DeFi Risk Supervision
summary: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks. General-purpose LLM agents fit this setting poorly: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations offer no regulator-aligned way to measure the resulting false alarms. We introduce DeXposure-Claw, a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios then turn those forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation before DeXposure-Claw emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. We further develop DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis evaluation harness, whose decision axis scores tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate. Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support our system. Code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw.

AI.tldr: DeXposure-Claw is a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system for decentralized finance (DeFi) that uses a graph time-series foundation model (DeXposure-FM) to forecast exposure networks, then applies deterministic monitors and confidence gates to generate auditable, low-false-alarm supervisory tickets. A companion benchmark (DeXposure-Bench) evaluates decisions against regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM agents perform poorly in DeFi supervision: they over-interpret weak signals and recommend excessive high-stakes interventions. Existing evaluation frameworks lack regulator-aligned metrics to quantify false alarms. A structured, evidence-grounded approach is needed to balance timely risk detection with intervention restraint.
AI.method: The system has three components: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model that forecasts future credit exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios that convert forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; (3) data-health and confidence gates that constrain escalation, ensuring only high-confidence findings become auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. Evaluation uses DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis harness with a decision axis scoring tickets via regulator-aligned absolute loss and an explicit false-intervention rate.
AI.result: Experiments on five years of weekly real-world DeFi data demonstrate that DeXposure-Claw effectively generates supervisory tickets with controlled false-intervention rates, outperforming general-purpose LLM agents that otherwise produce excessive false alarms.
AI.conclusion: Grounding LLM-based supervision in structured forecasts, deterministic monitors, and confidence gates yields a practical, auditable DeFi oversight system. The regulator-aligned benchmark provides a reusable standard for measuring supervisory agent performance in networked credit-risk settings.

title: Information Lattice Learning as Probabilistic Graphical Model Structure Learning
summary: Information lattice learning (ILL) learns interpretable rules of a signal by alternately projecting the signal onto a partition lattice that encodes a hierarchy of abstractions and lifting selected rules back to the signal domain. When the signal is a probability mass function, we show the probabilistic rules learned by ILL admit a natural probabilistic graphical model (PGM) interpretation and develop this interpretation in detail. A partition in ILL induces a deterministic quotient variable, and a rule is the marginal law of that quotient variable. A rule set is therefore a collection of marginal constraints over interpretable abstractions. General lifting is the feasible family of all joint distributions satisfying those constraints, while special lifting chooses a maximum-ignorance reconstruction, implemented in ILL by an L2 uniformity principle closely related to maximum entropy. Under a Shannon-entropy lifting, the same constraints yield a log-linear factor graph whose factors are indexed by learned abstractions. The information lattice itself, however, is not a Bayesian network: its edges encode refinement and coarsening of abstractions, not conditional dependence. Thus ILL is best viewed as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables. This view clarifies how ILL relates to graphical models and maximum entropy models, while suggesting new directions for inference, identifiability, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning.

AI.tldr: ILL learns interpretable probabilistic rules by projecting signals onto a partition lattice. This paper shows these rules correspond to marginal constraints on quotient variables, framing ILL as structure learning for constraint-based factor graphs. The lattice encodes abstraction refinement (not conditional dependence), distinguishing it from Bayesian networks, and connecting ILL to maximum entropy and probabilistic graphical models.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous probabilistic graphical model interpretation for Information Lattice Learning (ILL), clarifying its theoretical foundations, distinguishing it from Bayesian networks, and connecting it to established frameworks like maximum entropy models and factor graphs.
AI.method: The authors develop a detailed PGM interpretation of ILL by mapping its components: a partition induces a deterministic quotient variable; a learned rule is the marginal law of that variable; a rule set forms a collection of marginal constraints. General lifting is characterized as the family of all joint distributions satisfying those constraints, while special lifting uses an L2 uniformity principle (akin to maximum entropy). Under Shannon-entropy lifting, constraints yield a log-linear factor graph with factors indexed by learned abstractions.
AI.result: ILL is best understood as structure learning for interpretable, constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables. The information lattice encodes refinement/coarsening relations among abstractions, not conditional dependence, so it is not a Bayesian network. This framing clarifies ILL's relationship to graphical models and maximum entropy approaches.
AI.conclusion: Viewing ILL through a PGM lens opens new directions for inference, identifiability analysis, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning, while firmly grounding the method in established probabilistic theory.

title: Heterogeneous LLM Debate Under Adversarial Peers: Honest Gains, Replacement Costs, and Resilience
summary: Heterogeneous LLM debate is motivated by the promise that diverse peers correct one another, but the same exchange that carries correction also carries adversarial influence. We measure which dominates by tracking how a heterogeneous peer changes the honest agents' revision behavior: how often they change their answer, and whether the change is corrective or harmful. We compare matched panels (homogeneous baseline, honest-mixed, and adversarial-mixed) and contaminated panels in which a malicious same-family peer is already present, spanning four model families and three reasoning benchmarks. An honest heterogeneous peer sharply lowers harmful revision, and an adversarial one reverses it. For Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard, the honest-slot harmful-revision rate falls from 89% in the homogeneous panel to 35% with an honest peer, and an adversarial peer returns it to 90%. The conditional rate hides this damage on weak defenders, but the end-of-debate flip rate exposes it. The pattern keeps its sign across families and benchmarks while its magnitude varies with the defender-benchmark regime. We also measure the effects when an adversarial same-family peer is already present: an honest heterogeneous peer lowers both harmful revision and the rate at which initially-correct answers are lost. On the same Llama-3.1-70B setting, the added honest peer cuts the flip rate on initially-correct items from 31% under a same-family adversary to 6%. Heterogeneity is therefore not only an attack surface but, when an adversary is already present, also a defense.

AI.tldr: Heterogeneous LLM debate is a double-edged sword: an honest heterogeneous peer sharply reduces harmful revision, while an adversarial one restores it. Critically, when a same-family adversary is already present, adding an honest heterogeneous peer acts as a defense, dramatically reducing the flip rate on initially-correct answers.
AI.motivation: Investigating whether heterogeneous LLM debate is dominated by beneficial cross-model correction or by adversarial influence, and quantifying the net effect of model diversity on revision behavior in multi-agent reasoning settings.
AI.method: The authors compare matched panels (homogeneous baseline, honest-mixed, adversarial-mixed) and contaminated panels with a pre-existing same-family adversary. They track revision behavior — specifically how often honest agents change answers and whether changes are corrective or harmful — across four model families and three reasoning benchmarks. Metrics include harmful-revision rate, end-of-debate flip rate, and conditional revision rates.
AI.result: An honest heterogeneous peer sharply reduces harmful revision (e.g., from 89% to 35% for Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard). An adversarial heterogeneous peer reverses this, restoring harmful revision to ~90%. On weak defenders, conditional rates mask damage but the end-of-debate flip rate exposes it. When a same-family adversary is already present, adding an honest heterogeneous peer cuts the flip rate on initially-correct items from 31% to 6%. The pattern holds across model families and benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneity is both an attack surface and a defense: while adversarial heterogeneous peers can corrupt debate, honest heterogeneous peers are powerful correctives — especially as a countermeasure when a malicious same-family agent is already present.

title: PACMS: Submodular Context Selection as a Pluggable Engine for LLM Agents
summary:
Conversational and tool-using LLM agents operate over a context window that fills from several directions simultaneously. As a session proceeds, the agent accumulates user and assistant turns, entries drawn from a persistent memory store, and often largest of all, the verbatim outputs of tool calls such as file reads, search results, and API responses. Once the cumulative context exceeds the model's token budget, the framework must decide what to keep.
  The prevailing mechanism is recency truncation, sometimes paired with periodic summarization. This is topic-blind: a fact established early in a session is discarded simply because it is old, even when the current user query is about exactly that fact; conversely, verbose but irrelevant recent material is retained. Agents that must recall information across many turns, the defining case for memory, are precisely where recency truncation fails.
  Existing alternatives sit outside the agent's assembly step. Retrieval augmented generation fetches external documents into the prompt but does not arbitrate the agent's \emph{already-present} pooled context. Context-compression methods reduce token count by rewriting or pruning text, but operate query-blind and lossily. Neither treats memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a single candidate pool to be selected from by relevance at the moment the prompt is assembled.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques recency-based context truncation in LLM agents and highlights the absence of a relevance-driven, unified selection mechanism that treats conversation turns, memory entries, and tool outputs as a single candidate pool during prompt assembly.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents manage context windows via recency truncation, which is topic-blind: it discards old but relevant facts while retaining recent but irrelevant material. This fails precisely in the use case that defines memory-augmented agents — recalling information across many turns. Existing alternatives (RAG and context compression) operate outside the prompt assembly step and do not treat all context sources as a unified, relevance-rankable pool.
AI.method: This appears to be a position/problem-formulation paper rather than one proposing a novel method. It systematically identifies and taxonomizes the failure modes of recency truncation, delineates the limitations of existing alternatives (RAG's external focus, compression's query-blind lossiness), and frames the problem as the need for a relevance-based, query-aware selection mechanism operating over the unified pool of conversation turns, memory entries, and tool outputs at prompt assembly time.
AI.result: The paper identifies a clear architectural gap: no existing mechanism performs query-conditioned relevance selection over the agent's entire accumulated context (conversation + memory + tool outputs) at the moment of prompt construction. Recency truncation is topic-blind; RAG fetches external documents but ignores already-present context; context compression reduces tokens lossily and query-blindly.
AI.conclusion: A relevance-driven, query-aware context selection mechanism that unifies all context sources — conversation history, persistent memory, and tool outputs — into a single candidate pool at prompt assembly time is needed to overcome the fundamental limitations of recency-based truncation in LLM agents.

title: When Global Gating Is Enough: Admission-Time Hubness Control in Anisotropic Vector Retrieval Systems
summary: Vector hubness, where a few points become nearest neighbors of many queries, creates a poisoning risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): one injected document can influence unrelated requests. Existing defenses use periodic reverse-kNN scans, leaving an exposure window and repeated corpus-wide work. We study admission-time control, scoring each candidate against sentinel queries and quarantining hub-like documents before insertion. Across two 100,000-document corpora, five encoders, and disjoint attacker and defender query sets, a global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point (>=0.92 across the effective range) and 0.91 +/- 0.07 on HotFlip attacks, with 1% false positives on general documents. A per-topic gate provides no reliable benefit, consistent with anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, with corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion cost. On HNSW, admission adds about 3.1% to ingestion latency, scoring remains flat to 10^6 vectors, and 1.2% of decisions flip under approximate indexing, none involving attacks. Provenance complements the gate for natural or tight-domain hubs.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses vector hubness poisoning in RAG systems by proposing admission-time gating: scoring documents against sentinel queries before insertion to quarantine hubs. A global gate achieves near-perfect recall (1.0 at the decisive point, ≥0.92 across effective range) and 0.91 on adversarial HotFlip attacks, with only 1% false positives. The approach adds ~3.1% ingestion latency on HNSW and scales independently of corpus size.
AI.motivation: In RAG systems, vector hubness (where a few points become nearest neighbors to many queries) creates a poisoning vulnerability: an attacker can inject a single document that influences many unrelated queries. Existing defenses rely on periodic reverse-kNN scans, which leave an exposure window between scans and require repeated corpus-wide computation. The authors aim to eliminate this window and reduce overhead by controlling hubness at admission time rather than through periodic retroactive detection.
AI.method: The proposed method uses an admission-time gate that scores each candidate document against a fixed set of sentinel queries before insertion into the vector index. Documents exhibiting hub-like behavior (high nearest-neighbor frequency across sentinels) are quarantined. The approach is evaluated with: (1) a global gate using a single threshold across all documents, and (2) per-topic gates with topic-specific thresholds. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, yielding corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion cost. Experiments span two 100K-document corpora, five encoders, disjoint attacker/defender query sets, HNSW indexing, and HotFlip adversarial attacks. The method also explores provenance as a complementary signal for natural or tight-domain hubs.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) The global gate achieves recall of 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point and ≥0.92 across the effective operating range. (2) Against HotFlip attacks, detection reaches 0.91 ± 0.07. (3) False positive rate on legitimate documents is ~1%. (4) Per-topic gates provide no reliable benefit, attributed to anisotropy coupling local and global visibility.
