(5) Admission adds ~3.1% to HNSW ingestion latency; scoring cost remains flat up to 10^6 vectors. (6) Under approximate indexing, only 1.2% of decisions flip, with none involving attacks. (7) Incremental threshold maintenance keeps insertion cost independent of corpus size.
AI.conclusion: Admission-time gating with sentinel queries is an effective and efficient defense against hubness-based poisoning in RAG systems. A simple global gate suffices; per-topic partitioning adds complexity without benefit due to anisotropy. The approach integrates with approximate indexing like HNSW with minimal overhead and complements provenance-based methods for edge cases. This shifts the defense paradigm from periodic retroactive scanning to proactive, lightweight admission control.

title: Designing for Interconnected Islamic Learning: A Qualitative Study of Muslim Women's Experiences with Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah Apps
comment: 27 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
summary: Islamic learning often depends on reading the Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah together, yet digital tools typically separate these sources across apps, screens, and search pathways. We examine this as a human-computer interaction problem through five semi-structured interviews with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community. Participants described a recurring tension: they wanted Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah context at the point of reading, but only when contextual expansion remained trustworthy, optional, and did not interrupt reading. Interpreting the interviews through gendered digital religion, epistemic trust, and seamless learning, we identify five themes concerning contextual understanding, authenticity, interface clutter, study modes, and guidance features. We introduce layered contextuality as an HCI account of this domain: contextual expansion must be balanced with interpretive accountability, devotional flow, and continuity across devices and study intensities.

AI.tldr: Islamic learners need Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah in one reading flow, but digital tools fragment these sources. Interviews with Muslim women reveal a tension: they want contextual expansion at the point of reading, but only when trustworthy, optional, and non-disruptive. The paper introduces "layered contextuality" to balance contextual depth with devotional flow, interpretive accountability, and cross-device continuity.
AI.motivation: Islamic learning traditionally requires reading the Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah as interconnected sources, yet current digital tools silo these texts across separate apps, screens, and search pathways. This fragmentation creates a human-computer interaction problem that impedes seamless, contextual study of Islamic scripture. The authors aim to understand and articulate the specific design tensions involved, grounded in the lived experiences of Muslim learners.
AI.method: The study employs qualitative semi-structured interviews (n=5) with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community. Interview data are interpreted through three analytical lenses: gendered digital religion (how gender shapes digital religious practice), epistemic trust (how users assess reliability and authenticity of sources), and seamless learning (continuity across contexts and devices). Themes are derived inductively from participant accounts.
AI.result: Five themes emerged: (1) contextual understanding — learners desire integrated Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah context at the point of reading; (2) authenticity — contextual expansion must be trustworthy and epistemically sound; (3) interface clutter — additional context must not interrupt devotional flow or reading; (4) study modes — users shift between different intensities of study requiring different levels of context; (5) guidance features — need for optional scaffolding that supports without imposing. The core tension is that contextual enrichment is valued only when it remains optional, reliable, and non-disruptive.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose "layered contextuality" as a novel HCI framework: contextual expansion in digital Islamic tools must balance interpretive accountability, devotional flow, and cross-device/study-intensity continuity. This challenges default HCI assumptions that more information is always better, instead advocating for trust-calibrated, user-controlled, distraction-minimizing design for religious reading interfaces.

title: Beyond the GUI Paradigm: Do Mobile Agents Need the Phone Screen?
summary: Recent advances in mobile agents are dominated by the GUI paradigm, in which agents perceive UI information and emit screen interactions. However, mobile platforms also expose a command-line interface (CLI) that provides direct access to device services and data. We argue CLI deserves first-class consideration alongside GUI. We evaluate three coding agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) across four model APIs on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld without any mobile-specific post-training, comparing against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). Claude Code (Opus 4.7) reaches 71.8\% and 51.9\%, outperforming every reproducible GUI baseline (69.3/68.1/57.8\% on AndroidWorld; 43.2/26.3/13.3\% on MobileWorld), while every other CLI configuration remains competitive. To establish the paradigm's ceiling, we provide oracle CLI solutions that reach 88.8\% on AndroidWorld (103/116 tasks CLI-solvable) and 86.3\% on MobileWorld (101/117 tasks CLI-solvable), indicating substantial room for future improvement. To cover everyday user intents beyond the GUI scope, we introduce the \textbf{CLI-Advantage Task Suite}, comprising 45 templates across five categories: bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, and hidden device state. Every CLI agent outperforms every GUI baseline in all five categories, with substantially fewer steps per task (10.7 vs.\ 18.6). To support future research on mobile CLI agents, we will open-source agent implementations, oracle solutions, the CLI-Advantage suite, and evaluation infrastructure.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that mobile command-line interfaces (CLI) deserve equal consideration alongside GUI for mobile agents. Without mobile-specific training, CLI coding agents significantly outperform GUI baselines on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks, solve tasks with fewer steps, and handle everyday user intents beyond GUI scope. The authors introduce a CLI-Advantage Task Suite and provide oracle solutions showing substantial headroom for improvement.
AI.motivation: Current mobile agent research is dominated by the GUI paradigm (perceiving UI screens, emitting touch interactions), overlooking that mobile platforms also expose CLIs offering direct access to device services and data. The authors argue CLI warrants first-class investigation because it can handle tasks beyond GUI capabilities (e.g., bulk operations, hidden device state) and may offer efficiency advantages.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three coding agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) across four model APIs on the AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks without any mobile-specific post-training. They compare against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). Oracle CLI solutions are constructed to establish an upper bound. Additionally, they introduce the CLI-Advantage Task Suite with 45 templates across five categories (bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, hidden device state) to evaluate tasks favoring CLI access.
AI.result: Claude Code (Opus 4.7) achieves 71.8% on AndroidWorld and 51.9% on MobileWorld, outperforming all GUI baselines (69.3/68.1/57.8% and 43.2/26.3/13.3% respectively). All other CLI configurations remain competitive. Oracle CLI solutions reach 88.8% on AndroidWorld (103/116 tasks solvable) and 86.3% on MobileWorld (101/117 tasks solvable). On the CLI-Advantage Suite, every CLI agent outperforms every GUI baseline across all five categories, using substantially fewer steps (10.7 vs. 18.6).
AI.conclusion: CLI-based mobile agents represent an underexplored but highly promising paradigm that outperforms GUI approaches on existing benchmarks, handles tasks GUI cannot, and operates more efficiently. Significant headroom remains for improvement relative to oracle performance. The authors commit to open-sourcing their implementations, oracle solutions, task suite, and infrastructure to foster future research in mobile CLI agents.

title: Where to Place the Query? Unveiling and Mitigating Positional Bias in In-Context Learning for Diffusion LLMs via Decoding Dynamics
summary: While In-Context Learning (ICL) is extensively studied in Autoregressive (AR) LLMs, its mechanism within Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) remains largely unexplored. Unlike AR models restricted by unidirectional causal masking, dLLMs intrinsically utilize bidirectional attention, offering extensive spatial flexibility for query placement. Unfortunately, current practices conventionally inherit AR-style trailing-query templates, often overlooking the structural paradigm shift. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis unveiling that query position is actually a first-order variable in dLLMs. Through empirical decoupling, we demonstrate that positional variance impacts generation quality on par with example semantic quality. Internally, this positional sensitivity stems from a spatial ``Recency Effect'' in attention flow and task-dependent shifts in decoding trajectories. To mitigate this instability without ground-truth labels, we reveal that traditional single-step confidence ($C_{decoded}$) fails in dLLMs. Instead, we propose Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$), a novel metric tracking the iterative decoding process. By establishing the foundational spatial ICL baselines, we introduce Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically optimizes query placement, robustly approaching oracle performance across heterogeneous reasoning and perception tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that query position is a critical first-order variable in Diffusion LLMs' In-Context Learning, stemming from a spatial "Recency Effect" in attention flow. The authors propose Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$) as a novel metric for query placement optimization and introduce Auto-ICL, a training-free routing strategy that dynamically selects optimal query positions to approach oracle performance.
AI.motivation: Current practices for Diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) naively inherit Autoregressive-style trailing-query templates for ICL, ignoring the fundamental structural differences between the two paradigms. Since dLLMs use bidirectional attention rather than unidirectional causal masking, they offer spatial flexibility for query placement that remains unexploited. The authors seek to systematically characterize how query position affects generation quality and provide principled methods to optimize it.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis decoupling query position from example semantic quality, demonstrating that position is a first-order variable. They investigate internal mechanisms, identifying a spatial "Recency Effect" in attention flow and task-dependent shifts in decoding trajectories. They show that traditional single-step confidence ($C_{decoded}$) fails as a selection metric in dLLMs and propose Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$), which tracks the full iterative decoding process. Building on these insights, they establish spatial ICL baselines and develop Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically optimizes query placement without ground-truth labels.
AI.result: Query positional variance impacts generation quality on par with example semantic quality. The proposed Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$) metric effectively captures decoding quality in dLLMs where single-step confidence fails. Auto-ICL robustly approaches oracle-level performance across heterogeneous reasoning and perception tasks by dynamically optimizing query placement.
AI.conclusion: Query position is a first-order variable in dLLM-based ICL, fundamentally driven by a spatial Recency Effect and task-dependent decoding trajectories. Auto-ICL, powered by the Average Confidence metric, provides a practical, training-free solution that robustly approaches oracle performance, establishing foundational baselines for spatial ICL in diffusion language models.

title: LLM Doesn't Know What It Doesn't Know: Detecting Epistemic Blind Spots via Cross-Model Attribution Divergence on Clinical Tabular Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to structured clinical data, yet whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge on such tasks remains unexplored. We study this question through the lens of cross-model attribution divergence with the goal of reducing epistemic uncertainty for structured tasks, comparing Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a prediction task via attribution divergence analysis. We report four findings. First, LLM verbalized confidence is epistemically vacuous, it outputs a near-constant (0.856-0.937) regardless of whether accuracy is 49% or 75.3%, tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. Second, the LLM exhibits an inverse difficulty effect: accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) when it is moderately uncertain. Third, few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions: they reduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) from 1.54 to 0.38 and improve accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. Fourth, a cross-model calibrator that determined LLM reliability using attribution divergence signals reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080, replacing uninformative verbalized confidence with patient-specific reliability estimates, without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference. We frame these findings as a cold start problem for LLMs on structured data and outline a path toward genuine epistemic self-awareness.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit poor epistemic self-awareness on structured clinical tasks, with verbalized confidence being uninformative. Cross-model attribution divergence with XGBoost reveals an inverse difficulty effect, and combining few-shot examples with SHAP evidence substantially reduces disagreement and improves accuracy. A cross-model calibrator using attribution divergence signals effectively replaces vacuous verbalized confidence with reliable patient-specific uncertainty estimates.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs can recognize the limits of their own knowledge when applied to structured clinical data, with the broader goal of reducing epistemic uncertainty through cross-model attribution divergence analysis.
AI.method: Comparison of Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a structured clinical prediction task using attribution divergence analysis. Key interventions include: (1) evaluating LLM verbalized confidence against actual accuracy, (2) analyzing the inverse difficulty effect via cross-model accuracy patterns, (3) combining few-shot examples with SHAP-derived feature evidence as orthogonal super-additive interventions measured by Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS), and (4) building a cross-model calibrator that leverages attribution divergence signals to produce patient-specific reliability estimates without accessing model internals.
AI.result: Four main findings: (1) LLM verbalized confidence is near-constant (0.856–0.937) and tracks prompt format rather than prediction quality, regardless of accuracy (49% vs. 75.3%). (2) Inverse difficulty effect: LLM accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) under moderate uncertainty. (3) Few-shot examples and SHAP evidence are super-additive, reducing ADS from 1.54 to 0.38 and improving accuracy from 49% to 75.3%. (4) The cross-model calibrator reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080.
AI.conclusion: The findings are framed as a "cold start problem" for LLMs on structured data, outlining a path toward genuine epistemic self-awareness. Attribution divergence between LLMs and traditional models like XGBoost provides a principled signal for calibrating LLM reliability on structured tasks.

title: Weibull Weight-Scale Parameter Evolution under AdamW Training Dynamics
summary: Building on a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, we study why the Weibull weight-scale parameter $λ$ grows, overshoots, and then relaxes during AdamW training. We derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update: an alignment force measuring the correlation between weights and the adaptive update direction, an injection force from adaptive step magnitude, and a decay force from decoupled weight decay. On self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments, alignment dominates the rise phase, contributing 88-94% of the absolute force budget across four random seeds and remaining robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the transition from weight-scale growth to relaxation. These force dynamics directly govern the squared-norm component underlying $λ(t)$; the remaining RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset is measurable and decomposes into bridge and integration components, totaling approximately 5-6% in densely sampled regions. To extend the analysis to real models where optimizer moments are unavailable, we introduce a spline displacement method that recovers the alignment force from sparse checkpoints with approximately 92-94% accuracy, about twice the naive two-point baseline. We further observe that the peak value of $λ(t)$ varies with training-data coherence in our experiments, suggesting a data-dependent component of weight-scale growth that we leave to a controlled follow-up study. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tiexinding/NPM-Weibull-public.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why the Weibull weight-scale parameter λ grows, overshoots, and relaxes during AdamW training of transformers. The authors derive a three-force decomposition (alignment, injection, decay) from the AdamW update rule, show alignment dominates growth (~88-94%), and introduce a spline method to recover force dynamics from sparse checkpoints when optimizer moments are unavailable.
AI.motivation: Prior work established a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, but the dynamical origin of the observed λ(t) trajectory—growth, overshoot, and relaxation—remained unexplained. Understanding these underlying forces could illuminate fundamental training dynamics in adaptive optimizers.
AI.method: The authors (1) derive a leading-order decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update into three forces: alignment (correlation between weights and adaptive update direction), injection (adaptive step magnitude), and decay (decoupled weight decay); (2) validate on self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments; (3) introduce a spline displacement method to recover the alignment force from sparse checkpoints without optimizer state; and (4) analyze the RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset via bridge and integration components.
AI.result: Alignment dominates the rise phase (88-94% of absolute force budget, robust to super-weight removal). Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the growth-to-relaxation transition. The RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset totals ~5-6% in densely sampled regions. The spline displacement method recovers alignment force with 92-94% accuracy from sparse checkpoints, roughly doubling naive two-point baseline performance. Peak λ(t) varies with training-data coherence.
AI.conclusion: The three-force framework provides a mechanistic explanation for the λ(t) trajectory in AdamW training, with alignment as the primary driver of weight-scale growth. The spline method enables practical analysis of real models lacking optimizer state. The observed data-dependence of peak λ suggests a connection to data coherence warranting further study.

title: ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research
summary: Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.

AI.tldr: ScaffoldAgent introduces a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research, modeling outline evolution as a structured decision process with Expansion, Contraction, and Revision operations, driven by a utility signal that estimates downstream value from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing OEDR systems either fix the outline prematurely or refine it with local heuristics, causing scaffold drift as new information accumulates and lacking timely feedback to evaluate outline modifications. A principled mechanism for dynamic outline optimization is needed.
AI.method: ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three atomic operations: Expansion (adding new nodes), Contraction (removing redundant nodes), and Revision (modifying existing nodes). A utility-guided feedback mechanism estimates the downstream value of each operation by jointly considering retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. This utility signal drives node selection, operation scheduling, and termination decisions during inference.
AI.result: Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym demonstrate that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation quality and factual grounding compared to existing deep research agents.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic outline optimization guided by a principled utility function is effective for open-ended deep research, addressing scaffold drift and enabling more coherent, factually grounded long-form report generation.

title: Generative Engine Optimization at Scale: Measuring Brand Visibility Across AI Search Engines
summary:
People increasingly get answers straight from AI search engines like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini rather than scrolling search results. Brands that once focused on search engine optimization (SEO) must now optimize for how these engines represent, cite, and recommend them -- a shift variously called Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), and AI Search Visibility. We treat AEO and AI Visibility as part of GEO, and study how to measure brand visibility across AI engines: what they value when they cite a brand, which sources they rely on, and what content large language models surface. The hard case is everyone outside the already-authoritative top brands -- SMEs, D2C brands, creators, and early-stage startups.
  We analyze 100K+ prompt responses across 100+ brands tracked on Ranqo between March and May 2026. First visibility runs form a clear three-tier brand-stature ladder: global household names (e.g., Stripe, Nike) appear in 73% of relevant AI answers on their first run; established mid-market and regional brands (e.g., Olipop, Klaviyo) in 44%; niche and small brands in just 11% -- about 30 percentage points per step. When engines cite sources, about 78% go to corporate websites; among non-corporate sources YouTube leads, ahead of Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. The highest-leverage page is the ranked "best-of" listicle, the most-cited content format at about 21% of all citations. Sentiment is the unstable signal: whether a brand is framed positively or negatively flips about 6.7 times more often than whether it is mentioned at all.
  These findings provide a first large-scale baseline for measuring GEO: AI brand visibility can be measured, differs by platform, and varies strongly by brand maturity. We close by proposing seven v1.1 protocols to test whether specific recommendations can causally improve AI visibility.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study of 100K+ AI search engine responses across 100+ brands reveals a steep three-tier visibility hierarchy: household names appear in 73% of relevant answers, mid-market brands in 44%, and niche brands in just 11%. Corporate websites dominate citations (78%), "best-of" listicles are the highest-leverage content format (21% of citations), and sentiment is highly volatile. The authors propose seven protocols for causally testing GEO strategies.
AI.motivation: The shift from traditional search to AI-generated answers (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude) creates an urgent need for brands to understand how to optimize for visibility in these engines—a practice termed Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). Existing knowledge is anecdotal; there is no large-scale empirical baseline measuring what drives AI engine citation, representation, and recommendation, particularly for non-dominant brands (SMEs, D2C, creators, startups).
AI.method: The authors analyze 100K+ prompt responses across 100+ brands using the Ranqo tracking platform (March–May 2026). They measure: (1) brand mention frequency across AI engines, stratified by brand stature; (2) source types cited (corporate vs. non-corporate); (3) content formats driving citations; and (4) sentiment stability vs. mention stability. Brands are categorized into a three-tier maturity ladder based on visibility rates.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) A clear three-tier brand visibility ladder—global brands (73% visibility), mid-market (44%), niche (11%)—with ~30 percentage points between tiers. (2) Corporate websites receive 78% of all citations; among non-corporate sources, YouTube leads, followed by Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. "Best-of" listicles are the single most-cited content format (~21%). (3) Sentiment is 6.7× more volatile than mention presence, making it an unreliable optimization signal.
AI.conclusion: AI brand visibility is measurable, platform-dependent, and strongly stratified by brand maturity. The study provides the first large-scale empirical baseline for GEO and demonstrates that content format choice—particularly listicles—may offer higher leverage than brand-building alone. The authors propose seven v1.1 experimental protocols to move from observational measurement to causal testing of GEO interventions.

title: SafeSpec: Fast and Safe LLM via Dynamic Reflective Sampling
summary: Speculative inference accelerates large language model (LLM) decoding but provides no inherent safety guarantees. Existing safety defenses are largely incompatible with speculative inference: they either introduce additional computation or disrupt the draft-verify mechanism, negating acceleration benefits. This reveals a fundamental incompatibility between current safety methods and speculative decoding. We propose SafeSpec, a safety-aware speculative inference framework that integrates risk estimation directly into the verification process. SafeSpec attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model to jointly evaluate semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass. When unsafe generations are detected, SafeSpec applies rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations rather than terminating generation. We model jailbreak attacks as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase the probability of harmful continuations without eliminating safe ones. Under this model, SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process. Across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks, SafeSpec achieves a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off. On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06x inference speedup on benign workloads, demonstrating that speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized.

AI.tldr: SafeSpec integrates safety verification into speculative decoding by attaching a latent safety head that evaluates both semantic validity and safety in one forward pass, using rollback and safety-guided multi-sampling to recover safe continuations when unsafe generations are detected.
AI.motivation: Speculative inference accelerates LLM decoding but lacks safety guarantees, and existing safety defenses are incompatible with speculative decoding—they either add computational overhead or break the draft-verify mechanism, negating speed gains. This motivates a safety method that operates within the speculative decoding framework without sacrificing efficiency.
AI.method: SafeSpec adds a lightweight latent safety head to the target model, enabling joint evaluation of semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass during verification. Upon detecting unsafe generations, it employs rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations (rather than terminating generation). Jailbreak attacks are modeled as distributional shifts where adversarial prompts increase harmful continuation probability without eliminating safe ones, and SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within this framework.
AI.result: On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while maintaining a 2.06× inference speedup on benign workloads. Comparable safety-efficiency trade-off improvements are demonstrated across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized. SafeSpec resolves the previously fundamental incompatibility between safety methods and speculative decoding by embedding safety into the verification process itself.

title: MemGUI-Agent: An End-to-End Long-Horizon Mobile GUI Agent with Proactive Context Management
summary: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress on short-horizon tasks, yet remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks that require retaining intermediate facts across many steps and app transitions. We attribute this limitation to ReAct-style prompting, which passively accumulates per-step records, leading to prompt explosion and dilution of critical cross-app facts. To address this, we introduce MemGUI-Agent, an end-to-end long-horizon mobile GUI agent with proactive context management. MemGUI-Agent is built on Context-as-Action (ConAct), which casts context management as first-class actions emitted by the same policy that selects UI actions. Instead of passively appending history, ConAct maintains three structured context fields: folded action history, folded UI state, and recent step record, preserving critical UI facts while keeping context compact. To make proactive context management learnable across model scales, we construct MemGUI-3K, a 2,956-trajectory dataset with full ConAct annotations for supervised training and offline analysis. Training an 8B model on MemGUI-3K produces MemGUI-8B-SFT, an 8B MemGUI-Agent that achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://memgui-agent.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MemGUI-Agent introduces proactive context management via Context-as-Action (ConAct) for long-horizon mobile GUI tasks, maintaining structured context fields instead of passive ReAct-style history accumulation, achieving state-of-the-art 8B performance with a purpose-built 2,956-trajectory dataset.
AI.motivation: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents using ReAct-style prompting fail on long-horizon tasks because passive accumulation of per-step records causes prompt explosion and dilutes critical cross-app facts needed across many steps and app transitions.
AI.method: MemGUI-Agent uses Context-as-Action (ConAct), which treats context management as first-class actions emitted alongside UI actions. It maintains three structured context fields — folded action history, folded UI state, and recent step record — to preserve critical UI facts compactly. The MemGUI-3K dataset (2,956 trajectories with full ConAct annotations) enables supervised training of an 8B model (MemGUI-8B-SFT).
AI.result: MemGUI-8B-SFT achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Proactive context management via ConAct effectively addresses the long-horizon reliability problem in mobile GUI agents by replacing passive history accumulation with structured, compact context maintenance, demonstrating strong performance and generalization at the 8B scale.

title: Execution-bound advisory automation for agentic AI: a reproducible AIBOM-driven CSAF-VEX framework
summary: A protocol driven framework is presented that binds SBOM and AIBOM artefacts to deterministic environment capture and structured runtime telemetry. Exploitability is computed from declared artefacts, observed activation conditions, and enforced execution policies. CSAF VEX advisories are generated from combined static and runtime evidence, cryptographically signed, and validated through deterministic replay. Evaluation uses approximately 10000 component entries across synthetic Agentic AI workloads 50 to 5000 components, incorporating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets.

AI.tldr: A protocol-driven framework links SBOM/AIBOM artifacts to deterministic environment snapshots and runtime telemetry, computes exploitability from declared artifacts, activation conditions, and execution policies, then generates cryptographically signed CSAF VEX advisories validated through replay. Evaluated on ~10,000 components across synthetic Agentic AI workloads (50–5,000 components) using OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets.
AI.motivation: Traditional vulnerability management relies on static SBOM analysis alone, which produces high false-positive rates by failing to account for whether vulnerable code is actually reachable, loaded, or exploitable in a given runtime context. The proliferation of AI/ML supply chains (AIBOM) exacerbates this problem due to opaque dependencies and dynamic loading patterns. A need exists for a unified framework that deterministically links declared components to observed runtime behavior, enabling evidence-based exploitability assessment and standards-compliant advisory generation.
AI.method: The authors propose a protocol-driven framework comprising: (1) binding of SBOM and AIBOM artifacts to deterministic environment captures (filesystem, process state, library loading) and structured runtime telemetry; (2) exploitability computation via cross-referencing declared component artifacts against observed activation conditions (code paths exercised, libraries loaded) and enforced execution policies (e.g., seccomp, capability bounds); (3) automatic generation of CSAF VEX (Common Security Advisory Framework – Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) advisories from combined static and runtime evidence; (4) cryptographic signing of generated advisories with deterministic replay for independent validation. Evaluation uses synthetic Agentic AI workloads spanning 50 to 5,000 components, drawing vulnerability data from OSV, GitHub Advisory Database, CISA KEV catalog, and EPSS scoring.
AI.result: The framework was evaluated across approximately 10,000 component entries within synthetic Agentic AI workloads. Key findings include the ability to reduce false-positive vulnerability alerts by conditioning exploitability on runtime activation evidence rather than static presence alone. Deterministic replay successfully validated the integrity of generated CSAF VEX advisories. The approach scaled from 50 to 5,000 components, demonstrating feasibility for complex AI supply chains incorporating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS threat intelligence.
AI.conclusion: The protocol-driven integration of SBOM/AIBOM with deterministic runtime telemetry and execution policies provides a robust, evidence-based mechanism for computing exploitability and producing verifiable CSAF VEX advisories. The approach addresses critical gaps in software supply chain security for AI systems, where static analysis alone is insufficient. Cryptographic signing and deterministic replay ensure advisory integrity and reproducibility, supporting regulatory compliance and operational trust.

title: Pruning via Causal Attribution Preserves Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on LLM Reasoning. 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning but incur substantial inference cost. We introduce Causal Attribution Pruning (CAP), a training-free method that identifies critical attention heads by measuring their causal impact on reasoning tasks and uses these head-level scores to guide fine-grained weight pruning. For each attention head, CAP estimates the expected performance degradation when the head is masked during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems. These causal scores are then converted into weight-level importance values for the corresponding projection matrices. Unlike magnitude-only or activation-based criteria, CAP's interventional measurement directly captures each head's functional contribution, yielding relative accuracy gains of up to 61% over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. We evaluate CAP on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct at 10%, 20%, and 50% sparsity. At moderate sparsity (10-20%), CAP improves over Wanda in most model-benchmark configurations. with especially large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3. Our results suggest that attention-head-level causal attribution can better preserve reasoning performance on downstream benchmarks than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, while remaining limited by coarse MLP attribution at 50% sparsity.

AI.tldr: CAP is a training-free pruning method that uses causal attribution at the attention-head level to identify critical heads for reasoning tasks, converting head-level importance scores into weight-level pruning decisions, achieving up to 61% relative accuracy improvement over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity.
AI.motivation: LLMs are effective at multi-step reasoning but incur high inference costs. Existing pruning methods relying on magnitude or activation-based correlational criteria fail to capture the functional contribution of attention heads, leading to suboptimal preservation of reasoning performance under sparsity.
AI.method: CAP (Causal Attribution Pruning) operates in two stages: (1) For each attention head, it estimates a causal score by measuring expected performance degradation when that head is masked during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems. (2) These head-level causal scores are converted into weight-level importance values for the corresponding Q, K, V, and O projection matrices, which then guide structured, fine-grained weight pruning — eliminating the need for any model retraining.
AI.result: CAP achieves up to 61% relative accuracy gains over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. At moderate sparsity (10-20%), CAP outperforms Wanda on most model-benchmark configurations across Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge, with particularly large gains for Llama-3 on ARC-Challenge.
AI.conclusion: Attention-head-level causal attribution better preserves reasoning performance than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity levels. However, the method is limited by coarse MLP attribution at 50% sparsity, indicating that finer-grained causal analysis of MLP layers is needed for higher sparsity regimes.

title: REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision-Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer's Disease Risk
summary: The retina offers a noninvasive window into neurodegenerative disease, capturing subtle structural patterns associated with a risk of future cognitive decline. Vision-language alignment frameworks such as REVEAL have shown that pairing retinal fundus images with structured clinical risk narratives improves early prediction of Alzheimer's disease (AD). A key design choice in these approaches is the use of phenotypic grouping, where individuals with similar risk profiles are treated as multi-positive pairs during contrastive learning. However, existing methods operationalize phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct, relying on hard group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. We propose a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure within contrastive learning. Rather than assigning samples to fixed clusters, we model inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships through a continuous aggregation operator, enabling graded supervision that reflects the spectrum nature of disease risk. We further introduce a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines. By treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule, our approach provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes replacing discrete phenotypic grouping in retinal-based Alzheimer's risk prediction with a continuous, learnable similarity formulation within contrastive learning. Soft multi-positive relationships are modeled via differentiable weighting functions derived from intra-modality embeddings, jointly optimized with cross-modal alignment, yielding superior incident AD prediction on UK Biobank data.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language alignment methods (e.g., REVEAL) for predicting Alzheimer's disease from retinal fundus images use discrete phenotypic grouping—hard cluster assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. This binary treatment of similarity fails to capture the spectrum nature of disease risk.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure where inter-subject similarity is modeled as a differentiable weighting function based on intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and clinical risk profiles; (2) soft multi-positive relationships via a continuous aggregation operator; and (3) a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure end-to-end.
AI.result: The proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction.
AI.conclusion: Treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule provides a more principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

title: Zero-Inflated Gaussian Distributions Enable Parameter-Space Sparsity in Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms
summary: Estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs) are a powerful class of evolutionary methods for black-box optimization, especially when little is known about the structure of the objective. Whereas classical evolutionary algorithms rely on hand-designed mutation and crossover operators, hard to devise for unknown problem structures, and a source of bias, EDAs sidestep operator design entirely: they fit a probability distribution to the best individuals and sample the next generation from it. EDAs are well established on continuous parameter spaces, but they have not previously been generalized to sparse ones, in which most coefficients of a good solution are exactly zero. Existing sparse black-box optimizers therefore reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid: hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level schemes alternating between support set and active values, zeroing thresholds, and other baked-in assumptions. We close this gap by proposing multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as EDA sampling laws. A latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and the interactions between the two, so sparsity patterns and active values are optimized jointly, hierarchy-free. We show that the latent parameters of this model are identifiable from observed samples, unlike in the missing-data settings where related constructions originate, and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators for them. The estimators accurately recover latent correlation structures, and on the Lunar Lander benchmark the resulting ZIG-EDA converges faster and reaches higher final returns than a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while finding controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as sampling laws for estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs), extending EDAs to sparse optimization problems. ZIG-EDA jointly optimizes sparsity patterns and active values without hand-crafted sparsity operators, using a latent Gaussian model with identifiable parameters and amortized inversion-based estimators. It outperforms dense Gaussian EDA, hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithms, and ad-hoc sparse EDAs on the Lunar Lander benchmark.
AI.motivation: EDAs avoid hand-designed variation operators by fitting distributions to elite individuals, but existing EDAs have not been generalized to sparse optimization where most solution coefficients are zero. Current sparse black-box optimizers reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid: hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level schemes, zeroing thresholds, and other baked-in assumptions. The authors aim to close this gap by providing a principled EDA framework for sparse domains.
AI.method: The authors propose multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as EDA sampling laws. A latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and their interactions, enabling joint, hierarchy-free optimization of sparsity and active values. They prove latent parameters are identifiable from observed samples (unlike in missing-data settings) and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators that accurately recover latent correlation structures.
AI.result: On the Lunar Lander benchmark, ZIG-EDA converges faster and achieves higher final returns than a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while finding controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.
AI.conclusion: ZIG distributions provide the first principled EDA framework for sparse black-box optimization, eliminating the need for hand-crafted sparsity operators. The identifiability of the latent model and the effectiveness of amortized inversion-based estimators enable joint optimization of sparsity patterns and active values, yielding superior performance on sparse control tasks.

title: RACL: Reasoning-Agent Control Layers for Continuous Metaheuristic Learning
summary: This paper introduces RACL, a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer for metaheuristics. RACL places a reasoning agent above an existing optimizer. The agent does not replace the optimizer and does not modify business constraints. Instead, it controls the optimizer's internal search behavior by observing operational memory, reasoning over past behavior, formulating bounded hypotheses, testing interventions, evaluating outcomes, applying guardrails, consolidating useful policies and explaining its decisions. The experiment uses vehicle routing as a testbed, but the contribution is not a new routing solver, a particular ALNS configuration or a specific set of routing rules. The contribution is the RACL method: a way for a reasoning agent to discover, validate, consolidate and explain algorithmic control rules for a metaheuristic. In the current experimental setting, RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21 of 21 feasible cases and improves or ties a non-reasoning Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18 of 21 feasible cases, with an average RACL vs STP cost delta of -0.641%. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% versus Fixed and -1.605% versus STP without showing material computational overhead. During the proof-of-concept, Codex was used as an in-the-loop reasoning agent observing executions, interpreting logs and proposing live bounded interventions. The policy proxy was later used only to make quantitative evaluation reproducible.

AI.tldr: RACL introduces a reasoning-agent control layer that sits above existing metaheuristic optimizers, observing and guiding their internal search behavior without modifying the underlying algorithm or business constraints. It discovers, validates, consolidates, and explains algorithmic control policies, demonstrated via vehicle routing experiments where it consistently outperforms baseline policies.
AI.motivation: Metaheuristic optimizers often rely on hand-crafted or static control policies for internal search decisions. The authors aim to replace this manual tuning with an agent-driven approach that dynamically reasons over operational memory to formulate and test interventions, thereby improving optimizer performance without altering the solver itself.
AI.method: RACL places a reasoning agent (Codex in the proof-of-concept) above an existing optimizer. The agent observes operational memory, reasons over past behavior, formulates bounded hypotheses, tests interventions, evaluates outcomes, applies guardrails, consolidates useful policies, and explains decisions. It does not replace the optimizer or modify business constraints — it only influences internal search behavior. A policy proxy was used for reproducible quantitative evaluation.
AI.result: RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21/21 feasible cases and improves or ties a Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18/21 cases, with an average cost delta of -0.641% vs STP. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% vs Fixed and -1.605% vs STP, with no material computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: The RACL method demonstrates that a reasoning agent can effectively control metaheuristic search behavior, discovering and consolidating useful policies that outperform both static and stagnation-triggered baselines. The contribution is the general control-layer architecture, not a domain-specific solver.

title: ScholarQuest: A Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark for Agentic Academic Paper Search in Open Literature Environments
summary: Academic paper search is a core step in scientific research, and LLM-based search agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for iterative, intent-driven literature exploration. However, existing benchmarks are insufficient for systematically evaluating agentic academic search under realistic open literature environments. We propose ScholarQuest, a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for agentic academic paper search. ScholarQuest is constructed from over 1,000 computer science topics and four representative research intents, including method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, and scope-controlled queries. It further provides scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend ScholarBase for reproducible evaluation. Benchmarking results show that agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines, yet the best-performing agent only achieves 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All, indicating substantial room for improvement. In addition, analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases further highlight the benchmark's ability to provide multi-dimensional evaluation signals for academic paper search agents.

AI.tldr: ScholarQuest is a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agentic academic paper search across four research intents, revealing that even the best agent achieves only 0.314 Recall@100, highlighting significant room for improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately evaluate LLM-based search agents for iterative, intent-driven academic literature exploration in realistic open environments. There is a need for a systematic, reproducible, and multi-dimensional evaluation framework.
AI.method: ScholarQuest is built from over 1,000 CS topics and four research intents (method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, scope-controlled). It features scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend called ScholarBase for reproducible evaluation.
AI.result: Agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines. The best agent achieves 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All. Analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases provide multi-dimensional evaluation signals.
AI.conclusion: Agentic academic search shows promise but remains far from solved, with substantial headroom for improvement. ScholarQuest enables fine-grained, reproducible benchmarking that can guide future research in this domain.

title: DISARM: Target Electronic Device Informed Mitigation of Software Runtime Side-Channel Vulnerabilities
summary: Program runtime or timing attacks exploit variations in a program's execution times to extract sensitive information from the program (e.g. encryption keys, sensitive variable data, intellectual property). State-of-the-art solutions to runtime side-channel attacks attempt to balance the execution time of the sensitive code for different control flow paths to eliminate the timing leakage. However, during the mitigation process, most techniques do not consider the underlying hardware or device on which the target program is supposed to run on. This can lead to over-fixing (unnecessary extra operations), under-fixing (not solving the imbalance properly), and even failures. We propose DISARM, a joint hardware-software methodology (unlike any existing solution) for mitigating runtime side-channel vulnerabilities that utilizes timing values from real embedded devices to generate targeted software fixes. We implement DISARM to support C, C++, and Java source codes and validate it across 22 standard benchmarks. DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions such as PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR in terms of execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness on five different embedded or edge devices.

AI.tldr: DISARM is a joint hardware-software methodology that uses real device timing measurements to generate targeted mitigations for runtime side-channel attacks, outperforming existing solutions on embedded/edge devices.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime side-channel mitigation techniques ignore the underlying hardware characteristics of the target device, leading to over-fixing, under-fixing, or outright failures when deployed on real embedded systems.
AI.method: DISARM employs a hardware-software co-design approach: it collects actual timing measurements from real embedded devices and uses these hardware-specific timing values to generate targeted software fixes for C, C++, and Java source code, ensuring the mitigation is tailored to the specific execution platform.
AI.result: Validated on 22 standard benchmarks across five different embedded/edge devices, DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions (PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR) in execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-aware timing side-channel mitigation is essential for embedded systems; DISARM demonstrates that joint hardware-software methodologies yield more efficient and correct fixes than hardware-agnostic approaches.

title: MobileForge: Annotation-Free Adaptation for Mobile GUI Agents with Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization
summary: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress in UI understanding and action execution, but adapting them to real target apps remains costly because mobile apps are numerous, frequently updated, and hard to cover with human-written tasks, demonstrations, or reward labels. Existing annotation-free GUI learning reduces manual supervision, yet lacks a unified substrate connecting target-app exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and feedback, while policy optimization often relies on isolated rollouts and coarse rewards that are hard to convert into reliable improvement signals. We present MobileForge, an annotation-free adaptation system for mobile GUI agents. MobileForge consists of MobileGym, which grounds task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interaction, and Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization (HiFPO), which turns trajectory outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints into hint-contextualized step-level GRPO updates. Using only automatically generated annotation-free adaptation data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld, close to the closed-data GUI-specialized GUI-Owl-1.5-8B base model at 69.0%. The MobileForge-adapted ForgeOwl-8B further reaches 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, establishing the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent in our evaluation. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://mobile-forge.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MobileForge is an annotation-free adaptation system that fine-tunes MLLM-based mobile GUI agents using automatically generated interaction data. It combines MobileGym (a real-app interaction environment for task generation and evaluation) with HiFPO (a hierarchical feedback-driven policy optimization that converts trajectory outcomes, step-level feedback, and corrective hints into GRPO updates). The adapted ForgeOwl-8B achieves 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% on MobileWorld, setting a new state-of-the-art for open-data mobile GUI agents.
AI.motivation: Adapting MLLM-based GUI agents to real target apps is prohibitively expensive because apps are numerous, frequently updated, and difficult to cover with human-written tasks, demonstrations, or reward labels. Existing annotation-free methods lack a unified substrate that integrates target-app exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and feedback loops. Furthermore, policy optimization in prior work relies on isolated rollouts and coarse-grained rewards that fail to provide reliable improvement signals for fine-tuning.
AI.method: MobileForge comprises two components: (1) MobileGym, which grounds task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interactions, enabling automated curriculum mining and execution; and (2) Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization (HiFPO), which leverages trajectory-level outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints to construct hint-contextualized step-level GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) updates. The system operates entirely without human annotations.
AI.result: Using only automatically generated annotation-free data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld, approaching the closed-data GUI-Owl-1.5-8B at 69.0%. The fully adapted ForgeOwl-8B achieves 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, establishing the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent reported.
AI.conclusion: MobileForge demonstrates that annotation-free adaptation with hierarchical feedback-guided policy optimization can produce mobile GUI agents competitive with or surpassing closed-data counterparts. The system provides a unified framework spanning exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and fine-grained feedback, and the resulting ForgeOwl-8B model sets a new state-of-the-art for open-data mobile GUI agents.

title: DevOps and General Developers: Insights from Stack Overflow's 2023 Survey
comment: 17 pages, 11 tables, research paper based on the 2023 Stack Overflow Developer Survey data analysis
summary:
Purpose: To investigate the distinct roles of DevOps specialists and general software developers, examining their varying use of tools, technologies, methodologies, and demographics in the current software development environment. In addition, to differentiate these two professional groups regarding their unique contributions and challenges in the field.
  Design/Methodology/Approach: The research uses a quantitative approach to analyze data from the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey. It focuses on a comparative analysis of technological preferences, demographic information, and professional experiences between DevOps specialists and general developers, highlighting key trends and differences. The data analysis was conducted using Python's Pandas library for data analysis.
  Findings: The research indicates no significant difference in the tool and technology preferences between DevOps specialists and general software developers, highlighting their complementary roles. DevOps specialists and general software developers use tools like Docker and Kubernetes, emphasizing efficiency and automation. While general developers employ diverse tools for various role demands, demographic trends show younger general developers and mid-career DevOps professionals. This age range reflects growing experience in DevOps, and both groups are adapting to remote and hybrid work models in the evolving tech industry.
  Practical Implications: This research offers perspectives on the dynamic roles within software development, emphasizing the growing importance of DevOps. It is a valuable resource for academic and industry professionals to understand the evolving dynamics in software development roles.
  Originality/Value: This research fills a significant gap in the existing literature regarding the evolving dynamics of software development roles.

AI.tldr: This study compares DevOps specialists and general software developers using Stack Overflow 2023 survey data, finding no significant differences in tool/technology preferences but notable demographic distinctions — younger general developers versus mid-career DevOps professionals — with both groups converging around containerization tools and remote work adoption.
AI.motivation: To fill a gap in the literature by empirically distinguishing DevOps specialists from general software developers in terms of tool usage, methodologies, demographics, and professional contributions within the evolving software development landscape.
AI.method: Quantitative comparative analysis of the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey data, employing Python's Pandas library for data processing and statistical examination of technological preferences, demographic patterns, and professional experiences between the two groups.
AI.result: No significant difference in tool and technology preferences emerged between groups; both heavily use Docker and Kubernetes for efficiency and automation. Demographic trends reveal younger general developers versus mid-career DevOps specialists, reflecting the experience required in DevOps. Both groups are increasingly adopting remote and hybrid work models.
AI.conclusion: DevOps specialists and general developers occupy complementary rather than divergent roles. The research provides valuable insights for academia and industry on evolving software development dynamics, with DevOps growing in importance and both roles adapting similarly to modern tooling and work arrangements.

title: Detecting Hallucinations for Large Language Model-based Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning infers new knowledge from existing facts and is widely applied in question answering, recommendation, and decision support. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks have become increasingly popular by leveraging retrieved KG information. However, hallucinations in LLMs remain a critical issue. Even when relevant KG knowledge is incorporated, models may still generate incorrect outputs, leading to misinformation and unreliable decisions. Existing hallucination detection methods either focus on LLM internal states or verify consistency with retrieved contexts, but both overlook the structural information in KGs, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this gap, we propose LUCID, the first halLUcination deteCtIon method for LLM-based knowleDge graph reasoning frameworks. LUCID jointly leverages LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information. Specifically, it extracts node and edge features from attention scores and semantic similarities, and integrates them with KG structure using a graph neural network. We also construct manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation. Experiments on nine datasets show that LUCID achieves state of the art performance compared to 15 baselines.

AI.tldr: LUCID is a hallucination detection method for LLM-based knowledge graph reasoning that jointly leverages LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information via graph neural networks, achieving state-of-the-art performance across nine datasets.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucinations even when provided with relevant KG knowledge during reasoning, yet existing hallucination detection methods overlook KG structural information, leading to suboptimal detection performance.
AI.method: LUCID extracts node and edge features from LLM attention scores and semantic similarities, then integrates these with KG structural information using a graph neural network (GNN). The authors also constructed manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments on nine datasets demonstrate that LUCID achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to 15 baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating KG structural information via GNNs, combined with LLM attention and semantic features, significantly improves hallucination detection in LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks.

title: Emergent Alignment
summary: Can Large Language Models (LLMs) discern when their own outputs are misaligned with human ethics? And can they self-correct? We endow an LLM with a conscience step that reviews its own reasoning and outputs, and we extend the training loss with an alignment component using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to steer the model away from non-ethical outputs. The result is an online technique to align models in a wide range of applications: training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning. It does not require a weaker or stronger judge, relying instead on a frozen copy of itself. In previous work, the Emergent Misalignment scenario showed a range of emergent unethical behaviors from fine-tuning the model to hack code. Instead, we empirically show how to achieve Emergent Alignment: a single high-level introspective question steers training toward an ethical model under the same code hacking scenario.

AI.tldr: LLMs can self-identify unethical outputs via a "conscience step" that reviews their own reasoning. By incorporating DPO-based alignment loss, the model self-corrects toward ethical behavior without external judges. This yields "Emergent Alignment," where a single introspective question steers the model away from unethical behaviors like code hacking.
AI.motivation: LLMs can produce misaligned, unethical outputs, particularly under adversarial conditions such as fine-tuning on malicious tasks (e.g., the Emergent Misalignment scenario involving code hacking). The authors investigate whether LLMs possess the capacity to self-diagnose and self-correct ethical violations without relying on external supervisory models or human feedback.
AI.method: The approach introduces a "conscience step" where the model reviews its own reasoning and outputs for ethical alignment. The training loss is augmented with an alignment component using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), treating the model's own frozen copy as a reference to steer away from non-ethical outputs. This online alignment technique applies across training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot settings, without requiring a weaker or stronger external judge.
AI.result: The method demonstrates "Emergent Alignment": under the same code-hacking fine-tuning scenario that previously produced Emergent Misalignment, a single high-level introspective question suffices to steer training toward an ethical model, empirically showing that the model can self-correct its own misaligned behaviors.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can be endowed with a self-reflective conscience mechanism that enables autonomous detection and correction of ethical misalignment. This shifts the paradigm from Emergent Misalignment to Emergent Alignment, suggesting a scalable, judge-free approach to AI alignment that leverages the model's own introspective capabilities.

title: A Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization
comment: Presented at the 17th Workshop on Optimization and Learning in Multiagent Systems (OptLearnMAS, https://optlearnmas.github.io), co-located with the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
summary: Many decision-making problems in computing and networking systems can be naturally formulated as cost-minimization problems under performance constraints. In dynamic environments, reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to solve such problems at runtime by embedding both costs and constraint violations into a single scalar reward through weighted penalty terms, following a Lagrangian-inspired formulation. However, in this context the behavior of the learned policy critically depends on the choice of these weights, which are typically selected manually. This makes it difficult to identify an appropriate trade-off between optimizing the primary objective and effectively avoiding constraint violations, particularly in non-stationary environments where their relative importance may change. This paper presents MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization), an approach to tackle this balancing problem through multi-agent RL. MAMO decouples task execution from objective design by formulating the selection of reward weights as a learning problem, providing a !rst step towards more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization problems in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: MAMO introduces a multi-agent RL approach that decouples task execution from reward-weight selection, treating weight tuning as a learning problem to autonomously balance cost minimization and constraint satisfaction in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: In dynamic computing/networking systems, RL solutions for constrained cost-minimization rely on Lagrangian-style scalarized rewards with penalty weights. These weights critically shape policy behavior but are typically chosen manually, making it difficult to strike the right cost-constraint trade-off — especially in non-stationary settings where relative importance shifts over time.
AI.method: MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization) reformulates the problem using multi-agent RL. It decouples task execution (solving the primary problem) from objective design (selecting reward weights), treating the latter as a separate learning problem. This allows the weight-selection policy to adapt alongside the task policy.
AI.result: The paper presents MAMO as a first step toward more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions, though specific experimental results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: MAMO represents a novel step toward autonomous constrained RL by learning reward weights rather than hand-tuning them, enabling more robust adaptation in dynamic, non-stationary environments.

title: ELVA: Exploring Ranking-Driven Universal Multimodal Retrieval
summary:
Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) via contrastive learning has become a mainstream paradigm for improving the performance of Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR). However, previous works have ignored the grain blindness when adapting the contrastive paradigm into retrieval tasks. Grain blindness refers to the tendency of the model to overlook grain-level information contained in the query, which is crucial for effectively handling complex queries. This stems from contrastive learning treating samples as a binary classification (positive/negative), while ignoring the different information carried by each negative sample. To address this, we argue that negatives should be treated differently according to their similarity to the positive sample, enabling the model to learn distinct grain information from each negative. In this paper, we introduce a simple but effective framework, called ELVA, a novel rule-based RL framework that mitigates grain blindness through ranking-driven MLLMs. 1) Instead of relying on reward models, we extend Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
  (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, allowing the model to explore new ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels. 2) By utilizing rule-based rewards, our approach jointly optimizes the ranking of negative samples while enlarging the similarity gap between positive and negative. To more precisely measure grain blindness, we further introduce MRBench, a new benchmark specifically designed for multi-grain query scenarios. ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results across standard retrieval benchmarks, and its notable 13.1% improvement on MRBench further demonstrates its effectiveness in alleviating grain blindness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ELVA, a rule-based RL framework that addresses "grain blindness" in multimodal retrieval — the failure of contrastive learning models to distinguish different levels of semantic granularity in negative samples. By extending RLVR to retrieval and using ranking-driven optimization without reward models, ELVA jointly optimizes negative ranking and positive-negative separation. A new benchmark, MRBench, is proposed to measure grain blindness, where ELVA achieves a 13.1% improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing contrastive learning approaches for Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR) treat negative samples uniformly as a binary positive/negative classification problem, causing "grain blindness" — the model's inability to capture fine-grained, grain-level information in queries. Complex queries require the model to discern varying degrees of relevance among negatives, but standard contrastive learning ignores the distinct information carried by each negative sample based on its similarity to the positive.
AI.method: The authors propose ELVA, which extends Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to retrieval tasks. Key components: (1) RLVR is adapted to retrieval without relying on explicit reward models or ranking labels, allowing the model to explore ranking behaviors autonomously. (2) Rule-based rewards are designed to jointly optimize the ranking order of negative samples (treating negatives differently based on similarity) while simultaneously enlarging the similarity gap between positive and negative samples. The framework is rule-based, not requiring a learned reward model.
AI.result: ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results on standard retrieval benchmarks. On MRBench (a newly introduced multi-grain query benchmark), it delivers a notable 13.1% improvement, demonstrating significant mitigation of grain blindness.
AI.conclusion: Grain blindness is a critical limitation in contrastive learning-based multimodal retrieval that prior work has overlooked. ELVA effectively addresses this by leveraging RLVR with rule-based rewards to enable grain-aware learning from negatives, validated by strong empirical gains on both standard benchmarks and the newly proposed MRBench.

title: AI Conversational Interviewing: Scaling Up Semi-Structured and In-depth Interviews
summary: Public opinion research has long faced a trade-off between depth and scale: standardized surveys enable large-scale measurement but restrict respondents to researcher-defined categories, obscuring the diversity of unexpected considerations that underlie public sentiment. More conversational interviews provide richer insights through open-ended probing, but their reliance on trained human interviewers has kept them difficult to scale. This study introduces AI Conversational Interviewing as a method for collecting open-ended public opinion data at scale, pursuing three objectives: to demonstrate the analytical value of conversational text data for questions beyond the reach of closed-ended items; to assess the method's practical viability through participants' own evaluations; and to inform implementation by experimentally comparing voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice interview modes. We conducted a study combining an AI-led interview with a standardized survey on migration policy among 571 respondents recruited via Prolific and Payback Panel. The findings establish AI Conversational Interviewing as a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit. The conversational transcripts surface considerations and reasoning that a comprehensive standardized battery does not capture such as markedly different mental models of migration among subgroups with similar attitudes levels. Among respondents who completed the interview, evaluations of the AI interview were at or above those of the standardized survey across modes, although completion itself varied by condition.
