By releasing open data and open-source pipeline materials, the study contributes to a growing literature on harnessing artificial intelligence to expand the methods of public opinion measurement.

AI.tldr: The study introduces AI Conversational Interviewing as a scalable method for collecting open-ended public opinion data, demonstrating that AI-led interviews capture reasoning and mental models missed by standardized surveys, with participant evaluations matching or exceeding those of traditional surveys.
AI.motivation: Public opinion research faces a fundamental trade-off: standardized surveys offer scale but constrain responses to researcher-defined categories, while conversational interviews yield richer insights but are difficult to scale due to reliance on trained human interviewers. The authors seek to resolve this tension by leveraging AI to conduct open-ended interviews at scale.
AI.method: A study was conducted with 571 respondents (recruited via Prolific and Payback Panel) who completed both an AI-led conversational interview and a standardized survey on migration policy. The design experimentally compared three interview modes — voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice — to assess implementation trade-offs. Participants evaluated both the AI interview and the standardized survey to gauge practical viability.
AI.result: AI conversational transcripts revealed considerations and reasoning — including markedly different mental models of migration among subgroups with similar attitude levels — that the comprehensive standardized battery failed to capture. Participant evaluations of the AI interview were at or above those of the standardized survey among completers, though completion rates varied by condition.
AI.conclusion: AI Conversational Interviewing is a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit, capable of surfacing nuanced public reasoning at scale. The authors contribute open data and open-source pipeline materials to support further methodological development in AI-augmented public opinion measurement.

title: JustDiag!: A Diagnostic Justification Engine for Accountable Root Cause Analysis
summary: Large language models can produce fluent root cause analyses, but fluent final answers alone are insufficient evidence for accountability in high-stakes operations. In real incident response, engineers need to know what evidence supported a diagnosis, which alternatives were considered, where contradictions remained, and whether the system resolved the case or preserved uncertainty. We address this gap with JustDiag, a diagnostic justification engine for RCA that maintains an explicit process state over evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks. We evaluated the system on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer protocol that separately scores final-answer quality and process quality. Relative to a matched control without diagnostic justification, JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores, while accepting slightly lower terminal completion due to more calibrated non-closure. These results suggest that accountable RCA requires explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not only fluent final answers.

AI.tldr: JustDiag is a diagnostic justification engine that enhances root cause analysis (RCA) by explicitly tracking evidence, hypotheses, conflicts, and decision processes. Evaluated on 66 real-world incidents, it outperformed baseline systems in both outcome and process quality, while appropriately leaving more cases unresolved rather than forcing fluent but unjustified answers.
AI.motivation: Fluent final answers from LLMs are insufficient for high-stakes incident response; engineers need transparent evidence trails, consideration of alternatives, awareness of contradictions, and calibrated uncertainty. Current RCA systems lack explicit diagnostic justification and process-aware evaluation.
AI.method: JustDiag maintains an explicit process state tracking evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks during RCA. The system was evaluated on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer protocol: one layer scores final-answer quality, another scores process quality (evidence support, alternative consideration, contradiction handling, uncertainty calibration). A matched control without diagnostic justification served as baseline.
AI.result: JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores compared to the control. Terminal completion was slightly lower due to more calibrated non-closure — the system appropriately declined to close cases when evidence was insufficient rather than producing fluent but unsupported answers.
AI.conclusion: Accountable RCA requires explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not merely fluent final answers. Diagnostic transparency and calibrated uncertainty are essential for trustworthiness in high-stakes operational settings.

title: Sign-Language Datasets at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey on Resources, Benchmarks, and Annotation Standards
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. 27 pages, 5 figures
summary: Sign languages are expressive visual languages used by Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) communities. Despite substantial progress in sign-language recognition, translation, and production, advances remain constrained by fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Existing benchmarks often fail to reflect real-world communication needs, and systematic analyses of these limitations remain limited. In this survey, we present a comprehensive index of sign-language datasets, covering 120 resources across 35 sign languages. We analyze key challenges such as modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias, and outline considerations for future dataset design. We also introduce a 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet and release a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/Ginqwerty/Open-Sign-Language) to support standardized documentation and reproducible evaluation. Overall, our work provides a unified and practical foundation for developing inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey indexing 120 sign-language datasets across 35 languages, analyzing key challenges (modality imbalance, annotation granularity, signer bias), and proposing a standardized 24-field datasheet plus a public repository to support reproducible, inclusive sign-language technology development.
AI.motivation: Sign-language recognition, translation, and production research is constrained by fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Existing benchmarks often fail to capture real-world communication needs, and no systematic analysis of these shortcomings exists. This survey aims to fill that gap by providing a unified resource and critical assessment.
AI.method: The authors survey and index 120 sign-language datasets spanning 35 sign languages. They systematically analyze dataset characteristics across dimensions including modality balance, annotation granularity, and signer diversity. They introduce a standardized 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet for documentation and release a public GitHub repository for reproducible evaluation and community contribution.
AI.result: The survey reveals persistent issues: modality imbalance (e.g., over-reliance on isolated signs vs. continuous signing), inconsistent annotation granularity, signer bias (limited demographic diversity), and poor real-world ecological validity. The proposed datasheet and repository provide practical tools to mitigate these issues in future dataset construction.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified, practical foundation for building more inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies by standardizing dataset documentation and enabling reproducible benchmarking across the research community.

title: ITNet: A Learnable Integral Transform That Subsumes Convolution, Attention, and Recurrence
summary: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers each encode different inductive biases -- locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction -- and have remained mathematically distinct since their inception. We show that this fragmentation reflects not a fundamental diversity in how signals should be processed, but rather incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object: a learnable integral transform. We introduce the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified architecture built around a learnable kernel that depends jointly on positions and features. This kernel is implemented as a small neural network, specifically an MLP, that models pairwise interactions, enabling the model to adapt its behavior from data. We show that convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (including LSTM, GRU, S4, and Mamba) arise as special cases under appropriate parameterizations, and that ITNet is a universal approximator of continuous operators. To make this practical, we develop tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization, enabling efficient and scalable computation. A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K , GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA\,v2 and NLVR2. The results demonstrate that a single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three architectural families from data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified neural architecture based on a learnable integral transform with a content- and position-dependent kernel (MLP). Convolutions, self-attention, and recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU, S4, Mamba) emerge as special cases. ITNet matches or surpasses specialized architectures across vision, language, 3D, and multimodal tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing dominant architectures — CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers — encode distinct inductive biases (locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction) and have remained mathematically separate. The authors argue this fragmentation stems from incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object: a learnable integral transform. The goal is to unify these paradigms under one framework, demonstrating that a single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three families from data.
AI.method: ITNet is built around a learnable kernel implemented as a small MLP that depends jointly on positions and features, modeling pairwise interactions. The kernel is integrated via importance-weighted Monte Carlo. Three innovations enable practicality: (1) tiled kernel fusion, (2) importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and (3) learned low-rank factorization. Convolutions, multi-head self-attention, and autoregressive recurrence (LSTM, GRU, S4, Mamba) are shown to be special parameterizations. The architecture uses a shared ITNet operator with lightweight modality-specific encoders, and ITNet is proven to be a universal approximator of continuous operators.
AI.result: A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K (vision), GLUE (language), ModelNet40 (3D), VQA v2 and NLVR2 (vision-language). This demonstrates that one learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers from data.
AI.conclusion: The fragmentation of CNN, RNN, and Transformer architectures is not fundamental but reflects incomplete views of a single underlying learnable integral transform. ITNet unifies these paradigms, matches or beats specialized models across diverse modalities, and suggests that future architecture design may focus on learning the kernel form from data rather than hand-designing inductive biases.

title: ProMUSE: Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty-guided Staged Evidential Alzheimer Disease Classification
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a fatal disorder that destroys memory and cognitive skills in the elderly population. Most treatments for AD are effective in the early stage, leading to an increasing demand for early AD diagnosis. AD diagnosis increasingly relies on multimodal data such as clinical assessments, structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging. However, MRI and PET acquisition remain costly and not universally accessible, making full-modality inference impractical in real-world clinical workflows. We propose ProMUSE, a Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty Guided Staged Evidential Network that adaptively determines when additional modalities are necessary, helping reduce the overall cost of data acquisition while maintaining accuracy. ProMUSE first performs evidential classification using low-cost clinical data and quantifies uncertainty via a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, ProMUSE progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty through Dempster-Shafer theory to obtain a calibrated multimodal prediction. This staged acquisition strategy enables accurate diagnosis while minimizing reliance on expensive imaging. Experiments on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks demonstrate that ProMUSE achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50-90%, yielding substantial cost savings. These results highlight ProMUSE as a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening.

AI.tldr: ProMUSE is a staged evidential network that uses clinical data for initial AD diagnosis and only requests costly MRI/PET scans when prediction uncertainty exceeds a threshold, reducing imaging usage by 50–90% while maintaining accuracy comparable to full-modality methods.
AI.motivation: MRI and PET imaging are expensive and not universally accessible, making full-modality AD diagnosis impractical in real clinical workflows. A method is needed that intelligently decides when costly modalities are necessary rather than requiring them for every patient.
AI.method: ProMUSE performs evidential classification on low-cost clinical data using a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model to quantify uncertainty. When uncertainty surpasses a learned threshold, it progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty via Dempster-Shafer theory for calibrated multimodal prediction.
AI.result: On ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS datasets across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks, ProMUSE matched or exceeded full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50–90%.
AI.conclusion: ProMUSE offers a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening by adaptively determining when expensive imaging is needed.

title: Phoenix: Safe GitHub Issue Resolution via Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: We present Phoenix, a multi-agent LLM system that resolves GitHub issues from triage through pull-request creation, combining seven layered safety controls with a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy. Phoenix decomposes the work across six specialized agents. Planner, reproducer, coder, tester, failure analyst and Pull Request (PR) agent, all coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Every change is checked against a baseline test run before a pull request is opened. On a 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite. run on the production webhook path, Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% of instances with no pass-to-pass regressions on successful runs; this curated slice is not directly comparable to full-split leaderboard results, and we discuss the limits of the comparison. A complementary pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories yields 100% correctness preservation (CP; mean 122s on the hard tier). Manual inspection shows that about half of the resulting pull requests are well-targeted fixes. The other half place code at incorrect paths, a planner localization limitation we are addressing with retrieval. We also report the deployment failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI) that motivated each safety mechanism.

AI.tldr: Phoenix is a multi-agent LLM system that autonomously resolves GitHub issues using six specialized agents with seven layered safety controls. It achieves 75% oracle-resolution on a curated SWE-bench Lite slice with zero pass-to-pass regressions, and 100% correctness preservation on a pilot of 42 real issues across 14 repos. About half of generated PRs are well-targeted; the remainder suffer from planner localization errors.
AI.motivation: Automated issue-to-PR pipelines using LLMs face significant deployment risks: generating incorrect patches, introducing regressions, violating repository conventions, and encountering real-world failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI). The authors aim to build a production-grade system that balances autonomy with safety, ensuring no regressions are introduced when resolving issues automatically.
AI.method: Phoenix employs six specialized agents — Planner, Reproducer, Coder, Tester, Failure Analyst, and PR Agent — orchestrated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. The system enforces seven layered safety controls, including a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy: every change is checked against a baseline test run before a PR is opened, preventing pass-to-pass regressions. Evaluation uses a curated 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite (production webhook path) and a complementary pilot on 42 real GitHub issues across 14 repositories.
AI.result: On the 24-instance SWE-bench Lite slice, Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% of instances with zero pass-to-pass regressions. On 42 real issues across 14 repositories, it achieves 100% correctness preservation (CP), with a mean resolution time of 122s on the hard tier. Manual inspection reveals approximately half of PRs are well-targeted fixes; the rest place code at incorrect paths due to planner localization limitations. Deployment failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI) are documented as motivation for each safety mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Phoenix demonstrates that multi-agent LLM systems can safely and effectively automate GitHub issue resolution at production scale, provided robust safety controls and baseline-aware testing are in place. The primary limitation is planner localization accuracy, which the authors are addressing through retrieval-based improvements. The work highlights the importance of safety mechanisms grounded in real deployment failure modes.

title: Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation is an emerging paradigm that has shown promise in industrial recommendation systems, aiming to predict users' next interactions from their historical behaviors. At the core of generative recommendation lies item tokenization, which bridges item semantics and recommendation models. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively organize and inject complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts into recommendation models simultaneously. On the one hand, existing graph-based integration methods, such as graph serialization and graph neural networks, either suffer from scalability issues or exploit only local graph information. On the other hand, existing semantic tokenization methods typically rely on heuristics and lack explicit supervision signals, which may lead to inaccurate or suboptimal semantic representations. To address these limitations in user interest context modeling, we propose G2Rec, a scalable framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization for industrial-scale generative recommendation. Overall, G2Rec enables recommendation models to capture holistic and semantically grounded user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth user interests, thereby providing more comprehensive and accurate modeling of user behavior contexts in industrial sequential recommendation. Online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of G2Rec over existing methods.

AI.tldr: G2Rec is a scalable generative recommendation framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic item tokenization, enabling recommendation models to capture comprehensive user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth labels.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods struggle with two limitations: (1) graph-based integration approaches (serialization, GNNs) are either unscalable or capture only local graph information; (2) semantic tokenization relies on heuristics without explicit supervision, yielding suboptimal representations. A unified framework addressing both issues simultaneously is needed for industrial-scale deployment.
AI.method: G2Rec combines holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization in a unified framework. It captures global graph structures for user interest context and employs semantically grounded tokenization with explicit supervision, avoiding reliance on ground-truth user interests while producing comprehensive user behavior representations.
AI.result: Online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that G2Rec outperforms existing generative recommendation methods.
AI.conclusion: G2Rec successfully addresses the dual challenges of scalable graph context modeling and supervised semantic tokenization in generative recommendation, providing more accurate user behavior modeling for industrial sequential recommendation systems.

title: Low-Cost Multi-Precision Systolic Arrays for Accelerating FHE NTTs on AI ASICs
summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) ensures robust data privacy but suffers from prohibitive computational overhead. Accelerating FHE on AI hardware like Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) is promising, yet fundamentally limited by a precision mismatch: TPUs are optimized for 8-bit arithmetic, whereas FHE and its critical parts such as the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), demand high precision. Current approaches bridge this gap using matrix decomposition to execute NTT computations on low-precision matrix engines. However, reconstructing the full-precision results requires shift-and-add accumulation that does not match the dataflow of matrix multiplication. This forces offloading full-precision reconstruction from matrix engines to vector processors that disrupts the matrix multiplication dataflow, creating significant performance bottleneck. To resolve this limitation, we propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that performs full-precision output reconstruction natively within the array in sync with low-precision matrix multiplication under a uniform dataflow. Synthesized at 7nm with OpenRoad, our design incurs negligible hardware overhead. Cycle-accurate simulations using SCALE-Sim demonstrate that natively executing NTTs on the proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33x speedup, for transform sizes 2^12 to 2^16 on 128x128 matrix engines, successfully enabling standard AI hardware to support high-precision FHE acceleration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that natively performs full-precision output reconstruction within the array, enabling efficient NTT computation for FHE on TPU-like AI hardware without disrupting the matrix multiplication dataflow.
AI.motivation: FHE requires high-precision arithmetic (e.g., for NTT), but TPUs are optimized for low-precision (8-bit) matrix engines. Existing matrix decomposition approaches offload full-precision reconstruction to vector processors, breaking the matrix multiplication dataflow and creating a severe performance bottleneck.
AI.method: Design a multi-precision systolic array with minimal modifications that performs full-precision shift-and-add accumulation natively within the array, synchronized with low-precision matrix multiplication under a unified dataflow. Evaluated via 7nm synthesis (OpenRoad) and cycle-accurate simulation (SCALE-Sim) on 128×128 matrix engines across transform sizes 2^12 to 2^16.
AI.result: The proposed design incurs negligible hardware overhead and achieves at least 1.33× speedup for NTT execution across all tested transform sizes compared to baseline approaches that offload reconstruction to vector processors.
AI.conclusion: By enabling native full-precision reconstruction within the systolic array under a uniform dataflow, the proposed architecture successfully bridges the precision gap, allowing standard AI hardware (TPUs) to efficiently support high-precision FHE acceleration.

title: Editorial Alignment: A Participatory Approach to Engaging Editorial Expertise in LLM-mediated Knowledge Dissemination
summary: The emergence of LLM-driven information services is reshaping the conditions under which public knowledge institutions operate, threatening to absorb the editorial function these institutions exist to exercise. While LLMs offer powerful new affordances for knowledge dissemination, editorial authority is challenged by pretrained LLMs that arrive already aligned with the values and dissemination strategies of their commercial developers. This paper investigates editor participation in re-aligning LLM interfaces to editorial standards through design workshops, in a case study where we design and implement an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface with a Nordic public knowledge institution. We introduce editorial alignment as a design practice within Participatory AI, framing AI alignment as a design process and positioning the editorial standard as a design artefact that translates editorial practice and values into alignment objectives for technical implementation. Last, we discuss how editorial alignment can create space for ongoing participation and give editors agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "editorial alignment" as a design practice within Participatory AI, using a case study with a Nordic public knowledge institution to show how editors can participate in realigning LLM interfaces to uphold editorial standards rather than defaulting to commercial developer values.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven information services threaten to absorb the editorial function of public knowledge institutions, as pretrained LLMs come pre-aligned with commercial developers' values rather than the editorial standards of institutions like libraries and encyclopedias. There is a need for methods that give editors agency in shaping how LLMs mediate knowledge dissemination.
AI.method: The authors conducted design workshops with editors from a Nordic public knowledge institution, collaboratively designing and implementing an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface. They frame editorial alignment as a Participatory AI design practice, treating the editorial standard as a design artefact that translates editorial values and practices into concrete alignment objectives for technical implementation.
AI.result: The case study demonstrates that editorial alignment can successfully create space for ongoing editor participation and give editors meaningful agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination. The editorial standard, as a design artefact, effectively bridges editorial practice with technical alignment objectives.
AI.conclusion: Editorial alignment offers a viable Participatory AI approach for public knowledge institutions to reclaim editorial authority over LLM-mediated information services, positioning AI alignment not merely as a technical problem but as a collaborative design process centered on institutional values.

title: OpenRath: Session-Centered Runtime State for Agent Systems
summary: Modern agent systems often suffer from fragmented runtime state: transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded separately and become difficult to inspect or reproduce. OpenRath addresses this issue with a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent, multi-session systems. The analogy concerns the role of a central first-class runtime abstraction, not tensor computation. Its core abstraction is Session, the runtime value passed between agents and workflows. A Session is branchable, inspectable, replayable, backend-aware, and composable. It records conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence, while defining where memory interactions enter the runtime record. Since this state is carried by the same value used in program execution, fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations rather than states reconstructed from external traces. OpenRath further defines Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector, with Selector turning control flow into runtime-routed decisions. This report presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. Its claims are limited to controlled runtime properties, while broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are left for follow-on evaluation. The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition.

AI.tldr: OpenRath introduces a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent systems centered on a first-class runtime abstraction called Session, which unifies fragmented runtime state (transcripts, tool effects, memory, lineage) into a branchable, inspectable, replayable, and composable value, enabling fork/merge/replay as explicit runtime operations rather than reconstructed traces.
AI.motivation: Modern agent systems suffer from fragmented runtime state — transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace state, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded separately across different subsystems, making inspection and reproduction difficult. There is a need for a unified runtime abstraction that consolidates these disparate state artifacts into a single coherent value that flows through program execution.
AI.method: OpenRath proposes a programming model where Session is the central first-class runtime abstraction, analogous to PyTorch's Tensor but for agent orchestration rather than tensor computation. A Session carries conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence. The model defines complementary abstractions: Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector (which turns control flow into runtime-routed decisions). Fork, merge, and replay are implemented as explicit operations on Session values rather than external trace reconstruction.
AI.result: This is a design/architecture report presenting the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. The claims are deliberately scoped to controlled runtime properties; broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are explicitly deferred to follow-on work.
AI.conclusion: The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition. By making runtime state a native, branchable, and composable value that participates directly in program execution, OpenRath enables more transparent, reproducible, and inspectable multi-agent, multi-session systems.

title: Quantifying Aleatoric Uncertainty of In-Context Learning for Robust Measure of LLM Prediction Confidence
summary: In-Context Learning (ICL) allows LLMs to adapt to new tasks from a few demonstrations, but its reliability remains a concern: predictions are highly sensitive to both prompt design and the model's ability to understand the context, obscuring whether failures arise from data properties or model limitations. Uncertainty decomposition-separating aleatoric from epistemic sources-is particularly crucial in this setting, yet existing methods, designed for standard generation tasks, fail to capture the unique dynamics of ICL. To address this, we introduce a concept of self-function vectors, built upon Bayesian views and the mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors leverage internal model representations to model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting, thereby enabling a direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework and circumventing the reliance on brittle input or decoding manipulations. Given the lack of established benchmarks and suitable evaluation protocols, we also propose the first and rigorous evaluation protocol, in which data is manipulated in controlled ways so as to quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely and separately from epistemic uncertainty. With this new evaluation framework, initially grounded in synthetic tasks for conceptual development and subsequently extended to real-world datasets, we show that our proposed methodology can measure uncertainty of LLM predictions made under ICL more reliably than existing alternative methods. Moreover, we show it can be used as a practical tool for trustworthy-related applications, such as hallucination detection. Our findings pave a new direction for connecting the quantitative view of uncertainty with the mechanistic understanding of model behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces self-function vectors—latent representations capturing the concept learned during in-context prompting—to estimate aleatoric uncertainty in LLM predictions under ICL within a Bayesian framework. It also provides a rigorous evaluation protocol with controlled data manipulations to disentangle aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty, demonstrating superior reliability over existing methods and practical utility for tasks like hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: In-context learning reliability is undermined by sensitivity to prompt design and ambiguity about whether failures stem from data properties (aleatoric uncertainty) or model limitations (epistemic uncertainty). Existing uncertainty decomposition methods, designed for standard generation, fail to capture ICL's unique dynamics. A method tailored to ICL is needed to separately quantify these uncertainty sources reliably.
AI.method: The authors propose self-function vectors grounded in Bayesian principles and mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting from internal model representations, enabling direct aleatoric uncertainty estimation without brittle input or decoding manipulations. They also construct a controlled evaluation protocol where data is systematically manipulated to isolate and quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely from epistemic uncertainty, tested on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.result: The proposed self-function vector method measures ICL prediction uncertainty more reliably than existing alternatives. The evaluation framework successfully separates uncertainty types, and the approach demonstrates practical value in trustworthiness applications such as hallucination detection.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a novel connection between quantitative uncertainty estimation and mechanistic model understanding, offering both a principled uncertainty decomposition method for ICL and a rigorous evaluation protocol, with promising implications for building more trustworthy LLM systems.

title: Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
summary: Recent position papers argue that the classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty framework is insufficient for interactive large language model (LLM) agents and call for underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations that can unlock new agent capabilities such as proactive clarification seeking and shared mental-model building. Practical deployment constraints -- black-box APIs, interactive latency budgets, and the absence of labeled trajectories -- rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based estimation as the most viable family for surfacing such signals at deployment time. We answer this call with a simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u), enabling the agent to ask for clarification when the task specification is ambiguous. To evaluate it, we introduce two clarification-augmented benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification) in which 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified, and systematically compare the proposed decomposition against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B) on these variants together with the standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection. Averaged across the five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM, and leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, indicating that the gains generalize beyond a single LLM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a simple prompt-based method that decomposes LLM agent outputs into action confidence and request uncertainty (u), enabling proactive clarification-seeking when task specifications are ambiguous. Evaluated on two new clarification-augmented benchmarks across five LLM backbones, the approach substantially outperforms ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM), with gains averaging 73% and 36% respectively on ALFWorld-Clarification F1 scores.
AI.motivation: Existing aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty frameworks are inadequate for interactive LLM agents. Deployment constraints — black-box APIs, latency budgets, and absence of labeled trajectories — render logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods infeasible, making prompt-based estimation the only viable approach. The authors aim to address the call for underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations that enable clarification-seeking behavior.
AI.method: A prompt-based decomposition separates the agent's output into two signals: action confidence (how sure the agent is about what to do) and request uncertainty (u), which flags whether the task specification is ambiguous enough to warrant asking for clarification. Two new benchmarks, WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification, are introduced with 50% deliberately underspecified tasks. The method is compared against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones: GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, and GPT-OSS-120B, evaluated on both clarification-augmented and standard benchmarks (WebShop, ALFWorld, REAL).
AI.result: Averaged across five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and 36% over UAM. It leads clarification F1 on every backbone for WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones for ALFWorld-Clarification, demonstrating strong cross-model generalization. Results on standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection are also reported.
AI.conclusion: The proposed prompt-based action-confidence/request-uncertainty decomposition effectively enables LLM agents to recognize underspecified tasks and seek clarification, significantly outperforming existing uncertainty estimation methods. The gains generalize across diverse LLM backbones, validating the practical utility of the approach under real-world deployment constraints.

title: cAPM: Continual AI-Assisted Pace-Mapping with Active Learning
summary: Ventricular tachycardia is a life-threatening rhythm disorder and a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Pace-mapping is a clinical procedure for identifying the intervention target during catheter ablation of VT. It requires clinicians to pace different sites in the ventricles and rapidly interpret the resulting electrocardiograms to determine where to pace next or whether a target site has been identified. Active learning AI models have been proposed to guide clinicians to the next pacing site, showing promise in reducing the number of pacing sites and improving the efficiency of pace-mapping. Existing methods require retraining each target without the ability to transfer knowledge across multiple VTs within the same patient or across patients. We introduce cAPM for continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping to capture and transfer knowledge accumulated from past pace-mapping data to reduce the number of pace-mapping data needed for future target VTs. This is made possible by a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that learns the mapping from pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology, an active-learning strategy that refines this surrogate model by selecting the most informative pacing site for each target, and a continual learning strategy to do so sequentially while retaining knowledge from prior targets. Evaluated on an in-silico testbed consisting of sequentially-presented localization tasks across different physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM with and without replay of past data samples achieved an 81% probability of localizing within clinical tolerance (5 mm accuracy) using 4.5 pace-mapping sites, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving 38% probability using 13.7 pacing sites. These results provide a strong basis for preparing cAPM towards in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies where it can be used to guide pace-mapping.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes cAPM, a continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping framework that uses continual learning and a task-agnostic surrogate neural network to transfer knowledge across multiple ventricular tachycardia (VT) localization tasks, dramatically reducing the number of pacing sites needed (4.5 sites for 81% localization accuracy vs. 13.7 sites for 38% with prior SOTA).
AI.motivation: Existing active-learning methods for VT pace-mapping require retraining from scratch for each new target VT and cannot transfer knowledge across VTs within the same patient or across patients. This inefficiency motivates a continual learning approach that accumulates and reuses knowledge from past pace-mapping procedures.
AI.method: cAPM combines three components: (1) a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that maps pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology; (2) an active-learning strategy that selects the most informative next pacing site to refine the surrogate model; and (3) a continual learning strategy that sequentially updates the model across targets while retaining prior knowledge, with an optional replay mechanism for past data samples.
AI.result: On an in-silico testbed with sequential localization tasks across varying physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM achieved 81% probability of localizing within 5 mm clinical tolerance using only 4.5 pacing sites on average. In contrast, the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieved only 38% probability requiring 13.7 pacing sites.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that continual knowledge transfer across VT pace-mapping tasks substantially improves data efficiency and localization accuracy, providing a strong foundation for advancing cAPM toward preclinical and clinical in-vivo studies.

title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

AI.tldr: Introduces Contagion Networks, a framework for measuring evaluator bias propagation among LLM agents. A 3-agent experiment with DeepSeek-chat shows consistent bias contagion (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]). Homogeneous-model contagion is 3-5x weaker than cross-model. Increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.motivation: When LLMs act as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases can propagate through the agent network, distorting collective judgments. Prior work has not formally characterized the mechanisms or magnitude of this bias contagion, nor provided a measurement framework or actionable mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The authors propose Contagion Networks — a formal framework for measuring evaluator bias spread. They conduct a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), measuring the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Γ₃. Propagation regimes are characterized by the spectral radius ρ(Γ_N). Mitigation is tested by varying evaluator committee size (k=1 to k=3).
AI.result: Evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same model. Homogeneous-model contagion coefficients are 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients from prior work (MM-EPC: γ ≈ 0.85–1.3), placing them in the suppression regime (ρ < 1). Increasing committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.conclusion: LLM evaluator bias contagion is a measurable, systematic phenomenon governed by spectral properties of the contagion matrix. Using homogeneous models and larger evaluator committees are effective mitigation strategies. The open-source Contagion Network framework is released for further study.

title: Cost-Optimal LLM Routing with Limited User Feedback under User Satisfaction Guarantees
summary: Inference costs for large language model (LLM) applications are rapidly growing, driven by surging demand and rising infrastructure cost. Users expect high-quality responses, and in commercial settings this is formally codified in Service Level Agreements (SLAs), creating a fundamental tension between cost and quality. Recent progress on cost-aware LLM request routing has shown potential to resolve this tension, but existing approaches rely on complete feedback signals, offline training, extensive per-workload tuning, and most lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity. We introduce SLARouter, an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy from the sparse, one-sided user feedback available in production systems. SLARouter provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance. Experiments across a wide range of LLM benchmarks show that SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without the need for per-benchmark tuning, reducing operating cost by up to 2.2x over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: SLARouter is an online LLM request routing algorithm that learns cost-optimal policies from sparse, one-sided user feedback while providing theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance, achieving up to 2.2x cost reduction over baselines without per-benchmark tuning.
AI.motivation: Rising inference costs for LLM applications conflict with user expectations for high-quality responses, formalized in SLAs. Existing cost-aware routing methods require complete feedback, offline training, and lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity — creating a need for an online approach that works with realistic, sparse production feedback.
AI.method: SLARouter is an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy using only the sparse, one-sided user feedback naturally available in production systems, with theoretical guarantees for cost optimality and strict SLA compliance without per-workload tuning.
AI.result: Across diverse LLM benchmarks, SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without per-benchmark tuning and reduces operating costs by up to 2.2x compared to existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: SLARouter successfully bridges the cost-quality tension in LLM serving by enabling online, SLA-guaranteed routing from sparse feedback, demonstrating significant practical cost savings while maintaining compliance.

title: FFinRED: An Expert-Guided Benchmark Generation and Evaluation Framework for Financial LLM Red-Teaming
summary: Existing safety benchmarks target general adversarial scenarios but miss finance-specific risks. Financial LLMs face regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion that require targeted evaluation. We introduce FinRED, an expert-guided red-teaming framework for financial LLM safety evaluation developed with financial experts. FinRED uses a novel two-level taxonomy mapping global standards (e.g., FATF and EU DORA) to threats ranging from regulatory evasion to complex fraud, integrated with a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into context-rich red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) through an expert-defined schema. Rigorous expert validation confirms seed plausibility and realism for meaningful LLM safety evaluation. We also provide an expert-validated, finance-specific rubric that goes beyond disclaimer checks, aligns more closely with human experts than static one-size-fits-all rubrics, and reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. Aligned with internationally adopted risk-management and information-security standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 27001), FinRED is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute (FSI) regulatory sandbox for generative AI security evaluation in real financial services. To mitigate dual-use risks, the dataset, generation pipeline, prompt template, and evaluation framework are gated for qualified researchers at https://github.com/selectstar-ai/FinRED-paper and https://huggingface.co/datasets/datumo/FinRED.

AI.tldr: FinRED is an expert-guided red-teaming framework for evaluating financial LLM safety, featuring a two-level taxonomy aligned with global standards (FATF, EU DORA), a pipeline converting real financial documents into context-rich prompts, and an expert-validated finance-specific rubric that reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. It is deployed in South Korea's FSI regulatory sandbox.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks target general adversarial scenarios but miss finance-specific risks such as regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion. Financial LLMs require targeted, domain-specific safety evaluation.
AI.method: FinRED uses (1) a novel two-level taxonomy mapping global regulatory standards (FATF, EU DORA) to finance-specific threats; (2) a scalable pipeline converting real financial documents into context-rich red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) via an expert-defined schema; and (3) an expert-validated, finance-specific evaluation rubric that goes beyond simple disclaimer checks. Rigorous expert validation ensures seed plausibility and realism.
AI.result: The finance-specific rubric aligns more closely with human expert judgment than static, generic rubrics and reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. The framework is deployed operationally in South Korea's Financial Security Institute (FSI) regulatory sandbox for generative AI security evaluation.
AI.conclusion: FinRED provides a rigorous, standards-aligned red-teaming framework tailored to financial LLM safety, bridging the gap between general AI safety benchmarks and domain-specific regulatory requirements. The gated release mitigates dual-use risks while enabling qualified research access.

title: Organizing in the Digital Age: Understanding Community, Challenges, and Consequences in Digitally-facilitated Labor Organizing
summary: The contemporary American labor force is highly dispersed, necessitating the use of digital communication tools to bridge spatial and temporal gaps in union organizing. This study provides an in-depth analysis of how workers within various labor unions utilize digital, text-based communication platforms -- including Discord, WhatsApp, and Slack -- for labor organizing. Through 17 qualitative interviews, we examine the challenges and opportunities presented by digital organizing, identifying both technical and social obstacles. Our findings reveal that although digital tools are integral to contemporary labor successes, they also introduce new complexities, such as navigating technical security, managing information overload, and building trust and consensus. Based on these insights, we draw connections to broader understandings of digital organizing and the role of digital tools in unions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how dispersed American workers use digital communication platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for union organizing, revealing that while these tools are essential for modern labor success, they introduce challenges around security, information overload, and trust-building.
AI.motivation: The contemporary American workforce is highly geographically dispersed, creating spatial and temporal gaps that traditional face-to-face union organizing cannot bridge. Digital communication tools have become necessary, yet their role, opportunities, and challenges in union organizing remain underexamined.
AI.method: The authors conducted 17 qualitative interviews with workers across various labor unions who utilize digital, text-based communication platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing purposes.
AI.result: Findings show that digital tools are integral to contemporary labor organizing successes but introduce new complexities: navigating technical security concerns, managing information overload, and building trust and consensus among dispersed members. Both technical and social obstacles were identified.
AI.conclusion: The study draws connections between these insights and broader understandings of digital organizing, highlighting the dual nature of digital tools as both enablers and complicating factors in union activities.

title: FAPO: Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization of Multi-Step LLM Pipelines
summary: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail through interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, so prompt-only optimization can miss bottlenecks in the chain. We present FAPO (Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization), a framework that lets Claude Code optimize an LLM pipeline inside a standardized codebase. FAPO evaluates a pipeline, inspects intermediate steps, diagnoses failures, proposes scoped changes, and validates variants repeatedly to optimize against a score function. It first tries prompt edits and, only when prompt optimization appears insufficient, changes chain structure within the permitted scope when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck. Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the baseline GEPA in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. In 11 model-benchmark comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean $\pm$ trial-standard-deviation ranges, and the mean FAPO-GEPA gain is +14.1 pp. In the six HoVer and IFBench comparisons where prompt-first search escalated to structural changes, FAPO wins all six with a mean gain of +33.8 pp. FAPO also improves performance on security tasks: on CTIBench-RCM, a security CVE-to-CWE task, prompt-only FAPO lifts test accuracy by +4.0 pp on GPT-5, +7.1 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct, and +2.0 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning. These results position FAPO as a state-of-the-art pipeline optimization technique for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks.

AI.tldr: FAPO is an autonomous optimization framework that lets Claude Code iteratively improve multi-step LLM pipelines by first tuning prompts and, when necessary, restructuring the pipeline itself. It outperforms the baseline GEPA across 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons, with particularly large gains (+33.8 pp) when structural changes are triggered, and also improves security-task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt-only optimization methods miss bottlenecks that arise from interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps in multi-step LLM pipelines. There is a need for an autonomous system that can diagnose and fix both prompt-level and structural-level failures in a unified framework.
AI.method: FAPO operates within a standardized codebase and uses Claude Code to iteratively: (1) evaluate the pipeline against a score function, (2) inspect intermediate steps, (3) diagnose failures via attribution, (4) propose scoped changes (prompt edits first; structural changes only when prompts are insufficient), and (5) validate variants. The framework repeats this loop to converge on an optimized pipeline.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats GEPA in 15/18 comparisons, with a mean gain of +14.1 pp. In 11 comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean ± trial-SD ranges. On six HoVer and IFBench comparisons where structural changes were triggered, FAPO wins all six with a mean gain of +33.8 pp. On CTIBench-RCM (CVE-to-CWE), prompt-only FAPO improves accuracy by +4.0 pp (GPT-5), +7.1 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct), and +2.0 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning).
AI.conclusion: FAPO is a state-of-the-art pipeline optimization technique effective for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks, demonstrating that autonomous, attribution-driven optimization combining prompt and structural edits significantly outperforms prompt-only baselines.

title: Granularity-Regulated Adaptive Computational Efficiency for Optimal Verification in Test-Time Scaling
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs) by investing additional compute at inference time. A central component of TTS is the \emph{verifier}, which selects or scores candidate solutions to guide the search process. While prior work has explored the benefit of verification, a fundamental question remains underexplored: \emph{what is the optimal granularity of verification under a given compute budget?} Coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) and fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) represent two extremes, yet neither alone achieves compute-optimality across all regimes. In this paper, we establish a unified theoretical framework, called \textbf{GRACE} (\underline{G}ranularity-\underline{R}egulated \underline{A}daptive \underline{C}omputational \underline{E}fficiency), that characterizes the optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. We prove that there exists a phase transition: fine-grained verification dominates when either the compute budget is large or the problem is hard, whereas coarse-grained verification is preferred in the low-budget, easy-problem regime. Our theory unifies Best-of-$N$, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality framework, and motivates an adaptive granularity strategy that provably achieves the compute-performance Pareto frontier. Empirical results on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks corroborate all four theoretical claims, with our adaptive strategy outperforming fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1\% accuracy at matched compute.

AI.tldr: GRACE is a theoretical framework that identifies the optimal verification granularity for test-time scaling as a function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. It proves a phase transition: fine-grained verification is optimal for hard problems or large budgets, while coarse-grained verification excels for easy problems with low budgets. An adaptive strategy achieves the Pareto frontier, with up to 3.1% gains over fixed baselines.
AI.motivation: Prior work uses either coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) or fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) for verification in test-time scaling, but the fundamental question of optimal verification granularity under a given compute budget remains unanswered. Neither extreme is compute-optimal across all regimes, motivating a unified theory.
AI.method: The authors propose GRACE, a unified theoretical framework that models optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. They prove a phase transition phenomenon, unify Best-of-N, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality framework, and derive an adaptive granularity strategy that provably achieves the compute-performance Pareto frontier.
AI.result: Empirical validation on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks confirms all four theoretical claims. The adaptive granularity strategy outperforms fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1% accuracy at matched compute budgets.
AI.conclusion: There is no universally optimal verification granularity; the best choice depends on problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. The phase transition suggests adaptive granularity as a principled path to compute-optimal test-time scaling.

title: Analyzing the Narration Gap in LLM-Solver Loops
summary: Formal tools such as SAT and SMT solvers are increasingly embedded in language model reasoning pipelines when a safety or security critical question can be formulated in logic. Unlike chain of thought whose steps are sampled from the model distribution without formal guarantee, a solver produces a sound and independently verifiable answer. However, the soundness guarantee can be lost in the interaction between the solver and the model. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work has studied the formalization and decision, but not narration, which is the step that turns a formal tool's output into the user answer. To fill the narration gap, we first model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure. We further evaluate five open-sourced models under prompt injection, and we find certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, while an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. We study the mitigation through hardened prompt that reduces injection significantly but cannot eliminate it and still suffers under adaptive attack. Combining the formal analysis and empirical studies, we show in the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not reach to the answer that the user finally reads.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and analyzes the "narration gap" in LLM-solver hybrid pipelines: while the solver's output is formally sound, the LLM's narration step (translating solver output into user-facing answers) can be compromised via prompt injection, breaking the overall soundness guarantee. Certificate gating preserves soundness, but adversaries can invert conclusions across phrasings and channels; hardened prompts reduce but cannot eliminate this vulnerability.
AI.motivation: The increasing use of SAT/SMT solvers in LLM pipelines for safety-critical reasoning creates an implicit trust in formal soundness. However, prior work only examined formalization and decision steps, overlooking the narration step where the LLM translates solver output into natural language. This gap means the end-to-end soundness guarantee may be lost at the final human-readable output stage.
AI.method: The authors (1) formally model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure, (2) empirically evaluate five open-source models under prompt injection attacks targeting the narration step, (3) test certificate gating as a defense, (4) assess adversarial inversion across different phrasings and communication channels, and (5) study hardened prompts as mitigation, including under adaptive attack scenarios.
AI.result: Certificate gating successfully preserves solver verdict soundness. However, without gating, an adversary can invert a verified conclusion simply by varying phrasing or communication channels. Hardened prompts significantly reduce injection success but cannot eliminate it entirely and remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks.
AI.conclusion: In LLM-solver hybrid pipelines, end-to-end robustness does not extend to the final user-facing answer. The narration step is a critical weak link that undermines the formal soundness guarantees provided by the solver, and current mitigations are insufficient against determined adversaries.

title: Protein Representation Learning with Secondary-Structure and Energy-Filtered Hydrogen-Bond Graphs
summary: Graph-based representations are widely used in protein modeling, yet many existing approaches rely primarily on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which only partially reflect the principles governing protein folding. Proteins instead adopt complex three-dimensional conformations organized around secondary structure elements, such as $α$-helices and $β$-sheets, which encode recurring local motifs and stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions. In this work, we introduce a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning. Residue-level node representations are augmented with secondary structure assignments, and graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by their energetic strength. This design enables the model to capture both local structural context and long-range couplings that are central to protein stability and function. We evaluate the proposed approach on commonly used protein benchmarks and observe consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods. In addition, the resulting graph representations offer enhanced biological interpretability, as the learned connectivity aligns with established structural motifs. These findings suggest that incorporating secondary structure and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning. The code is released at https://github.com/mohamedmohamed2021/SSProNet

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a graph neural network that incorporates secondary structure (α-helices, β-sheets) and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond interactions as edges, outperforming standard proximity/adjacency-based protein GNNs while offering better biological interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing protein graph models rely on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which fail to capture the true organizing principles of protein folding — namely secondary structure elements and hydrogen-bond networks that govern stability and long-range interactions.
AI.method: A secondary-structure-aware GNN where: (1) residue-level node features are augmented with secondary structure assignments (α-helix, β-sheet, loop); (2) graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by energetic strength rather than simple distance cutoffs. This yields a topology that reflects genuine stabilizing interactions.
AI.result: The proposed model achieves consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods on standard protein benchmarks. The learned graph connectivity aligns with known structural motifs, providing enhanced biological interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating secondary structure awareness and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology serves as an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning, improving both predictive performance and mechanistic interpretability.

title: Denoising Implicit Feedback for Cold-start Recommendation
summary: Implicit feedback is widely used in recommender systems due to its accessibility and generality, yet it usually presents noisy samples (e.g., clickbait, position bias). Meanwhile, recommenders inevitably face the item cold-start problem due to the continuous influx of new items. We identify that cold items are more prone to noisy samples due to the aforementioned factors, and researchers often overlook the significance of denoising implicit feedback for cold items. Previous denoising studies usually identify noisy samples based on heuristic patterns, such as higher loss values, and mitigate noise through sample selection or re-weighting. However, these methods have limited adaptability and are ineffective in cold-start scenarios. To achieve denoising implicit feedback for cold-start recommendation, we propose a model-agnostic denoising method called DIF. First, user preferences for content remain stable, which allows us to infer pseudo-labels indicating whether a user is interested in a cold item through content-similar warm items. Furthermore, to improve pseudo-label accuracy, we model the confidence of pseudo-labels based on the content similarity between the cold item and warm items, and then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels for each sample. Finally, we explicitly estimate the uncertainty of the noisy sample label by considering its relative entropy and the cold-start status of the item, which adaptively guides the role of pseudo-labels to correct the noisy labels at the sample level. DIF's superiority is supported by both theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The method has been deployed on a billion-user scale short video application Kuaishou and has significantly improved various commercial metrics within cold-start scenarios.

AI.tldr: DIF is a model-agnostic denoising method for cold-start recommendation that uses content-similar warm items to generate confidence-weighted pseudo-labels, then adaptively corrects noisy implicit feedback by modeling sample uncertainty based on relative entropy and cold-start status.
AI.motivation: Implicit feedback (e.g., clicks) is noisy due to clickbait and position bias, and cold-start items are disproportionately affected. Existing denoising methods rely on heuristic patterns (e.g., high loss values) and fail in cold-start scenarios where interaction data is sparse. The gap is that no prior work addresses denoising implicit feedback specifically for cold items.
AI.method: DIF operates in three stages: (1) infer pseudo-labels for cold items by leveraging stable user content preferences and identifying content-similar warm items; (2) model pseudo-label confidence based on content similarity between cold and warm items, then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels per sample; (3) explicitly estimate sample-level label uncertainty using relative entropy and the item's cold-start status, which adaptively weights the pseudo-labels to correct noisy labels.
AI.result: The method is theoretically justified and validated via extensive experiments on real-world datasets. It has been deployed on Kuaishou, a billion-user short video platform, achieving significant improvements across multiple commercial metrics in cold-start scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DIF effectively addresses the overlooked problem of denoising implicit feedback for cold-start recommendation. Its model-agnostic design, theoretical soundness, and real-world deployment at scale demonstrate both academic and practical value.

title: AutoTam: Specifying Secure Protocol Implementations with Tamarin Model Generation
summary:
Formal verification is a challenging but important task for ensuring the security of cryptographic protocols. While modern protocol verification tools significantly reduce verification effort, modelling remains challenging to practitioners without a background in formal verification. In addition, transferring verification results to a concrete protocol implementation requires expert knowledge.
  In this paper, we present a novel language-first method for verification of trace properties using a domain-specific language for protocol implementations. We target the Tamarin prover for verification, and we prove that verified universal trace properties translate back to the implementation. We additionally integrate symbolic execution in order to analyse the memory safety of protocol implementations. We use our tool to implement and generate accurate models for a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol, and for the WireGuard VPN protocol. Our WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when using our interpreter, and achieves acceptable performance. We formally prove our implementations secure using a combination of symbolic execution and verification of the generated Tamarin models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a language-first approach to cryptographic protocol verification using a domain-specific language (DSL). Protocol implementations written in this DSL are automatically translated into Tamarin prover models, and verified universal trace properties are proven to carry back to the implementation. Symbolic execution is also integrated for memory safety analysis. The approach is validated on a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and WireGuard VPN, with the WireGuard implementation being interoperable with existing implementations.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of cryptographic protocols is critical for security but remains challenging for practitioners without formal methods expertise. Two key pain points are: (1) the difficulty of creating accurate formal models, and (2) the gap between verified abstract models and concrete implementations, which requires expert knowledge to bridge correctly.
AI.method: A language-first methodology where a domain-specific language (DSL) serves as the single source for both protocol implementation and verification. The DSL is used to write protocol implementations, from which Tamarin models are automatically generated. The authors formally prove that verified universal trace properties in Tamarin translate back to the implementation. Symbolic execution is integrated to additionally verify memory safety properties of the implementation.
AI.result: The tool was used to implement and verify a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and the WireGuard VPN protocol. The WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing WireGuard implementations when using the authors' interpreter and achieves acceptable performance. Both implementations were formally proven secure through a combination of symbolic execution and Tamarin model verification.
AI.conclusion: The language-first approach successfully bridges the gap between formal verification and concrete protocol implementation, making formal verification more accessible to practitioners. The method ensures that verified properties are preserved in the actual implementation, reducing the risk of implementation flaws that escape formal analysis.

title: DataMagic: Transforming Tabular Data into Data Insight Video
summary: Data videos integrate dynamic charts, voice narration, and synchronized animations to communicate data insights as temporal narratives, making them an effective medium for improving data consumption efficiency in the data management lifecycle. However, producing high-quality data videos requires expertise spanning data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing approaches fall short: static visualization tools (e.g., BI dashboards) lack narrative logic and animation; authoring tools require users to pre-prepare visualizations rather than working from raw data; pixel-level video generation models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance. We demonstrate DataMagic, an end-to-end interactive system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos. To ensure data fidelity, DataMagic introduces the declarative specification DVSpec, which binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields through data-driven semantic references. To address the combinatorial explosion of the design space, DataMagic adopts a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that generates candidate scenes in parallel and then optimizes narrative coherence through global orchestration. Leveraging DVSpec's decoupling of logic and rendering, the system further supports three interaction modes and structured provenance-based data Q&A, transforming one-way videos into explorable interactive data interfaces. Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of the DataMagic. Homepage: https://datamagic-home.github.io/

AI.tldr: DataMagic is an end-to-end system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos, using a declarative specification (DVSpec) for data fidelity, a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture for narrative coherence, and interactive modes for explorability.
AI.motivation: Producing high-quality data videos requires combined expertise in data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing solutions fall short: static BI dashboards lack narrative logic and animation; authoring tools demand pre-prepared visualizations rather than raw data; and generative video models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance. A system is needed that automates the full pipeline from raw data to interactive narrative videos while maintaining data integrity.
AI.method: The system is built around three core components: (1) DVSpec, a declarative specification that binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields via data-driven semantic references, ensuring data fidelity and decoupling logic from rendering; (2) a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that first generates candidate scenes in parallel (tackling design-space combinatorial explosion) and then globally orchestrates them for narrative coherence; (3) three interaction modes and structured provenance-based data Q&A that transform one-way videos into explorable interactive interfaces, leveraging DVSpec's logic-rendering decoupling.
AI.result: Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validated the effectiveness of the DataMagic system.
AI.conclusion: DataMagic successfully bridges the gap between raw data and high-quality narrative data videos by combining declarative data-video binding, multi-agent orchestration, and interactive post-hoc exploration, offering a practical and validated end-to-end solution.

title: StaminaBench: Stress-Testing Coding Agents over 100 Interaction Turns
summary: We introduce StaminaBench, a benchmark that measures the stamina of coding agents: how many consecutive interaction turns (change requests) they can handle before failing. Unlike the prevailing fraction-of-tasks-solved metric, this matches real vibe-coding where sessions run dozens or hundreds of turns. In StaminaBench, agents implement a REST API server and modify it across a tunable number of procedurally generated follow-up change requests - 100 in our experiments, resulting in codebases of up to 6,000 lines.
