Tests are generated fully programmatically without LLM involvement, ensuring reproducibility and reliability; change sequences are drawn from either a hardcoded or LLM-driven sampler, both constrained to a structured action space to ensure changes are valid. The agent and the server run in an isolated environment and communicate with the benchmark through HTTP, making testing fully black-box and language-agnostic. We evaluate six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each and find that: (1) all the tested models fail within 5-6 turns, confirming that vibe-coding-style programming without thorough testing produces bugs; (2) passing test feedback back to the agent and allowing it to retry improves passed turn count by up to 12x; and (3) a good harness is required for strong performance: stronger models exhibit up to a 6x gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail with any harness. We release the benchmark and the generated tasks to enable further research into multi-turn coding agent behavior. Benchmark code and data: github.com/amazon-science/StaminaBench.

AI.tldr: StaminaBench is a benchmark measuring coding agents' ability to handle long sequences of consecutive change requests (stamina), where all tested models fail within 5-6 turns without test feedback, but passing test feedback back improves performance up to 12x, and harness quality strongly influences stronger models.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks use a fraction-of-tasks-solved metric that fails to capture real-world "vibe-coding" scenarios where sessions involve dozens or hundreds of consecutive interaction turns. There is a need to evaluate agent stamina—how many turns an agent can sustain before failure—rather than just one-shot task completion rates.
AI.method: StaminaBench procedurally generates 100-turn change request sequences for implementing and modifying a REST API server, producing codebases up to ~6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically (no LLM involvement) for reproducibility. Change sequences come from hardcoded or LLM-driven samplers within a structured action space. The agent and server communicate via HTTP in an isolated black-box, language-agnostic environment. Six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs are evaluated across 20 scenarios.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) All models fail within 5-6 turns without test feedback; (2) Passing test feedback with retry capability improves passed turn count by up to 12x; (3) Harness quality matters significantly—stronger models show up to a 6x performance gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail regardless of harness.
AI.conclusion: Vibe-coding-style programming without thorough testing is unsustainable beyond a few turns. Test feedback loops and high-quality agent harnesses are critical for long-horizon coding tasks. The benchmark and data are publicly released to spur research on multi-turn coding agent behavior.

title: Trustworthy Multi-Agent Systems: Mitigating Semantic Drift with the Argent Signaling Protocol
summary:
When multi-agent LLM systems produce bad answers, not all failures are equal: some answers are grounded in the right material but incomplete, while others are simply ungrounded and should be stopped. Current retry strategies treat both cases identically (try again and hope for the best), leaving human supervisors unable to tell whether a retry was warranted or whether the system should have halted instead.
  We introduce the Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP), a compact machine-readable header that accompanies every AI-generated response with structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index that classifies the evidentiary basis of each claim. These signals enable a controller to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures and route each case differently.
  We evaluate ASP in two modes. In standalone mode, a 27-question document-grounded QA benchmark over the Array BioPharma/Ono license agreement compares baseline prompts against ASP-instrumented controller actions across three local GGUF models. On Qwen~(0.8B), ASP improves pass rate from 11.1% to 33.3% and mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; on Dobby~(8B), ASP produces 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; on SmolLM3~(3B), ASP alternates between repair and containment per question. Aggregate improvement is meaningful (12/81 to 21/81 passes). In multi-agent mode, an ASP sidecar sits between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent; the sidecar blocks 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs from reaching the downstream agent (24/27 blocked, 0 ungrounded propagations).

AI.tldr: ASP is a machine-readable protocol header that tags LLM outputs with quality signals (certainty, grounding, stochasticity, assumption index) so a controller can distinguish repairable failures from ungrounded ones and route them differently, improving QA pass rates and blocking ungrounded propagation in multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: Current LLM retry strategies treat all failures identically, conflating grounded-but-incomplete answers with ungrounded ones. Human supervisors cannot determine whether a retry was justified or the system should have halted. A mechanism is needed to classify failure types and enable differentiated routing.
AI.method: The Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP) appends a structured header with four signals — certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index — to every AI response. A controller interprets these signals to route outputs: repairable failures get retried, containment failures get halted. Evaluated in standalone mode (27-question document QA benchmark on a legal contract, three GGUF models: Qwen 0.8B, Dobby 8B, SmolLM3 3B) and multi-agent mode (ASP sidecar between retrieval and decision agents, blocking ungrounded upstream outputs).
AI.result: Standalone: Qwen 0.8B pass rate 11.1%→33.3%, mean term coverage 36.7%→65.4%; Dobby 8B pass rate 33.3%→44.4% with 4 fail-to-pass recoveries; SmolLM3 3B alternates repair/containment per question; aggregate passes 12/81→21/81. Multi-agent: ASP sidecar blocked 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs (24/27 blocked, 0 ungrounded propagations).
AI.conclusion: ASP provides a lightweight, interpretable mechanism for classifying and differentially routing LLM failures, yielding meaningful improvements in both standalone QA and multi-agent settings. It prevents ungrounded information from cascading downstream while preserving repairable responses for retry.

title: Configurable Clinical Information Extraction with Agentic RAG: What Works, What Breaks, and Why
summary: Patient contexts span hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, yet the document-level metadata that AI systems need for retrieval and triage is absent or incomplete. Standard retrieval-augmented generation fails on this data, mishandling temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata. We deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) at University Medicine Essen: an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in source passages for clinician verification. We quantify the metadata gap, trace the architectural decisions it shaped, and evaluate extraction alongside an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study, in which nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources. Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5\% of extractions, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80\% to 99\%.

AI.tldr: ACIE is an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline deployed at University Medicine Essen that extracts structured clinical information from heterogeneous patient documents. In a lymphoma registry study with 7,326 clinician judgments, 96.5% of extractions were accepted, with per-type accuracy ranging from 80%–99%.
AI.motivation: Patient contexts contain hundreds of documents and thousands of structured data points, but critical document-level metadata for AI retrieval and triage is missing or incomplete. Standard RAG fails due to poor temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and absent metadata. There is a demonstrated "metadata gap" that necessitates a different architectural approach.
AI.method: The authors deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction), an on-premise agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The system reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in cited source passages to enable clinician verification. It is evaluated through an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study where nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources.
AI.result: Across 7,326 clinician judgments in the lymphoma registry study, 96.5% of extractions were accepted. Per-type acceptance rates ranged from a low of 80% to a high of 99%.
AI.conclusion: An agentic RAG architecture that reasons over complete patient contexts with source-grounded outputs can achieve clinically acceptable extraction accuracy, addressing the metadata gap that causes standard RAG to fail on real-world clinical data.

title: Physics-Informed Discovery of Yield Functions in Plasticity via Convex Neural Representations
summary: Identifying anisotropic yield functions remains challenging since yielding is not directly observed in full-field mechanical measurements, directional calibration can require many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. This study proposes a physics-informed framework for discovering yield functions from full-field displacement data and reaction force data, without stress observations, plastic strain measurements, direct yield surface data, or a prescribed parametric yield function. The framework identifies the yield function as a mechanically constrained constitutive component inside elastoplastic stress integration, rather than through direct stress-space supervision. The yield function is represented by a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one while imposing the assumed tension-compression symmetry, and this neural yield function is trained with a differentiable stress update and a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases. The proposed framework is validated using finite element (FE) benchmark studies with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions, assessing yield contour agreement, displacement-noise sensitivity, identifiability through plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and polynomial-surrogate deployment. This study provides a mechanics-constrained pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while keeping the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed framework is proposed to discover anisotropic yield functions directly from full-field displacement and reaction force data, without requiring stress observations, plastic strain measurements, or a pre-specified yield function form. The yield function is represented as a convex neural network embedded within elastoplastic stress integration, trained via a differentiable stress update and force equilibrium loss, and validated on benchmark yield functions.
AI.motivation: Identifying anisotropic yield functions is challenging because yielding is not directly observable in full-field measurements, directional calibration demands many loading cases, and choosing an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. Existing methods typically require stress-space supervision or a prescribed parametric form, limiting their applicability.
AI.method: The framework uses a convex neural network to represent the yield function, enforcing convexity, positive homogeneity of degree one, and tension-compression symmetry. This neural yield function is embedded as a constitutive component within elastoplastic stress integration. Training employs a differentiable stress update and a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases, using only full-field displacement data and reaction force data. Validation uses FE benchmarks with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions, assessing yield contour agreement, displacement-noise sensitivity, identifiability via plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and polynomial-surrogate deployment.
AI.result: The framework successfully recovers yield surfaces consistent with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d benchmarks. Assessments demonstrate robust yield contour agreement, sensitivity analysis to displacement noise, identifiability through plastically active stress states, quantification of epistemic uncertainty, and feasibility of deploying the learned yield function as a polynomial surrogate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a mechanics-constrained, data-driven pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data, keeping the identified component fully integrated within the elastoplastic stress integration structure, thus avoiding the need for direct stress-space supervision or pre-specified parametric forms.

title: A Measurement Study of Cryptographic Misuse in Embodied AI Mobile Applications
summary: Embodied AI (EAI) mobile applications are evolving from auxiliary user interfaces into active control-path components, directly linking mobile-side cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust. Despite this shift, existing security research predominantly focuses on embodied AI devices and cloud infrastructures, leaving the mobile control layer largely unexplored as a critical attack surface. To bridge this gap, we present the first large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse within the EAI mobile ecosystem. We construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world applications across six EAI domains, and employ an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to measure the prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes. Our measurement yields 12,975 misuse findings (with an evaluated precision of 80.74\%), revealing that these cryptographic failures are driven by EAI-specific engineering constraints rather than random developer errors. We uncover structural security trade-offs: latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport protection, while the heavy reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates the local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Through real-world case studies, we demonstrate how these mobile-side cryptographic flaws bypass nominal network protections, enabling adversaries to intercept command channels and hijack the physical control of EAI entities. Ultimately, our findings highlight that mobile applications have become a fragile, yet overlooked, cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems.

AI.tldr: First large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse in embodied AI mobile apps (507 apps, 6 domains), finding 12,975 misuse instances (80.74% precision). Reveals EAI-specific engineering constraints — latency-sensitive control paths and legacy IoT SDKs — systematically weaken transport security and hardcode credentials, enabling device hijacking via mobile-side flaws.
AI.motivation: Embodied AI mobile apps are increasingly becoming active control-path components bridging cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust, yet the mobile control layer remains an unexplored critical attack surface. Existing research focuses only on EAI devices and cloud infrastructure, leaving a gap in understanding mobile-side cryptographic vulnerabilities.
AI.method: Constructed EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world EAI mobile applications across six domains. Employed an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to measure prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes. Validated findings through real-world case studies.
AI.result: Identified 12,975 cryptographic misuse findings with 80.74% evaluated precision. Cryptographic failures stem from EAI-specific engineering constraints, not random errors: latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport protection; offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbate local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Demonstrates mobile-side flaws bypass nominal network protections, enabling command channel interception and physical control hijacking.
AI.conclusion: Mobile applications have become a fragile yet overlooked cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems. The findings underscore the need for the security community to address EAI-specific constraints in mobile control-layer design.

title: Characterizing Narrative Content in Web-scale LLM Pretraining Data
comment: 8 pages of main content, 28 total pages. 30 figures
summary: The narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored even though narrative is a fundamental mode of human communication. We present the first fine-grained study of narrative features in Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open pretraining corpus. Drawing on narrative theory, we design a framework spanning three core narrative elements (agency, setting, and events) operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. After sampling and annotating a diverse set of 400 passages, we finetune and validate NarraBERT, a RoBERTa-based model for fine-grained narrative prediction. We apply NarraBERT to 3M passages, resulting in a new dataset, NarraDolma. We find (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data, (ii) we uncover a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlying web text, and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics in ways that current curation practices neither measure nor account for. Our framework, dataset, and analyses provide a foundation for understanding how narrative qualities are distributed in LLM pretraining data and for studying how data composition affects narrative reasoning tasks. We publicly release NarraDolma and NarraBERT.

AI.tldr: First fine-grained study of narrative features in LLM pretraining data (Dolma corpus), introducing a theory-driven framework with 11 dimensions, a prediction model (NarraBERT), and a 3M-passage dataset (NarraDolma), revealing measurable, multidimensional, and unequally distributed narrative structures across web-scale pretraining corpora.
AI.motivation: Despite narrative being a fundamental mode of human communication, the narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored. Current data curation practices neither measure nor account for narrative qualities, leaving a gap in understanding how narrative structure in pretraining data may affect downstream narrative reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: The authors draw on narrative theory to design a framework spanning three core narrative elements — agency, setting, and events — operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. They sample and annotate 400 diverse passages from Dolma (a 3-trillion-token open corpus), then fine-tune and validate NarraBERT (a RoBERTa-based model) for fine-grained narrative prediction. NarraBERT is applied to 3 million passages to produce NarraDolma, a large-scale dataset of narrative annotations.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous web data; (ii) a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlies web text; and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics — variations that current curation practices neither measure nor account for.
AI.conclusion: The framework, NarraBERT model, and NarraDolma dataset provide foundational tools for understanding narrative quality distribution in LLM pretraining data and for investigating how data composition influences narrative reasoning tasks. All artifacts are publicly released.

title: Which Pairs to Compare for LLM Post-Training?
summary: Preference-based post-training has become a central paradigm for aligning language models. A common data-collection strategy is to generate a small set of completions for each prompt and label the resulting comparison pairs. However, human preference labels are often much more expensive than generating additional completions, suggesting a different use of the same labeling budget: generate a larger pool of completions, but label only the most informative comparison pairs. This paper studies which pairs should be compared in preference-based post-training. We formulate comparison curation as a sampling-design problem and evaluate designs by the quality of the final policy under the preference-based post-training objective. We instantiate this framework for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), analyzing how the choice of labeled pairs propagates through DPO training to downstream policy performance. Our main results provide matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap of the DPO-trained policy. The bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream performance through a single design-dependent information matrix, which links label allocation to parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation and motivates practical sampling designs for selecting informative pairs from large generated completion pools. Experiments on synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks show that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes comparison curation in DPO post-training as a sampling-design problem, deriving matching upper/lower bounds on policy suboptimality that depend on a design-dependent information matrix. This yields an optimization criterion for selecting the most informative comparison pairs from large completion pools, improving sample efficiency over naive heuristics.
AI.motivation: Human preference labels are far more expensive than generating completions. Current practice wastes labeling budget on comparing randomly chosen completions rather than selecting the most informative pairs. The paper addresses how to optimally allocate a fixed labeling budget across candidate comparison pairs to maximize downstream policy quality.
AI.method: The authors frame comparison curation as an optimal experimental design problem under the DPO objective. They derive non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the suboptimality gap of the DPO-trained policy relative to the optimal policy, showing the gap depends on a design-dependent information (Fisher-like) matrix. This matrix encodes how label allocations propagate through parameter estimation to policy performance. They then derive an explicit optimization criterion (e.g., D-optimal or A-optimal design) for selecting which pairs to label, and propose practical sampling strategies for informative pair selection from large pools.
AI.result: The derived bounds establish that the information matrix is the key sufficient statistic linking comparison design to downstream policy suboptimality. The proposed optimal-design-based sampling strategies consistently outperform random pairing and other common heuristics on both synthetic settings and real language-model post-training benchmarks in terms of sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Comparison curation is a principled design problem with a clear optimization criterion. Budgeted labeling should target pairs that maximize information gain in parameter space, not random pairs. The framework provides practical, theoretically-grounded sampling designs that improve DPO sample efficiency.

title: Multi-Agent Transactive Memory
summary: The decentralized deployment of LLM agents with diverse capabilities across diverse tasks motivates infrastructure for knowledge sharing across heterogeneous agent populations. Just as search engines index human-generated artifacts to support human problem solving, retrieval systems can organize agent-generated artifacts for reuse across agent populations. We extend retrieval-augmented generation - which demonstrates the value of human-authored artifacts to individual agents - to retrieval of agent-generated artifacts supporting a population of agents. In particular, agent trajectories encode reusable procedural knowledge, yet these artifacts are typically discarded after a single use or retained only by the producing agent, forcing newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover existing solutions. We propose Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of agent-generated trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. We focus on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena), where trajectories are long and encode especially rich procedural structure. Our experiments demonstrate that retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces interaction steps without coordination or joint training. These results position MATM as a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems.

AI.tldr: MATM is a framework where LLM agents share task execution trajectories through a population-level repository, enabling agent populations to retrieve and reuse procedural knowledge, which improves task performance and efficiency without coordination or joint training.
AI.motivation: LLM agent trajectories encode reusable procedural knowledge but are typically discarded after single use or siloed within individual agents. This forces newly instantiated agents to wastefully rediscover existing solutions. Just as web search indexes human artifacts, agent populations need infrastructure for sharing agent-generated artifacts.
AI.method: MATM extends retrieval-augmented generation from human-authored to agent-generated artifacts. Producer agents contribute execution trajectories to a shared repository; consumer agents retrieve relevant trajectories to guide their own task execution. The framework is evaluated on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena) where trajectories are long and contain rich procedural structure.
AI.result: Retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces the number of interaction steps required, without any coordination mechanisms or joint training between agents.
AI.conclusion: MATM serves as an effective design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems, enabling heterogeneous agent populations to benefit from collective procedural memory.

title: Accelerating Trust Convergence in IIoT: A ML Approach for Dynamic Network Conditions
summary: In Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments, trust management plays a vital role in securing systems, especially when dealing with resource-constrained devices. Traditional trust models often overlook the impact of fluctuating network quality, leading to slower trust convergence and inaccurate assessments. In this paper, we propose a dynamic trust management solution, known as the Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach, which integrates Machine Learning (ML) to accelerate trust convergence under poor network conditions. Our model predicts the number of time units needed for trust convergence based on key network metrics and dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model to enhance convergence speed. Using a simulation framework that incorporates realistic Wi-Fi channel conditions based on the IEEE 802.11 standard, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the TCA-based approach, achieving up to a 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging conditions. Furthermore, the proposed solution exhibits resilience in scenarios involving malicious nodes, improving trust evaluation accuracy. This work provides a scalable and adaptive trust framework for IIoT systems in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach that uses machine learning to dynamically accelerate trust convergence in IIoT environments under poor network conditions, achieving up to 28.6% reduction in convergence time.
AI.motivation: Traditional trust models in IIoT ignore fluctuating network quality, resulting in slow trust convergence and inaccurate assessments, particularly problematic for resource-constrained devices in dynamic industrial environments.
AI.method: The TCA approach employs ML to predict the number of time units required for trust convergence based on key network metrics (e.g., Wi-Fi channel conditions per IEEE 802.11). It dynamically adapts transition probabilities within the trust model to accelerate convergence. Validation is performed via a simulation framework incorporating realistic channel conditions.
AI.result: The TCA-based approach achieved up to 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging network conditions and demonstrated resilience against malicious nodes, improving trust evaluation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed solution offers a scalable and adaptive trust framework suitable for IIoT systems operating in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance regardless of varying network conditions.

title: Creating Multilingual Mental Health Dialogue Datasets: Limits of Persona-Based Localization via Nationality and Language
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 2026 Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026), co-located with ACL 2026
summary: AI and large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools to address global mental health challenges. Despite the global nature of these challenges, there remains a critical shortage of high-quality datasets for training and evaluating such systems. To mitigate this gap, researchers increasingly generate synthetic clinical personas to simulate user data and test digital mental health support systems. However, most validated personas rely on English-centric contexts. This paper investigates whether similar persona-based methods can be used to generate multilingual mental health datasets. We modified nationality and language parameters in personas to generate clinical dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. We then examined how different LLMs perform when evaluating the depression severity of these generated multilingual datasets against the baseline in English. Our findings indicate that just adding nationality and language parameters in personas might not be adequate, as it can introduce clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judge models often exhibit inaccuracies in assessing depression severity in non-English texts, with performance varying across different models. This exposes the systemic limitations of applying English-centric personas to multilingual contexts. Ultimately, our work highlights the urgent need for culturally responsive data generation to ensure equitable mental health systems globally.

AI.tldr: Modifying nationality and language parameters in English-centric personas to generate multilingual clinical dialogues (Mandarin, Bengali, Hindi) introduces clinical inconsistencies, and LLM evaluators show variable inaccuracies when assessing depression severity in non-English texts.
AI.motivation: There is a critical shortage of high-quality, non-English datasets for training and evaluating AI-driven mental health support systems. While synthetic persona generation is widely used to simulate clinical data, existing validated personas are predominantly English-centric, raising questions about their applicability to multilingual contexts.
AI.method: The authors modified nationality and language parameters in existing clinical personas to generate mental health dialogue datasets in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. They then benchmarked multiple LLMs as "judge" models to evaluate depression severity in these generated multilingual dialogues and compared performance against the English baseline.
AI.result: Simply adding nationality and language parameters proved insufficient, introducing clinical inconsistencies across languages. LLM judge models exhibited inaccuracies in assessing depression severity in non-English texts, with performance variability across different models, exposing systemic limitations of English-centric persona generation.
AI.conclusion: The work underscores the urgent need for culturally responsive data generation methods rather than superficial parameter adjustments, to ensure equitable and clinically valid mental health AI systems globally.

title: Prompt Quality and Pull Request Outcomes: A Stage-Based Empirical Study of LLM-Assisted Development
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering workflows, yet little is known about how prompt structure influences downstream pull request (PR) outcomes. Prior studies primarily examine conversational helpfulness, productivity, or coarse-grained adoption metrics, leaving the role of prompt structure in collaborative integration behavior insufficiently understood. We analyze 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions derived from self-admitted ChatGPT usage in open-source pull requests. Building on prior research on developer-facing artifacts and prompt engineering, we operationalize prompt structure using three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification. We first evaluate whether LLM-assisted annotation can reliably reproduce human judgments of prompt structure, finding substantial variation across dimensions and workflow contexts. Specificity shows the most stable agreement with human judgments; Context is systematically under-scored by the LLM; and Verification remains difficult to assess consistently, motivating a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy. Using this validated framework, we then examine how prompt structure influences actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth across AI-assisted PR workflows. Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification emerges as the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context. Overall, our findings show that prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows, influencing downstream adoption and integration through contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how prompt structure (Context, Specificity, Verification) in ChatGPT-assisted pull requests influences downstream outcomes — actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth — using 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions from open-source PRs. A hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy is developed due to inconsistent LLM-only assessments.
AI.motivation: Despite growing use of LLM-powered tools like ChatGPT in collaborative software engineering, prior work focuses on conversational helpfulness or coarse-grained adoption metrics, leaving the role of prompt structure in PR outcomes poorly understood. The authors aim to close this gap by systematically characterizing how prompt design influences multi-stage collaborative integration behavior.
AI.method: The authors collected 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions extracted from self-admitted ChatGPT usage in open-source pull requests. Prompt structure is operationalized along three dimensions — Context (background/grounding information), Specificity (task precision and detail), and Verification (evaluability cues). They first test whether LLM-assisted annotation can reliably reproduce human judgments, finding uneven agreement, and consequently adopt a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy. Using this validated framework, they then statistically examine associations between the three prompt dimensions and three downstream outcomes: actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth.
AI.result: LLM-only annotation shows substantial variation: Specificity achieves the most stable agreement with human judgments; Context is systematically under-scored by the LLM; and Verification is inconsistently assessed. In the outcome analysis, Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification is the primary predictor of code adoption; and Context is most strongly associated with integration depth. Prompt characteristics thus exert distinct, stage-dependent effects.
AI.conclusion: Prompt structure matters in AI-assisted software engineering, but its effects are not uniform — they are stage-dependent. Contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues each influence different phases of the PR workflow (generation, adoption, integration), underscoring the need for prompt-aware tool design and process guidance in collaborative AI-assisted development.

title: Reliability without Validity: A Systematic, Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge Models Across Agreement, Consistency, and Bias
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for language models, but judge validation in practice relies on exact-match agreement, a metric that does not correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability. We present the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge to date: 21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench, evaluated under three protocols (agreement, consistency, bias audit) over 118 runs and approximately 541,000 individual judgments. Four findings emerge, consistent across the full cohort, including the April 2026 frontier: kappa deflation between exact match and Cohen's kappa is universal (33--41 pp on MT-Bench), judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks, high test--retest reliability (>0.95) coexists with severe position bias (>0.10) in two production-deployed judges (instantiating a consistency--bias paradox), and verbosity bias is small (<0.011) across our cohort under a single pairwise rubric. We distill these into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper conducts the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge, assessing 21 judges across three benchmarks under three protocols (~541K judgments). It finds that exact-match agreement systematically overstates judge quality; Cohen's kappa reveals universal deflation (33–41 pp), judge rankings shift dramatically across benchmarks, and a consistency–bias paradox emerges where high test–retest reliability coexists with severe position bias. The authors distill findings into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-as-a-Judge validation practices rely on exact-match agreement, which fails to correct for chance agreement and systematically inflates perceived discriminative ability. There is no standardized, rigorous validation protocol, leaving practitioners with misleading quality assessments. The work aims to establish empirical baselines and a principled validation framework.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 21 LLM judges from nine providers on MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench using three protocols: (1) agreement (exact-match vs. Cohen's kappa), (2) consistency (test–retest reliability), and (3) bias audit (position bias, verbosity bias). The study spans 118 runs and approximately 541,000 individual judgments, including frontier models as of April 2026.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Cohen's kappa deflation relative to exact-match agreement is universal, ranging 33–41 percentage points on MT-Bench; (2) judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions depending on the benchmark used; (3) a consistency–bias paradox: two production-deployed judges exhibit high test–retest reliability (>0.95) yet severe position bias (>0.10); (4) verbosity bias is small (<0.011) across the cohort under a single pairwise rubric.
AI.conclusion: Exact-match agreement is an inadequate validation metric; Cohen's kappa should be adopted as standard. Judge quality is not monolithic — rankings are benchmark-dependent. The consistency–bias paradox shows that reliability alone is insufficient; bias auditing is essential. The proposed Minimum Viable Validation Protocol synthesizes these lessons into a practical framework for rigorous LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation.

authors: Antonio de Sousa Leitão Filho; Allan Kardec Duailibe Barros Filho; Fabrício Saul Lima; Selby Mykael Lima dos Santos; Rejani Bandeira Vieira Sousa
title: Toten: Knowledge-Based Ontological Tokenization Of Physical Quantities And Technical Notation In Brazilian Portuguese
summary: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization is statistically efficient for vocabulary compression, but semantically blind to structured technical entities, fragmenting physical quantities, numbers, units, and symbolic expressions into lexically arbitrary subwords. We present TOTEN, a knowledge-based ontological tokenization framework that replaces statistical derivation with declarative classification grounded in a formal ontology of engineering entities (OEE). We formalize TOTEN as the triple <O, classify, {inst_tau}>: the ontology gathers types, structural principles, composition relations, and preservable invariants; the classification function maps raw text into typed regions; and the instantiator family yields a self-descriptive structured representation. Robustness derives from deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional), Unicode Character Database (typographic), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Intrinsic evaluation covers four properties verifiable by construction -- ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction -- over an internal, physically validated benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1771 eligible cases). We also report detection recall, distinguishing coverage from conditional atomicity. Against eight state-of-the-art baselines, TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts and numerical reconstruction of 0.775-0.904 on external corpora, vs. 0.627-0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity of the control benchmark. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint, the oracle from which the system inherits dimensional authority.

AI.tldr: TOTEN is a knowledge-based tokenization framework that replaces statistical Byte-Pair Encoding with ontology-driven classification, achieving superior atomicity for engineering entities (quantities, units, numbers) by grounding tokenization in a formal ontology and three external oracles.
AI.motivation: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization, while statistically efficient, is semantically blind: it fragments structured technical entities like physical quantities, units, and symbolic expressions into arbitrary subwords. This undermines downstream NLP tasks in scientific and engineering domains where preserving the integrity of such entities is critical.
AI.method: TOTEN is formalized as a triple: an ontology (OEE) defining types, composition relations, and invariants; a classification function that maps raw text into typed regions; and an instantiator family producing self-descriptive structured representations. Robustness is ensured through deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional analysis), the Unicode Character Database (typographic classification), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). The framework is evaluated intrinsically on four properties verifiable by construction: ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction.
AI.result: On external Brazilian Portuguese corpora (N=1,771), TOTEN achieves numerical reconstruction scores of 0.775–0.904 versus 0.627–0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3). On the internal EngQuant benchmark (N=800), TOTEN scores 0.780 vs. 0.340 for Quantulum3. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint. Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity.
AI.conclusion: TOTEN demonstrates that knowledge-based, ontology-grounded tokenization significantly outperforms statistical methods for preserving the structural integrity of engineering entities. The framework's deterministic coupling with authoritative oracles provides robust, verifiable guarantees that statistical tokenizers cannot offer, establishing a new paradigm for domain-specific tokenization.

title: Emyx: Fast and efficient all-atom protein generation
summary: Computational enzyme design requires generating proteins that scaffold catalytic residues and ligands, a task that demands both geometric accuracy and structural diversity from the underlying generative model. Current all-atom generators inherit expensive architectures from structure prediction, leading to high training costs and limited sample diversity. We argue that much of this complexity is unnecessary for generators, which condition on sparse geometric constraints rather than rich co-evolutionary signals. Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that concentrates capacity within standard transformer blocks, replacing heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity. We additionally derive an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, bridging flow matching training efficiency with state-of-the-art sampling methods designed for diffusion models without retraining. Despite being the smallest model, Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 against the AME enzyme design benchmark across success rate under strict evaluation requiring both global fold recovery and catalytic geometry accuracy, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity, while training in just $682$ GPU-hours, roughly $4\times$ less than RFdiffusion3.

AI.tldr: Emyx is a lightweight 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model for computational enzyme design that outperforms larger models (Proteína-Complexa, RFdiffusion3) on the AME benchmark while requiring only 682 GPU-hours (~4× less than RFdiffusion3). It achieves this by replacing heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and bridging flow matching with EDM noise-level sampling.
AI.motivation: Current all-atom generators for enzyme design inherit expensive architectures from structure prediction models, resulting in high training costs and limited sample diversity. The authors argue this complexity is unnecessary because enzyme design conditions on sparse geometric constraints (catalytic residues and ligands) rather than rich co-evolutionary signals, motivating a streamlined architecture that retains geometric accuracy while improving diversity and efficiency.
AI.method: Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that: (1) concentrates capacity within standard transformer blocks instead of heavy embedding stacks; (2) uses lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity; and (3) introduces an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, enabling flow matching training efficiency combined with state-of-the-art diffusion sampling methods without retraining.
AI.result: On the AME enzyme design benchmark, Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 across multiple metrics: success rate under strict evaluation (requiring both global fold recovery and catalytic geometry accuracy), structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity. It achieves this while training in only 682 GPU-hours, approximately 4× less than RFdiffusion3, despite being the smallest model.
AI.conclusion: Heavy architectures inherited from structure prediction are unnecessary for generative enzyme design. A streamlined flow matching model with lightweight conditioning and EDM-compatible sampling can achieve superior performance in both quality and diversity at a fraction of the training cost, setting a new state-of-the-art on the AME benchmark.

title: When Does Streaming Tool Use Help? Characterizing Tool-Intent Stabilization in Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Streaming RAG) reduces user-perceived latency by issuing tool queries in parallel with ongoing user input, before the utterance is complete. Reported gains are aggregate, yet the mechanism's benefit is fundamentally query-intrinsic: speculation can only help when the correct tool query becomes determinable before the user stops speaking or typing. We isolate and measure this property -- tool-intent stabilization, the point in the input stream at which a speculative query's retrieval converges to the answer-bearing result. On the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions) we (i) measure the distribution of stabilization, (ii) derive a model-agnostic bound H on the portion of tool latency that can be hidden behind the user's remaining input, as a function of tool latency L and input cadence δ, (iii) validate against a working streaming pipeline that realized savings meet or exceed this bound, and (iv) identify which query properties predict early versus late stabilization. The study requires no model training and runs on commodity CPU hardware. We find that at a realistic operating point (L=600ms, δ=3w/s, θ=0.8), 73.9% of queries across the full benchmark admit substantial latency hiding -- a blended figure that mixes sufficiency stabilization on the 21.3% of questions where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable (95.2% streamable on this favorable slice) with a grounding-free top-1-settling fallback on the remainder. On the favorable slice, φ_suf is bracketed to [0.26, 0.281] by exact and relaxed grounding -- both early. Question type produces a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, epsilon^2=0.04), directly informing when a learned speculative trigger is worth its cost.

AI.tldr: This paper measures tool-intent stabilization — the point during user input when a speculative tool query's retrieval result converges to the final answer-bearing result — and derives a model-agnostic bound on how much tool latency can be hidden behind remaining user input. On the CRAG benchmark, 73.9% of queries admit substantial latency hiding at realistic operating parameters.
AI.motivation: Streaming RAG reduces perceived latency by speculatively issuing tool queries before the user finishes speaking/typing, but its benefit is fundamentally query-intrinsic: speculation only helps when the correct tool query becomes determinable early. The paper aims to isolate and quantify this stabilization property, which prior work only measured in aggregate.
AI.method: Authors measure tool-intent stabilization on the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions) by simulating streaming input word-by-word and tracking when retrieval results converge. They derive a model-agnostic bound H = (L/δ) × θ relating latency hiding to tool latency L and input cadence δ. Two stabilization criteria are used: sufficiency stabilization (φ_suf, where gold evidence is verbatim-present and retrievable via BM25) and grounding-free top-1-settling. No model training is required; all experiments run on commodity CPU.
AI.result: At L=600ms, δ=3 words/second, θ=0.8: 73.9% of all CRAG queries admit substantial latency hiding. On the favorable slice (21.3% of questions with verbatim-present gold evidence), 95.2% are streamable, with φ_suf bracketed to [0.26, 0.281] (early stabilization). Question type yields a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, ε²=0.04).
AI.conclusion: Tool-intent stabilization is an intrinsic, measurable query property that determines Streaming RAG's effectiveness. The derived bound H enables latency-hiding prediction without running a full pipeline. The significant split by question type directly informs when learned speculative triggers are worth their computational cost, enabling selective deployment.

title: GNSS Spoofing Threat for V2X communications
comment: 2026 IEEE\@. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) constitute a core technology for delivering crucial positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services in the Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) domain, where they are indispensable for generating Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM) that uphold network reliability and vehicular safety. Yet, GNSS signals are acutely exposed to spoofing, an advanced attack in which an adversary transmits crafted signals that replicate legitimate satellite characteristics, misleading the receiver into computing a false position. This work presents a methodology for conducting physical spoofing with inexpensive Software Defined Radio (SDR), describing a coordinate generation pipeline that employs Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization to emulate constant velocity, and linear interpolation to produce high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The proposed attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OnBoard Unit (OBU) and RoadSide Unit (RSU) devices using a HackRF One across three scenarios that emulate synthetic trajectories at steady speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h. The most significant contribution of this paper is the demonstration that V2X communications are not secured, as they are susceptible to GNSS spoofing attacks, which cause service degradation without being detected.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a low-cost GNSS spoofing attack against V2X OnBoard and RoadSide Units using an SDR, demonstrating that V2X communications are vulnerable to undetected spoofing that degrades safety-critical PNT services.
AI.motivation: GNSS is essential for V2X Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM), which underpin vehicular safety and network reliability. However, GNSS signals are highly susceptible to spoofing attacks. The authors aim to expose the practical vulnerability of real V2X hardware to low-cost physical spoofing, thereby highlighting a critical security gap in vehicular communication systems.
AI.method: The methodology comprises: (1) a coordinate generation pipeline using Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization for constant velocity emulation, and linear interpolation; (2) physical spoofing attack implementation using a HackRF One SDR to transmit crafted GPS baseband signals; (3) experimental validation on real Commsignia OBU and RSU devices across three synthetic trajectory scenarios at constant speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h.
AI.result: The spoofing attack successfully misled both OBU and RSU devices into computing false positions across all three tested velocity scenarios. The attack caused service degradation in V2X communications without triggering any detection mechanisms, confirming the susceptibility of production V2X hardware to GNSS spoofing.
AI.conclusion: V2X communications are not secured against GNSS spoofing attacks. Low-cost SDR equipment can execute physical spoofing that degrades V2X services undetectably, underscoring an urgent need for robust anti-spoofing countermeasures in vehicular communication standards and hardware.

title: Beyond Uniform Forgetting: A Study of Sequential Direct Preference Optimization Across Preference Settings
summary: Aligning language models with human preferences often requires optimising multiple behavioural objectives. A practical approach is to apply these objectives sequentially using preference optimisation methods such as Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO), but it remains unclear whether later training uniformly degrades preferences learned earlier or whether the effect depends on the relationship between objectives. We study sequential DPO across four preference settings covering distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters, we evaluate all objectives after every stage with a fixed base-model reference. We find that sequential DPO does not produce a single forgetting pattern; preference change ranges from partial degradation to stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order. Pair-level analysis using length-normalised policy margins shows that aggregate metrics can mask heterogeneous changes across preference pairs, whereas quartile decomposition reveals that high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve depending on the setting. Mechanistic diagnostics show that Stage~2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective across all settings, providing little evidence that direct gradient opposition is the primary driver. These findings suggest that future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength, rather than assuming that later objectives affect earlier preferences uniformly.

AI.tldr: Sequential DPO training does not cause uniform forgetting of earlier preferences. Instead, outcomes range from degradation to stability, redistribution, or positive transfer, depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order. Gradient analysis shows near-orthogonal adapter updates across stages, suggesting direct gradient opposition is not the primary mechanism.
AI.motivation: Practical alignment often requires applying multiple behavioural objectives sequentially via DPO, but it is unclear whether later training uniformly overwrites earlier preferences or whether the effect depends on how objectives relate. The work seeks to replace the assumption of uniform degradation with a nuanced understanding of when and why forgetting occurs.
AI.method: The authors conduct sequential DPO experiments using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters across four settings: distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. All objectives are evaluated after every stage using a fixed base-model reference. Pair-level analysis employs length-normalised policy margins and quartile decomposition. Mechanistic diagnostics measure gradient and adapter update orthogonality between stages.
AI.result: Sequential DPO yields four distinct outcomes: partial degradation, stability, pair-level redistribution, and positive transfer. Aggregate metrics mask heterogeneous pair-level changes. High-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve depending on the setting. Stage-2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective, indicating that direct gradient opposition is not the primary cause of forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength rather than assuming uniform degradation. The near-orthogonality of updates suggests forgetting arises from more subtle mechanisms than direct gradient conflict.

title: LaViSA: A Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity Benchmark
summary: Structural ambiguity arises when a single sentence admits multiple valid interpretations due to its syntactic structure, posing a fundamental challenge for language understanding. Visual scenes serve as useful cues for resolving such ambiguity, and Vision and Language Models (VLMs) need to be capable of deriving possible semantic interpretations from visual scenes. We introduce Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity (LaViSA), a benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of VLMs to resolve structural ambiguity leveraging visual scenes. LaViSA consists of ambiguous sentences, their disambiguated sentences, and corresponding images of these disambiguated sentences across seven ambiguity categories. Using LaViSA, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of diverse VLMs, including both proprietary and open-source models with varying parameter scales and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that although recent VLMs can leverage visual scenes to resolve structural ambiguity to a some extent, they still struggle with certain ambiguity types and visually subtle semantic distinctions, indicating remaining limitations in resolving structural ambiguity using visual scenes.

AI.tldr: LaViSA is a benchmark evaluating VLMs on resolving syntactic structural ambiguity using visual scenes across seven categories. Experiments reveal current VLMs can partially leverage visual cues but struggle with specific ambiguity types and subtle semantic distinctions.
AI.motivation: Structural ambiguity — where a sentence has multiple valid syntactic parses — is a fundamental challenge in language understanding. While visual scenes can help disambiguate such sentences, there is no systematic benchmark to evaluate how well Vision-Language Models (VLMs) use visual information to resolve these ambiguities.
AI.method: The authors introduce LaViSA, a benchmark comprising ambiguous sentences paired with their disambiguated counterparts and corresponding images, spanning seven ambiguity categories. They evaluate a diverse set of VLMs (both proprietary and open-source, across parameter scales and reasoning capabilities) on their ability to resolve structural ambiguity using visual cues.
AI.result: Recent VLMs demonstrate some capacity to leverage visual scenes for structural ambiguity resolution, but performance remains limited — particularly on certain ambiguity types and cases requiring fine-grained visual-semantic discrimination.
AI.conclusion: Despite progress, current VLMs exhibit clear limitations in using visual scenes to resolve structural ambiguity, highlighting an important area for future improvement in vision-language understanding.

title: AI4SE and SE4AI Exploration: A Decade Looking Back and Forward
summary: The March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and Systems Engineering (SE) became the most downloaded issue in the publication's history and launched a research community that now draws over 250 registrants to its annual workshop. In this article, we trace the progress in AI and SE across three phases (labeled here foundational, applied, and LLM inflection) based on the authors' reading of the field's core papers, and describe our opinions of where the community has converged and where critical gaps remain. Separately, a human-AI agreement literature review leveraging both human expertise and six AI models was performed to assess the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. The results identify five critical research gaps and offer guidance for practitioners navigating AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE. We share the agreement data and the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application so readers can compare their own relevance judgments with the human and AI raters.

AI.tldr: This paper traces the evolution of AI and Systems Engineering (SE) integration across three phases, identifies five critical research gaps through a large-scale human-AI agreement study of 1,712 INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications, and provides an interactive web tool for comparative relevance assessment.
AI.motivation: The growing convergence of AI and SE—evidenced by record readership and workshop attendance—demands a systematic understanding of the field's progress, areas of consensus, and unresolved gaps to guide practitioners in AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation.
AI.method: The authors (1) conducted a qualitative literature synthesis tracing AI and SE progress across three phases: foundational, applied, and LLM inflection; and (2) performed a human-AI agreement literature review where both human experts and six AI models independently assessed the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications to AI4SE/SE4AI topics.
AI.result: The analysis converged on five critical research gaps in AI4SE/SE4AI. The agreement study data and an accompanying AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application were released publicly, enabling readers to benchmark their own relevance judgments against both human and AI raters.
AI.conclusion: The AI and SE community has matured significantly since the 2020 inflection point, but substantial gaps remain. Practitioners are advised to focus on AI assurance, measured adoption strategies, and workforce transformation, while leveraging the shared tools and data for continued research alignment.

title: A Hybrid GNN-FEM Framework for Phase-Field Fracture Simulation. Physics-Preserving Hybridization for Generalizable Surrogate Modeling
summary: Scientific machine learning (SciML) has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating simulations of complex physical systems, yet achieving physically consistent and generalizable predictions for nonlinear, history-dependent problems remains a central challenge. In this study, we propose a hybrid GNN--FEM framework for efficient and generalizable phase-field fracture modeling. While phase-field approaches provide a robust variational framework for simulating complex crack evolution, their high computational cost limits practical applications because they require solving coupled, nonlinear, and history-dependent systems within an incremental finite element procedure. To address this challenge, a graph neural network surrogate is integrated into the conventional staggered scheme, replacing the phase-field update at each load increment while retaining the FEM-based displacement solver to enforce mechanical equilibrium and boundary conditions. By preserving the incremental solution structure, the framework remains consistent with history-dependent fracture evolution without requiring the surrogate to approximate the full solution trajectory. This selective surrogate strategy emphasizes the identification of a physically meaningful and incrementally structured learning target, rather than relying on brute-force data generation to learn the full fracture process. The proposed framework achieves strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations through dimensionless feature design, a graph-based formulation on mesh-based domains, and a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field equation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the hybrid approach reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy compared with conventional FEM, and exhibits robust predictive performance across diverse problem settings.

AI.tldr: A hybrid GNN-FEM framework is proposed for phase-field fracture modeling, where a graph neural network replaces only the phase-field update step within the conventional staggered scheme while retaining FEM for displacement, achieving computational speedup with strong generalization across geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations.
AI.motivation: Phase-field fracture models, while robust, are computationally prohibitive due to solving coupled, nonlinear, history-dependent systems incrementally in FEM. Existing SciML surrogates struggle with generalization and physical consistency for such nonlinear, history-dependent problems. The authors aim to reduce computational cost while preserving accuracy and generalizability.
AI.method: The authors propose a hybrid GNN-FEM framework that selectively replaces only the phase-field update in the staggered solution scheme with a graph neural network surrogate, while retaining the FEM displacement solver to enforce equilibrium and boundary conditions. Key design choices include: (1) dimensionless feature design to promote generalization, (2) a graph-based formulation operating on mesh domains, and (3) a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field PDE to enforce physical consistency.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that the hybrid GNN-FEM approach reduces computational cost compared to conventional FEM while maintaining accuracy. The framework exhibits robust predictive performance and strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and mesh discretizations.
AI.conclusion: Selectively replacing the phase-field update with a GNN surrogate within an incremental staggered FEM framework is an effective strategy for achieving physically consistent, generalizable, and computationally efficient phase-field fracture modeling, without requiring the surrogate to learn the full solution trajectory.

title: TrustMix: How to Mix Messages in a Mobile Ad-hoc Network
summary:
Mix networks are a highly effective way to achieve anonymity, defending against a wide range of traffic-analysis attacks. However, mix networks are usually designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied in the context of mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). The few existing solutions for MANETs require advance knowledge of the topology or a trusted central party.
  In this paper, we present TrustMix, a mix protocol for MANETs that operates without any central trusted party. In TrustMix, parties join groups and then messages are forwarded via multiple groups to provide anonymity. With TrustMix, users only need to find a party nearby that they consider trusted. They then forward the message to this party's group, and the party shuffles messages before forwarding to other groups, meaning that the original message and the forwarded message cannot be linked. Furthermore, even if the chosen party is adversarial, they can only break the anonymity if all parties in their group are adversarial as all of them contribute to the shuffling. In addition to anonymity, TrustMix also enforces rate limits on the number of messages through the use of linkable ring signatures, which allows detecting that parties send more messages that allowed without revealing identities.
  We prove the security of our protocol in the random oracle model. We evaluate its anonymity using an existing mix-network simulator and show that TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept Android implementation and show that TrustMix achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices.

AI.tldr: TrustMix is a decentralized mix network protocol for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs) that provides anonymous communication without requiring a trusted central party or advance topology knowledge. It uses group-based message shuffling combined with linkable ring signatures for rate limiting.
AI.motivation: Existing mix networks are designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied to MANETs. The few MANET-specific solutions either require advance knowledge of the network topology or rely on a trusted central party — both unrealistic assumptions in decentralized, dynamic mobile environments.
AI.method: TrustMix organizes parties into groups. A sender forwards a message to a nearby trusted party's group, where all group members collaboratively shuffle messages before forwarding to subsequent groups. This multi-hop group shuffling ensures unlinkability between original and forwarded messages. Linkable ring signatures enforce per-party rate limits, detecting violations without revealing identities. Security is proven in the random oracle model.
AI.result: Simulation using an existing mix-network simulator shows TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. A proof-of-concept Android implementation with 5 mobile devices demonstrates acceptable throughput, confirming practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: TrustMix successfully brings mix-network anonymity to MANETs in a fully decentralized manner, requiring only local trust decisions. The combination of group shuffling and linkable ring signatures provides both strong anonymity and enforceable rate limiting, with demonstrated practicality on mobile devices.

title: Learning to Prompt: Improving Student Engagement with Adaptive LLM-based High-School Tutoring
summary: LLMs can personalize education, although current static-prompt tutoring systems struggle to adapt to diverse academic disciplines. We develop and test a system with subject-aware prompting, based on 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) extracted from raw transcripts. We first train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment, and then deploy it for online adaptation with actual high-school students. The simulation benchmark shows the router outperforming two static baselines ($0.694$ vs. $0.647$ and $0.64$, $p<0.001$). A/B testing ($N=656$ conversations from 359 students) shows sim-to-real transfer where the model switches from analytical to scaffolding learning strategies. Our adaptive prompt selection mechanism improves instructional efficiency, maintains pedagogical quality and reduces interactions by around 3 turns ($p=0.007$). While a greedy router achieves a comparable exercise conversion rate with the baseline ($19.1\%$ vs. $19.6\%$), a stochastic router that samples strategies leads to a higher conversion rate ($28.1\%$).

AI.tldr: An adaptive LLM tutoring system using subject-aware prompt routing based on pedagogical features from transcripts outperforms static prompts in simulation and real-world A/B testing, with a stochastic router boosting exercise conversion rates to 28.1%.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based tutoring systems use static prompts that fail to adapt across diverse academic disciplines. Personalized education requires dynamic pedagogical strategies tailored to subject-specific needs, motivating the development of an adaptive prompt selection mechanism.
AI.method: 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) are extracted from raw tutoring transcripts. A prompt routing model is trained in a simulation environment, then deployed online with high-school students. Two routers are compared: a greedy router and a stochastic router that samples strategies. A/B testing involves 656 conversations from 359 students to evaluate sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: In simulation, the router significantly outperforms two static baselines (0.694 vs. 0.647 and 0.64, p<0.001). In real deployment, the system successfully shifts between analytical and scaffolding strategies, reduces interactions by ~3 turns (p=0.007), and maintains pedagogical quality. The greedy router achieves comparable exercise conversion (19.1% vs. baseline 19.6%), while the stochastic router substantially improves conversion to 28.1%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive prompt selection based on pedagogical features enables effective sim-to-real transfer, improving instructional efficiency and reducing interaction length. A stochastic routing strategy yields superior engagement outcomes, suggesting that strategy diversity benefits student conversion rates in LLM-based tutoring.

title: Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective
summary: Electronic design automation (EDA) is inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy. Design artifacts, flow scripts, and engineering decisions cross tool, session, and organizational boundaries before final implementation, signoff, or release. Each transfer carries explicit and implicit requirements that may not be fully captured by stage-local checks. LLM-based agents now invoke EDA tools directly, embed retrieved knowledge in executable scripts, and hand off state across sessions and stages. Once their outputs condition downstream engineering decisions, the transferred object must satisfy a handoff contract and meet the assumptions of its next consumer. This survey introduces handoff validity as its organizing principle. A handoff is valid when the transferred object satisfies the consumer's acceptance conditions and carries sufficient context, evidence, and provenance for downstream use. We review 82 systems and classify them into three boundary classes. Stage-Bound systems establish validity within a single EDA stage or bounded verification task. Flow-Bound systems preserve coherent workflow state across tools, invocations, and sessions. Organization-Bound systems maintain source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries. For each class, we analyze handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. These analyses motivate a five-layer EDA agent communication protocol (EACP), covering the agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security and IP protocols. We aim to provide a common vocabulary and research agenda for trustworthy agentic EDA.

AI.tldr: This survey introduces "handoff validity" as an organizing principle for LLM-based agents in EDA, classifying 82 systems into Stage-Bound, Flow-Bound, and Organization-Bound classes, analyzing how each ensures transferred artifacts satisfy downstream consumer requirements, and proposing a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP).
AI.motivation: EDA workflows are multi-stage and handoff-heavy, with design artifacts crossing tool, session, and organizational boundaries. Stage-local checks often fail to capture the full set of explicit and implicit requirements needed by downstream consumers. As LLM-based agents increasingly drive EDA tool invocation and decision-making, there is no systematic framework for ensuring that transferred objects satisfy handoff contracts with sufficient context, evidence, and provenance.
AI.method: The authors survey 82 LLM-based EDA systems and classify them into three boundary classes: (1) Stage-Bound — validity within a single EDA stage or bounded verification task; (2) Flow-Bound — coherence across tools, invocations, and sessions; (3) Organization-Bound — source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries. For each class, they analyze handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. They synthesize findings into a proposed five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP): agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security/IP.
AI.result: The taxonomy reveals that Stage-Bound systems dominate current work but lack cross-stage validity guarantees. Flow-Bound systems address state continuity but rarely formalize contracts. Organization-Bound systems are the least explored yet most critical for production deployment, requiring provenance chains and authority-based admissibility. The proposed EACP layers provide a common vocabulary for addressing gaps at each boundary level.
