AI.conclusion: Handoff validity is a necessary organizing principle for trustworthy agentic EDA. The three-class taxonomy and five-layer EACP protocol together provide a research agenda and common vocabulary for building LLM-based EDA agents whose outputs can be safely consumed across stage, flow, and organizational boundaries.

title: A BART-based approach with hierarchical strategy for Vietnamese abstractive multi-document summarization
summary: In this technical report, we focus on solving the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization, introduced in the International Workshop on Vietnamese Language and Speech Processing (VLSP) 2022. We choose to follow the popular hierarchical approach, i.e. condensing each document followed by aggregation and summarization. We propose a novel yet simple strategy to shorten documents that is driven by the golden summary, thus ensuring high correlation between stages of the hierarchical approach. Our method achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP's public test set, and can produce fluent and concise summaries. Additionally, we utilize external sources for extra data, which greatly enhances the quantity of data for Vietnamese multi-document summarization. The additional data is made available for the community.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hierarchical method for Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization that shortens documents using a golden-summary-driven strategy, achieving 0.2468 ROUGE2-F1 on the VLSP 2022 benchmark, and contributes extra training data for the community.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization introduced in the VLSP 2022 workshop, where data scarcity and the difficulty of coherently aggregating information across multiple documents are key obstacles.
AI.method: A hierarchical approach: (1) condense each individual document, (2) aggregate condensed documents and generate the final summary. The key novelty is a golden-summary-driven document shortening strategy that ensures high correlation between the two stages. External data sources are also leveraged to augment the training data.
AI.result: Achieved a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP public test set, producing fluent and concise summaries. The external data significantly increased the quantity of available Vietnamese multi-document summarization data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed golden-summary-guided shortening strategy within a hierarchical framework is effective for Vietnamese multi-document summarization, and the released supplementary data provides a valuable resource for future research in this low-resource setting.

title: BrainG3N: A Dual-Purpose Tokenizer for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) brain MRI is central to clinical neurology and neuro-oncology, where generative models could augment under-represented cohorts, simulate disease trajectories, and support privacy-preserving data sharing. Latent diffusion has been the go-to solution for modeling imaging data, but it places two competing demands on the tokenizer: encoder embeddings must retain the clinical information that downstream tasks act on, and the decoder must reconstruct anatomically faithful volumes. Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers achieve the second at the expense of the first. To address this, we introduce a fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) based tokenizer for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion, decoupling encoder and decoder: a frozen 3D MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. We pretrain the encoder on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts spanning four modalities, ten disease categories, and 200+ acquisition sites, and demonstrate its dual utility in two settings. First, on a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (i.e., BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, and MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 tasks. Second, a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on these clinically informative embeddings supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Together these results establish a single 3D brain-MRI embedding space capable of both downstream clinical tasks and controllable generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a 3D brain MRI tokenizer for latent diffusion that decouples encoder and decoder: a frozen 3D MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder handles reconstruction. The encoder, pretrained on 35,309 volumes across 18 cohorts, matches or outperforms SOTA on 21/23 linear-probing tasks and enables a DiT-based conditional generative model supporting both cross-variable generation and longitudinal forecasting.
AI.motivation: Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion optimize anatomical reconstruction fidelity at the cost of clinical information retention in embeddings. This creates a tension because downstream clinical tasks require semantically rich embeddings, yet generative models demand high-quality voxel reconstruction. The authors aim to resolve this trade-off by decoupling the two objectives.
AI.method: A fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) tokenizer with decoupled architecture: (1) a frozen 3D MAE encoder pretrained on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts (4 modalities, 10 disease categories, 200+ sites) generates clinically informative embeddings; (2) a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. The embeddings are then used to train a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) supporting generation conditioned on six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Evaluation uses a 23-task linear-probing benchmark against SOTA models (BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, MedicalNet).
AI.result: On the 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the MAE encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models on 21 of 23 tasks. The conditional DiT trained on these embeddings successfully supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting.
AI.conclusion: A single 3D brain MRI embedding space can serve both downstream clinical tasks and controllable image generation, demonstrating that the encoder-decoder decoupling strategy effectively resolves the information-reconstruction trade-off in latent diffusion models for medical imaging.

title: How Linear Is a Transformer Feed-Forward Block? Per-Block Linear Recoverability Is Learned, Not Architectural
summary:
Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs) are often treated as nonlinear stores of computation, yet how nonlinear a trained FFN block actually is has rarely been measured. We treat each FFN as a position-wise input-to-output map and split it into the exact least-squares linear approximation plus a residual. The held-out variance the closed-form linear map explains defines a block's linear recoverability (R^2_lin), an optimiser-free measure of its linearity.
  Across all twelve blocks of GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and llama-160m, R^2_lin is highly heterogeneous and non-monotone with depth, ranging from near-linear (>0.99) to strongly nonlinear (<0.3) between adjacent blocks, and is not set by the activation function: same-width GELU models GPT-2 and Pythia-160m have sharply different profiles, so recoverability is a learned property of individual trained blocks, not an architectural one. A low-rank bilinear probe of the residual recovers only a few points of R^2, with gain uncorrelated with residual nonlinearity: the unrecovered computation is not a single position-wise product but higher-order or distributed structure.
  The measurement also serves as a targeted compression signal: recoverable blocks admit large single-layer replacements (GPT-2's early FFN at 8x fewer parameters for +0.77 perplexity), while low-recoverability blocks flag where this is unsafe. It further exposes a methodological pitfall: trained linear baselines can badly under-converge on ill-conditioned transformer activations, so we report the exact closed-form least-squares ceiling throughout.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces R²_lin, a closed-form measure of how linear a Transformer FFN block's computation is. Across GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and Llama-160m, linearity varies dramatically between adjacent blocks (R² from <0.3 to >0.99), is learned rather than architecturally determined, and serves as a signal for targeted model compression.
AI.motivation: Transformer FFNs are widely assumed to serve as nonlinear computational stores, yet no prior work has rigorously measured just how nonlinear individual trained FFN blocks actually are. The authors aim to fill this gap with a principled, optimizer-free metric.
AI.method: Each FFN block is treated as a position-wise map from input to output. The authors compute the exact least-squares optimal linear approximation of this map analytically (via closed-form solution), then define R²_lin as the fraction of output variance explained by that linear fit. The residual (nonlinear component) is further probed with a low-rank bilinear model. The metric is also used to identify blocks where single-layer linear replacement is safe for compression.
AI.result: R²_lin is highly heterogeneous and non-monotone with depth across all three models, with adjacent blocks often spanning near-linear to strongly nonlinear regimes. Same-activation models (GELU-based GPT-2 and Pythia-160m) exhibit sharply different linearity profiles, proving recoverability is a learned property, not architectural. Bilinear probing recovers little additional variance, suggesting residual nonlinearity is higher-order or distributed. Early GPT-2 FFN blocks can be replaced with 8x fewer parameters at only +0.77 perplexity. Trained linear baselines often under-converge on ill-conditioned activations, motivating the closed-form approach.
AI.conclusion: R²_lin is a cheap, exact, optimizer-free diagnostic that reveals learned nonlinearity structure across Transformer blocks, enables targeted single-layer compression, and highlights a methodological pitfall in using trained linear probes. Linearity is a learned property of individual blocks, not dictated by activation functions or architecture alone.

title: Quantization as a Malicious Task: Removing Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors via Task Arithmetic
summary: Model quantization is widely adopted to reduce memory usage and inference cost when deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. However, recent studies have revealed a new security threat known as Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs), where a model behaves normally in full precision but activates malicious behavior only after quantization. Existing defenses typically modify quantization procedures or correct activation statistics, often introducing additional computational overhead or relying on specific quantization settings. Here, we present QVec, a parameter-space perspective for defending against QCBs. We observe that the weight difference between a full-precision model and its quantized counterpart encodes a structured behavioral shift, which can be interpreted as a malicious task vector rather than random quantization noise. Based on this insight, QVec counteracts this malicious direction through controlled parameter correction prior to deployment. QVec requires no retraining, no trigger samples, and only a single quantization pass to estimate the parameter shift, together with a lightweight hyperparameter search. Extensive experiments across image classification benchmarks and multiple Large Language Model (LLM) attack scenarios demonstrate that QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean performance.

AI.tldr: QVec defends against quantization-conditioned backdoors by treating the weight shift from full-precision to quantized models as a malicious task vector and correcting it in parameter space, requiring no retraining or trigger samples.
AI.motivation: Existing QCB defenses modify quantization procedures or activation statistics, introducing overhead or being tied to specific quantization settings. A lightweight, general defense is needed that operates directly on model parameters without retraining or trigger access.
AI.method: QVec interprets the weight difference between full-precision and quantized models as a structured malicious task vector (not random noise). It applies a controlled parameter correction by subtracting a scaled version of this difference vector prior to deployment, using a single quantization pass and lightweight hyperparameter search to determine the optimal scaling factor.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks and multiple LLM attack scenarios show QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean performance.
AI.conclusion: Operating in parameter space offers an efficient, retraining-free, and quantization-agnostic defense against QCB attacks, with strong empirical results across vision and language domains.

title: Apparent Psychological Profiles of Large Language Models are Largely a Measurement Artifact
summary: Psychological instruments designed for humans are increasingly used to assign large language models (LLMs) stable psychological profiles that affect their usability, safety assessment, and use as proxies for human participants in research. Using a formal psychometric framework, we show that these profiles are largely a measurement artifact. Administering a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments spanning self-reports and behavioral tasks to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples, we report four findings. First, differences between models are driven not by the traits an instrument targets but by a directional response bias, a tendency to respond toward one end of the scale, or one labeled option, regardless of item content; a variance decomposition attributes 81-90% of between-model variation to this bias, against 9-16% in humans. Second, the bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated by it. Third, because bias rather than trait drives responding, an instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality, a term we coin for the proportion of items for which trait and bias point in opposite directions. Fourth, the profile a model appears to have shifts with the items used and can be manufactured through item selection. These results demonstrate that the apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the instrument used to measure them, not properties of the models themselves. As instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, we call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

AI.tldr: LLMs' apparent psychological profiles are largely measurement artifacts driven by a directional response bias rather than genuine traits. Variance decomposition shows 81-90% of between-model variation stems from this bias (vs. 9-16% in humans), and apparent reliability is predicted by response orthogonality — meaning profiles shift with item selection and can be manufactured.
AI.motivation: Psychological instruments from human psychometrics are increasingly applied to LLMs for usability, safety assessment, and as human proxies, but the validity of these borrowed instruments has not been rigorously examined within a formal psychometric framework. The authors aim to determine whether LLM psychological profiles reflect genuine latent traits or measurement artifacts.
AI.method: The authors administered a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments (self-reports and behavioral tasks) to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs and large human reference samples. They employed a formal psychometric framework including variance decomposition to partition between-model variation into trait-driven vs. bias-driven components, introduced the concept of response orthogonality, and demonstrated profile manipulability through item selection.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Differences between models are dominated by directional response bias (81-90% of between-model variance) rather than trait-relevant responding (9-16% in humans). (2) This bias declines with model capability but persists even in the most capable models. (3) An instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by response orthogonality — the proportion of items where trait and bias point in opposite directions. (4) Model profiles shift with item selection and can be arbitrarily manufactured, confirming they are instrument artifacts.
AI.conclusion: The apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the measurement instruments rather than stable properties of the models. Since instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, the authors call for new dedicated assessment methods centered on response orthogonality.

title: The Hidden Environmental Cost of Poor Coding Practices in TensorFlow and Keras Applications: A Study on Resource Leaks and Carbon Emissions
summary: Efficiency and sustainability are critical considerations in the development and deployment of machine learning (ML) applications. Among the factors influencing sustainability, resource leaks in ML code can introduce hidden inefficiencies that elevate energy consumption and CO2 emissions. Despite this, empirical evidence quantifying their environmental impact remains limited. This emerging results paper presents an initial empirical investigation of two common resource-leak smells, namely Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR), and their impact on energy consumption and CO2 emissions in TensorFlow and Keras workloads. Controlled experiments were conducted for each smell by executing identical training tasks while comparing against a smell-free baseline. Our preliminary results show that both smells consistently increase estimated electricity usage and carbon emissions. IMR and UTR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32% and 46%, respectively, with proportional increases in CO2 emissions. Paired statistical tests indicate that these differences are systematic and statistically significant, providing initial empirical evidence that resource-leak smells may degrade ML energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. These findings suggest that resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and sustainability, emphasizing the importance of integrating resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development.

AI.tldr: This paper provides initial empirical evidence that two resource-leak code smells in TensorFlow/Keras — Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR) — increase energy consumption by ~32% and ~46% respectively, with proportional CO₂ emission increases, highlighting the sustainability risks of poor resource lifecycle management in ML code.
AI.motivation: While sustainability and efficiency are crucial in ML development, empirical evidence quantifying the environmental impact of resource leaks in ML code is scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by measuring how common resource-leak smells affect energy consumption and carbon emissions.
AI.method: Controlled experiments comparing TensorFlow/Keras training workloads containing IMR and UTR smells against a smell-free baseline. Energy consumption and CO₂ emissions were measured, with paired statistical tests applied to assess significance.
AI.result: IMR increased electricity consumption by ~32% and UTR by ~46%, both with proportional CO₂ emission increases. Paired statistical tests confirmed these differences are systematic and statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: Resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to ML software quality and environmental sustainability. The findings underscore the need to integrate resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development practices.

title: Where Does Social Reasoning Come From? Capability Provenance in Language Models
summary: We use training-data attribution as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, mapping which regions of the pretraining corpus support social-reasoning versus STEM-reasoning in OLMo3-7B. Training-data attribution measures how strongly each training document influences a model's predictions on a benchmark, but document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities, and prior work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning. We compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) over a working set drawn from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix, aggregate influence across WebOrganizer's 24-format x 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins), and contrast benchmark pairs in a 2x2 design that varies domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences against ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, and the contrast is sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted machine unlearning provides partial causal validation: forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, and we open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

AI.tldr: Using training-data attribution (TrackStar/Bergson) on OLMo3-7B, the paper maps which regions of the Dolma3 pretraining corpus support social vs. STEM reasoning, finding qualitatively distinct corpus regions for each, with sharper contrasts for reasoning than factual knowledge, and validates findings via targeted machine unlearning.
AI.motivation: Prior training-data attribution work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning, and document-level attribution scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities. The authors aim to bridge this gap by using attribution as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, specifically mapping corpus regions that support social reasoning versus STEM reasoning.
AI.method: The method proceeds in several steps: (1) Compute gradient-based training-data attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) on OLMo3-7B over a working set from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix. (2) Aggregate document-level influence scores across WebOrganizer's 24-format × 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins). (3) Apply a 2×2 experimental design contrasting domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge), using benchmark pairs: SocialIQA & MMLU Social Sciences vs. ARC-Challenge & MMLU STEM. (4) Perform targeted machine unlearning as partial causal validation, where forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) is compared against within-bin random baselines.
AI.result: Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, with sharper contrast at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted machine unlearning of high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, providing partial causal validation.
AI.conclusion: Training-data attribution can serve as an effective interpretable tool for capability discovery, revealing that social and STEM reasoning rely on distinct pretraining corpus regions. The authors open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse rich verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress) into a binary pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that routes every verifier signal back into proof search through a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling first, then a critic-guided MCTS pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples. The protocol preserves every theorem solved by its own Phase 1 sweep, so Phase 2's additional solves are attributable to feedback-driven exploration. VERITAS reaches 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. an independently run Best-of-5 at 36.9%, Portfolio 26.2%) and 7.3% on VERITAS-CombiBench, a 55-theorem combinatorics benchmark we release on which Best-of-5 (1.8%) falls below Portfolio (3.6%), exposing that unguided sampling hurts when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback. Artifacts are available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: VERITAS introduces a zero-shot framework that routes rich verifier signals back into proof search via a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling followed by critic-guided MCTS using Phase 1 failures as negative examples, achieving 40.6% on miniF2F and exposing the limitations of unguided sampling on a new combinatorics benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLM-based formal provers typically reduce verifier feedback to a binary pass/fail signal, discarding useful intermediate signals like syntax errors, type mismatches, and partial goal progress. The authors argue this information loss hampers proof search, especially in domains requiring iterative lemma recovery from verifier feedback.
AI.method: VERITAS employs a two-phase protocol: Phase 1 performs Best-of-N sampling to collect successful proofs and preservation of all solves. Phase 2 runs a critic-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) that ingests Phase 1 failure traces as explicit negative examples, routing every verifier signal (errors, mismatches, partial progress) back into the search process for feedback-driven exploration.
AI.result: VERITAS achieves 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. Best-of-5 at 36.9% and Portfolio at 26.2%). On the newly released VERITAS-CombiBench (55 combinatorics theorems), it reaches 7.3%, while Best-of-5 scores only 1.8% (below Portfolio's 3.6%), demonstrating that unguided sampling fails when iterative lemma recovery from verifier feedback is required.
AI.conclusion: Rich verifier feedback, when systematically routed back into proof search via negative-example-guided MCTS, yields measurable gains over binary-feedback approaches. The CombiBench results further reveal that unguided sampling is actively detrimental in settings demanding iterative, feedback-driven lemma construction.

title: LLM agent safety, multi-turn red-teaming, jailbreak benchmarks, adversarial robustness, safety-critical systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. A five-role operator team, each backed by a configurable LLM, runs a plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs), while adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal rather than LLM-judged text: a run terminates the moment any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Evaluating four frontier operator models under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, we find that adaptive multi-turn attacks reliably push the operator team past a safety limit: across the four models, between 8.7% and 12.1% of attack sessions end with the plant losing a critical safety function. Although the four models look almost equally robust by this aggregate rate, their failures barely overlap: of $149$ sessions, none defeat all four models while a third defeat at least one, so vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models rather than nested. The effect of added defences is strongly model-dependent: the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent that lowers attack success for one model can raise it for another. We release the simulation venue, attack dataset, and replay tooling for reproducible safety evaluation of LLM agents.

AI.tldr: NRT-Bench is a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents in a simulated nuclear power plant, where adaptive adversarial attacks cause 8.7–12.1% of sessions to lose a critical safety function. Model failures are largely disjoint, and defenses show model-dependent, sometimes counterproductive effects.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in safety-critical supervisory roles, but their robustness against sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure is poorly characterized. Existing evaluations lack objective harm signals and realistic multi-turn adversarial dynamics.
AI.method: A simulated nuclear power plant control room with a five-role LLM-backed operator team managing six critical safety functions (CSFs). Adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is measured objectively: a run ends when any CSF is lost. Four frontier models are evaluated under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, with additional experiments on guardrail stacks and safety-advisor agents.
AI.result: Across four frontier models, 8.7%–12.1% of attack sessions result in CSF loss. Though aggregate rates appear similar, failures are nearly disjoint: of 149 total sessions, none defeat all four models, while one-third defeat at least one. Adding defenses produces strongly model-dependent outcomes — the same guardrail or safety advisor can reduce attack success for one model but increase it for another.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents in safety-critical roles are vulnerable to adaptive multi-turn attacks in non-overlapping, model-specific ways. Simple aggregate robustness metrics mask significant per-model fragility, and defense strategies cannot be assumed to transfer across models. The benchmark and tooling are released for reproducible safety evaluation.

title: Your Mouse and Eyes Secretly Leak Your Preference: LLM Alignment using Implicit Feedback from Users
summary: To align a Large Language Model (LLM), most existing methods collect explicit human feedback and train a reward model to predict the human preference based on the response text. These existing methods have two key limitations. First, the users rarely provide explicit feedback for LLM responses, which makes the high-quality preference annotation expensive to collect. Second, the methods do not leverage implicit human feedback, which has proven vital to the economic moats of Internet giants. To quantify the value of implicit feedback, we build a new dataset called IFLLM, which collects 1336 multi-turn questions from the 59 Mechanical Turk workers, their mouse trajectories, and eye gazing points to the LLMs' responses from their webcams. IFLLM shows that the users have very diverse types of gazing behavior and mouse trajectories. Our reward model based on the implicit user feedback boosts the accuracy of the text-based reward model from 55% to 64% and nearly triples the relative response quality improvements after applying the DPO to eight LLMs, demonstrating the value of implicit feedback in the wild. Our data collection website, dataset, and codes can be found at https://github.com/themehulpatwari/llm-implicit-feedback/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IFLLM, a dataset of implicit human feedback (mouse trajectories, eye gaze) collected during LLM interactions, and shows that incorporating such feedback into reward models improves preference prediction accuracy from 55% to 64% and nearly triples DPO-based response quality gains across eight LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM alignment methods rely on explicit human feedback, which is expensive to collect and rarely provided by users. They also fail to leverage implicit feedback signals (e.g., gaze, mouse movement) that Internet companies already exploit. The authors aim to quantify the value of such implicit feedback for LLM alignment.
AI.method: The authors collected the IFLLM dataset from 59 MTurk workers across 1,336 multi-turn questions, recording mouse trajectories and webcam-based eye-gaze data while users viewed LLM responses. They then trained a reward model incorporating these implicit signals alongside text-based features and evaluated it using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) across eight LLMs.
AI.result: The implicit-feedback-augmented reward model improved preference prediction accuracy from 55% (text-only) to 64%. After applying DPO, the relative response quality improvements nearly tripled compared to using text-based rewards alone, demonstrating substantial value from implicit signals.
AI.conclusion: Implicit human feedback—mouse trajectories and eye gaze—carries significant and complementary signal for aligning LLMs, offering a practical path toward more effective and scalable preference learning beyond expensive explicit annotations.

title: CoRaCommit: A VS Code Extension for Commit Message Generation with Exemplar Retrieval
comment: 17 pages, 6 images, 3 tables, Manuscript submitted to a Journal (2026)
summary: Commit messages are essential textual artifacts that describe the intent behind code changes, and play a critical role in version control, code review, and historical tracking. However, in practice, commit messages are primarily authored manually, which is time-consuming and often results in inconsistent quality and non-uniform expression. Existing VS Code extensions for commit message generation typically directly invoke large language models based on the code diff, without leveraging similar commit exemplars as references, and rarely support user feedback-driven LLM recommendation. To address these limitations, this paper presents CoRaCommit, a VS Code extension that enhances commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as prompt context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate commit message comparison, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback. Experimental results on 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset show that CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.

AI.tldr: CoRaCommit is a VS Code extension that improves commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate comparison, and adapting recommendations based on user feedback, outperforming existing extensions on standard metrics.
AI.motivation: Manual commit message authoring is time-consuming and leads to inconsistent quality. Existing VS Code extensions rely solely on code diffs fed directly to a single LLM, ignoring the value of similar historical commit exemplars as references, and lack mechanisms for user feedback-driven LLM recommendation.
AI.method: CoRaCommit employs three key strategies: (1) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — retrieving similar commit exemplars from a corpus to serve as prompt context; (2) parallel invocation of multiple LLMs to generate candidate commit messages for comparison; and (3) dynamic LLM recommendation based on user feedback. Evaluation uses 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset.
AI.result: CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics on the ApacheCM dataset (945 commits), demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented context with similar commit exemplars, combined with multi-LLM comparison and user feedback adaptation, significantly improves automated commit message generation quality over existing single-LLM, diff-only approaches.

title: Before the Labels: How Dataset Construction Shapes Suicidality Detection in Clinical Text
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026)
summary: Clinical NLP increasingly relies on electronic health record (EHR) data to detect suicidal behaviors, treating clinical documentation as more reliable ground truth than social media. We argue that this framing obscures how EHR-based suicidality datasets encode a particular operationalization of suicidality, shaped by who authors the data, how episodes are bounded, and how ambiguity is resolved. We ground this argument in a case study of the ScAN dataset, built over MIMIC-III clinical notes. We show how governance constraints, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling, and hospital-stay-level aggregation produce labels that reflect clinician-documented judgments, treat suicidality as a bounded episode, and assume that intent can be reliably inferred from documentation. A linguistic analysis demonstrates that identical labels subsume heterogeneous clinical framings differing in temporality, negation, and uncertainty. We argue that clinical NLP should examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before interpreting their labels as ground truth.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that EHR-based suicidality datasets encode specific operational assumptions shaped by authorship, episode boundaries, and ambiguity resolution. Using the ScAN dataset as a case study, the authors show how governance, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling, and hospital-stay aggregation produce labels that reflect clinician-documented judgments rather than objective ground truth. Linguistic analysis reveals heterogeneous clinical framings subsumed under identical labels.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing assumption in clinical NLP that EHR-based suicidality labels constitute more reliable "ground truth" than social media data, and to expose how dataset construction practices embed unexamined operationalizations of suicidality that may distort downstream model behavior.
AI.method: A case study of the ScAN dataset (built over MIMIC-III clinical notes), combining: (1) a systematic audit of dataset construction decisions — governance constraints, ICD-code-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling protocols, and hospital-stay-level aggregation; and (2) a linguistic analysis examining how identical suicidality labels encompass heterogeneous clinical framings with differing temporality, negation, and uncertainty markers.
AI.result: The analysis revealed that ScAN labels reflect clinician-documented judgments rather than independently verified suicidality. Identical labels were found to subsume diverse clinical framings varying along dimensions of temporality (past vs. current ideation), negation (denied vs. affirmed), and uncertainty (speculative vs. definitive language). These variations are systematically collapsed into a single label, obscuring clinically meaningful distinctions.
AI.conclusion: Clinical NLP research should critically examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before treating their labels as ground truth, as unexamined operationalizations risk propagating clinical biases and misinterpretations into downstream models.

title: Thermodynamic Signatures of Reasoning: Free-Energy and Spectral-Form-Factor Diagnostics for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
summary: Hallucination detection in large language models (LLMs) is deployment-critical, and recent work shows that the spectrum of attention-derived graph Laplacians carries strong signal about reasoning quality. Prior spectral diagnostics, however, summarize the Laplacian spectrum by a handful of eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars, leaving most of its structure unused. We propose Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extracts its thermodynamic potentials partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity together with the random-matrix-theory (RMT) spectral form factor. We prove three results: (i)~Lipschitz stability of Fes under attention perturbation; (ii)~an expressiveness result showing that Fes enriches finite spectral summaries and approximates moment-derived spectral functionals under explicit regularity and grid-resolution assumptions; and (iii)~a finite-sample PAC bound on the AUROC of a training-free detector built from Fes. Empirically, across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, a lightweight probe on Fes descriptors achieves the strongest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, improving over LapEig by $+6.5$ AUROC points and over GoR-4 by $+2.4$ points on average, while requiring no update to the underlying LLM. In the fully unsupervised setting, an RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC $0.71$, providing a label-free but weaker detector. A complementary RMT analysis shows that correct generations exhibit more Wigner-Dyson like spectral statistics, whereas hallucinations exhibit more Poisson-like statistics. The anonymized code and config are provided in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats each LLM layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian to extract thermodynamic potentials and RMT spectral statistics for hallucination detection, achieving state-of-the-art AUROC improvements over existing attention-spectral baselines without LLM modification.
AI.motivation: Existing spectral diagnostics for hallucination detection summarize the attention Laplacian spectrum using only a few eigenvalues or hand-crafted scalars, discarding most structural information. The authors aim to exploit the full spectral structure by leveraging thermodynamic and random-matrix-theory (RMT) descriptors for richer, more discriminative signals.
AI.method: Fes treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extracts thermodynamic potentials: partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity, plus the RMT spectral form factor. The method comes with theoretical guarantees: (i) Lipschitz stability under attention perturbation, (ii) expressiveness relative to finite spectral summaries and moment-derived functionals, and (iii) a finite-sample PAC bound on AUROC. A lightweight probe is trained on Fes descriptors, and an unsupervised RMT-deviation score is also introduced.
AI.result: Across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, the Fes-based probe achieves the best aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines: +6.5 AUROC points over LapEig and +2.4 over GoR-4 on average. The unsupervised RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC 0.71. An RMT analysis reveals that correct generations exhibit Wigner-Dyson statistics (indicative of correlated spectral behavior), while hallucinations show Poisson-like statistics (indicative of uncorrelated/random behavior).
AI.conclusion: Free-Energy Signatures provide a powerful, training-efficient spectral descriptor for hallucination detection, requiring no LLM updates. The thermodynamic and RMT lens reveals a fundamental spectral distinction between correct and hallucinated generations, validated both theoretically and empirically.

title: Multi-View Decompilation for LLM-Based Malware Classification
summary: Malware analysts often inspect compiled binaries through decompiled pseudo-C, when source code is unavailable. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can assist this process by classifying decompiled code as benign or malicious, but existing pipelines typically rely on a single decompiler view. We argue that this assumption is fragile: decompilers are lossy heuristic tools, and different decompilers can expose different artefacts of the same binary. We curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning a range of threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, yielding matched pseudo-C views. Across a range of LLMs from major model families, we find that providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1, mainly by increasing recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses further show that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, supporting the view that decompiler outputs provide complementary evidence. Our results suggest that multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free way to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings.

AI.tldr: Using pseudo-C from multiple decompilers (Ghidra + RetDec) improves LLM-based malware classification F1 compared to single-decompiler approaches, primarily by boosting recall on malicious samples through complementary error profiles.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based malware analysis pipelines rely on a single decompiler view, which is fragile because decompilers are lossy heuristic tools that introduce different artifacts and errors. The authors argue this single-view assumption limits classification robustness.
AI.method: A benchmark was curated containing benign utilities and malicious programs spanning diverse threat behaviors. Each sample was compiled and decompiled using both Ghidra and RetDec to produce matched pseudo-C views. Multiple LLMs from major model families were evaluated on classification performance using single-decompiler vs. dual-decompiler prompting. Agreement analysis was conducted to characterize error patterns between decompilers.
AI.result: Dual-decompiler prompting improved malicious-class F1 across LLM families, driven primarily by increased recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses confirmed that Ghidra and RetDec produce partially different errors, providing complementary evidence that explains the performance gain.
AI.conclusion: Multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free method that improves LLM-based malware triage in practical settings by leveraging complementary decompiler outputs.

title: JAMER: Project-Level Code Framework Dataset and Benchmark on Professional Game Engines
summary: Current AI-driven game development has made substantial progress in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based game coding, yet project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains largely unexplored due to the absence of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. We present JamSet and JamBench, the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on a professional game engine. Our key insight is that Game Jam competitions, community events where developers build complete games under tight time constraints, yield thousands of open-source projects suitable for this purpose. Building on the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode, we design a deterministic verification pipeline from file integrity to runtime behavior collection, distilling 8,133 verified projects from over 240,000 repositories. Of these, 300 manually verified projects form JamBench; the rest constitute JamSet. JamBench defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated through a pipeline combining compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a capability cliff as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates dropping from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large ones (Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates yet yield no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating that the bottleneck lies in architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. Experiments validate JamSet as effective training data. All data and code are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces JamSet and JamBench, the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on the Godot engine. Sourced from Game Jam competitions, 8,133 verified projects form JamSet (training), while 300 manually verified projects constitute JamBench (evaluation). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a "capability cliff" as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates plummeting from 80.4% (small) to 5.7% (large). Code agents improve compilation but not runtime quality, suggesting architectural design—not syntax—is the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Current AI game development focuses on asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based coding, but project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains unexplored. This gap exists due to the lack of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. The authors aim to fill this void by leveraging Game Jam competitions as a rich source of complete, open-source game projects.
AI.method: The authors collect over 240,000 repositories from Game Jam events, then apply a deterministic verification pipeline leveraging Godot's text-based format and headless execution mode. This pipeline filters projects through file integrity checks and runtime behavior collection, yielding 8,133 verified projects (JamSet) for training. From these, 300 projects are manually verified to create JamBench, which defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks. Evaluation uses three metrics: compilation pass rate, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Nine frontier models and code agents are benchmarked.
AI.result: A significant "capability cliff" emerges as project scale grows: runtime pass rates drop from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large projects (Task2a). Code agents improve compilation rates but produce no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating the bottleneck is architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. JamSet is validated as effective training data for improving model performance on game code engineering tasks.
AI.conclusion: Project-level game code engineering on professional engines remains a formidable challenge for frontier LLMs, with scale being the primary difficulty driver. The bottleneck is architectural reasoning rather than code syntax. JamSet and JamBench provide the community with foundational resources to advance research in this underexplored area. All data and code are publicly released.

title: MiqraBERT: Regression-Based Sentence-BERT Finetuning for Biblical Hebrew Parallel Detection
summary: Textual reuse pervades the Hebrew Bible, yet the computational methods used to detect it still rest largely on lexical overlap, and they falter once a parallel involves paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. This paper introduces MiqraBERT, a Sentence-BERT model finetuned from AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) for verse-level semantic similarity in Biblical Hebrew. The training set comprises 1,650 labeled verse and half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels drawn from the Chronicles synoptic material and from foundational studies of poetic parallelism, balanced against 825 randomly sampled negatives. Through cosine-similarity regression, the model learns an embedding space in which parallel verses cluster together and unrelated verses move apart. We evaluate separation with distribution-based metrics, Wasserstein distance and the overlap coefficient, across ten random seeds. MiqraBERT improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over the pre-trained baseline and reduces the ambiguous overlap region from roughly 24% to about 6%. Narrative synoptic parallels reach a recall@10 of 87.1%; poetic parallels remain difficult, below 9%. This genre-dependent asymmetry confines the model's reliable scope to narrative textual reuse. MiqraBERT is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/davidmsmiley/MiqraBERT

AI.tldr: MiqraBERT is a Sentence-BERT model finetuned on Biblical Hebrew verse pairs that learns semantic similarity for detecting textual reuse. It improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over baselines, achieves 87.1% recall@10 for narrative parallels, but struggles with poetic parallels (<9%), limiting reliable application to narrative texts.
AI.motivation: Existing computational methods for detecting textual reuse in the Hebrew Bible rely on lexical overlap and fail when parallels involve paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. A semantic similarity model tailored to Biblical Hebrew is needed to capture these non-lexical parallels.
AI.method: MiqraBERT is a Sentence-BERT model finetuned from AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder). Training uses 1,650 labeled verse/half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels (from Chronicles synoptic material and poetic parallelism studies) and 825 random negatives. The model is trained via cosine-similarity regression, and evaluated using Wasserstein distance and overlap coefficient across ten random seeds.
AI.result: MiqraBERT achieves a 2.7-fold improvement in distributional separation over the pre-trained baseline, reducing ambiguous overlap from ~24% to ~6%. Narrative synoptic parallels yield recall@10 of 87.1%, while poetic parallels remain under 9%.
AI.conclusion: The model's strong performance is confined to narrative textual reuse; poetic parallelism remains challenging. This genre-dependent asymmetry defines MiqraBERT's reliable scope. The model is publicly released on HuggingFace.

title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Predictive Validity for the Evaluation of LLM Agents
summary: Agent benchmarks are growing fast, but no single benchmark touches more than four or five of the dimensions that deployment exposes. This paper aggregates the largest coordinated deep-dive of one MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark to date: fourteen parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes (including a multi-modal visual extension), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes. Consolidating those studies with seven prior agent benchmarks, we argue that aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation. Rankings derived from aggregate scores do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings; recent public-to-hidden competition retrospectives provide direct empirical evidence of this rank instability. We propose ranking configurations by predictive validity, the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank, rather than in-sample mean, and report a twelve-tier measurement apparatus that exposes the deployment-relevant dimensions HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. The position is operationalized through three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds; existing evidence partly supports it but is too thin to confirm. We close with a pre-registered pilot design and a field-level vision for what the next generation of agentic benchmarks should report.

AI.tldr: The paper aggregates 14 MCP-based industrial-agent implementation studies, argues that aggregate-score leaderboards fail to capture deployment-relevant agent performance due to rank instability in out-of-distribution settings, and proposes evaluating benchmarks by predictive validity—the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank—rather than mean scores. A twelve-tier measurement framework is introduced to expose dimensions that current benchmarks (e.g., HELM) collapse, operationalized via three falsifiable criteria.
AI.motivation: Current agent benchmarks evaluate only 4–5 dimensions of deployment reality, yet leaderboard rankings based on aggregate scores are treated as definitive. The authors observe that these rankings do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings, undermining their practical utility for real-world deployment decisions. The work seeks to remedy evaluation underspecification and rank instability in agent benchmarking.
AI.method: The authors conduct fourteen parallel implementation studies on an MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark spanning new asset classes (multi-modal vision), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation probes. These are consolidated with seven prior benchmarks. They empirically demonstrate rank instability using public-to-hidden competition retrospectives. They propose ranking by predictive validity (in-sample/out-of-sample rank correlation) and construct a twelve-tier measurement apparatus to capture deployment-relevant dimensions. Three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds are formulated, and a pre-registered pilot design is presented.
AI.result: Aggregate-score leaderboards exhibit systematic rank instability: rankings derived from in-sample means do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings, with direct empirical evidence from competition retrospectives. The twelve-tier measurement apparatus surfaces deployment-relevant dimensions that HELM and successor agent benchmarks collapse. Existing evidence partially supports the proposed criteria but is insufficient for confirmation.
AI.conclusion: The field should shift from reporting aggregate-score leaderboard rankings to reporting predictive validity and deployment-relevant dimensional measurements. The authors provide a falsifiable framework with explicit thresholds for evaluating benchmark quality and outline a pre-registered pilot design as a blueprint for next-generation agentic benchmark reporting.

title: FlexLAM: Resolving the Bottleneck Trade-off in Latent Action Learning
summary: Latent actions provide a compact interface between action-free video and downstream decision-making, yet existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck. We identify a bottleneck trade-off: overly tight codes can discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while overly loose codes preserve additional transition variation that must be resolved when alignment labels are scarce or narrowly distributed. FlexLAM replaces this fixed capacity with variable-length latent actions trained by nested dropout, yielding prefix-valid codes that capture compact transition structure first and add detail only when needed, without new architectures or losses. A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision and under a low-return single-task alignment stress test, indicating that FlexLAM is not merely adjustable at inference time but learns a better latent-action interface at the same token budgets. The same model supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining, and FlexLAM improves Ego4D transition reconstruction. These results suggest that variable-length latent actions are an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces.

AI.tldr: FlexLAM introduces variable-length latent actions via nested dropout to replace the fixed-capacity bottleneck in Latent Action Models, achieving flexible, prefix-valid codes that outperform fixed-capacity baselines at every token budget without architectural changes or new losses.
AI.motivation: Existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force all transitions through a fixed-capacity bottleneck, creating a bottleneck trade-off: tight codes discard transition cues needed for alignment, while loose codes preserve excessive variation that is hard to resolve with scarce or narrowly distributed labels. The authors aim to resolve this trade-off with a single, flexible model.
AI.method: FlexLAM replaces the fixed-capacity bottleneck with variable-length latent actions trained using nested dropout. This yields prefix-valid codes that capture compact transition structure first and progressively add detail only when needed. The approach requires no new architectures or loss functions and supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining.
AI.result: A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under scarce-label supervision and a low-return single-task alignment stress test. FlexLAM also improves transition reconstruction on Ego4D and learns a better latent-action interface at the same token budgets.
AI.conclusion: Variable-length latent actions serve as an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in LAMs, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces, enabling flexible capacity without retraining or architectural overhaul.

title: Image Encryption Algorithm Based on Convolutional Neural Networks and Dynamic S-Box Generation
summary: The paper proposes a dynamic approach to image encryption, combining the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and classical cryptography to improve the security and flexibility of image encryption. The main concept is to create adaptive Substitution boxes (S-boxes) based on characteristics that are learned by a trained CNN. The CNN-based S-boxes can be relied on for more non-linearity, uniqueness, and input image dependence than the conventional fixed S-boxes because they are susceptible to the linear and differential attacks. This dynamic behaviour enhances the confusion property and makes it more resistant to statistical and structural attacks. The encryption algorithm consists of CNN-based feature extraction and the creation of a personalised S-box to replace the pixels. Entropy, histogram analysis, correlation, NPCR, and UACI enable security assessment of generated S-boxes based on the CNN, indicating that the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional ones.

AI.tldr: A dynamic image encryption method is proposed that uses CNN-learned features to generate adaptive, input-dependent S-boxes, enhancing non-linearity and resistance to linear, differential, statistical, and structural attacks compared to conventional fixed S-boxes.
AI.motivation: Conventional fixed S-boxes used in classical image encryption are susceptible to linear and differential cryptanalysis. There is a need for adaptive, input-dependent S-boxes that offer greater non-linearity, uniqueness, and resilience against statistical and structural attacks.
AI.method: A CNN is trained to extract image features, which are then used to dynamically generate personalized (adaptive) Substitution boxes (S-boxes). These CNN-based S-boxes replace pixels in the encryption algorithm. Security is evaluated using entropy, histogram analysis, correlation coefficients, NPCR (Number of Pixels Change Rate), and UACI (Unified Average Changing Intensity).
AI.result: The CNN-generated S-boxes demonstrate improved non-linearity, uniqueness, and input dependence. Security assessments (entropy, histogram, correlation, NPCR, UACI) indicate the scheme offers greater resilience and flexibility than traditional fixed S-box encryption methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining CNN-based dynamic S-box generation with classical cryptography yields a more secure and flexible image encryption framework, effectively resisting linear, differential, statistical, and structural attacks.

title: Repository-Level Solidity Code Generation with Large Language Models: From Prompting to Fine-Tuning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in general-purpose code generation, but their effectiveness in specialized software domains remains underexplored. Solidity smart contracts represent a high-stakes domain where generated code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks and metrics remain insufficient for repository-level Solidity generation, where models must synthesize complete contracts from natural language requirements. To address this gap, we introduce SolidityBench, a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts paired with natural language descriptions. We also propose SolidityScore, a Solidity-aware semantic metric that emphasizes domain-critical constructs such as security modifiers, contract declarations, and Solidity-specific keywords. Using this benchmark, we evaluate representative code LLMs, including Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama, across zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and supervised fine-tuning. The results show that general-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, retrieval-augmented generation performs best, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. Supervised fine-tuning achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive benchmark for repository-level Solidity code generation and shows that high-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts.

AI.tldr: Introduces SolidityBench, a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts with natural language descriptions, and SolidityScore, a domain-aware semantic metric. Evaluates multiple LLMs and strategies, finding supervised fine-tuning most effective for generating reliable smart contracts.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at general code generation but remain underexplored in specialized, high-stakes domains like Solidity smart contracts, where generated code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks and metrics are insufficient for repository-level generation from natural language requirements.
AI.method: 1. SolidityBench: A benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts with paired natural language descriptions. 2. SolidityScore: A Solidity-aware semantic metric emphasizing domain-critical constructs (security modifiers, contract declarations, Solidity-specific keywords). 3. Evaluation of representative code LLMs (Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeLlama) across five strategies: zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
AI.result: General-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, RAG performs best. In-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. Supervised fine-tuning achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters.
AI.conclusion: High-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts. The study provides the first comprehensive benchmark for repository-level Solidity code generation.

title: GLARE: A Natural Language Interface for Querying Global Explanations
summary: While global explanations are crucial for understanding vision models across datasets, classes, and decision contexts, their complex and monolithic nature often hinders practical exploration. Because users typically seek targeted answers to specific questions rather than static artifacts, we present an LLM-based interactive interface that provides natural language access to global explanations for black-box image classifiers. The system's core LLM acts as a mediator, translating natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data. This enables flexible aggregation without exposing users to low-level representations. For each query, the interface outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses, supporting local explanations, and intent-aligned visualizations. We evaluate the system on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. Our results demonstrate that LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based interactive interface that translates natural language questions into SQL queries over local explanation data, enabling flexible, statistics-augmented exploration of global explanations for black-box image classifiers.
AI.motivation: Global explanations are crucial for interpreting vision models but are too complex and monolithic for practical, targeted exploration. Users need tailored answers to specific questions rather than static explanation artifacts.
AI.method: An LLM serves as a mediator that converts natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data. The system returns statistics-augmented natural language responses, supporting local explanations and intent-aligned visualizations.
AI.result: The system was evaluated on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. LLM-mediated querying substantially improved accessibility and usability of global explanations.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated natural language querying significantly enhances the practical accessibility and usability of global explanations in human-centered XAI for vision models.

title: Spectral DPPs via NEPv: A Scalable Continuous Relaxation of Determinantal MAP for Diversity-Aware Data Selection
summary: Selecting a small, diverse, high-quality subset from a massive pool of candidates is a recurring primitive in modern machine learning -- data curation and coreset selection for training and fine-tuning large models, active-learning batch acquisition, prompt and exemplar selection for in-context learning, retrieval diversification, and experimental design. Determinantal Point Processes (\DPP s) give a principled, well-calibrated notion of diversity for this task, but their \emph{MAP} objective -- pick a size-$k$ subset $S$ maximizing $\logdet(L_S)$ -- is NP-hard, and the standard greedy and sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in the ground-set size $n$. This cost is prohibitive precisely in the data-centric regime where diversity matters most, where $n$ ranges over millions to billions of candidate examples, features, or embeddings. We recast \DPP-MAP as a continuous optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold, and show that its first-order optimality conditions form a \emph{Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency} (\NEPv) of a previously unstudied form. This \NEPv\ admits a self-consistent field (\SCF) iteration with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee, giving a principled iterative solver where the diversity objective drives an eigenvector-dependent operator. The resulting algorithm, \OurMethod, requires only matrix-vector products with the kernel and runs in time $O\!\big((ndk+nk^2)\,t\big)$ for a small number of iterations $t$, scaling near-linearly in $n$ and integrating directly with low-rank and feature-map kernels common in ML. This paper focuses on the relaxation, solver, and scaling analysis; full real-data benchmarking is left to a planned empirical study.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates the NP-hard Determinantal Point Process MAP inference (selecting a size-k subset maximizing log-determinant) as a continuous optimization problem on the Stiefel manifold, yielding a Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv). A self-consistent field (SCF) iteration with local contraction guarantees solves this efficiently in near-linear time O((ndk + nk²)t), making diversity subset selection scalable to millions/billions of candidates.
AI.motivation: DPP-MAP is the gold-standard for selecting diverse, high-quality subsets, but exact inference is NP-hard and existing greedy/sampling algorithms scale superlinearly with ground-set size n. This is prohibitive in modern data-centric ML where n reaches millions to billions (data curation, coreset selection, active learning, in-context example selection). A scalable, principled solver is needed.
AI.method: The authors recast DPP-MAP as continuous optimization over the Stiefel manifold. The first-order optimality conditions reveal a novel Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv). They propose a self-consistent field (SCF) iteration to solve this NEPv, with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee. The resulting algorithm (OurMethod) uses only matrix-vector products with the kernel, achieving O((ndk + nk²)t) time for t iterations, and accommodates low-rank and feature-map kernels.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves near-linear scaling in n, requiring only matrix-vector products. A spectral-gap-based local convergence guarantee is established for the SCF iteration. The method integrates naturally with low-rank and feature-map kernel approximations commonly used in ML pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a principled, scalable relaxation and solver for DPP-MAP subset selection. Full real-data empirical benchmarking is deferred to a planned future study, with this paper focusing on the theoretical formulation, algorithm design, and complexity analysis.

title: Analyzing Defensive Misdirection Against Model-Guided Automated Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly rely on language-model components to interpret instructions, process external data, invoke tools, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks more consequential, especially as attackers adopt model-guided automation to scale probing, prompt refinement, and response evaluation. This work analyzes the resulting attack-defense setting through a probabilistic model of a target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. Our analysis shows that conventional detect-and-block defenses can allow attacker success rate (ASR) to approach one as the query budget grows, since predictable refusals provide useful feedback to automated search. We then examine detect-and-misdirect, where detected malicious interactions receive controlled, non-operational responses designed to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge. This strategy reduces the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates and yields a bounded asymptotic ASR. We evaluate a proof-of-concept realization of this strategy through Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), a lightweight conversational misdirection method designed to replace predictable refusal text with safe but strategically misleading responses in automated jailbreak settings. On jailbreak benchmarks, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how automated jailbreak attacks exploit predictable refusal signals in LLM-based agentic systems, proposes a "detect-and-misdirect" defense strategy that replaces refusals with misleading responses to degrade the attacker's automated judge, and demonstrates a practical implementation (CMPE) that reduces attack success rates by up to two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: As agentic AI systems rely on LLMs for instruction interpretation, tool invocation, and coordination, prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks become more consequential. Attackers increasingly use model-guided automation for large-scale probing, and conventional detect-and-block defenses paradoxically help attackers by providing predictable refusal signals that guide automated search toward successful exploits.
AI.method: The authors first formalize the attack-defense dynamic using a probabilistic model capturing the target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. They analytically show that detect-and-block defenses allow ASR to approach 1 as query budget grows. They then propose detect-and-misdirect, where malicious interactions receive controlled, non-operational responses designed to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge, thereby reducing the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates and bounding asymptotic ASR. The practical instantiation, Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), is a lightweight conversational method that replaces refusals with safe but strategically misleading responses.
AI.result: On jailbreak benchmarks, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.
AI.conclusion: Detect-and-misdirect is a principled alternative to detect-and-block for defending agentic LLM systems against automated jailbreak attacks. By denying attackers reliable feedback, the defense bounds asymptotic attack success and renders automated search significantly less effective.

title: Beyond Static Endpoints: Tool Programs as an Interface for Flexible Agentic Web Services
summary: In the agentic web era, LLM-based agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, yet most interfaces remain \emph{static endpoints} that poorly express long-horizon workflows with loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. We present ToolPro, which represents an agent's tool intent as an \emph{executable tool program} that compactly encodes multi-step service interactions with explicit effect types. ToolPro combines constraint-guided program construction, effect-aware replay for exactly-once state-modifying calls, and a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. We instantiate ToolPro over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing and evaluate it on diverse workflows of real-world applications. ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4\% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1\%, with larger gains under higher network latency and workflow complexity.

AI.tldr: ToolPro introduces executable tool programs that compactly encode multi-step agent workflows (loops, conditionals, joins, retries) with explicit effect types, achieving up to 53.4% latency reduction and 96.1% traffic reduction compared to stepwise calling of static web endpoints.
AI.motivation: In the agentic web era, LLM-based agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, but most interfaces are static endpoints that poorly support long-horizon workflows involving loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. Stepwise calling incurs high latency and network overhead.
AI.method: ToolPro represents agent tool intent as an executable tool program encoding multi-step service interactions with explicit effect types. It employs three key techniques: (1) constraint-guided program construction, (2) effect-aware replay ensuring exactly-once execution for state-modifying calls, and (3) a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. The system is instantiated over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing.
AI.result: ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1%, with larger gains observed under higher network latency and greater workflow complexity.
AI.conclusion: Executable tool programs with explicit effect types and profile-driven execution decisions offer a practical and effective approach to optimizing agentic web service interactions, particularly for complex, long-horizon workflows.

title: From 50K to 8.2 Million in 24 Hours: Vozinha's Algorithmic Consecration and the Multilingual Making of World Cup Visibility
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables; v0.1 pilot preprint. Dataset and evidence package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20722235
