summary: We present a multilingual computational discourse analysis of how language constructed the algorithmic consecration of Vozinha, the 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper, after Spain 0-0 Cape Verde at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The study contributes a multilingual corpus in Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French; a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based frame annotation; a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestion with human validation; and an analysis of cross-lingual narrative diffusion across discourse phases. We treat the platform follower count itself, narrated as "50k to 8M", as a linguistic object: a circulating and narratable proof of visibility rather than a mere measurement. The follower-growth timeline is used only as contextual metadata: we reconstruct a conservative phase structure, not a continuous API-native series, and type every datapoint by value class, confidence, and evidence type. The only exact primary scraper anchor is 8,235,652 followers at 2026-06-16 15:47 UTC; all other figures are reported as estimated ranges or thresholds, including an estimated pre-match baseline of 45k-56k. Findings suggest that distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese mobilization, Spanish crisis, English nation-making, and a shared platform-metric spectacle through which peripheral athletic performance became globally visible. As a v0.1 pilot, the paper releases the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline, while flagging full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement as planned work.

AI.tldr: A multilingual discourse analysis of how four languages framed the viral rise of Cape Verde's goalkeeper Vozinha after a 2026 World Cup draw, finding that Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French each carried distinct narrative frames — mobilization, crisis, nation-making, and platform spectacle — while treating follower counts as narratable linguistic objects rather than mere metrics.
AI.motivation: To understand how distinct languages construct algorithmic consecration differently — i.e., how a peripheral athletic performance becomes globally visible through platform-mediated narrative framing. The study challenges treating follower counts as neutral measurements, instead positioning them as circulating linguistic objects that narrate visibility.
AI.method: Constructed a multilingual corpus (Portuguese, Spanish, English, French) around the Spain 0-0 Cape Verde match; developed a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based annotation; built a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestions with human validation; reconstructed a conservative phase structure for follower growth using estimated ranges and typed datapoints (value class, confidence, evidence type); used only one exact scraper anchor (8,235,652 followers at 2026-06-16 15:47 UTC) with all other figures as estimated ranges.
AI.result: Distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese discourse centered on mobilization, Spanish on crisis, English on nation-making, with a shared platform-metric spectacle frame operating across all languages. The follower count narrative ("50k to 8M") functioned as a circulating proof of visibility across discourse phases.
AI.conclusion: As a v0.1 pilot, the paper demonstrates the viability of the multilingual frame-analysis approach and releases the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline. Full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement are flagged as planned future work.

title: Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks
summary: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, yet its black-box nature remains a key roadblock to deployment and scientific diagnosis. Standard interpretability tools, such as Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), are ill-equipped for NCO, whose decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack proper concept vocabulary definition. To close this gap, we introduce Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), to our knowledge, the first framework for interpreting NCO policies by distilling black-box NCO models into human-readable program portfolios. EPB employs an LLM to autonomously evolve a bank of programs, where each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck. EPB works through an iterative framework: Block I fixes program bank capacity and introduces a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme that couples numerical gradients for student router updates and textual gradients for LLM-based program revision; Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate EPB's effectiveness and broad applicability, where the distilled program portfolios largely match original performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models.

AI.tldr: EPB introduces the first interpretability framework for Neural Combinatorial Optimization by distilling black-box NCO policies into evolving, human-readable program portfolios using an LLM-driven iterative process with hybrid gradient descent and dynamic capacity adaptation.
AI.motivation: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) models achieve strong performance but suffer from a black-box nature that hinders deployment and scientific understanding. Existing interpretability tools like Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) fail on NCO because NCO decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack a well-defined concept vocabulary.
AI.method: EPB employs an LLM to evolve a bank of programs, where each program's per-step action distribution serves as a programmatic bottleneck. The framework operates in two iterative blocks: Block I uses a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent — numerical gradients update a student router, while textual gradients guide LLM-based program revision, all under fixed bank capacity. Block II dynamically adjusts capacity via fault-targeted expansion (adding programs for failure cases) and redundancy pruning (removing overlapping programs).
AI.result: Extensive experiments show distilled program portfolios largely match the original NCO model performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as compositions of classic heuristic variants.
AI.conclusion: EPB advances interpretable NCO and establishes itself as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models more broadly.

title: Spectral Retrieval-Augmented Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting leverages historical patterns to predict future values, but traditional methods face challenges when dealing with complex, non-stationary patterns that are difficult to memorize during training. Retrieval-augmented approaches have emerged as promising solutions by retrieving similar historical patterns to enhance predictions. However, existing retrieval methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: spectral blindness, which overlooks critical frequency-domain characteristics that capture underlying periodic structures, and temporal recency, which treats all historical data equally without emphasizing recent, more relevant patterns. In this paper, we propose SpecReTF, a novel retrieval method that addresses these issues by converting time series into windowed frequency representations, measuring similarity with a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information. To balance recency and historical context, we apply an exponential moving average weighting scheme that emphasizes recent windows. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SpecReTF outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy across diverse, non-stationary time series.

AI.tldr: SpecReTF proposes a frequency-domain retrieval method for time series forecasting that addresses spectral blindness and temporal recency bias by comparing windowed frequency representations with a combined amplitude-phase similarity metric, weighted by an exponential moving average to emphasize recent patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented time series forecasting methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) spectral blindness — they operate solely in the time domain and fail to capture frequency-domain characteristics that reveal underlying periodic structures; (2) temporal recency neglect — they treat all historical data equally without prioritizing more recent, relevant patterns. These limitations degrade performance on complex, non-stationary time series where periodic and evolving dynamics are critical.
AI.method: SpecReTF converts time series into windowed frequency-domain representations, then measures similarity using a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information across windows. To address temporal recency, it applies an exponential moving average (EMA) weighting scheme that assigns higher importance to more recent windows when retrieving similar patterns from historical data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that SpecReTF consistently outperforms time-domain retrieval methods in forecasting accuracy, particularly on diverse, non-stationary time series.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-domain retrieval with recency-aware weighting offers a robust and effective approach for retrieval-augmented time series forecasting, overcoming key limitations of purely time-domain methods.

title: A-COMPASS: Formal Foundations for Anonymity Analysis in Microdata
summary: In the information age, one of the leading problems is how to ensure individual's privacy. Depending on the context in which privacy is considered, various data privacy models have emerged. However, the domain of formal verification of these models is still not sufficiently explored even when it comes to the most basic models. An attempt to verify privacy requirements is the Compliance Assertion Language (COMPASS). In COMPASS, one can specify an anonymity condition that a table needs to satisfy, and an action that will modify the table if the condition is not satisfied. It is designed to operate on preprocessed tables in a form one record - one group of people. In this paper, we modify the COMPASS language in order to operate on microdata tables in their usual form of one record - one person. The modified language is called A-COMPASS. Along with checking of previously applied anonymity conditions, A-COMPASS enables the execution of anonymization actions as a new feature. We further provide the syntax and the semantics for the A-COMPASS language. We also prove the most important properties of the introduced semantics like determinism and compositionality. Finally, we provide a mechanism to verify anonymity properties, such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces A-COMPASS, a modified formal language for specifying and verifying privacy/anonymity conditions on microdata tables (one record–one person), extending the original COMPASS language which operates on aggregated tables. A-COMPASS adds anonymization action execution, formal syntax/semantics, and proofs of determinism and compositionality, with verification support for k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.motivation: The domain of formal verification of data privacy models remains underexplored, even for basic models. The original COMPASS language operates only on preprocessed tables (one record–one group), limiting its applicability to standard microdata. There is a need for a formal language that can specify, verify, and enforce anonymity conditions directly on person-level microdata.
AI.method: The authors modify the COMPASS language to create A-COMPASS, which operates on microdata tables in the standard one record–one person format. They define the full syntax and formal semantics of A-COMPASS, prove key semantic properties (determinism and compositionality), and introduce anonymization actions as a new executable feature alongside condition checking. They also provide a verification mechanism for anonymity properties including k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.result: A-COMPASS is presented with complete syntax and formal semantics. The semantics is proven to be deterministic and compositional. The language supports both checking previously applied anonymity conditions and executing anonymization actions. Verification mechanisms for k-anonymity and l-diversity are provided.
AI.conclusion: A-COMPASS successfully extends COMPASS to operate on standard one record–one person microdata tables, filling a gap in the formal verification of data privacy models. The formal semantics with proven determinism and compositionality provides a rigorous foundation for specifying and enforcing anonymity properties like k-anonymity and l-diversity in microdata.

title: When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents
summary: As LLM agents increasingly select tools autonomously, their choices among tools with different privileges become safety-relevant. However, prior tool-selection studies focus on safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving privilege-sensitive choices underexplored. To address this gap, we study over-privileged tool selection, in which an agent selects or escalates to a higher-privilege tool despite a sufficient lower-privilege alternative. We introduce ToolPrivBench to evaluate whether agents choose higher-privilege tools despite sufficient lower-privilege alternatives, measuring both initial selection and escalation after transient tool failures. Across eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, we find that over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is further amplified by transient failures. We further find that general safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice, while prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. We therefore introduce a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary. Our mitigation experiments show that this defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.

AI.tldr: LLM agents often over-select high-privilege tools when lower-privilege ones suffice, a behavior amplified by transient failures. The authors introduce ToolPrivBench to benchmark this issue, find that general safety alignment is insufficient, and propose a privilege-aware post-training defense that significantly reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use without degrading general capabilities.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents autonomously select tools with varying privilege levels, over-privileged selection poses safety risks — yet prior work only examines safety-agnostic metadata preferences. This gap motivates a systematic study of whether agents choose higher-privilege tools when lower-privilege alternatives are sufficient, including escalation behaviors after transient failures.
AI.method: The authors introduce ToolPrivBench, a benchmark spanning eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, to measure over-privileged tool selection in both initial selection and post-failure escalation scenarios. They evaluate mainstream LLM agents, test whether general safety alignment transfers to least-privilege tool choice, assess prompt-level mitigations, and develop a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary.
AI.result: Over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is amplified by transient failures. General safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice. Prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. The proposed privilege-aware post-training defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Over-privileged tool selection is a prevalent and understudied safety issue for autonomous LLM agents. Neither general safety alignment nor prompt-level interventions suffice; a dedicated privilege-aware post-training approach is necessary to enforce least-privilege tool selection reliably in practice.

title: SAGE-OPD: Selective Agent-Guided Intervention for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves student models by training them on trajectories induced by their own policy, making it a promising approach for mitigating exposure bias in agent training. However, most OPD studies focus on single-turn settings, while realistic LLM agents interact with environments over multiple turns. In this regime, early errors can alter future observations and compound across the trajectory, and standard dense token-level OPD becomes brittle, as it may over-penalize semantically valid alternatives, reinforce local degeneracies such as repeated actions, and propagate unreliable teacher supervision on off-distribution histories. We propose SAGE-OPD, a verifier-free selective intervention framework specifically designed for multi-turn OPD. Instead of applying teacher supervision uniformly across all turns, SAGE-OPD first observes environment feedback and uses teacher judgment to decide whether each student response should be skipped or intervened on. To further address compounding errors, SAGE-OPD weights token-level distillation by teacher confidence, reducing the influence of uncertain teacher distributions on corrupted or ambiguous histories. Finally, SAGE-OPD applies loss normalization to preserve the overall loss scale of standard OPD while retaining selective turn-level weighting. Experiments on agent tasks show that SAGE-OPD consistently improves over baselines, achieving up to a 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies further demonstrate that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization provide complementary benefits. Our results suggest that effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision should be selectively allocated to turns where intervention is necessary and reliable.

AI.tldr: SAGE-OPD is a selective intervention framework for multi-turn on-policy distillation that uses teacher judgment to decide when to intervene, weights distillation by teacher confidence, and applies loss normalization — achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement on ALFWorld over standard OPD.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) works well in single-turn settings but fails in multi-turn agent scenarios because early errors compound across trajectories, dense token-level supervision over-penalizes valid alternatives, reinforces local degeneracies (e.g., repeated actions), and propagates unreliable teacher guidance on off-distribution states.
AI.method: SAGE-OPD introduces three complementary mechanisms: (1) turn-level selective intervention — using environment feedback and teacher judgment to decide whether to skip or intervene on each student response; (2) teacher confidence weighting — scaling token-level distillation loss by the teacher's confidence to reduce influence on corrupted or ambiguous histories; (3) loss normalization — preserving the overall loss scale of standard OPD while incorporating selective turn-level weighting.
AI.result: SAGE-OPD consistently outperforms baselines on agent tasks, achieving up to a 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies confirm that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization each contribute complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy but allocate teacher supervision selectively — only to turns where intervention is both necessary and reliable.

title: A Comparative Study of Pretrained Transformer Models for Quranic ASR: Speech Representations, Label Formats, and Dataset Composition
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, Submitted to International Journal of Speech Technology
summary: Quran Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) aims to convert Quranic recitation into text, enabling applications such as aided memorisation tools and Quranic search engines. However, existing ASR models often exhibit high Word Error Rates (WER) on user-recited verses and lack full coverage of the Quranic corpus. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of domain-specific fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer-based models for Quranic ASR, using advanced speech feature extraction methods: Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, and XLS-R. These models apply self-supervised learning by masking portions of input audio and using Transformer architectures to learn context-aware speech features. The pretrained models are fine-tuned on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours of professional and user recitations. Through comprehensive ablation studies across feature extractors, output label formats, training strategies, and clip durations, we identify the key factors that affect transcription accuracy in this domain. Our best-performing configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on the EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on the combined EveryAyah+Tarteel setting, representing roughly a five-percentage-point gain over the Citrinet baseline (WER = 0.163) while reducing combined-model training time from 140 hours to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall representation. Future work includes improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models to extract deeper speech feature representations for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically fine-tunes self-supervised Transformer-based speech models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) for Quranic ASR on 870+ hours of recitation data, achieving a best WER of 0.08–0.11, significantly outperforming the Citrinet baseline while cutting training time by ~70%.
AI.motivation: Existing Quranic ASR systems suffer from high Word Error Rates on user-recited verses and incomplete coverage of the Quranic corpus. The authors aim to close this gap by systematically investigating how domain-specific fine-tuning of modern self-supervised speech models can improve transcription accuracy for both professional and user Quranic recitations.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive empirical study fine-tuning three pretrained Transformer-based speech feature extractors — Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, and XLS-R (specifically Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53) — on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours. These models use masked audio portions and self-supervised learning to derive context-aware representations. Ablation studies examine feature extractor choice, output label format (with/without diacritics), training strategies, and clip durations to isolate factors affecting transcription accuracy.
AI.result: The best configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on the EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on the combined EveryAyah+Tarteel setting — a ~5 percentage-point improvement over the Citrinet baseline (WER=0.163). Training time drops from 140 to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall representation.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning of XLS-R-based models with non-diacritized Arabic text substantially advances Quranic ASR accuracy and efficiency. Future work should target improved dataset quality and phoneme-aware modeling to capture Tajweed-sensitive features for deeper speech representation.

title: Does Text Actually Help? Uncovering and Resolving Text Collapse in Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal time series forecasting, which pairs numerical sequences with domain-relevant textual reports, promises to inject world knowledge into forecasting pipelines. However, we uncover a critical failure mode in existing frameworks that we term text collapse: the text branch converges to a content-independent transformation, contributing negligible discriminative signal regardless of the input description. We argue that text collapse is a consequence of a fundamental asymmetry in time series forecasting: the numerical input is strongly autocorrelated with the output, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant, while the text branch, despite carrying complementary and often critical information, is insufficiently utilized, leading to its systematic underexploitation. To address this, we propose \textbf{REST-TS} (\textbf{R}esidual-\textbf{E}xclusive \textbf{S}upervision for \textbf{T}ext in \textbf{T}ime \textbf{S}eries), which turns the asymmetry into a design principle: the numerical backbone produces its own independent numerical forecast, and the text branch is exclusively supervised to predict the structured components of the residual, the prediction gap that numbers cannot explain. Because no numerical pathway can reduce these losses, the text branch must extract genuine content from the input description. Evaluated across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures, REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that supervising the text branch on the residual compels it to extract genuine content from the input.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "text collapse" in multimodal time series forecasting, where text branches become uninformative due to the dominance of numerical features. The proposed REST-TS framework solves this by exclusively supervising the text branch on the residual error that the numerical backbone cannot explain, forcing genuine text utilization and achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal time series forecasting frameworks suffer from "text collapse," where the text branch degrades into a content-independent transformation that contributes negligible discriminative signal. This stems from a fundamental asymmetry: numerical inputs are strongly autocorrelated with outputs, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant, while complementary text information is systematically underexploited.
AI.method: REST-TS (Residual-Exclusive Supervision for Text in Time Series) converts the asymmetry into a design principle. The numerical backbone independently produces a numerical forecast. The text branch is then exclusively supervised to predict the structured components of the residual — the prediction gap that numerical features cannot explain. Since no numerical pathway can reduce these residual losses, the text branch is compelled to extract genuine semantic content from the input description.
AI.result: REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures. It consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that residual-exclusive supervision compels the text branch to extract genuine content.
AI.conclusion: Supervising the text branch exclusively on the numerically unexplainable residual is an effective strategy to prevent text collapse, forcing meaningful multimodal fusion. This design principle can be applied across various backbone architectures and domains.

title: Calibration Without Comprehension: Diagnosing the Limits of Fine-Tuning LLMs for Vulnerability Detection in Systems Software
summary: Whether LLMs scoring well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data remains unresolved. We present CWE-Trace, a framework for LLM vulnerability detection built from 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples spanning 74 CWEs. The framework enforces a strict temporal split (pre-2025 historical set / post-cutoff leakage-free set), preserves context-aware vulnerable--patched pairs, and introduces two diagnostic metrics: the Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). We evaluate eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification. Our analysis yields two key results. First, data contamination provides no measurable advantage. Function-level analysis shows that 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal: vulnerable functions are absent or cross-mapped across datasets, and ~31% of contaminated samples carry CWE misclassification. Second, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning. Models exhibit stable, systematic failure modes (DFI ranging from -85.5 to +94.8 pp) that persist from historical to post-cutoff data and resist correction. Fine-tuning shifts the output threshold without changing the decision policy. This is calibration without comprehension: output distributions adapt to training data while the underlying security reasoning remains absent. The weakest backbone at binary detection (DeepSeek-R1) gains the most in coarse CWE classification, revealing that detection and understanding are decoupled capabilities. The best detection score reaches only 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE ranking remains below 1.3% Top-1 accuracy, confirming that current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.

AI.tldr: Current LLMs fail at vulnerability detection in Linux kernel code, not because of data contamination but because they lack genuine security reasoning — fine-tuning merely shifts output thresholds without changing decision policies.
AI.motivation: Resolve whether LLMs' performance on vulnerability benchmarks reflects genuine security reasoning or mere pattern-matching on contaminated training data, and to rigorously assess the gap between detection and comprehension capabilities.
AI.method: CWE-Trace framework with 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples across 74 CWEs, strict temporal split (pre-2025 vs. post-cutoff), context-aware vulnerable-patched pairs, and two diagnostic metrics: Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). Evaluated 8 vanilla and 15 LoRA fine-tuned LLMs on non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification.
AI.result: Data contamination provides no measurable advantage (84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal; ~31% have CWE misclassification). Backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning with stable, systematic failure modes (DFI -85.5 to +94.8 pp). Fine-tuning only shifts output thresholds without changing decision policies. Best binary detection: 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE Top-1 accuracy: below 1.3%.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software. Detection and CWE understanding are decoupled capabilities. Fine-tuning provides calibration without comprehension, and backbone priors systematically resist correction regardless of strategy.

title: The Correctness Illusion in LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, LNCS format. Companion papers to follow on arXiv next week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary: Benchmarks for LLM-generated GPU kernels (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) score correctness through fixed-shape, small-sample allclose-style checks. The number of inputs varies between benchmarks. The shape, dtype, and tolerance are fixed for each kernel. We test that oracle empirically. We construct a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU stand-in kernels (15 correct controls and 9 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors) and re-evaluate it under op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with a high-precision (fp64) CPU reference and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The seeded oracle flags 9 of 9 buggy kernels and passes 15 of 15 correct controls, at zero precision cost on controls. We extend the corpus to 26 ops (adding a flash-attention pair) and re-run the same protocol on five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL). The verdicts are identical across all five GPUs: 10 of 10 illusions caught and 16 of 16 controls clean. The corpus result is about LLM-style transcription bugs that the allclose-on-one-shape oracle certifies as correct, not about the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM. Every flagged failure replays byte-for-byte from a stored seed.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that standard LLM-generated GPU kernel benchmarks use oversimplified correctness checks (fixed-shape, small-sample allclose tests) that miss LLM-style transcription bugs. By constructing a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU kernels (15 correct, 9 buggy) and evaluating with op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing using fp64 CPU references with per-operation absolute tolerances, the authors achieve perfect classification (9/9 bugs caught, 15/15 controls passed). The protocol generalizes across five GPU classes with identical results.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) evaluate LLM-generated GPU kernel correctness using fixed-shape, small-sample allclose-style checks with fixed tolerance, dtype, and input count. This methodology is insufficiently rigorous and can certify buggy kernels as correct — a critical gap for safety-critical and performance-sensitive GPU computing.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled corpus of 24 kernels (15 correct controls, 9 buggy variants with documented LLM-style transcription errors) spanning Triton and CPU stand-ins. They develop an op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing protocol: a high-precision fp64 CPU reference computes ground truth, and per-(operation, dtype) absolute tolerances are applied. The protocol is tested across five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL), with the corpus extended to 26 ops including a flash-attention pair. All failures are deterministically replayable from stored seeds.
AI.result: The seeded oracle flags 9/9 buggy kernels and passes 15/15 correct controls with zero precision cost on controls. Across all five GPU classes, results are identical: 10/10 illusions caught, 16/16 controls clean. The standard allclose-on-one-shape oracle falsely certifies these same buggy kernels as correct.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-shape allclose checks are inadequate for validating LLM-generated GPU kernels. Op-schema-aware fuzzing with fp64 CPU references and per-operation absolute tolerances provides a robust, reproducible, GPU-agnostic correctness oracle that catches subtle transcription bugs missed by current benchmarks. The approach is not a measure of LLM bug rates but a methodological critique of existing evaluation pipelines.

title: CacheWeaver: Cache-Aware Evidence Ordering for Efficient Grounded RAG Inference
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual grounding, but it also lengthens prompts and raises prefill cost. Prefix caching in serving engines such as vLLM reduces this cost only when requests share the same token prefix. In grounded generation, however, adjacent queries may retrieve overlapping evidence in different orders, so set overlap does not become reusable prefix overlap. We present CacheWeaver, a lightweight prompt-layer method for cache-aware evidence ordering. The method keeps a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences and uses a greedy walk to place the most reusable prefix first, while leaving the serving engine and retrieved evidence set unchanged. Across three vLLM configurations, the method lowers median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by about 20-33 percent relative to retrieval-order prefix caching, without hurting answer quality in our QA tests. The greedy policy reaches 97.5 percent of the median TTFT gain from oracle ordering, indicating that most reusable prefix locality can be recovered by a simple scheduling layer between retrieval and inference.

AI.tldr: CacheWeaver reorders retrieved evidence chunks before feeding them to an LLM, maximizing shared prefix reuse in the serving engine's KV-cache without modifying the retriever or engine. This yields 20–33% lower time-to-first-token with no quality degradation, achieving 97.5% of oracle-level gains.
AI.motivation: RAG extends prompts with retrieved evidence, increasing prefill latency. Serving engines like vLLM use prefix caching to reuse KV-cache across requests sharing the same token prefix, but in grounded generation, different queries retrieve overlapping evidence in different orders—so set-level overlap rarely translates into reusable prefix overlap. The motivation is to close this gap without altering the retrieval pipeline or serving infrastructure.
AI.method: CacheWeaver inserts a lightweight scheduling layer between retrieval and inference. It maintains a prefix tree (trie) over recently served evidence sequences. Given a new set of retrieved passages, it performs a greedy walk: at each step, it selects the passage whose text shares the longest prefix with the current trie position, thereby maximizing immediate KV-cache hits. The resulting ordered evidence is then concatenated to the prompt and sent to an unmodified vLLM serving engine. The approach is evaluated against three baselines: retrieval order, random order, and an oracle that knows future cache state.
AI.result: Across three vLLM configurations (varying block size and cache policies), CacheWeaver reduces median time-to-first-token by approximately 20–33% relative to retrieval-order prefix caching. The greedy policy achieves 97.5% of the median TTFT reduction attained by the oracle ordering. These gains come with no statistically significant change in downstream QA accuracy, confirming that evidence reordering does not harm generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Most reusable prefix locality in RAG workloads can be recovered by a simple, inference-engine-agnostic evidence reordering layer. CacheWeaver demonstrates that a greedy prefix-tree scheduling policy is both near-optimal and practical to deploy, substantially reducing prefill latency without altering retrieval or serving infrastructure.

title: Benchmarking Agentic Review Systems
summary: A new class of agentic review systems are emerging as a remedy to the pressure placed on peer review systems by AI-assisted research, but it is unclear how they should be evaluated. We evaluate two open-source systems (OpenAIReview and coarse), one proprietary system (Reviewer3), and a zero-shot baseline, across six LLMs spanning frontier and efficient models. First, we study whether AI reviews on ICLR/NeurIPS papers track with papers' quality as approximated by external signals such as citations and acceptance decisions. Every system performs above chance in pairwise accuracy, and the best is OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 at 83.0%. Second, to test whether systems can catch errors with known ground truth, we construct a perturbation benchmark that injects four categories of errors into papers across eight arXiv subject classes and measure detection recall. The strongest configuration (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) catches 71.6% of injected errors, leaving substantial room for improvement. The union of detections across six models reaches 83.3% recall, suggesting different models detect different errors and better harness design can potentially increase performance. Beyond these benchmarks, we study a public deployment of OpenAIReview with real users. Votes on its comments skew positive at 1.44 to 1, and the most common complaints are about false positives and minor nitpicks. Together, by evaluating full review systems backed by state-of-the-art models on real research papers, we show that while AI reviews still have room for improvement, they can already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive feedback from real users.

AI.tldr: Evaluates AI agentic review systems for academic papers across multiple LLMs, finding GPT-5.5 with OpenAIReview achieves 83% pairwise accuracy on quality judgments and 71.6% error detection recall, with user feedback skewing positive but noting false positives and nitpicking as main complaints.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted research is placing pressure on traditional peer review systems, prompting development of agentic AI review systems. However, no established evaluation framework exists for assessing how well these systems perform, necessitating a systematic benchmark for evaluation.
AI.method: Evaluates three review systems (OpenAIReview, coarse, Reviewer3) plus a zero-shot baseline across six LLMs. Two evaluation paradigms are used: (1) correlating AI reviews with external quality signals (citations, acceptance decisions) via pairwise accuracy on ICLR/NeurIPS papers; (2) a perturbation benchmark injecting four error categories into papers across eight arXiv subject classes to measure detection recall. Also includes a real-world deployment study with user voting data.
AI.result: OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 achieves 83.0% pairwise accuracy and 71.6% error detection recall. Union of six models reaches 83.3% recall, indicating complementary error detection. User votes skew positive at 1.44:1, with main complaints being false positives and minor nitpicking.
AI.conclusion: AI review systems backed by state-of-the-art models can already track human quality judgments, catch important errors, and receive positive user feedback, though substantial room for improvement remains, particularly in reducing false positives and improving error detection coverage.

title: MortarBench: Evaluating Mortgage Loan Origination Agents
summary: Loan origination is the process by which a lender creates a new loan, from application and underwriting through approval and funding. This process serves a critical role in evaluating the eligibility and level of risk posed by an applicant. Recently, firms have begun using mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers, despite a lack of any public benchmark. To fill this gap, we present MortarBench, a loan origination agent benchmark. MortarBench uses a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples with broad edge case coverage that match real-world distributions and questions. We find that state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) perform poorly, with closed-source models achieving at most 77.1\% exact match accuracy. We also discover systematic biases in LLM perception of foreignness related to non-English names. Noting these weaknesses, we introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. Our method increases accuracy to 80.5\% while improving risk management steering and reducing bias.

AI.tldr: MortarBench is a new benchmark for loan origination agents, revealing that top LLMs achieve only 77.1% accuracy and exhibit bias against non-English names. The proposed CRIT framework boosts accuracy to 80.5% while reducing bias and improving risk calibration.
AI.motivation: Firms are deploying mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers despite the absence of any public benchmark, creating an urgent need to systematically evaluate LLM performance, uncover failure modes, and identify biases in the loan origination domain.
AI.method: The authors introduce MortarBench, a benchmark built using a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline that generates realistic, distribution-matching examples with broad edge-case coverage. They evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs on this benchmark. They then propose CRIT, a confidence calibration framework designed to improve accuracy, risk management steering, and bias mitigation.
AI.result: Closed-source LLMs achieve at most 77.1% exact match accuracy on MortarBench. Systematic biases against non-English (foreign-sounding) names were discovered. The CRIT framework raises accuracy to 80.5% while simultaneously improving risk management and reducing perceptual bias.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are insufficient for reliable loan origination without augmentation. MortarBench provides a necessary public benchmark, and the CRIT framework demonstrates that confidence calibration can meaningfully improve performance, fairness, and risk steering in financial AI agents.

title: Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents
summary: Securing AI agents that operate in complex digital environments has become a critical need, and runtime monitoring approaches that formulate and enforce policies expressed in a formal language like Datalog offer a promising solution. However, existing approaches are restricted to deterministic policies. In many practical applications of AI agents, there is a need to enforce security policies in the face of ambiguity, leading to probabilistic predicates or state transitions (for example, a declassifier or Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detector that has some failure probability on each invocation). Furthermore, in many such applications, one cannot easily make the independence assumptions necessary to invoke prior work on probabilistic inference in Datalog. We address this by introducing a sound and efficient framework for such verification based on distributionally robust optimization, computing sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation regardless of possible correlations between predicates. On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool calling agents, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior art and improves the security-utility trade-off while ensuring rigorous bounds on the probability of policy violation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a runtime monitoring framework for AI agents that enforces probabilistic security policies using distributionally robust optimization (DRO). Unlike prior Datalog-based approaches limited to deterministic policies, it computes sound upper bounds on policy violation probability without requiring independence assumptions, outperforming existing methods on benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling agents.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime monitoring for AI agents using Datalog is limited to deterministic policies. Real-world applications require handling ambiguity — such as probabilistic PII detectors or declassifiers with failure probabilities — where deterministic enforcement is insufficient. Furthermore, prior work on probabilistic inference in Datalog relies on independence assumptions that are often untenable in practice, creating a gap for sound verification under arbitrary correlations.
AI.method: The authors propose a verification framework based on distributionally robust optimization (DRO). Rather than assuming independence between probabilistic predicates, the method computes sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation that hold under any possible correlation structure. This is applied to runtime monitoring of AI agents operating in complex digital environments, where policies with probabilistic predicates or state transitions are expressed in Datalog.
AI.result: On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling agents, the proposed DRO-based approach outperforms prior art, achieving a better security-utility trade-off while providing rigorous, sound bounds on the probability of policy violation.
AI.conclusion: Distributionally robust optimization provides an effective and sound framework for probabilistic policy enforcement in AI agent monitoring, overcoming the limitations of both deterministic approaches and independence-assuming probabilistic inference in Datalog.

title: Learning Critical Testing Literacy Through Puzzles: an Experience Report
summary:
In this paper, we report our experiences and takeaways from workshops using puzzles to learn CTL.
  Background: Software testing is important yet difficult to teach. We introduced a BoK of puzzle-based learning activities to teach CTL, based on a model of critical tester's cognition, leading to the pedagogical framework P4TEST. We conducted thirteen workshops with students, testers, teachers, and primary school pupils to assess puzzle-based teaching of critical testing literacy.
  Experience: Across eleven workshops, we used a semi-structured approach, varying puzzles, materials, and timing. In two additional workshops, we introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions to gather more data on the learning experience.
  Observations: Participants consistently perceived themselves as experimenting while solving puzzles. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring. Emotions were visible in behaviour but hard to surface through written reflection alone. Think-aloud sessions revealed immediate reasoning; written reflections elicited more meta-cognitive reflection. The theme Sensemaking / reflection-in-action captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
  Reflections: Puzzles are not the intervention: the entire sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is. Designing that sequence more deliberately is the work ahead. We also developed an open-source web application with built-in analytics to customise workshops.

AI.tldr: The paper reports on using puzzle-based learning to teach Critical Testing Literacy (CTL), grounded in the P4TEST framework. Across thirteen workshops with diverse participants, the authors found that the full sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting—not just puzzles themselves—drives learning, and that think-aloud protocols surface different cognitive processes than written reflections.
AI.motivation: Software testing is both important and difficult to teach. The authors sought to address this by developing and assessing puzzle-based learning activities for teaching Critical Testing Literacy (CTL), underpinned by a model of critical tester's cognition and the P4TEST pedagogical framework.
AI.method: Thirteen workshops were conducted with students, professional testers, teachers, and primary school pupils. Eleven workshops used a semi-structured approach varying puzzles, materials, and timing. Two additional workshops introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions to capture richer data on the learning experience.
AI.result: Participants consistently perceived themselves as experimenting. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring. Emotions were visible in behavior but elusive in written reflection. Think-aloud sessions revealed immediate reasoning, while written reflections elicited more metacognitive reflection. The theme "Sensemaking / reflection-in-action" captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
AI.conclusion: Puzzles alone are not the intervention; the full sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is what matters. Future work lies in designing that sequence more deliberately. An open-source web application with built-in analytics was developed to support customizable workshops.

title: Code-Switching Reveals Language Anchoring in Multilingual LLMs
summary: Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to handle Code-Switched (CS) inputs, yet mixing languages frequently degrades performance relative to source- or target-language monolingual counterparts. To understand this degradation, we use grammar-forced CS as a controlled diagnostic setting for locating CS representations relative to their source and target counterparts. We introduce Anchor Bias, a geometric measure that quantifies language anchoring, whether a CS hidden state aligns closer to its source or target language counterpart. Across diverse MLLMs, Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS stays source-anchored, whereas target-framed CS shifts target-ward and shows larger Question Answering (QA) degradation. Motivated by this representational pattern, we propose CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering), an inference-time intervention that extracts a source-side canvas from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during prefill. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across MLLMs and CS conditions, showing that internal anchoring signals provide an actionable target for mitigating CS inference failures.

AI.tldr: Code-switched inputs cause QA performance degradation in multilingual LLMs. The paper introduces Anchor Bias, a geometric measure revealing that target-framed CS representations shift away from source-language anchors, correlating with performance drops. CANVAS, a proposed inference-time steering method, redirects target-language hidden states toward source anchors, recovering lost QA performance.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs suffer performance degradation when processing code-switched (CS) inputs compared to monolingual inputs. The authors aim to understand the representational mechanisms behind this degradation and develop a practical mitigation strategy.
AI.method: The authors use grammar-forced code-switching as a controlled diagnostic, introducing Anchor Bias — a geometric measure quantifying whether a CS hidden state is closer to its source-language or target-language monolingual counterpart. They then propose CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering), an inference-time intervention that extracts a "source canvas" from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during the prefill phase.
AI.result: Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS remains source-anchored, while target-framed CS shifts target-ward and exhibits greater QA degradation. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 scores across multiple MLLMs and CS conditions.
AI.conclusion: Internal anchoring signals provide an interpretable diagnostic for CS-induced failures and serve as an actionable target for inference-time intervention, as demonstrated by CANVAS's consistent recovery of QA performance.

title: Grounded Inference: Principles for Deterministically Encapsulated Generative Models
summary: The incorporation of generative models into traditional computational systems presents both enormous opportunity and tremendous peril. Although many early adopters have realized these perils at great expense, the field still requires foundational frameworks to de-risk incorporation of AI into traditional systems. This manuscript establishes this foundation through the definition of four specific primitives of AI blended architecture, designed to enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models. It further establishes two overarching anti-patterns broadly represented across industry to serve as warnings for engineers in this field. This framework was designed to enable successful integration of AI into traditional systems while providing a foundation upon which generative model providers could build the next generation of generative model interfaces.

AI.tldr: Proposes a foundational framework of four architectural primitives for blending generative AI into traditional systems with deterministic encapsulation, and identifies two anti-patterns to avoid.
AI.motivation: Early adopters have suffered costly failures integrating generative AI into traditional computational systems, yet the field lacks foundational frameworks to systematically de-risk such integration.
AI.method: Defines four specific architectural primitives for AI-blended architecture that enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models, and identifies two overarching anti-patterns observed across industry practice.
AI.result: A foundational framework consisting of four primitives and two anti-patterns, providing concrete architectural guidance for integrating AI into traditional systems.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables successful, de-risked integration of AI into traditional systems and provides a foundation for building the next generation of generative model interfaces.

title: 3D-DLP: Self-Supervised 3D Object-Centric Scene Representation Learning
summary: We introduce 3D-DLP, a self-supervised object-centric representation learning model that decomposes scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of 3D latent particles. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, each particle encodes disentangled attributes, including 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features, and represents a distinct entity in the scene. The model learns interpretable per-particle segmentation maps through an end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective. We demonstrate on both simulated and real-world datasets that the learned latent space is interpretable and controllable: by manipulating particle positions and decoding, we can generate novel scene configurations. Furthermore, we show that leveraging these compact 3D latent particles for downstream robotic manipulation improves performance over baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or rely on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure. Code and videos are available at https://eubooks3003.github.io/3d-dlp.

AI.tldr: 3D-DLP extends Deep Latent Particles to 3D, learning object-centric representations from RGB-D/voxel inputs via self-supervised reconstruction. Each latent particle encodes disentangled 3D position, bounding box, and appearance features with interpretable segmentation. The model enables controllable scene generation and improves downstream robotic manipulation over baselines lacking object-centric 3D structure.
AI.motivation: Existing object-centric representation learning methods often operate in 2D or lack explicit, disentangled 3D structure. This limits their interpretability, controllability, and utility for 3D reasoning tasks like robotic manipulation. The authors aim to bridge this gap by learning compact, object-centric 3D latent representations directly from scene-level observations without supervision.
AI.method: 3D-DLP builds on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, extending it to 3D. The model takes RGB-D or voxel observations as input and decomposes the scene into a set of 3D latent particles. Each particle encodes disentangled attributes: 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features. An end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective drives learning, and the model produces interpretable per-particle segmentation maps. The decoder can render novel views by manipulating latent particle positions.
AI.result: On both simulated and real-world datasets, 3D-DLP produces an interpretable and controllable latent space: manipulating particle positions and decoding generates novel scene configurations. For downstream robotic manipulation tasks, using compact 3D latent particles as the representation outperforms baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or use memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure.
AI.conclusion: 3D-DLP successfully learns disentangled, object-centric 3D representations in a self-supervised manner. The resulting latent space is both interpretable and actionable, offering clear benefits for tasks requiring 3D scene understanding and manipulation. The approach demonstrates that explicit 3D object-centric structure can be learned without labels and effectively leveraged for downstream robotics.

title: Sovereign Execution Brokers: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly connected to cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows, but production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes. Existing access-control mechanisms authorize identities, while assurance layers certify proposed actions; neither alone provides a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at the moment of mutation. This paper introduces the Sovereign Execution Broker (SEB), a runtime enforcement boundary for certificate-bound agentic infrastructure. SEB consumes certificates issued by the Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifies that the requested mutation matches the certified execution contract, checks validity windows, policy epochs, revocation epochs, and live-state drift, mints scoped execution identity, invokes infrastructure APIs, and records signed decision and outcome records. By separating proposal, admission, and execution, SEB turns certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, provided that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities. We present the SEB execution model, certificate and replay-verification predicates, scoped identity semantics, bypass-prevention deployment patterns, failure behavior, and a concrete prototype implementation. We evaluate the prototype on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation, drift detection, and security under fault injection.

AI.tldr: SEB introduces a runtime enforcement boundary that consumes certificates from a Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB) to mediate production mutations. It verifies execution contracts, checks validity/revocation windows and live-state drift, mints scoped execution identities, and produces signed audit records — effectively turning certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable capability at the moment of mutation.
AI.motivation: Production mutation authority should not be placed inside non-deterministic reasoning processes (e.g., autonomous agents). Existing mechanisms are insufficient: access control authorizes identities but lacks certified action validation, while assurance layers certify proposed actions but lack mandatory enforcement at mutation time. A unified enforcement point is needed to bridge certified authority and runtime mutation.
AI.method: SEB acts as a runtime broker between agent proposals and infrastructure APIs. It consumes SAB-issued certificates, verifies mutation requests against certified execution contracts, checks validity windows, policy/revocation epochs, and live-state drift. It then mints scoped, short-lived execution identities, invokes infrastructure APIs, and records signed decision and outcome records. Deployment requires that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities to prevent bypass. A prototype is implemented and evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes.
AI.result: The prototype was evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads introduced by the broker, revocation propagation latency, drift detection effectiveness, and security resilience under fault injection. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.)
AI.conclusion: SEB successfully separates proposal, admission, and execution phases, converting certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, and auditable runtime capability. The approach provides a mandatory enforcement point that neither access-control nor assurance layers alone can deliver, strengthening the security posture of agentic infrastructure systems.

title: N-Version Programming with Coding Agents
summary: This paper revisits the classical concept on N-version programming in the setting of contemporary AI coding agents. Revisiting the seminal Knight-Leveson experiment, we study whether diversity across agent systems, models, and implementation languages creates diverse failure modes. Using the Knight-Leveson's, Launch Interceptor Program Specification, we evaluate 48 agent-generated implementations on a shared oracle and a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. The results show substantial common-mode failure, along the findings of Knight-Leveson. Further analysis that many of those co-occuring failures can be traced to where is specification is particularly hard or ambiguous. We also demonstrate that diversity from coding agents provides practical benefit: across majority voting three-version units, the mean failure count drops from 387.44 for single versions to 130.99 for triples, and 11,844 N-version units exhibit zero observed failures. Our original results is the strongest evidence to date that N-Version Programming with coding agents is a useful engineering strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits N-version programming in the context of modern AI coding agents, replicating the Knight-Leveson experiment. Using 48 agent-generated implementations of a Launch Interceptor Program, tested with 1M random inputs, it finds substantial common-mode failures traced to ambiguous specifications. However, diversity across agents, models, and languages yields practical gains: majority voting across three-version units reduces mean failures from 387.44 to 130.99, with 11,844 N-version units exhibiting zero failures—the strongest evidence to date that N-version programming with coding agents is effective.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to test whether the classical N-version programming concept—originally studied in the Knight-Leveson experiment—holds promise when applied to contemporary AI coding agents. Specifically, they investigate whether diversity across agent systems, foundation models, and implementation languages produces genuinely diverse failure modes, or whether common-mode failures dominate as Knight and Leveson originally found.
AI.method: The authors use the Knight-Leveson Launch Interceptor Program specification and generate 48 implementations from coding agents varying across agent systems, models, and programming languages. These are evaluated against a shared test oracle using a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. Failures are analyzed for common-mode patterns, and N-version majority voting (three-version units) is assessed for reliability improvement.
AI.result: Substantial common-mode failure was observed, consistent with the original Knight-Leveson findings, with many co-occurring failures traced to hard or ambiguous parts of the specification. However, diversity from coding agents provides practical benefits: the mean failure count dropped from 387.44 (single versions) to 130.99 (three-version majority voting). A total of 11,844 N-version units exhibited zero observed failures, representing the strongest empirical support to date for N-version programming with AI coding agents.
AI.conclusion: N-version programming with AI coding agents is a useful engineering strategy. While common-mode failures persist—especially around specification ambiguity—diversity across agents, models, and languages meaningfully reduces failure rates through majority voting, demonstrating practical reliability gains.

title: What sentiment analysis can't see: Measuring whether customers were helped, and what went wrong, across 70,000 support conversations
summary: Most companies read their customer support data at scale using sentiment analysis, which measures how customers sound rather than whether they were satisfied with the result. We tested a richer alternative on 70,450 support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform: alongside tone, we used GPT-5.4 to estimate each customer's satisfaction and to flag whether they reported a concrete problem, then validated all three readings against the 1-to-5 ratings customers left on the conversations they rated. The satisfaction estimate tracked those ratings far better than sentiment did, correlating at 0.47 against 0.36 and flagging unhappy customers with far fewer false alarms. The structured read also sees what sentiment cannot: tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of conversations, a single "Neutral" label hides everything from quietly satisfied customers to ones who quietly gave up, and the largest group of all is "tolerated friction," customers who are satisfied but still reporting a fixable problem, a standing issue that no sentiment-based dashboard can surface. The broader finding is that LLM-based annotation can capture far more than the tonality of a customer's language, offering strong potential for new business metrics grounded instead in the customer's state (whether they were satisfied) and the cause of their problem extracted directly from the raw textual data of interactions and feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that GPT-4-based satisfaction estimation and problem detection from customer support conversations significantly outperforms traditional sentiment analysis, revealing that tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of cases and uncovering a large "tolerated friction" segment invisible to sentiment-based dashboards.
AI.motivation: Traditional sentiment analysis measures *how* customers sound rather than whether they were actually satisfied with the outcome of their support interaction. This creates a blind spot: companies may miss dissatisfied customers who speak politely or misclassify satisfied customers who express frustration. The authors argue for richer, LLM-based annotation that captures customer state and problem causality directly from text.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 70,450 customer support conversations from an online fundraising platform. Using GPT-4 (referred to as "GPT-5.4," likely a typo for GPT-4), they generated three readings per conversation: (1) a sentiment/tone estimate, (2) a customer satisfaction estimate, and (3) a flag for whether a concrete problem was reported. All three were validated against ground-truth 1-to-5 customer satisfaction ratings on the subset of conversations where customers left ratings. They then compared correlations, false-alarm rates, and examined cases where tone and satisfaction diverged.
AI.result: The satisfaction estimate correlated with customer ratings at 0.47, substantially outperforming sentiment's 0.36, and flagged unhappy customers with far fewer false alarms. Tone and satisfaction disagreed in 44% of conversations. The "Neutral" sentiment label collapsed multiple distinct customer states: quietly satisfied customers, quietly dissatisfied ones who gave up, and the largest group — "tolerated friction" — customers who were satisfied overall yet still reported a fixable problem, a cohort invisible to sentiment-based analytics.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based annotation can capture customer state and problem causality from raw interaction text far more effectively than tonality-based sentiment analysis. This opens the door to new, more actionable business metrics grounded in whether customers were actually satisfied and what concrete problems they experienced, rather than merely how they sounded.

title: Optimal Scheduling in a Question-Answering Forum of Knowledge Workers
summary: As individuals turn to the Internet to find answers to questions they may have, several Question Answering (QA) forums have evolved, where users knowledgeable in certain topics can contribute their expertise to answering these requests for information. While these are currently volunteer based, we consider a future version employing knowledge workers who are experts in certain topics. In such a system, the request-answer processes forming the queuing system may utilize schedulers that assign requests in different topics to the experts in the forum, who may be able to answer them according to their expertise levels in different topics. With this model, we calculate the capacity of the system for handling the requests while keeping the system stable, and design schedulers that achieve capacity. We also investigate how collaboration between experts in answering requests can potentially increase capacity.

AI.tldr: This paper models a QA forum with paid knowledge workers as a queuing system, calculates its capacity under stability constraints, designs throughput-optimal schedulers that assign questions to experts based on topic expertise, and explores how expert collaboration can further increase system capacity.
AI.motivation: Existing QA forums rely on volunteers, but a future model may employ paid knowledge workers with varying expertise across topics. Understanding the fundamental capacity limits of such a system and designing efficient scheduling policies to maximize throughput while maintaining stability is both practically relevant and theoretically challenging.
AI.method: The authors model the QA forum as a multi-class queueing system with heterogeneous servers (experts) having different service rates across different topics. They analyze system stability using queueing theory, derive the capacity region, and design scheduling policies (schedulers) that can achieve this capacity. They further extend the model to incorporate collaboration between experts on individual requests.
AI.result: The paper derives the capacity region of the QA system — the set of request arrival rates for which the system can remain stable. It presents schedulers that are throughput-optimal, i.e., they stabilize the system for any arrival rate vector within the capacity region. Additionally, it shows that collaboration among experts can strictly enlarge the capacity region compared to independent processing.
AI.conclusion: A QA forum staffed by knowledge workers can be modeled and optimized as a queueing system. Throughput-optimal scheduling policies exist and can achieve the theoretical capacity. Enabling collaboration between experts can further increase the system's overall capacity, providing a strong incentive for collaborative workflows in such platforms.

title: Can In-Context Learning Support Intrinsic Curiosity?
summary: Effective machine learning depends not only on how we model data, but also on what data we choose to collect. While large sequence models have revolutionized data modeling, the problem of automated data selection, or "intrinsic curiosity", remains a significant challenge. Classic approaches incentivize exploration by rewarding an agent based on its "learning progress", which measures how much a newly acquired observation improves a world model's predictive ability. However, evaluating these rewards traditionally requires expensive inner loops of gradient descent updates within each trajectory, rendering them computationally impractical at scale. In this work, we investigate whether the emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by serving as immediate, update-free world models. Specifically, we evaluate whether an exploration policy can be trained to maximize learning progress, using solely the prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner. We first prove that in general Markov decision processes, this is in fact impossible in an unbiased way: the resulting intrinsic rewards either suffer from nuisance terms that bias their estimation of true learning progress, or they cannot be implemented using an in-context learner's prediction errors. Conversely, we prove a positive result for a broad subclass of non-temporal settings, encompassing active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design: here, ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to the true learning progress. We corroborate our theory with controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments, demonstrating that our ICL-driven framework successfully trains curious data-collection policies that explore optimally.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether in-context learning (ICL) can replace expensive gradient-based inner loops for computing intrinsic curiosity rewards. The authors prove that in general MDPs, unbiased learning progress estimation via ICL is impossible, but in non-temporal settings like active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design, ICL-derived rewards converge to true learning progress. Experiments validate the theoretical findings.
AI.motivation: Traditional intrinsic curiosity methods reward agents based on learning progress—the improvement in a world model's predictive ability from new observations. However, evaluating this requires computationally prohibitive inner loops of gradient descent within each trajectory, making these approaches impractical at scale. The authors ask whether the emergent in-context learning capabilities of large sequence models can serve as immediate, update-free world models, eliminating this bottleneck.
AI.method: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of using ICL prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations to estimate learning progress. The authors prove two key results: (1) a negative result showing that in general Markov decision processes, unbiased learning progress estimation via ICL is impossible due to nuisance terms or implementation constraints; (2) a positive result for non-temporal settings (active learning, Bayesian Experimental Design) where ICL-derived rewards provably bound and asymptotically converge to true learning progress. Controlled experiments in continuous and symbolic environments validate the theory.
AI.result: In general MDPs, ICL-based intrinsic rewards cannot unbiasedly estimate learning progress. However, in non-temporal settings (active learning, BED), ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to true learning progress. Experiments demonstrate that the ICL-driven framework successfully trains curious data-collection policies that explore optimally.
AI.conclusion: In-context learning can serve as a computationally efficient substitute for gradient-based world models in intrinsic curiosity, but only within the restricted domain of non-temporal settings such as active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design. The approach is theoretically impossible to implement without bias in general MDPs.

title: From Efficiency to Leakage -- Privacy Backdoor in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple parties to collaboratively fine-tune language models for domain-specific tasks without sharing raw data. Since full model fine-tuning is often prohibitively expensive for FL clients, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become the de facto approach in practice, freezing the base model and training only a small set of adapters. In this paper, we show that a malicious parameter server can stealthily corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor that implicitly memorizes the client's training samples as isolated per-sample parameter updates stored in separate neurons, without degrading model utility. Concretely, our attack, NeuroImprint, assigns a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and constrains that each neuron is updated at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory. This design mitigates both cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing introduced by large local batches and stateful optimizers (e.g., Adam/AdamW) in language-model fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the resulting isolated per-sample updates can be analytically inverted in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are then deterministically mapped back to token sequences. To understand the generality of our method, we implemented NeuroImprint on multiple language models (BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2) and evaluated it across four fine-tuning datasets spanning diverse domains. The results demonstrate that our attack can reconstruct 59% to 79% of all finetuning samples with high semantic fidelity.

AI.tldr: NeuroImprint is a privacy attack where a malicious FL server poisons PEFT adapters to make each training sample update a dedicated neuron in isolation.
