This enables closed-form inversion of per-sample updates to reconstruct original text, achieving 59–79% recovery across multiple LLMs and datasets without harming model utility.
AI.motivation: Federated learning with PEFT is widely used for privacy-preserving domain adaptation, but the security assumption that a malicious server cannot recover client data through PEFT adapters remains underexplored. The authors aim to demonstrate that PEFT is not inherently safe against server-side privacy attacks.
AI.method: NeuroImprint crafts a malicious adapter initialization (a "privacy backdoor") that assigns one dedicated memorization neuron per training sample. It constrains each neuron to be updated at most once during local fine-tuning, preventing cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing from large batches and stateful optimizers (Adam/AdamW). After training, the per-sample parameter deltas are isolated, and a closed-form analytical inversion recovers text embeddings, which are deterministically mapped back to token sequences via nearest-neighbor lookup in the embedding matrix.
AI.result: Evaluated on BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2 across four diverse fine-tuning datasets, NeuroImprint reconstructs 59% to 79% of all fine-tuning samples with high semantic fidelity, all while maintaining task utility indistinguishable from benign PEFT training.
AI.conclusion: PEFT adapters in FL are not inherently privacy-safe; a malicious server can implant a privacy backdoor that enables high-fidelity training data reconstruction. This calls for rethinking server-side trust assumptions and developing defenses against such adapter-level privacy leakage.

title: Qiskit Code Migration with LLMs
summary: The rapid evolution of Quantum Development Kits (QDKs) introduces a specific form of technical debt that compromises code maintainability and hinders software reuse. In the specialized domain of Quantum Software Engineering (QSE), this challenge is intensified by the scarcity of high-quality training data and the high volatility of emerging frameworks, which often lead general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce unreliable or hallucinated results. This paper proposes a hybrid approach integrating LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to automate the migration of Qiskit code across versions. The proposed methodology enhances the precision and reliability of migration suggestions by leveraging an automatically generated taxonomy of migration scenarios as the structured, version-specific knowledge source to guide the models. The approach is implemented through an automated, extensible workflow evaluating LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5 and OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) under different retrieval schemes (unconstrained and restrictive). Results demonstrate that the taxonomy-based RAG architecture, particularly under the restrictive scheme, significantly reduces hallucinations and improves descriptive quality, with Google Gemini Flash-2.5 showing superior performance in detecting complex refactoring scenarios. These findings confirm the potential of this data-centric methodology to foster technological independence and provide robust, intelligent assistants that mitigate API obsolescence, ensuring the long-term availability of quantum algorithms within a rapidly shifting ecosystem and flattening the learning curve within Quantum Software Engineering (QSE).

AI.tldr: A hybrid LLM + Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach using a taxonomy of migration scenarios is proposed to automate Qiskit code migration across versions, reducing hallucinations and improving reliability compared to general-purpose LLMs.
AI.motivation: Quantum Development Kits (QDKs) evolve rapidly, creating technical debt that undermines code maintainability and software reuse. General-purpose LLMs produce unreliable, hallucinated outputs due to scarce training data and high framework volatility in Quantum Software Engineering (QSE).
AI.method: A hybrid LLM-RAG architecture is built around an automatically generated, version-specific taxonomy of migration scenarios. The workflow evaluates two LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5, OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) under two retrieval schemes: unconstrained and restrictive. The taxonomy serves as the structured knowledge source guiding retrieval and generation.
AI.result: The taxonomy-based RAG architecture, especially under the restrictive retrieval scheme, significantly reduces hallucinations and improves descriptive quality. Google Gemini Flash-2.5 outperforms in detecting complex refactoring scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The data-centric, taxonomy-driven RAG methodology holds strong potential for fostering technological independence, mitigating API obsolescence, ensuring long-term availability of quantum algorithms, and flattening the QSE learning curve.

title: TerraMARS: A Domain-Adapted Small-Language-Model Pipeline for Mars Terraforming Literature
summary: Researchers are interested in learning about Mars so that it may eventually become habitable for humans. To achieve this, there is a need for comprehensive knowledge of the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation environment, and spatial features through the scientific literature. These contain valuable information and meaningful quantitative constraints that can be used in other models and studies, such as habitability assessment and future terraforming studies. We present TerraMARS, an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that combines a domain-adapted Small Language Model to answer Mars terraforming-related questions and convert unstructured Mars science text into machine-readable structured outputs in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. A corpus of open-access papers is collected and processed using a multistage retrieval and chunking framework. Google Gemma 3 1B was adapted to the domain using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The resulting pipeline generates both types of output and provides a foundation for integrating knowledge from scientific literature into downstream applications like digital twins and habitability modeling for Mars. The output from this pipeline looks promising, but further improvements are needed to increase extraction accuracy and factual consistency.

AI.tldr: TerraMARS is an information extraction pipeline that uses a fine-tuned Small Language Model (Gemma 3 1B with QLoRA) to convert unstructured Mars scientific literature into structured JSON outputs, supporting habitability assessment and terraforming studies.
AI.motivation: Comprehensive knowledge of Mars' atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation, and spatial features is needed to assess habitability and plan terraforming, but this information is scattered across unstructured scientific literature. Extracting it into machine-readable structured formats would enable downstream modeling and digital twin applications.
AI.method: A multistage retrieval and chunking framework processes a corpus of open-access Mars papers. Google Gemma 3 1B is domain-adapted via QLoRA fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The pipeline outputs both direct answers to terraforming-related questions and structured JSON extractions.
AI.result: The pipeline generates promising structured outputs from Mars scientific literature, providing a foundation for integrating scientific knowledge into digital twins and habitability models.
AI.conclusion: TerraMARS demonstrates a viable approach for extracting structured information from Mars science papers, though further improvements are needed to enhance extraction accuracy and factual consistency.

title: Beyond Entropy: Learning from Token-Level Distributional Deviations for LLM Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning; however, it faces a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates precipitate entropy collapse, leading to premature convergence to suboptimal strategies, whereas excessive Shannon Entropy maximization can cause entropy explosion, driving blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning chains. To resolve this dichotomy, we introduce the Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework, which shifts the optimization focus from scalar uncertainty to the distributional properties of token logits. By leveraging the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logits distributions, ICT identifies tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points for guiding effective exploration in LLM reasoning. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in both Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy, proves that selectively updating on these tokens regulates policy concentration: it reduces the overall distribution uncertainty measured by Shannon entropy, while controlling probability concentration captured by second-order Rényi entropy. This dual effect prevents over-concentrated token generation from weakening exploration and effectively stabilizes the training landscape. Empirical results demonstrate that updating only the top 10% of unique tokens on Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B) models yields an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58%, with a maximum gain of 14.9%, over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines across seven benchmarks spanning math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework to resolve the RLVR optimization instability in LLM reasoning, where uniform token updates cause entropy collapse and excessive entropy maximization leads to incoherent exploration. ICT uses Jensen-Shannon divergence between token logit distributions to identify critical tokens for selective updating, theoretically grounded in both Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy. Empirical results show updating only the top 10% unique tokens yields up to 14.9% improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: RLVR for LLM reasoning suffers from a fundamental optimization dichotomy: uniform token updates cause entropy collapse (premature convergence to suboptimal strategies), while excessive Shannon Entropy maximization causes entropy explosion (blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning). Existing approaches fail to balance these competing forces, motivating a distributional rather than scalar approach to uncertainty management.
AI.method: The ICT framework shifts optimization from scalar uncertainty to token logit distributional properties. It computes Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logit distributions to identify tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points. The method selectively updates only these tokens (top 10% of unique tokens) rather than uniformly. Theoretical analysis proves this selective updating regulates policy concentration: it reduces Shannon entropy (overall distribution uncertainty) while controlling second-order Rényi entropy (probability concentration), preventing both over-concentration and diffusion.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, 7B), updating only the top 10% unique tokens achieves an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58% over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines, with a maximum gain of 14.9% across seven benchmarks covering math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: ICT effectively resolves the entropy collapse-explosion dichotomy in RLVR by focusing optimization on distributionally distinctive tokens, providing both empirical gains and theoretical justification through the dual entropy lens. The framework stabilizes LLM reasoning training without requiring full-parameter or full-token updates.

title: Insulin4RL: Real-Time Insulin Management in the Intensive Care Unit for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (ORL) offers the potential to improve the quality of clinical decision-making using historical electronic health record (EHR) data. Current training and evaluative practices in this field rely heavily on EHR datasets that have been temporally discretised into fixed, regular time intervals. Discretisation creates fictional representations of complex clinical scenarios and compromises the generalisability of retrospective model evaluations. In this paper, we introduce Insulin4RL, a healthcare ORL dataset featuring naturally irregular inputs and actions from real clinical trajectories. Derived from MIMIC-IV, Insulin4RL comprises over 375,000 labelled decisions across 12,209 patients requiring insulin infusion titration in the Intensive Care Unit. The dataset can thus be used for research into ORL model performance under realistic clinical sampling assumptions. We provide a description of the dataset's structure and characteristics, baseline performance metrics using model-free offline reinforcement learning, and a standardised evaluation protocol using fitted Q-evaluation. We conclude with suggested areas for future research that could be addressed using this resource.

AI.tldr: Insulin4RL is a new offline reinforcement learning dataset derived from MIMIC-IV, featuring over 375,000 clinical decisions for ICU insulin titration across 12,209 patients with naturally irregular time-series data, addressing the artificial discretization limitations of existing EHR-based ORL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current offline RL research in healthcare relies on EHR datasets discretized into fixed, regular time intervals, which creates fictional representations of clinical scenarios and undermines the generalizability of retrospective model evaluations. There is a need for datasets with naturally irregular inputs and actions reflecting real clinical trajectories.
AI.method: The authors constructed Insulin4RL from the MIMIC-IV database, curating insulin infusion titration episodes in the ICU. The dataset preserves naturally irregular observation and action timestamps. They provide baseline performance metrics using model-free offline RL algorithms and establish a standardized evaluation protocol based on fitted Q-evaluation.
AI.result: The resulting dataset contains over 375,000 labeled decisions from 12,209 patients. Baseline performance metrics and a standardized fitted Q-evaluation protocol are provided, demonstrating the dataset's utility for benchmarking ORL methods under realistic clinical sampling assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Insulin4RL addresses a critical gap in healthcare ORL by providing a realistic, irregularly-sampled benchmark. The authors highlight future research directions including handling irregular time series, policy learning under clinical constraints, and improved off-policy evaluation methods for healthcare settings.

title: SysML Modeling of Digital Twins for Renewable Energy Communities
comment: Presented at the Workshop on Digital Twin Experiences and Model-Based Testing Methods, 12 June 2026, Västerås, Sweden, co-located with the 30th Ada-Europe International Conference on Reliable Software Technologies (AEiC 2026)
summary: Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) are emerging as a key organizational model for local and global sharing of renewable generation, storage, and flexible loads. Engineering Digital Twins of RECs is made difficult by the heterogeneity of devices, contracts, and runtime data involved. In this paper, we take a first step toward a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for REC's Digital Twins. Starting from an industrially-validated REC domain model, we re-express a representative house subset in SysML using the open-source Modelio tool, yielding two Block Definition Diagrams - a device taxonomy and a community organizational view. We then discuss four semantic gaps that plain SysML leaves open and sketch how the SAREF4ENER ontology could be imported as a reference package to close them. Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins remains largely unexplored, and we position this paper as a first step along that line.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for creating Digital Twins of Renewable Energy Communities (RECs), using SysML diagrams to model device taxonomies and community organization, then identifies semantic gaps that the SAREF4ENER ontology could address.
AI.motivation: Engineering Digital Twins for Renewable Energy Communities is challenging due to the heterogeneity of devices, contracts, and runtime data. Current SysML-based modeling leaves semantic gaps that hinder interoperability and consistency across the REC domain.
AI.method: The authors re-express a validated REC domain model subset (representative house) in SysML v2 using the Modelio tool, producing Block Definition Diagrams for device taxonomy and community structure. They then analyze four semantic gaps in plain SysML and propose importing the SAREF4ENER ontology as a reference package to close them.
AI.result: Two SysML Block Definition Diagrams are produced: a device taxonomy and a community organizational view. Four semantic gaps are identified where SysML alone falls short, and SAREF4ENER is sketched as a bridging solution — though full integration remains unexplored.
AI.conclusion: Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins is a largely unexplored direction. The paper positions itself as a preliminary step toward an MBSE workflow that integrates ontology-based semantics to address REC modeling challenges.

title: FineREX: Fine-Tuned NER-RE for Human Smuggling Knowledge Graphs
summary: Court proceedings contain valuable evidence about human smuggling networks, but this information is often buried within unstructured, jargon-heavy legal documents. While large language models (LLMs) can support knowledge graph construction through automated information extraction, existing approaches rely on general-purpose models that are not tailored to the entity and relationship definitions required in this domain. We introduce FineREX, a streamlined knowledge graph construction pipeline built around a fine-tuned LLM for named entity recognition and relationship extraction (NER-RE). Using a manually annotated dataset of $512$ text chunks, FineREX achieves absolute improvements of 15.50% and 31.46% in entity and relationship F1-score, respectively, compared to a larger general-purpose baseline. These gains translate into higher-quality knowledge graphs, reducing legal noise by nearly half and lowering node duplication on long documents from 17.78% to 11.17%. By eliminating document rewriting and redundant extraction stages, FineREX also reduces end-to-end processing time by 50.0%. Our results demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning can substantially outperform larger general-purpose models while improving both the quality and efficiency of knowledge graph construction for illicit network analysis.

AI.tldr: FineREX is a domain-specific fine-tuned LLM pipeline for constructing knowledge graphs from legal documents about human smuggling, outperforming larger general-purpose models by 15.50% (entity F1) and 31.46% (relation F1) while halving noise and processing time.
AI.motivation: Court documents contain valuable but unstructured, jargon-heavy evidence about human smuggling networks. General-purpose LLMs lack the domain-specific entity and relationship definitions needed for accurate knowledge graph construction in this legal-intelligence context.
AI.method: FineREX is a streamlined knowledge graph construction pipeline that uses a fine-tuned LLM for Named Entity Recognition and Relationship Extraction (NER-RE). The model is trained on a manually annotated dataset of 512 text chunks. The pipeline eliminates document rewriting and redundant extraction stages present in prior approaches.
AI.result: On a manually annotated dataset of 512 text chunks, FineREX achieved absolute F1 improvements of 15.50% (entity) and 31.46% (relationship) over a larger general-purpose baseline. Legal noise was reduced by nearly half, node duplication on long documents dropped from 17.78% to 11.17%, and end-to-end processing time was reduced by 50.0%.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning substantially outperforms larger general-purpose models for knowledge graph construction in illicit network analysis, improving both extraction quality and computational efficiency. The approach is particularly effective for structured intelligence extraction from legal documents.

title: AgentFinVQA: A Deployable Multi-Agent Pipeline for Auditable Financial Chart QA
summary: Financial chart question answering in regulated settings demands more than accuracy: practitioners must know which answers to trust before acting on them, and many institutions cannot send client data to external model providers. Yet existing chart-QA agents are accuracy-focused and opaque, and most assume proprietary API access; to our knowledge, none combines auditability with on-premise deployability without significant accuracy compromise. We present AgentFinVQA, a multi-agent pipeline that decomposes each query into planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification, recording every step in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP) per sample. On FinMME, AgentFinVQA improves $+7.68$ pp over a primary-backbone matched zero-shot baseline with a proprietary backbone (Gemini-3 Flash; 71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar $p \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-16}$), and $+4.84$ pp with open-weights Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 served locally. The verifier's verdict also serves as a useful confidence signal (68.2% vs. 55.6% exact accuracy on confirmed vs. revised answers), enabling human-in-the-loop review routing. Error analysis shows that question misunderstanding, legend confusion and extraction error account for nearly two-thirds of failures and are the categories least detected by the verifier, identifying clear directions for future work. Together these results show that auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical and that the open-weights system keeps most of the accuracy gains while enabling full data residency. We release our code to support reproducible evaluation.

AI.tldr: AgentFinVQA is a multi-agent financial chart QA pipeline that achieves strong accuracy while providing full auditability via per-sample traceable Model Evaluation Packets and supporting on-premise deployment with open-weights models, with a verifier that doubles as a confidence signal for human-in-the-loop review.
AI.motivation: Financial chart QA in regulated environments requires both trustworthiness (knowing which answers to trust) and on-premise deployability (no external data sharing), yet existing solutions are accuracy-focused, opaque, and assume proprietary API access. No current system combines auditability with on-premise deployment without significant accuracy loss.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline decomposing each query into five stages: planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification. Every step is recorded in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP) per sample. The verifier also serves as a confidence signal. The system supports both proprietary backbones (Gemini-3 Flash) and open-weights models (Qwen3.6-27B-FP8) for local deployment.
AI.result: On FinMME, AgentFinVQA achieves +7.68 pp over a zero-shot baseline with Gemini-3 Flash (71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar p≈1.1×10⁻¹⁶) and +4.84 pp with open-weights Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 served locally. The verifier's confirmed-vs-revised accuracy split is 68.2% vs. 55.6%, providing an effective confidence signal for review routing. Error analysis reveals question misunderstanding, legend confusion, and extraction error account for ~2/3 of failures and are least detected by the verifier.
AI.conclusion: Auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical. The open-weights system retains most accuracy gains while enabling full data residency. The verifier's confidence signal enables human-in-the-loop workflows, and clear directions for future improvement are identified from error analysis. Code is released for reproducible evaluation.

title: Concept Flow Models: Anchoring Concept-Based Reasoning with Hierarchical Bottlenecks
summary: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enhance interpretability by projecting learned features into a human-understandable concept space. Recent approaches leverage vision-language models to generate concept embeddings, reducing the need for manual concept annotations. However, these models suffer from a critical limitation: as the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, information leakage increases, enabling the model to exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations and undermining interpretability. In this work, we propose Concept Flow Models (CFMs), which replace the flat bottleneck with a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree. Each internal node in the hierarchy focuses on a localized subset of discriminative concepts, progressively narrowing the prediction scope. Our framework constructs decision hierarchies from visual embeddings, distributes semantic concepts at each hierarchy level, and trains differentiable concept weights through probabilistic tree traversal. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs, while substantially mitigating information leakage by reducing effective concept usage. Furthermore, CFMs yield stepwise decision flows that enable transparent and auditable model reasoning with hierarchical class structures.

AI.tldr: Concept Flow Models (CFMs) replace the flat bottleneck of Concept Bottleneck Models with a hierarchical decision tree, where each node uses a localized subset of discriminative concepts. This reduces information leakage caused by high concept dimensionality while maintaining predictive performance and enabling stepwise, auditable reasoning.
AI.motivation: Flat Concept Bottleneck Models suffer from information leakage when the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, allowing the model to exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations, thereby undermining interpretability. A structurally constrained alternative is needed to mitigate this leakage without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: CFMs construct a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree from visual embeddings. Each internal node focuses on a localized subset of discriminative concepts. The framework distributes semantic concepts across hierarchy levels and trains differentiable concept weights via probabilistic tree traversal, progressively narrowing the prediction scope.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks show CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs while substantially mitigating information leakage by reducing effective concept usage. They also produce stepwise decision flows enabling transparent, auditable reasoning with hierarchical class structures.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical concept bottlenecks effectively address the information leakage problem inherent in flat CBMs, offering a practical path toward both high-performance and genuinely interpretable concept-based models with auditable decision processes.

title: NRITYAM: Language Models Meet Art and Heritage of Dance
summary: Language models have become essential tools in shaping modern workflows. However, their global effectiveness hinges on a nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts. To address this gap, we present NRITYAM, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the cultural comprehension capabilities of language models in the context of global dance traditions. NRITYAM comprises 9,260 carefully curated question-answer pairs spanning 12 languages, making it the largest dataset dedicated to evaluating cultural knowledge in dance. The dataset has been developed from the ground up through close collaboration with native dance artists and native speakers of the languages, who authored and validated culturally relevant questions specific to their regions. We evaluate a broad set of models, including large language models, small language models, multimodal large language models, and small multimodal language models. As a multilingual and multicultural benchmark, NRITYAM sets a new standard for evaluating the ability of AI systems to understand and reason about traditional performing arts. Detailed dataset samples are available at~\url{https://github.com/niladrighosh03/NRITYAM}.

AI.tldr: NRITYAM is a large-scale, multilingual benchmark (9,260 QA pairs, 12 languages) for evaluating cultural comprehension in language models through the lens of global dance traditions, created in collaboration with native artists and speakers.
AI.motivation: Language models lack nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts, limiting their global effectiveness. No comprehensive benchmark exists for evaluating cultural knowledge specifically in the domain of traditional performing arts like dance.
AI.method: The authors built NRITYAM from the ground up by collaborating with native dance artists and native speakers of 12 languages, who authored and validated culturally relevant question-answer pairs. They then evaluated a range of models — large and small language models, as well as multimodal large and small language models — on this benchmark.
AI.result: NRITYAM comprises 9,260 curated QA pairs across 12 languages, making it the largest dataset dedicated to evaluating cultural knowledge in dance. The benchmark exposes varying degrees of cultural comprehension across different model types and scales.
AI.conclusion: NRITYAM sets a new standard for evaluating AI systems' ability to understand and reason about traditional performing arts, highlighting the critical need for culturally grounded benchmarks in multilingual and multicultural AI evaluation.

title: ORAgentBench: Can LLM Agents Solve Challenging Operations Research Tasks End to End?
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for multi-step tasks in executable environments, yet their ability to perform realistic operations research (OR) work remains unclear. Existing OR evaluations often decouple modeling from solving, rely on pre-formalized or text-only instances, and rarely test the full workflow from operational artifacts to validated decisions. In this work, we introduce ORAgentBench, an execution-grounded benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents on challenging end-to-end operations research tasks. It contains 107 human-reviewed tasks across diverse operational scenarios, each packaged in an isolated environment with a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a required submission schema. Agents must write and run solution code, and their submissions are evaluated by hidden validators for schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Experiments with fourteen frontier agent-model configurations show that current agents remain far from reliable OR practice. The best agent passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks, and many feasible submissions still fall below the required quality threshold. Failure analysis further shows that errors are dominated by strategic weaknesses, including missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills increase hard-task feasibility, but do not reliably improve solution quality or pass rate. These results suggest that progress in OR agents requires moving beyond plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making.

AI.tldr: ORAgentBench is an execution-grounded benchmark with 107 human-reviewed end-to-end OR tasks requiring agents to go from natural-language briefs and multi-file artifacts to validated, constraint-satisfying, high-quality solutions. The best agent-model achieves only 35.51% pass rate overall and 20.59% on hard tasks, with failures dominated by strategic weaknesses rather than coding errors.
AI.motivation: Existing OR evaluations decouple modeling from solving, use pre-formalized or text-only instances, and fail to test the full pipeline from raw operational artifacts to validated decisions. There is a need to assess whether LLM agents can reliably perform realistic, end-to-end OR work.
AI.method: ORAgentBench comprises 107 tasks across diverse operational scenarios, each with an isolated environment containing a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a submission schema. Agents must write and execute solution code; submissions are auto-evaluated via hidden validators on schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Fourteen frontier agent-model configurations were tested.
AI.result: The best agent passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks. Many feasible submissions fall below the quality threshold. Failure analysis reveals strategic weaknesses dominate: missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills improve hard-task feasibility but not reliably solution quality or overall pass rate.
AI.conclusion: Progress in OR agents demands moving beyond generating plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making. Current LLM agents remain far from reliable OR practice, with strategic reasoning gaps being the primary bottleneck.

title: Algebraic Dead Directions in LayerNorm Transformers: A Forward-Pass-Only Diagnostic at LLM Scale
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Empirical companion to arXiv:2606.05957
summary: Pretrained transformers sit near singular minima of the loss, where the Fisher information metric degenerates along dead directions: directions in parameter space along which the directional Fisher vanishes. Locating such a direction normally needs a forward pass and an eigendecomposition of activations, or a sampling-based complexity estimate; none returns a direction computable from the network's parameters alone. We give one, for LayerNorm transformers. The inverse-scale direction $γ^{-1}/\|γ^{-1}\|$ of the LayerNorm affine is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance, for any input distribution, and induces a corresponding dead direction in parameter space. It is read from the LN scale parameter alone, with no forward or backward pass and no eigensolve: the cheapest dead-direction read, specific to LayerNorm. We test it on $14$ pretrained transformers ($9$ LayerNorm, $5$ RMSNorm; $160$M-$35$B; language and vision objectives). At random initialisation the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction (one forward pass, direct SVD) to four decimal places on $9/9$ LayerNorm models, and is correctly absent on $5/5$ RMSNorm models, which lack the mean-subtraction projector that creates it. On the trained checkpoint the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ${\sim}10^3\times$ and further dead directions open; the random-init-to-trained gap is a one-forward-pass, per-checkpoint readout of singular structure along the predicted coordinate. Two consequences follow in closed form: the residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on $13/14$ transformers measured on their own input distribution, the one exception (Gemma$4$-$31$B) a genuine dead direction the same read pinpoints; and the kernel direction's presence classifies a transformer's normalisation from the parameters alone.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for LayerNorm transformers, the inverse-scale direction of the LayerNorm affine parameter is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm activation covariance, yielding a dead direction (zero Fisher information) computable directly from parameters — no forward pass or eigendecomposition needed. This direction is validated on 14 pretrained transformers, deepens ~10³× after training, and enables block-to-block singular value preservation analysis and normalization-type classification from parameters alone.
AI.motivation: Identifying dead directions in the Fisher information metric of pretrained transformers typically requires expensive forward passes, activation eigendecompositions, or sampling-based estimates. The authors seek a dead direction computable purely from network parameters — eliminating computational overhead — specifically for the widely-used LayerNorm architecture.
AI.method: The authors derive analytically that the inverse-scale direction γ⁻¹/‖γ⁻¹‖ of the LayerNorm affine parameter is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance matrix, for any input distribution. This produces a dead direction in parameter space. They validate the result by: (1) comparing the predicted direction against the bottom singular direction from direct SVD at random initialization on 9 LayerNorm and 5 RMSNorm models, (2) measuring how the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens from random init to trained checkpoints (~10³×), and (3) testing whether the residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block across 14 transformers (160M–35B parameters, language and vision).
AI.result: At random initialization, the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction to four decimal places on all 9/9 LayerNorm models and is correctly absent on all 5/5 RMSNorm models. On trained checkpoints, the eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ~10³× and additional dead directions emerge. The residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on 13/14 transformers; the sole exception (Gemma 4-31B) is identified as a genuine dead direction by the same method. The presence of the kernel direction classifies normalization type from parameters alone.
AI.conclusion: The inverse-scale direction of LayerNorm affine parameters provides the cheapest possible dead-direction readout — requiring only the LN scale parameter with no forward/backward pass or eigensolve. This is a structural property specific to LayerNorm (absent in RMSNorm due to lack of mean subtraction), with practical consequences for understanding singular structure evolution during training, block-wise signal propagation, and architecture identification.

title: Token-Operations-Oriented Inference Optimization Techniques for Large Models
summary: Large model inference optimization serves as a key foundation for supporting the scalable, low-cost, and highly stable operation of large model services. Centered on token-oriented inference optimization technology, this paper proposes for the first time a four-layer technical architecture consisting of Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, and Compute-Network-Model Fusion. It systematically reviews the key technologies and current industry status across these four levels and analyzes the application value of related technologies in real-world business scenarios. This paper provides a practical technical path for reducing token production costs, improving token service efficiency, ensuring the stability of token supply, and driving the transition of large model services from being merely callable to being operable.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a four-layer technical architecture for token-oriented large model inference optimization, covering Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, and Compute-Network-Model Fusion, aiming to reduce token costs, improve efficiency, ensure stability, and enable operable large model services.
AI.motivation: Large model services require scalable, low-cost, and highly stable operation. Current inference systems need a systematic optimization framework to move beyond mere model callability toward fully operable, production-grade services centered on token-level performance.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel four-layer technical architecture: (1) Multi-model Fusion, (2) Model Optimization, (3) Compute-Model Fusion, and (4) Compute-Network-Model Fusion. They systematically review key technologies and industry practices at each layer, analyzing their application value in real-world business scenarios.
AI.result: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of token-oriented inference optimization technologies across four architectural layers and demonstrates their practical value in business deployments, offering a concrete technical pathway for cost reduction, efficiency improvement, and supply stability.
AI.conclusion: The four-layer architecture offers a practical, systematic path for reducing token production costs, improving token service efficiency, and ensuring stable token supply, thereby enabling large model services to transition from being merely callable to being truly operable at scale.

title: CombEval: A Framework for Evaluating Combinatorial Counting in Large Language Models
summary: We present CombEval, a dynamic benchmark for evaluating combinatorial counting in large language models. CombEval represents each problem as a typed Cofola specification over entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints, enabling controlled generation of natural-language counting problems with exact solver-verified answers. Unlike static collections, CombEval supports systematic variation of object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. We evaluate 11 LLMs under direct and code-augmented settings and find that models remain brittle on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relatively positional constraints, and nested object dependencies. Error analysis further identifies failures in constraint interpretation and counting principles. CombEval provides a diagnostic testbed for studying when and why LLMs fail at combinatorial reasoning. The code and generated benchmark suites are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/YuxuZhou-CN/combination-problem-generation}.

AI.tldr: CombEval is a dynamic benchmark for evaluating LLMs on combinatorial counting problems, featuring solver-verified answers and systematic variation of problem parameters. Evaluation of 11 LLMs reveals brittleness on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relative positional constraints, and nested dependencies, with failures rooted in constraint interpretation and counting principles.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for evaluating LLMs on combinatorial reasoning are static collections that lack controlled, systematic variation of problem parameters (object type, entity scale, constraint count, reasoning depth). This makes it difficult to diagnose precisely when and why models fail at combinatorial counting.
AI.method: The authors introduce CombEval, which represents each combinatorial counting problem as a typed Cofola specification — a formal schema capturing entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints. This specification enables programmatic generation of natural-language problems with exact answers verified by a solver. The benchmark supports systematic variation along four axes: object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. Eleven LLMs are evaluated under both direct prompting and code-augmented (tool-use) settings.
AI.result: Models consistently struggle with: (1) ordered objects (permutations), (2) indistinguishable elements (combinations with identical items), (3) relatively positional constraints, and (4) nested object dependencies. Error analysis reveals two dominant failure modes: misinterpreting constraints stated in natural language and incorrectly applying fundamental counting principles (e.g., rule of sum vs. rule of product, inclusion-exclusion).
AI.conclusion: CombEval serves as a diagnostic testbed that exposes systematic weaknesses in LLMs' combinatorial reasoning capabilities. The brittleness on specific problem dimensions suggests that current models lack robust, generalizable counting abilities, and the benchmark provides a framework for targeted improvement and deeper study of these failures.

title: Calibrating Generative Models to Feature Distributions with MMD Finetuning
summary: Generative models can produce individually plausible samples while deviating substantially from a target set in the distribution of key features. For example, a model pretrained on broad drug-like chemical space may generate molecules whose molecular features differ from those of a therapeutic class of interest, such as known antibiotics. Correcting such distributional miscalibration is challenging: direct finetuning on the target set can overfit and does not control which features are matched. To fill this gap, we introduce kernel Calibrating Generative Models (kCGM). kCGM minimizes a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator, with KL regularization to remain close to the pretrained model. On a target set of 174 antibiotics, direct finetuning sacrifices chemical validity for feature-distribution matching, whereas kCGM improves target feature matching while increasing validity. We further demonstrate kCGM in protein and DNA generation tasks, showing it can adapt autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models using only feature-level supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/smithhenryd/cgm.

AI.tldr: kCGM is a method for recalibrating pretrained generative models to match target feature distributions using MMD minimization with KL regularization, demonstrated across molecules, proteins, and DNA for autoregressive and diffusion models.
AI.motivation: Pretrained generative models often produce samples that are individually plausible but collectively deviate from a target distribution in key feature spaces (distributional miscalibration). Direct fine-tuning overfits and cannot control which features are matched, so a principled method is needed to align generated feature distributions with a target set while preserving validity and proximity to the pretrained model.
AI.method: kCGM minimizes the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between the generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator, combined with KL divergence regularization to keep the model close to the pretrained distribution. This operates using only feature-level supervision on the target set.
AI.result: On 174 antibiotics, direct fine-tuning improved feature matching but sacrificed chemical validity, whereas kCGM improved target feature matching while increasing validity. The method was further validated on protein and DNA generation tasks, successfully adapting autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models.
AI.conclusion: kCGM provides an effective, general-purpose framework for distributional recalibration of generative models using only feature-level feedback, avoiding overfitting and validity collapse while achieving superior feature distribution matching across diverse domains and model classes.

title: A Model-Driven Approach for Developing Families of Reinforcement Learning Environments
summary: Virtual training environments are software-intensive systems in which reinforcement learning (RL) agents learn, adapt, and demonstrate meaningful behavior. Virtual training environments offer a safe and cost-efficient alternative to training agents in real-world settings. However, to converge, most realistic RL problems require training in multiple, mostly similar but slightly different environments - i.e., families of environment variants. The typical development process of environment families is a labor-intensive and error-prone manual endeavor that does not scale well. To alleviate these issues, in this paper, we propose a model-driven approach for developing families of RL training environments. To obtain the family of environments, we develop an approach and prototype tool. In our approach, a hybrid genetic algorithm - a combination of population-based global search and heuristic local search - generates environment families. Mutations and constraints are expressed as model transformations and are operationalized into a search process by a state-of-the-art model transformation engine. We demonstrate the soundness of our approach in a wildfire mitigation scenario and curriculum learning - a particular learning paradigm that relies on environment families.

AI.tldr: Proposes a model-driven approach using a hybrid genetic algorithm (global + local search) to automatically generate families of RL training environments, addressing the manual, error-prone bottleneck of creating environment variants. Validated via wildfire mitigation and curriculum learning scenarios.
AI.motivation: Realistic RL problems require training across families of similar-but-slightly-different environment variants (e.g., for curriculum learning). The manual development of these environment families is labor-intensive, error-prone, and does not scale, creating a bottleneck in RL training pipelines.
AI.method: A model-driven approach where environment families are generated via a hybrid genetic algorithm combining population-based global search with heuristic local search. Mutations and constraints are formalized as model transformations and executed by a state-of-the-art model transformation engine. A prototype tool operationalizes the approach.
AI.result: The approach was demonstrated to be sound in two settings: a wildfire mitigation scenario and a curriculum learning paradigm that explicitly relies on sequenced environment families.
AI.conclusion: Model-driven engineering, specifically combining genetic algorithms with model transformation engines, can effectively automate the generation of RL environment families, reducing manual effort and improving scalability.

title: Clusters are All You Need: Pre-Training the Tsetlin Machine with Semantic Clusters from Language Models for Interpretability
summary: Pre-trained language models such as BERT achieve strong text classification performance but lack transparency, limiting their use in high-stakes settings. The Tsetlin Machine (TM) offers fully interpretable, clause-based reasoning but captures little semantic information, and prior attempts to bridge the two rely on static word embeddings that miss contextual meaning. We propose a semantic pre-training framework that transfers knowledge from a pre-trained language model into a TM without using embeddings. Text samples are grouped into semantically coherent clusters with K-means or Top2Vec, and the resulting cluster-sample pairs pre-train a non-negated TM with enhanced Type I feedback. The TM thereby learns interpretable semantic keywords that are fine-tuned on downstream tasks. Across five datasets, our method substantially outperforms vanilla and embedding-based TMs and reaches performance competitive with BERT while remaining interpretable.

AI.tldr: Proposes a semantic pre-training framework that transfers knowledge from BERT-like models into Tsetlin Machines via clustering without static embeddings, achieving BERT-competitive accuracy while retaining full interpretability.
AI.motivation: BERT achieves high text classification accuracy but is opaque; Tsetlin Machines are fully interpretable but lack semantic understanding. Prior hybridization attempts use static word embeddings that fail to capture contextual meaning, leaving a gap between performance and interpretability.
AI.method: Text samples are clustered into semantically coherent groups using K-means or Top2Vec. These cluster-sample pairs are used to pre-train a non-negated TM with enhanced Type I feedback, enabling the TM to learn interpretable semantic keywords. The pre-trained TM is then fine-tuned on downstream classification tasks.
AI.result: The method substantially outperforms both vanilla TMs and embedding-based TMs across five datasets, achieving performance competitive with BERT while maintaining full interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Semantic pre-training via clustering effectively bridges the gap between opaque deep language models and transparent rule-based classifiers, yielding a practical high-performance interpretable alternative for high-stakes NLP applications.

title: Think Again or Think Longer? Selective Verification for Budget-Aware Reasoning
summary: Test-time reasoning is increasingly used as a serving-time control knob, but extra reasoning is not uniformly valuable: it can repair failed attempts, waste compute on already-correct answers, or introduce harmful answer changes. We study this as a deployment allocation problem rather than a new-verifier problem. We introduce \sevra, Selective Verification for Reasoning Allocation, a serving-layer controller that decides whether to preserve a frozen solver's initial answer or invoke active verification. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B solver, we log intervention outcomes and train recoverability-aware gates from serving-visible attempt state. On \mathfive, selective verification reaches 76.3\% accuracy, compared with 75.5\% for always verifying, while reducing post-generation tokens by 26.8\% and harmful flips from 2.2\% to 1.0\%. However, an 8,192-token initial solve reaches 76.0\% accuracy with 28\% fewer total model tokens, showing that selective recovery is useful but not the best tested cost frontier. In frozen transfer to \gsm, the selective policy verifies only 3.0\% of examples, improves accuracy from 93.4\% to 94.5\%, and reduces verification tokens by 91.2\% relative to always verifying; again, a longer initial solve matches its accuracy with fewer realized tokens. On CommonsenseQA, always-on verification hurts, while Self-Consistency@5 improves accuracy at about five times the realized token cost. The resulting deployment rule is: tune the initial budget first, then use selective recovery when explicit checks, bounded retries, auditability, or regression-risk control matter.

AI.tldr: Selective verification (SevRA) uses a learned gating mechanism to decide when to invoke active verification on a frozen solver's outputs, recovering from failures while avoiding wasted compute and harmful answer flips. On MATH500, it achieves 76.3% accuracy vs. 75.5% for always-verifying, with 26.8% fewer post-generation tokens. However, a longer initial solve often matches or exceeds this at lower total cost, leading to the deployment rule: tune the initial budget first, then apply selective recovery when explicit checks or regression-risk control matter.
AI.motivation: Test-time reasoning (verification, self-correction) is increasingly used as a serving-time control knob, but extra reasoning is not uniformly valuable — it can fix failures, waste compute on already-correct answers, or introduce harmful flips (correct→incorrect). The authors frame this as a deployment allocation problem: given a frozen solver, how to decide at serving time whether to keep the initial answer or invoke verification, rather than treating it as a new-verifier design problem.
AI.method: SevRA (Selective Verification for Reasoning Allocation) is a serving-layer controller. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B solver, the authors log intervention outcomes (whether verification would have helped, hurt, or been redundant) and train recoverability-aware binary gates from serving-visible attempt state features. The gate decides per-example whether to preserve the initial answer or trigger active verification. They evaluate across MATH500, GSM8K, and CommonsenseQA, comparing against always-verify, never-verify, longer initial solves, and Self-Consistency baselines.
AI.result: On MATH500: selective verification reaches 76.3% accuracy (vs. 75.5% always-verify, 73.5% never-verify), reduces post-generation tokens by 26.8%, and reduces harmful flips from 2.2% to 1.0%. An 8,192-token initial solve reaches 76.0% with 28% fewer total model tokens. On GSM8K: selective policy verifies only 3.0% of examples, improves accuracy from 93.4% to 94.5%, and reduces verification tokens by 91.2% vs. always-verify. On CommonsenseQA: always-on verification hurts; Self-Consistency@5 improves accuracy but at ~5× token cost.
AI.conclusion: The core deployment rule: tune the initial solve budget first (longer single-pass generation often dominates), then use selective recovery when explicit checks, bounded retries, auditability, or regression-risk control are needed. Selective verification is useful but is not the best tested cost frontier on its own.

title: Interactive Pareto navigation for deep multi-task learning
summary: In multi-task learning, handling an increasing number of objectives can quickly become challenging, both in terms of the computational resources and the decision maker's capacity to choose appropriate trade-offs. A widely used approach is thus to aggregate the individual losses in a single loss function by a weighted sum. This often fails to capture either the decision maker's preferences as a result of the shape of the Pareto front, or requires multiple adjustments and computations which becomes prohibitively expensive in deep learning applications. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework, Preference Pareto Exploration (PPE), which enforces the decision maker's preferences while accounting for the geometry of the Pareto set in an interactive exploration process. PPE is based on a predictor-corrector method that performs predictor steps tangential to the manifold of Pareto-optimal solutions, following the decision maker's preference. The subsequent corrector step results in a new trade-off reflecting this preference. To avoid explicit Hessian computations when characterizing the tangent space of the manifold, we employ a Krylov subspace method that relies solely on matrix-vector products. These products can be efficiently obtained via automatic differentiation, ensuring both efficiency and robustness throughout the optimization process. The method's functionality and performance are demonstrated using both toy problems and examples from deep learning.

AI.tldr: PPE is a novel multi-task learning framework that enables interactive Pareto exploration by performing predictor-corrector steps tangential to the Pareto manifold, guided by user preferences, using Krylov subspace methods to avoid explicit Hessian computations.
AI.motivation: Weighted-sum aggregation in multi-task learning fails to capture decision maker preferences due to Pareto front geometry and becomes computationally prohibitive when multiple trade-off adjustments are needed, especially in deep learning contexts.
AI.method: PPE uses a predictor-corrector approach: predictor steps move tangentially along the Pareto-optimal solution manifold following user preferences, and corrector steps project back to yield a new Pareto-optimal trade-off. Tangent space characterization avoids explicit Hessians via a Krylov subspace method using only matrix-vector products obtainable through automatic differentiation.
AI.result: The method's functionality and performance are validated on both synthetic toy problems and deep learning examples, demonstrating efficiency and robustness.
AI.conclusion: PPE offers an efficient, preference-driven framework for interactive Pareto exploration in multi-task deep learning, overcoming the limitations of weighted-sum aggregation by respecting both user preferences and Pareto front geometry without costly Hessian computations.

title: AutoPass: Evidence-Guided LLM Agents for Compiler Performance Tuning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for code compilation tasks, but applying them to runtime performance tuning is difficult due to complex microarchitectural effects and noisy runtime measurements. We present AutoPass, a multi-agent framework for compiler performance tuning that uses compiler and runtime evidence to guide LLM-generated optimization decisions. Rather than treating the compiler as a black box like prior auto-tuning schemes, AutoPass opens up the compiler to the LLM, enabling it to query compiler-internal optimization states and analyze the intermediate representation to orchestrate compiler options. The search process iteratively refines optimization configurations using measured runtime feedback to diagnose regressions and guide latency-improving edits. AutoPass operates in an inference-only, training-free setting and requires no offline training or task-specific fine-tuning, making it readily applicable to new benchmarks and platforms. We implement AutoPass on the LLVM compiler and evaluate it on server-grade x86-64 and embedded ARM64 systems. AutoPass outperforms expert-tuned heuristics and classical autotuning methods, achieving geometric-mean speedups of 1.043x and 1.117x over LLVM -O3 on x86-64 and ARM64, respectively.

AI.tldr: AutoPass is a multi-agent LLM framework for compiler optimization tuning that exposes compiler internals (IR, optimization states) and runtime feedback to guide iterative optimization decisions, achieving 1.043x–1.117x speedup over LLVM -O3 without any training or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise for code tasks, but applying them to compiler runtime performance tuning is challenging due to complex microarchitectural effects and noisy runtime measurements. Prior auto-tuning methods treat the compiler as a black box, missing valuable internal optimization state that could inform better decisions.
AI.method: AutoPass is a multi-agent LLM framework that "opens up" the compiler, allowing LLM agents to query compiler-internal optimization states, analyze intermediate representation (IR), and use measured runtime feedback to iteratively refine optimization configurations. It operates in an inference-only, training-free setting with no offline training or task-specific fine-tuning. Implemented on LLVM, evaluated on x86-64 and ARM64.
AI.result: AutoPass outperforms expert-tuned heuristics and classical autotuning methods, achieving geometric-mean speedups of 1.043x over LLVM -O3 on x86-64 and 1.117x on ARM64 embedded systems.
AI.conclusion: Exposing compiler internals to LLM-based agents enables more effective automatic performance tuning than black-box approaches, and the training-free design makes AutoPass readily applicable to new benchmarks and platforms.

title: CREDENCE: Claim Reduction for Decomposition & Enhanced Credibility -- Semantic Metrics and Convergence Analysis
comment: 40 pages, 6 figures, 19 tables. Submitted to Language Resources and Evaluation
summary: Decomposing compound sentences into atomic, verifiable claims is a prerequisite for reliable automated fact-checking. Prior work has relied on token-overlap (Jaccard) metrics that systematically underestimate decomposition quality for paraphrastic claims, and has lacked formal termination analysis for the repair loop. We present Credence, a revised claim decomposition and evaluation framework addressing both shortcomings. Our contributions are: (1) Semantic-F1: we use BGE-large cosine similarity fidelity metric that resolves Jaccard's penalisation and improves downstream fact-checking accuracy; (2) Convergence theorems: we formally characterise four properties of the repair pipeline, establishing that rule-based repair is monotone and finitely terminating under an oracle parser assumption; LLM-based self-repair is provably non-monotone and requires an early-exit guard; (3) Three evaluation benchmarks spanning social-media, encyclopaedic, and news domains for cross-domain generalisation measurement; (4) Multi-model benchmarking across four decomposer models (3.8B-12B) and a closed API model. Experiments on SocialClaimSplit, WikiSplitBench, and ClaimDecompBench show that Semantic-F1 outperforms Jaccard-F1 by +15-32pp. EPR ranges from 0.94 to 1.00 on SocialClaimSplit and WikiSplitBench, while ClaimDecompBench includes lower base EPR cases (down to 0.824) due to harder news-domain constructions, and rule-repair reduces the Atomicity Violation Rate (AVR) by 47-100% relative to the base model without degrading fidelity.

AI.tldr: Credence introduces Semantic-F1 (using BGE-large cosine similarity) to replace Jaccard-based evaluation for claim decomposition, provides formal convergence proofs for rule-based and LLM-based repair pipelines, and benchmarks across three domains, demonstrating +15-32pp improvement over Jaccard-F1 and 47-100% reduction in atomicity violations via rule-repair.
AI.motivation: Existing claim decomposition evaluation relies on token-overlap metrics (Jaccard) that penalize paraphrastic claims and lack formal termination guarantees for the repair loop, undermining reliable automated fact-checking.
AI.method: Credence proposes: (1) Semantic-F1 based on BGE-large cosine similarity as a fidelity metric; (2) formal convergence theorems proving rule-based repair is monotone and finitely terminating (under oracle parser), while LLM-based self-repair is non-monotone requiring early-exit; (3) evaluation on SocialClaimSplit, WikiSplitBench, and ClaimDecompBench across four open-source decomposers (3.8B–12B) and one closed API model.
AI.result: Semantic-F1 outperforms Jaccard-F1 by +15–32pp; EPR ranges 0.94–1.00 on SocialClaimSplit and WikiSplitBench, dropping to 0.824 on harder news-domain ClaimDecompBench; rule-repair reduces Atomicity Violation Rate (AVR) by 47–100% relative to base models without fidelity degradation.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-F1 is a more robust evaluation metric for claim decomposition, and rule-based repair offers provably safe, effective refinement, while LLM-based self-repair requires explicit termination guards to prevent non-monotonic degradation.

title: Human-on-the-Loop Orchestration for AI-Assisted Legal Discovery
summary: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in electronic discovery (e-discovery), where compounding errors across multi-step reasoning chains can constitute legal malpractice. Unlike single-turn retrieval, agentic workflows operating over privileged document corpora exhibit a class of failure we term "trajectory collapse": an early misclassification silently propagates, rendering an entire privilege review invalid. This paper makes three contributions. First, we propose a structured taxonomy of agentic failures in legal information retrieval, organized by functional stage. Second, we introduce a four-layer verification architecture -- spanning planning, reasoning, execution, and uncertainty quantification -- designed to intercept these failures before they compound. Third, we present a preliminary simulation study on a synthetic e-discovery corpus that demonstrates how mandatory Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) escalation thresholds reduce privilege-waiver risk relative to fully autonomous baselines. Our results suggest that calibrated uncertainty thresholds can reduce privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% versus fully autonomous deployment, while routing fewer than one quarter of documents to attorney review.

AI.tldr: LLM agents in e-discovery are vulnerable to "trajectory collapse," where early errors compound silently. The paper proposes a failure taxonomy, a four-layer verification architecture with human-on-the-loop escalation, and demonstrates via simulation that calibrated uncertainty thresholds reduce privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% while routing under 25% of documents for human review.
AI.motivation: Autonomous LLM agents in e-discovery pose a unique risk: compounding errors across multi-step reasoning chains can constitute legal malpractice. Unlike single-turn retrieval, agentic workflows over privileged documents can suffer from "trajectory collapse," where an early misclassification silently propagates and invalidates the entire privilege review. Existing safeguards are insufficient for this class of sequential, compounding failure.
AI.method: The authors: (1) develop a structured taxonomy of agentic failures in legal information retrieval organized by functional stage; (2) propose a four-layer verification architecture covering planning, reasoning, execution, and uncertainty quantification to intercept failures before they compound; and (3) conduct a preliminary simulation study on a synthetic e-discovery corpus comparing mandatory Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) escalation against fully autonomous baselines.
AI.result: Calibrated uncertainty thresholds with mandatory HOTL escalation reduced privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% compared to fully autonomous deployment, while routing fewer than one quarter of documents to attorney review.
AI.conclusion: A layered verification architecture with calibrated uncertainty-based HOTL escalation significantly mitigates trajectory collapse and privilege-waiver risk in legal e-discovery, offering a practical balance between autonomy and human oversight without overwhelming human reviewers.

title: Techniques for Peak Memory Reduction for LoRA Fine-tuning of LLMs on Edge Devices
comment: Hassan Dbouk and Matthias Reisser contributed equally to this work
summary: Fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on an end-user's data offers personalized experiences while keeping data private, but faces severe memory constraints on consumer hardware. Peak memory during fine-tuning often exceeds device limits, especially for models with billions of parameters and long-context training data. This paper introduces a suite of complementary techniques to reduce memory footprint without sacrificing model quality: (1) base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization, (2) memory-efficient checkpointing combining selective activation caching and disk offloading, (3) softmax approximation using semantically relevant token subsets, and (4) logits masking. Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B demonstrate up to $26\times$ and $28\times$ reduction in peak memory, enabling fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes four complementary memory-saving techniques for fine-tuning LLMs with LoRA on consumer hardware: base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization, memory-efficient checkpointing with selective activation caching and disk offloading, softmax approximation using semantically relevant token subsets, and logits masking. Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B achieve up to 26× and 28× peak memory reduction, respectively.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning LLMs with LoRA on end-user data enables personalized experiences while preserving data privacy, but consumer hardware faces severe memory constraints. Peak memory during fine-tuning often exceeds device limits, particularly for billion-parameter models and long-context training data. Existing solutions fail to adequately address this memory bottleneck without degrading model quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce four complementary techniques: (1) Base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization — the base model weights are stored in low-precision quantized format and dequantized only when needed during computation. (2) Memory-efficient checkpointing combining selective activation caching and disk offloading — only a subset of activations are cached in memory while the rest are recomputed or offloaded to disk. (3) Softmax approximation using semantically relevant token subsets — instead of computing softmax over the full vocabulary, only a semantically relevant subset of tokens is considered. (4) Logits masking — further reduces memory by masking irrelevant logits during training.
AI.result: Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B demonstrate up to 26× and 28× reduction in peak memory usage, respectively, enabling fine-tuning on resource-constrained consumer devices without sacrificing model quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed suite of techniques effectively decouples fine-tuning capability from high-end hardware requirements, enabling privacy-preserving on-device LoRA fine-tuning of billion-parameter LLMs. This significantly expands the accessibility of personalized LLM adaptation to consumer-grade devices.

title: Probe-and-Refine Tuning of Repository Guidance for Coding Agents
summary: LLM-based coding agents need higher-level operational knowledge about a repository (which files house which subsystems, how to run the test suite, which workflows have historically led to wrong fixes) that does not exist in the code itself. Engineers typically maintain \texttt{AGENTS.md} files to supply this context as instructions for coding agents, but whether they help is contested: recent studies disagree on whether LLM-generated guidance improves or harms agent performance. In this paper we show that how the guidance is produced is the decisive variable, and introduce \emph{probe-and-refine tuning}: a procedure that uses synthetic bug-fix probes to iteratively diagnose and patch a repository's guidance file through single-shot LLM calls, with no agent loop or tool use during tuning. On SWE-bench Verified across four independent trials with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 200 steps, probe-and-refine achieves 33.0\,\% mean resolve rate vs.\ 28.3\,\% for the static knowledge base used to initialize it and 25.5\,\% for an unguided baseline ($p < 0.001$ for both probe-and-refine contrasts). The improvement comes from coverage rather than precision: refined guidance produces evaluable patches for 14.5 percentage points (pp) more instances while per-patch precision remains statistically constant ($\sim$59\,\%, $p = 0.119$), showing that improved guidance helps agents reach the correct file rather than improving the quality of the changes they make. Further, a step-budget experiment shows that guidance is what lets the agent use a larger step budget productively, and a cross-model experiment with NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B finds that the tuning loop degrades when the model cannot generate sufficiently diagnostic output, though per-patch precision remains constant even then.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "probe-and-refine tuning," a method that iteratively improves AGENTS.md guidance files for LLM-based coding agents using synthetic bug-fix probes. The refined guidance significantly boosts resolve rates by increasing coverage (reaching more correct files) rather than precision, and the approach depends critically on the tuning model's diagnostic capability.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding agents lack high-level operational knowledge about repositories (file-to-subsystem mapping, test procedures, failure-prone workflows) that isn't present in code. While engineers maintain AGENTS.md files to supply this context, existing studies disagree on whether such guidance helps or harms agent performance. The authors hypothesize that how the guidance is produced—not its mere presence—is the decisive variable.
AI.method: The authors propose probe-and-refine tuning: a procedure that uses synthetic bug-fix probes to iteratively diagnose and patch a repository's AGENTS.md guidance file through single-shot LLM calls, with no agent loop or tool use during tuning. The method is evaluated on SWE-bench Verified across four independent trials with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 200 steps, comparing against a static knowledge base baseline and an unguided baseline. Additional experiments include a step-budget analysis and a cross-model test with NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B.
AI.result: Probe-and-refine achieves 33.0% mean resolve rate vs. 28.3% for the static knowledge base and 25.5% for the unguided baseline (p < 0.001 for both contrasts). The improvement stems from coverage: refined guidance produces evaluable patches for 14.5 percentage points more instances, while per-patch precision remains statistically constant (~59%, p = 0.119). The step-budget experiment shows guidance enables productive use of larger step budgets. The cross-model experiment reveals the tuning loop degrades when the model cannot generate sufficiently diagnostic output, though per-patch precision still remains constant.
AI.conclusion: How guidance is produced is the decisive variable for agent performance. Probe-and-refine tuning improves resolve rates primarily by helping agents reach the correct file (coverage) rather than improving patch quality (precision). The approach is model-dependent: tuning efficacy requires a model capable of generating diagnostic output.

title: Leverage Is Not Reach: A Control-Window Law for Single-Neuron Steering in Language Models
summary: Aligned language models gate behaviors such as refusal and language routing through sparse feed forward neurons, yet no theory predicts when a single neuron intervention controls a behavior coherently rather than collapsing the output. We develop a budget normalized control window framework for single neuron steering. A dose along one write direction reduces to one control coordinate: the alignment between the residual stream and the write, driven along a universal saturation curve in units of a coherence budget set by the residual norm divided by the write norm. Coherent control exists when a behavior trigger lies below the collapse ceiling. The same coordinate governs benign mode switches and refusal; the ceiling follows from weights and one generic forward pass, while triggers are measured at rollout. On fifteen held out neurons, the predicted ceiling has mean absolute error 0.14, about 0.07 in bulk layers, and the committed open or closed verdict holds on eleven against a ten of fifteen majority baseline. Closed cases expose three failure modes rather than violations: collapse before trigger, too little depth to propagate, or a normalization that caps how far one neuron can push. The law explains why local gradient attribution anti predicts control: true controllers write off the readout axis and carry a near zero first order gradient. A forward only contrastive screen made precise by the window recovers controllers that attribution misses. On refusal, the hardest case, intervention success is typed, not scalar: coherent bypass and strict actionable reach separate, so a neuron can flip refusal in fluent, on task text with no actionable content, and genuine actionable reach appears only for three of six audited Llama pivots and only at later rollout horizons. Single neuron steering is therefore a budgeted, typed audit of controllability rather than a fixed dose anecdote.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework for single-neuron steering in language models, showing that control effectiveness is governed by a "coherence budget" set by the ratio of residual norm to write norm. A neuron can coherently control behavior only when its trigger lies below a predicted collapse ceiling. The framework explains why gradient attribution fails to identify true controllers and enables a forward-only screening method that recovers them. For refusal behaviors, the authors find intervention success is typed rather than scalar, with coherent bypass and actionable reach being distinct phenomena.
AI.motivation: No existing theory predicts when single-neuron intervention in aligned language models produces coherent behavioral control versus output collapse. Prior work demonstrates that sparse feed-forward neurons gate behaviors like refusal and language routing, but lacks a principled framework for understanding controllability, leaving intervention studies as anecdotal dose-finding exercises.
AI.method: The authors develop a "budget normalized control window" framework that reduces single-neuron steering to one control coordinate: the alignment between the residual stream and the write direction. This is governed by a universal saturation curve parameterized by a coherence budget (residual norm / write norm).
