A behavior trigger is measured at rollout and compared against a collapse ceiling predicted from weights and a single forward pass. They validate on 15 held-out neurons and audit six Llama model variants on refusal behaviors, distinguishing between coherent bypass and strict actionable reach.
AI.result: The predicted collapse ceiling achieves mean absolute error of 0.14 across 15 held-out neurons (~0.07 in bulk layers). The open/closed controllability verdict holds on 11 of 15 neurons against a 10/15 majority baseline. Three failure modes explain closed cases: collapse before trigger, insufficient depth for propagation, or normalization capping. The framework explains why gradient attribution anti-predicts control (true controllers write off the readout axis with near-zero first-order gradients). A forward-only contrastive screen recovers controllers that attribution misses. For refusal, coherent bypass and actionable reach are distinct: a neuron can flip refusal with fluent on-task text containing no actionable content; genuine actionable reach appears only in 3 of 6 audited Llama pivots and only at later rollout horizons.
AI.conclusion: Single-neuron steering is a budgeted, typed audit of controllability, not a fixed-dose anecdote. The coherence budget framework provides a predictive theory for when interventions succeed or fail, explains the failure of gradient-based attribution, and reveals that refusal intervention success separates into distinct types (coherent bypass vs. actionable reach) that must be audited independently.

authors: V V N K Someswara Rao Koduri
title: TelcoAgent: A Scalable 5G Multi-KPM Forecasting With 3GPP-Grounded Explainability
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE GLOBECOM 2026
summary: Key Performance Measurement (KPM) forecasting is essential for proactive network management of 5G and next-generation telecom networks. However, existing machine learning (ML) approaches face significant limitations in scalability and explainability, restricting their effectiveness in real-world deployments. We propose TelcoAgent, a foundation model-based framework that enables accurate, scalable, and explainable forecasting of multiple KPMs across diverse network cells without the need for site-specific training. Specifically, the framework comprises three key components: (i) an automated three-agent pipeline that constructs a 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) knowledge graph directly from specification documents, (ii) a scalable, time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline to deliver accurate, zero-shot forecasting, and finally (iii) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that provides actionable, domain-grounded diagnostics. Evaluated using a 3-month, real-world, city-scale 5G KPM dataset from a U.S.-based network operator, TelcoAgent demonstrates high forecasting accuracy for all 7 considered KPMs per cell across 200 cells, while delivering explainable insights and actionable instructions to address network degradations.

AI.tldr: TelcoAgent is a foundation model-based framework for 5G KPM forecasting that combines a 3GPP knowledge graph, a time-series foundation model for zero-shot prediction, and a reasoning pipeline for explainable diagnostics — achieving accurate, scalable forecasts across 200 cells without site-specific training.
AI.motivation: Existing ML approaches for KPM forecasting in 5G networks suffer from poor scalability (requiring per-cell training) and lack explainability, limiting real-world deployment. There is a need for a unified framework that can forecast multiple KPMs across diverse cells with zero-shot capability and provide actionable, domain-grounded explanations.
AI.method: TelcoAgent uses a three-component architecture: (1) an automated three-agent pipeline that extracts and constructs a 3GPP knowledge graph from specification documents; (2) a scalable time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline for zero-shot KPM forecasting across cells; and (3) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that leverages the knowledge graph to deliver actionable diagnostics for network degradations.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 3-month, city-scale, real-world 5G KPM dataset from a U.S. operator, TelcoAgent achieved high forecasting accuracy across all 7 KPM types over 200 cells, while also generating explainable insights and actionable instructions for addressing network issues.
AI.conclusion: TelcoAgent demonstrates that foundation model-based approaches can overcome the scalability and explainability bottlenecks of traditional ML in telecom, enabling accurate zero-shot multi-KPM forecasting with domain-grounded explanations suitable for proactive network management.

title: Tracking Representation Dynamics in Large Language Models with Persistent Homology
summary: Large language models are commonly aligned through supervised fine-tuning, yet little is known about how their internal representations evolve during this process. We study alignment dynamics using persistent homology by tracking the topology of activation spaces throughout fine-tuning. Across four transformer language models ranging from 1B to 7B parameters and three alignment objectives corresponding to helpful, harmless, and mixed training data, we find that the majority of topological reorganization occurs during the earliest stages of training. A dense checkpoint analysis reveals a transient peak in topological activity followed by rapid stabilization. We further show that different alignment objectives induce distinguishable topological trajectories, while instruction-tuned and pretrained models exhibit qualitatively different patterns of evolution. Our results suggest that persistent homology provides a complementary perspective on alignment, revealing representation-level changes that are not apparent from behavioral metrics alone.

AI.tldr: Using persistent homology to track activation space topology across four transformer LMs (1B–7B) and three alignment objectives, the authors find that most topological reorganization occurs early in fine-tuning, with a transient peak followed by rapid stabilization. Different objectives yield distinguishable trajectories, and instruction-tuned vs. pretrained models show qualitatively distinct evolution patterns.
AI.motivation: Little is known about how internal representations evolve during supervised fine-tuning for alignment. Behavioral metrics alone may miss representation-level changes that occur during this process.
AI.method: Persistent homology is applied to track the topology of activation spaces throughout fine-tuning. The study uses four transformer language models (1B–7B parameters), three alignment objectives (helpful, harmless, mixed), and dense checkpoint analysis to characterize the temporal dynamics of topological reorganization.
AI.result: The majority of topological reorganization occurs during the earliest stages of training. A transient peak in topological activity is followed by rapid stabilization. Different alignment objectives induce distinguishable topological trajectories, and instruction-tuned vs. pretrained models exhibit qualitatively different evolution patterns.
AI.conclusion: Persistent homology offers a complementary lens on alignment, capturing representation-level changes invisible to behavioral metrics alone, and suggests that alignment fundamentally reshapes internal representations early and in an objective-specific manner.

title: AtomMem: Building Simple and Effective Memory System for LLM Agents via Atomic Facts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning and generation abilities, but their fixed context windows limit long-term information accumulation and reuse across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems often construct memory in a coarse and unstable manner, relying on inefficient memory representations or unstable unconstrained updates. To address these challenges, we propose AtomMem, a long-term memory system designed for value-dense storage and stable memory evolution. AtomMem introduces a Fact Executor, which selectively extracts high value atomic facts from long form interactions to serve as highly efficient memory representations. Subsequently, AtomMem organizes these facts into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, capturing coherent episodic contexts and tracking dynamically evolving user attributes over time. During retrieval, the system activates an associative memory graph to connect fragmented memories. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark confirm that AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks, offering a scalable and economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents.

AI.tldr: AtomMem is a long-term memory system for LLMs that extracts high-value atomic facts, organizes them into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, and uses an associative memory graph for retrieval, achieving SOTA on the LoCoMo benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLMs are constrained by fixed context windows, limiting long-term information accumulation across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems suffer from coarse, unstable memory construction with inefficient representations and unconstrained updates.
AI.method: AtomMem proposes three core components: (1) a Fact Executor that selectively extracts high-value atomic facts from long-form interactions as efficient memory representations; (2) hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles that organize facts into coherent episodic contexts and track evolving user attributes over time; (3) an associative memory graph activated during retrieval to connect fragmented memories.
AI.result: AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks on the LoCoMo benchmark.
AI.conclusion: AtomMem provides a scalable and economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents with effective long-term memory capabilities.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Black-Box Uncertainty Estimation Methods for Large Language Models
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, their outputs often remain unreliable and may contain hallucinations, making uncertainty estimation (UE) essential for building trustworthy LLMs. In practice, many mainstream LLMs are only accessible through restricted APIs, where internal signals such as logits and hidden states are unavailable, making black-box UE especially important. However, existing work on black-box UE for LLMs remains fragmented in methodology and lacks a unified empirical comparison. To address this gap, we present a systematic review of black-box UE methods and organize them into five categories: verbalization-based, sampling-based, explanation-based, multi-agent, and hybrid methods. We further build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings. Our results show that no single method consistently dominates across all settings. Nevertheless, methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective, and hybrid methods that combine multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions. By releasing the benchmark data and a unified evaluation framework, we aim to facilitate reproducible comparisons and support future research, while our empirical findings provide practical guidance for developing future black-box UE methods for LLMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic review and benchmark of black-box uncertainty estimation methods for LLMs, categorizing 24 methods into five families and evaluating them across multiple models/datasets, finding that answer-space reasoning and hybrid approaches are generally most effective.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs are often unreliable and may contain hallucinations. Since many mainstream LLMs are only accessible via restricted APIs (no access to logits or hidden states), black-box uncertainty estimation is critical. However, existing work lacks systematic organization and unified empirical comparison.
AI.method: The authors organize black-box UE methods into five categories: (1) verbalization-based, (2) sampling-based, (3) explanation-based, (4) multi-agent, and (5) hybrid methods. They build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings.
AI.result: No single method consistently dominates all settings. Methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective. Hybrid methods combining multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions.
AI.conclusion: A unified taxonomy and benchmark are provided to facilitate reproducible comparisons. Practical guidance is offered: answer-space reasoning methods and hybrid approaches are recommended for developing future black-box UE methods for LLMs.

title: Predicting Mergeability of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Updates
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes it cheap to train many domain- and task-specific language model adapters, but whether two adapters can be merged is usually discovered only after both have been fully trained and evaluated. This late feedback is costly: adapters that are strong in isolation can interfere destructively once their updates are combined. We ask whether this outcome can be anticipated. We formalize adapter mergeability as the degree to which an adapter preserves its single-task utility after merging, and show that it can be forecast from signals measured in the first few percent of training -- chiefly how the low-rank updates and their gradients align across tasks and how much they disturb shared representations. We package these signals into MergeProbe, a lightweight predictor that estimates pairwise and set-level retention and turns the estimate into a concrete decision: merge directly, reweight, prune, or route. On MERGE-PEFT, a five-domain benchmark spanning math, code, science, instruction following, and safety, MergeProbe attains the best average and worst-case retention among strong interference-aware merge baselines while adding far less deployment overhead than full task routing. This turns LoRA merging from a post-hoc engineering step into an anticipatory measurement problem.

AI.tldr: MergeProbe predicts whether independently trained LoRA adapters can be successfully merged using signals from early training (first few percent), converting adapter merging from a costly post-hoc trial into an anticipatory decision with concrete actions: merge, reweight, prune, or route.
AI.motivation: LoRA makes adapter training cheap, but merge compatibility is discovered only after full training and evaluation — a costly late-feedback loop. Adapters strong in isolation can destructively interfere when merged, and the authors ask whether this outcome can be anticipated early in training to save compute.
AI.method: MergeProbe formalizes mergeability as post-merge single-task utility retention and forecasts it from early-training signals: (1) alignment of low-rank update directions and gradients across tasks, and (2) disturbance to shared representations. These signals are packaged into a lightweight predictor that estimates pairwise and set-level retention and outputs a concrete decision among four actions: direct merge, reweighting, pruning, or routing.
AI.result: On MERGE-PEFT, a five-domain benchmark (math, code, science, instruction following, safety), MergeProbe achieves the best average and worst-case retention compared to strong interference-aware merge baselines, with substantially lower deployment overhead than full task routing.
AI.conclusion: LoRA merging can be reframed from a post-hoc engineering step into an anticipatory measurement problem, where early-training signals reliably predict merge outcomes and enable compute-efficient intervention decisions.

title: Prompt, Plan, Extract: Zero-Shot Agentic LLMs Workflows for Lung Pathology Extraction from Clinical Narratives
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Affiliations: (1) Department of Health Outcomes and Biomedical Informatics, College of Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA; (2) Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, Department of Medicine, College of Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA; (3) College of Nursing, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
summary: Information extraction from pathology reports is essential for cancer staging, tumor registry population. Yet key data remains embedded in narrative reports, making manual extraction labor-intensive and error-prone. Traditional supervised Natural Language Processing pipelines address this through fully supervised Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction, but require expensive manual annotation and suffer cascading failures when upstream entities are missed. In this study, we developed a zero-shot, agentic workflow, and evaluated five open-source generative Large Language Models (LLMs) to populate 13 College of American Pathologists synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. We compared them against a state-of-the-art supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline using a novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework. The baseline achieved Micro-F1of 0.960, while the best zero-shot model (GPT-OSS-20B) achieved Micro-F1 of 0.893 (recall: 0.949), accurately extracting complex relations like Pathologic Stage without task-specific training. These results suggest that open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs are a low-cost solution for extracting lung pathology information.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot agentic LLMs (best: GPT-OSS-20B, Micro-F1 0.893) approach supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline (Micro-F1 0.960) for extracting 13 CAP synoptic fields from lung pathology reports, offering a low-cost alternative without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Manual extraction of structured data from narrative pathology reports for cancer staging and tumor registries is labor-intensive and error-prone. Supervised NER-RE pipelines require costly annotation and suffer cascading failures from missed upstream entities. A zero-shot approach could eliminate annotation costs and pipeline fragility.
AI.method: Developed a zero-shot, agentic workflow using five open-source generative LLMs to populate 13 College of American Pathologists (CAP) synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. Compared against a supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline using a novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework.
AI.result: The supervised GatorTron baseline achieved Micro-F1 of 0.960. The best zero-shot model (GPT-OSS-20B) achieved Micro-F1 of 0.893 with recall of 0.949, successfully extracting complex relations such as Pathologic Stage without task-specific training.
AI.conclusion: Open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs represent a viable low-cost solution for extracting lung pathology information, narrowing the performance gap with supervised methods while eliminating the need for manual annotation.

title: MetaResearcher: Scaling Deep Research via Self-Reflective Reinforcement Learning in Adversarial Virtual Environments
summary: Deep research agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous information gathering and synthesis, yet their training remains constrained by the static nature of simulated environments, the limits of fact-retrieval-only task designs, and the inefficiency of outcome-based reinforcement learning. In this work, we propose MetaResearcher, a novel framework that scales deep research agent training across four synergistic dimensions. First, we introduce an Evolving Virtual World that injects temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation into the training environment, forcing agents to develop source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution skills. Second, we design Discovery-Oriented Tasks -- including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution -- that transcend simple fact retrieval and push agents toward genuine research behaviors. Third, we propose a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism within the GRPO framework that jointly optimizes for answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity, directly addressing the repetitive action loop problem observed in prior work. Fourth, we introduce a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture comprising specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models that learn collaborative research strategies through coordinated reinforcement learning. Built upon the LiteResearcher infrastructure, MetaResearcher requires zero marginal API cost for training while targeting substantial improvements in both benchmark performance (GAIA, Xbench-DS) and epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions. We present the complete framework design, training methodology, and planned experimental validation.

AI.tldr: MetaResearcher is a training framework for deep research agents that scales across four dimensions: an Evolving Virtual World with temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation, Discovery-Oriented Tasks beyond fact retrieval, a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism for multi-objective RL optimization, and a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture. Built on LiteResearcher, it aims for zero marginal API training cost while improving benchmark performance and epistemic robustness.
AI.motivation: Current deep research agent training is limited by three key constraints: (1) static simulated environments that fail to reflect real-world information dynamics, (2) task designs restricted to fact retrieval that do not foster genuine research skills like hypothesis generation, and (3) inefficient outcome-based reinforcement learning that leads to repetitive action loops. These limitations prevent agents from developing critical capabilities such as source credibility assessment, temporal conflict resolution, and collaborative research strategies.
AI.method: MetaResearcher addresses these limitations through four synergistic components: (1) an Evolving Virtual World that injects temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation, compelling agents to assess source credibility and resolve temporal conflicts; (2) Discovery-Oriented Tasks including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution that go beyond fact retrieval; (3) a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism integrated into the GRPO framework, jointly optimizing answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity to combat repetitive action loops; and (4) a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm with specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models that learn collaborative strategies via coordinated reinforcement learning. The framework is built on LiteResearcher infrastructure to achieve zero marginal API training cost.
AI.result: The paper presents the complete framework design, training methodology, and planned experimental validation. Targeted outcomes include substantial improvements on GAIA and Xbench-DS benchmarks, along with enhanced epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions. Quantitative experimental results are not yet reported as this appears to be a framework/methodology paper with planned validation.
AI.conclusion: MetaResearcher offers a comprehensive solution to the training bottlenecks of deep research agents by scaling training across environment dynamics, task complexity, reward design, and agent architecture dimensions simultaneously. The framework's zero marginal API cost and focus on epistemic robustness position it as a practical and principled advance toward genuinely autonomous research agents capable of critical inquiry rather than mere information retrieval.

title: Displacement Is Not Direction: Evaluating Fidelity Metrics for Quantized LLM Deployment
summary: Fidelity metrics, such as per-token KL divergence (KLD) against a high-precision reference, are often used in practice as low-cost proxies for benchmark quality. We test this practice on a 28-quant cohort of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and a 41-quant cohort of Devstral-Small-2-24B, evaluated across a suite of downstream benchmarks. We find that KLD is strongly correlated with benchmark score over the full cohort ($ρ=-0.72$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.86$ on Devstral, both with $p<0.001$). However, this relationship collapses to non-significance in the near-baseline silent zone ($ρ=+0.00$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.24$, $p=0.36$, on Devstral). This collapse persists across 14 measurement variants, including different KLD aggregations, perplexity formulations, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, and context lengths. At the per-prompt level, KLD has only weak failure-prediction power on code, with failed-vs-passed geometric-mean ratios in $[1.08,1.22]$ across five models on LiveCodeBench, and fails as a cross-model router, achieving only $42.3\%-49.4\%$ accuracy on disagreement prompts. We trace the collapse to a structural decomposition: KLD primarily measures the volume of disagreement with the reference, with silent-zone composite $ρ=+0.94$ ($p<0.001$) on Qwen and $+0.55$ ($p=0.03$) on Devstral, while its relationship to the direction of those disagreements is weak and task-conditional.

AI.tldr: KLD correlates strongly with benchmark scores across broad quantization ranges, but this correlation collapses to non-significance in the near-baseline "silent zone," because KLD primarily measures disagreement volume rather than direction.
AI.motivation: Practitioners routinely use fidelity metrics like per-token KL divergence as cheap proxies for downstream benchmark quality. This paper tests whether that practice is actually valid, especially in the practically important regime of near-baseline (high-fidelity, low-degradation) models where subtle quality differences matter most.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a 28-quant cohort of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and a 41-quant cohort of Devstral-Small-2-24B across multiple downstream benchmarks. They correlate KLD (and 14 measurement variants including different aggregations, perplexity formulations, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, and context lengths) against benchmark scores. They also test KLD for per-prompt failure prediction on LiveCodeBench and cross-model routing. Finally, they structurally decompose KLD into volume and direction components to explain the collapse.
AI.result: Over the full cohort, KLD correlates strongly with benchmark score (Qwen: ρ=-0.72; Devstral: ρ=-0.86; both p<0.001). In the near-baseline silent zone, correlation collapses (Qwen: ρ=+0.00; Devstral: ρ=-0.24, p=0.36). This collapse persists across all 14 measurement variants. Per-prompt KLD has weak failure-prediction power on code (geometric-mean ratios 1.08–1.22). As a cross-model router, KLD achieves only 42.3%–49.4% accuracy. The structural decomposition reveals KLD primarily measures disagreement volume (silent-zone composite ρ=+0.94 on Qwen, +0.55 on Devstral), while directionality of disagreements is weak and task-conditional.
AI.conclusion: KLD is a reliable quality proxy only over large fidelity ranges. In the near-baseline regime where most practical deployment decisions are made, it fails to discriminate model quality. The root cause is structural: KLD conflates disagreement volume with disagreement direction, and volume alone is insufficient to predict downstream performance in high-fidelity models. Practitioners should not rely on KLD for fine-grained model selection.

title: Large Language Models Do Not Always Need Readable Language
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly prompted and interfaced with human-readable natural language, even when the intended reader is another model. This paper investigates whether semantic information can be encoded in compact, non-standard textual forms that sacrifice human readability while remaining recoverable by LLMs. We refer to this class of model-centric textual representations as BabelTele, approached here not as a fixed protocol but as an empirical probe into LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret such representations. Through readability diagnostics, model likelihood measures, human questionnaires, and downstream task evaluations, we find that BabelTele can substantially depart from ordinary natural language while preserving core semantics for instruction-tuned LLMs. As a task-agnostic representational paradigm, BabelTele demonstrates high information density, maintaining 99.5% semantic fidelity even when the text volume is condensed to 27.9% of its original length. We further evaluate its semantic robustness in cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication. Results suggest that BabelTele can reduce context overhead while generally maintaining reliable downstream performance, although its effectiveness depends on the compressor-reader pair and task setting. These findings indicate that human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled, opening a path toward model-native representations in future exploration of LLM systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "BabelTele," a class of compact, non-standard textual representations that sacrifice human readability but remain semantically recoverable by LLMs. Experiments show BabelTele can condense text to 27.9% of original length while retaining 99.5% semantic fidelity, suggesting human readability and model-side semantic recoverability can be decoupled.
AI.motivation: LLMs are typically prompted with human-readable natural language even when communicating with other models, creating unnecessary context overhead. The authors aim to explore whether semantic information can be encoded in compact, model-centric representations that sacrifice human readability while preserving recoverability by LLMs, thereby reducing communication costs in LLM systems.
AI.method: The authors empirically probe LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret "BabelTele" representations — compact, non-standard textual forms — without fixing a specific protocol. Evaluation employs readability diagnostics, model likelihood measures, human questionnaires, and downstream task evaluations. They assess semantic fidelity under text compression, cross-model transfer, agent memory scenarios, and multi-agent communication settings.
AI.result: BabelTele achieves 99.5% semantic fidelity while condensing text volume to 27.9% of original length. It maintains reliable downstream performance in cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication. However, effectiveness depends on the specific compressor-reader pair and task setting.
AI.conclusion: Human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled. BabelTele demonstrates a path toward model-native representations that reduce context overhead while preserving semantics, opening new directions for efficient LLM-to-LLM communication.

title: Understanding Key Features of Time Series Foundation Models from Epidemic Forecasting
summary: Seasonal influenza infects millions of people and causes substantial morbidity and mortality in the United States each year, making accurate short-term forecasting a core public-health need. Reliable forecasts of epidemic time series can inform vaccination timing, hospital staffing, and resource allocation, yet the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized. We address this gap through a systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting using influenza-like illness surveillance and influenza-associated hospitalization time series under both temporal and spatial generalization settings for 1-4-week-ahead prediction. We compare classical neural network architectures, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches. Across tasks, we demonstrate that a mixture-of-experts model that fuses multiple pretrained forecasters achieves the strongest overall performance, indicating that heterogeneous pretrained representations provide complementary predictive information. Our results further show that numerical transformer-based models produce reliable forecasts, while pretraining provides the largest gains at longer horizons, particularly when the pretraining domain is mechanistically aligned with influenza dynamics. In contrast, LLM-based time series methods underperform relative to numerical forecasters in this setting. Finally, we examine hospitalization information as both an auxiliary covariate and a pretraining source. Hospitalization signals provide complementary improvements in selected settings and clarify when additional surveillance streams enhance the robustness of multi-horizon forecasting. These findings provide actionable guidance on model selection, pretraining strategy, and auxiliary-signal use for influenza preparedness.

AI.tldr: A systematic evaluation of multiple forecasting architectures (classical neural networks, numerical transformers, pretrained foundation models, LLM-based methods) for 1-4-week-ahead influenza prediction reveals that a mixture-of-experts fusing heterogeneous pretrained forecasters performs best, with pretraining providing greatest gains at longer horizons when aligned with influenza dynamics, while LLM-based time series methods underperform.
AI.motivation: Accurate short-term influenza forecasting is critical for public health (vaccination timing, hospital staffing, resource allocation), yet the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting across temporal and spatial generalization settings for 1-4-week-ahead prediction, comparing classical neural networks, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches. A mixture-of-experts model fusing multiple pretrained forecasters is also introduced. Hospitalization signals are examined as both auxiliary covariates and pretraining sources.
AI.result: The mixture-of-experts model achieves the strongest overall performance, showing heterogeneous pretrained representations provide complementary information. Numerical transformer-based models yield reliable forecasts. Pretraining provides the largest gains at longer horizons, especially when the pretraining domain aligns mechanistically with influenza dynamics. LLM-based time series methods underperform relative to numerical forecasters. Hospitalization signals provide complementary improvements in selected settings.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer actionable guidance for model selection, pretraining strategy, and auxiliary-signal use in influenza forecasting. Heterogeneous pretrained forecasters fused via mixture-of-experts, mechanistically aligned pretraining, and selective use of hospitalization surveillance streams enhance multi-horizon forecasting robustness.

title: The Almost Intelligent Revolution: Options for Scaling Up Deliberation and Empowering People with AI
comment: Published in /Handbook of Democracy in the Era of Artificial Intelligence/ edited by Evangelos Pournaras, Srijoni Majumdar, Carina Ines Hausladen, and Dirk Helbing. 2026
summary: The increasing prominence of Large Language Models (LLMs) in public discourse presents both opportunities and challenges for democratic deliberation. While red teaming strategies help mitigate specific risks, broader concerns persist regarding linguistic constraints, biases, and the sycophantic tendencies of LLMs. This chapter explores how LLMs can be used to significantly scale up and democratise deliberation, particularly in fostering inclusivity and empowering traditionally marginalised groups. Drawing on concepts from Systemic-Functional Linguistics, the chapter examines how variations across language users (for example, with respect to socio-demographic groups) and across language use (for example, with respect to communicative functions) shape participation in AI-supported deliberation. The chapter presents AI-driven deliberation studies and assesses their potential to scaffold argumentation, enhance access, and reduce the influence of exclusionary linguistic norms and biases which are embedded in prestigious registers. At the same time, the chapter cautions against both overclaiming, which leads to unrealistic expectations, and underclaiming, which risks missed opportunities for AI-assisted engagement. The chapter concludes by identifying future research directions to maximise the democratic potential of AI-assisted participation while embedding ethical safeguards to counteract the reproduction of linguistic inequalities.

AI.tldr: This chapter examines how Large Language Models can scale up democratic deliberation by scaffolding argumentation and reducing exclusionary linguistic norms, while cautioning against overclaiming and underclaiming their potential, and calling for ethical safeguards against linguistic inequality.
AI.motivation: While LLMs are increasingly prominent in public discourse and red teaming addresses specific risks, broader concerns remain about linguistic constraints, biases, and sycophantic tendencies. The chapter is motivated by the need to explore how LLMs can democratise deliberation at scale, particularly by empowering marginalised groups who are often excluded by prestigious registers and dominant linguistic norms.
AI.method: The chapter draws on Systemic-Functional Linguistics (SFL) as its theoretical framework, examining how variations across language users (socio-demographic groups) and language use (communicative functions) shape participation in AI-supported deliberation. It presents and assesses AI-driven deliberation studies to evaluate their capacity to scaffold argumentation, enhance access, and reduce exclusionary linguistic biases.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that LLMs can scaffold argumentation, broaden access, and mitigate the influence of exclusionary linguistic norms embedded in prestigious registers. However, the chapter identifies risks of both overclaiming (unrealistic expectations) and underclaiming (missed opportunities for AI-assisted engagement), necessitating a balanced approach.
AI.conclusion: Future research should focus on maximising the democratic potential of AI-assisted participation while embedding ethical safeguards to prevent the reproduction of linguistic inequalities. A balanced perspective — avoiding both overclaiming and underclaiming — is essential for responsible integration of LLMs into democratic deliberation.

title: eCNNTO: A Highly Generalizable ConvNet for Accelerating Topology Optimization
summary: This work proposes an element-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to accelerate density-based Topology Optimization (TO), termed eCNNTO. TO generally undergoes a large number of iterations, where finite element analysis is performed in every iteration, leading to the efficiency bottleneck especially when dense meshes are used to achieve high-resolution designs. To address this limitation, eCNNTO is proposed to build upon Kallioras et al. (2020), where a Deep Belief Network (DBN) was trained for every element to predict its near-optimal density from its early history, thereby skipping the great majority of iterations and significantly accelerating the TO procedure. However, the method lacks spatial correlations among neighboring elements and may lead to disconnected features in the final structure. The proposed method employs CNN with residual connections to address this issue. On top of it, a novel training strategy is introduced to further enhance the optimization efficiency, where the training dataset consists of the final stage density histories rather than early ones. This change can also help reduce the required training data size. eCNNTO requires only a small dataset to train and yet it can be generalized to problems with largely different boundary conditions, loading cases, design domain geometries, mesh resolutions, as well as non-design domains. In the end, the generalization capabilities and efficiency of eCNNTO are demonstrated through a variety of examples in two and three dimensions, achieving up to 90% and 97% reduction of iterations, respectively.

AI.tldr: eCNNTO is an element-based CNN with residual connections that accelerates density-based topology optimization by predicting near-optimal element densities from final-stage history data, achieving up to 90% (2D) and 97% (3D) iteration reduction while generalizing across diverse problem setups.
AI.motivation: Topology optimization suffers from efficiency bottlenecks due to the large number of iterations requiring finite element analysis, especially with dense meshes for high-resolution designs. The prior DBN-based approach (Kallioras et al., 2020) lacked spatial correlations among neighboring elements, leading to disconnected structural features.
AI.method: An element-based CNN with residual connections is proposed to capture spatial correlations among neighboring elements. A novel training strategy uses final-stage density histories (rather than early-stage) as the training dataset, which reduces required data size. The model predicts near-optimal element densities, allowing the TO procedure to skip most iterations.
AI.result: eCNNTO achieves up to 90% reduction of iterations in 2D and up to 97% reduction in 3D. It generalizes to problems with different boundary conditions, loading cases, design domain geometries, mesh resolutions, and non-design domains, using only a small training dataset.
AI.conclusion: eCNNTO effectively addresses the limitations of prior element-wise deep learning approaches for TO acceleration by incorporating spatial correlations through CNN with residual connections and a more efficient final-stage training strategy, demonstrating strong generalization and significant computational savings.

title: Advances in Scientific Machine Learning for Coupled Fluid Flow and Transport
summary: This chapter reviews recent advances in Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) for modeling coupled fluid flow and transport phenomena governed by the incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport equations. Such systems, found in applications like turbidity currents and thermal convection, feature strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior that make high-fidelity simulations computationally expensive. To address this, the chapter surveys state-of-the-art SciML methods for building efficient surrogate models, including linear reduced-order techniques based on Singular Value Decomposition (such as Dynamic Mode Decomposition) and nonlinear neural network approaches like Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and $β$-Variational Autoencoders ($β$-VAEs). It first covers the authors' work combining these models with High Performance Computing strategies, including Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening (AMR/C) and scientific floating-point data compression. It then presents two new contributions: surrogate modeling of turbidity currents via PINNs, and the extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows using $β$-VAEs. Governing equations and representative benchmarks, including lock-exchange flows and Rayleigh-Bénard convection, illustrate these methodologies. The chapter is intentionally long, covering both the mathematical and physical foundations of coupled fluid flow and the computational aspects of state-of-the-art modeling. Overall, it demonstrates how SciML enables fast, accurate approximations of complex coupled systems within the specific data regimes and modeling assumptions considered, while substantially reducing computational cost relative to full-order simulations. Broader capabilities such as real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain active research directions whose feasibility depends strongly on the problem at hand.

AI.tldr: This chapter surveys Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) methods—including Dynamic Mode Decomposition, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, and β-Variational Autoencoders—for building efficient surrogate models of coupled Navier-Stokes and scalar transport systems, demonstrating significant computational cost reduction for applications like turbidity currents and thermal convection.
AI.motivation: Coupled fluid flow and transport systems (e.g., turbidity currents, Rayleigh-Bénard convection) exhibit strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior, making high-fidelity simulations prohibitively expensive. There is a pressing need for efficient surrogate models that can approximate these complex systems accurately at substantially lower computational cost.
AI.method: The chapter reviews linear reduced-order methods (Singular Value Decomposition, Dynamic Mode Decomposition) and nonlinear neural network approaches (PINNs, β-VAEs), combined with HPC strategies including Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening and scientific floating-point compression. Two novel contributions are presented: PINN-based surrogate modeling of turbidity currents and β-VAE extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows, demonstrated on lock-exchange and Rayleigh-Bénard convection benchmarks.
AI.result: SciML methods enable fast, accurate approximations of coupled fluid-thermal systems within the considered data regimes and modeling assumptions, with substantial computational savings relative to full-order simulations.
AI.conclusion: SciML demonstrates clear efficacy for accelerating simulations of coupled incompressible flow-transport systems. However, broader capabilities like real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain open research challenges whose viability is highly problem-dependent.

title: QMFOL: Benchmarking Large Language Model Reasoning via Quantifiable Monadic First-Order Logic Test Case Generation
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant progress in reasoning, particularly in deductive reasoning, which is crucial for high-stakes decision-making. As models improve, evaluation benchmarks should evolve to keep pace. However, existing benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and struggle to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency.
  To address these issues, we propose QMFOL, an automated framework for generating monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with quantifiable and controllable complexity. It constructs formal logical structures using conjunction and disjunction patterns, enabling precise control over reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors. These structures are then translated into natural language via LLMs, with logical consistency ensured through round-trip verification using an external prover. Based on our framework, we build QMFOLBench, a benchmark comprising 2880 instances with 960 configurations across diverse logical and semantic dimensions. Evaluations on six large reasoning models (LRMs) and two LLMs show that performance degrades and computational overhead increases with rising logical complexity. Models perform better on True-labeled tasks than on False or Unknown ones, and exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation. Overall, QMFOL offers a scalable and reliable approach for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

AI.tldr: QMFOL is an automated framework that generates first-order logic reasoning tasks with controllable complexity by constructing formal logical structures, translating them to natural language via LLMs, and verifying consistency with an external prover. The resulting benchmark (QMFOLBench, 2880 instances) reveals that model performance drops and computational cost rises with increasing logical complexity, with models performing better on True labels than False/Unknown.
AI.motivation: Existing deductive reasoning benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and fail to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency, making it difficult to precisely evaluate and track progress in LLM reasoning capabilities as models improve.
AI.method: The authors propose QMFOL, a framework that: (1) constructs formal monadic first-order logic structures using conjunction/disjunction patterns to control reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors; (2) translates these structures into natural language via LLMs; (3) ensures logical consistency through round-trip verification using an external theorem prover. They then build QMFOLBench with 2880 instances across 960 configurations, and evaluate six large reasoning models (LRMs) and two LLMs.
AI.result: Performance degrades and computational overhead (inference time/tokens) increases as logical complexity (depth, width) rises. Models show higher accuracy on True-labeled tasks compared to False or Unknown labels. Models also exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation in how logically identical problems are phrased.
AI.conclusion: QMFOL provides a scalable, reliable method for generating deductive reasoning benchmarks with precisely controllable complexity, enabling more rigorous evaluation of LLM reasoning capabilities and revealing systematic limitations in current models' handling of complex logical structures.

title: REDACT: A Systematically Controlled Multilingual Benchmark for Personal Information Detection
summary: Benchmark infrastructure for personally identifiable information (PII) detection remains limited: existing corpora cover few entity types, use ad hoc generation conditions, and do not show which surface conditions cause detector failures. We present REDACT, a systematically controlled multilingual PII benchmark with 13,427 records, 324,078 entity annotations, 51 entity types, 4,127 surface-form patterns, and 25 languages across 9 scripts. A strength-2 covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes: domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, and co-occurrence. Three entity-level metadata fields (disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier) enable stratified evaluation beyond aggregate or per-type F1. From the full benchmark, we evaluate five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, the OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,000 records. Aggregate F1 masks an architecture-dependent failure structure: the rule-based detector performs poorly on the highest-stakes data, including HIGH-sensitivity categories (recall 0.07) and non-verbatim disclosure forms, while the LLM detectors remain more robust, with the HIGH tier as their strongest sensitivity slice. A three-model reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment corroborates that sensitivity-tier assignment is the task's hardest axis. We release the benchmark, schema, prompts, and stratified evaluation harness.

AI.tldr: REDACT is a large, systematically controlled multilingual PII detection benchmark spanning 51 entity types, 25 languages, and 9 generation axes. Evaluation reveals that aggregate F1 masks critical failure patterns: rule-based detectors fail on high-sensitivity and non-verbatim disclosures, while LLM-based detectors prove more robust, with sensitivity-tier assignment being the hardest axis of the task.
AI.motivation: Existing PII detection benchmarks are limited in entity-type coverage, rely on ad hoc generation, and fail to reveal which surface conditions cause detector failures. There is a need for a systematically controlled benchmark that enables fine-grained, stratified evaluation beyond aggregate metrics.
AI.method: The authors construct REDACT, a benchmark with 13,427 records and 324,078 entity annotations, generated using a strength-2 covering-array sampler that systematically varies nine axes (domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, co-occurrence). Each entity carries three metadata fields: disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier. Five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6) are evaluated on a stratified 1,000-record sample. A three-model LLM-as-judge assessment is used for corroboration.
AI.result: Aggregate F1 conceals architecture-dependent failure modes. The rule-based detector (Presidio) achieves only 0.07 recall on HIGH-sensitivity categories and struggles with non-verbatim disclosures. LLM-based detectors are more robust, with HIGH sensitivity as their strongest slice. The LLM-as-judge assessment confirms sensitivity-tier assignment is the hardest axis.
AI.conclusion: REDACT enables stratified evaluation that exposes critical weaknesses masked by aggregate metrics, particularly for rule-based systems on high-stakes PII. The benchmark, schema, prompts, and evaluation harness are publicly released to facilitate more rigorous PII detection research.

title: The Tao of Agency: Autotelic AI, Embedded Agency and Dissolution of the Self
summary:
Most artificial intelligence systems are built on the assumption that goals are exogenous and specified by the designer. Exploring what happens when an agent begins generating its own goals opens the field of autotelic AI. Agents are expected not merely to pursue objectives but to discover them. In this article, we trace its consequences through intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness; the last of which is found to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Embeddedness individuates the agent at the cost of revealing that the individuation is non-unique, such that the same dynamics admit many valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self.
  The deepest problem with autotelic AI is therefore not how the agent generates goals, but how it generates and relativizes the self to which the goals are assigned. The agent must believe in its own boundary in order to act, and see through that boundary in order to understand. We consolidate these developments into a single framework and extend it along three directions: a quantum formulation in which the agent-environment cut becomes physical, a philosophical reading against non-dual contemplative traditions, and a concrete LLM-based agentic instantiation.

AI.tldr: The paper explores autotelic AI—agents that generate their own goals rather than receiving them exogenously. It argues that the core challenge is not goal generation per se, but how the agent constructs and relativizes its own self-boundary. The authors consolidate intrinsic motivation, causal-interventional learning, and embeddedness into a unified framework, extending it with a quantum formulation, non-dual philosophical analysis, and an LLM-based agentic implementation.
AI.motivation: Most AI systems treat goals as externally specified. The paper aims to systematically investigate the implications of agents that autonomously discover and generate their own goals, identifying the deepest conceptual challenge as the self-world boundary problem rather than goal-generation mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors trace consequences of autotelic agency through several frameworks: intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness. They consolidate these into a unified framework and extend it along three dimensions: (1) a quantum formulation where the agent-environment cut becomes physical, (2) a philosophical reading engaging non-dual contemplative traditions, and (3) a concrete LLM-based agentic instantiation.
AI.result: Embeddedness is identified as a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Embeddedness individuates the agent but reveals that individuation is non-unique—the same underlying dynamics admit multiple valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self. The deepest problem is therefore how the agent both believes in its own boundary (to act) and sees through it (to understand).
AI.conclusion: The central challenge of autotelic AI shifts from goal generation to self-generation and self-relativization. The agent must simultaneously reify and transcend its own boundary—a tension the authors address through quantum formalism, non-dual philosophy, and practical LLM-based implementation.

title: On the QUEST for Uncertainty Quantification via Highest Density Regions
comment: 27 pages, of which 10 are main text. Contains 7 figures, 4 tables, 1 algorithm in total
summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for reliable decision-making in safety-critical applications in probabilistic machine learning. For regression problems, dominant scalar UQ approaches - notably, those based on proper scoring rules - measure uncertainty via pointwise predictive risk. This can lead to counterintuitive results when the target statistic is not the conditional expectation. We propose an alternative framework, in which uncertainty is characterised by the volume of the most probable subset of a distribution's support. QUEST (Quantifying Uncertainty via highest dEnSiTy regions) is a novel approach to UQ based on the concentration of Lebesgue measure at a distribution's peak(s), evaluated at one or more values of a robustness parameter $α$. We establish connections between our measures and classical statistics from information theory and economics. We show that, unlike popular alternatives based on proper scoring rules, QUEST measures of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty satisfy a set of axioms adapted from the UQ literature, including monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts. Selective prediction benchmarks confirm that QUEST performs favourably against standard measures such as variance and differential entropy.

AI.tldr: QUEST proposes a new uncertainty quantification framework based on the volume of highest-density regions rather than pointwise predictive risk, satisfying key axioms like monotonicity under spread and location invariance, and outperforming variance and entropy on selective prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing scalar UQ methods for regression (e.g., those based on proper scoring rules) measure uncertainty via pointwise predictive risk, which yields counterintuitive results when the target statistic differs from the conditional expectation. The authors aim to address this limitation with a geometrically-grounded alternative.
AI.method: QUEST characterizes uncertainty via the Lebesgue measure (volume) of the highest-density region(s) of a predictive distribution, evaluated at user-specified robustness levels α. The approach draws connections to information theory and economics, and defines both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty measures that are axiomatically justified.
AI.result: QUEST measures satisfy axioms of monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts, unlike proper-scoring-rule-based alternatives. Empirical validation on selective prediction benchmarks shows QUEST performs favorably against variance and differential entropy.
AI.conclusion: The HDR-volume-based framework offers a theoretically principled and practically effective alternative to dominant scalar UQ methods, with stronger axiomatic foundations and competitive empirical performance.

title: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
summary: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit--DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.

AI.tldr: A lightweight pronunciation assessment framework using only native speech data. It combines surprisal from a token language model on discretized speech units with DTW alignment features guided by reference transcripts, achieving near-supervised performance on learner speech.
AI.motivation: Supervised pronunciation assessment models require costly labeled L2 error data or non-native corpora. The authors aim to circumvent this by leveraging only native speech resources, with optional light calibration from a small set of scored utterances.
AI.method: Learner speech is discretized via an SSL encoder and K-means codebook into acoustic tokens. A token language model trained on native token sequences computes surprisal (higher values signal phonotactic deviation). A Text2DUnit--DTW module predicts native token sequences from the reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens, producing error-sensitive alignment features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression to predict pronunciation scores.
AI.result: On SpeechOcean762, Pearson Correlation Coefficient improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, approaching supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent improvements.
AI.conclusion: The proposed native-only, transcript-guided framework achieves competitive pronunciation assessment without requiring labeled L2 data, demonstrating strong generalization across datasets.

title: PhysDrift: Bridging the Embodiment Gap in Humanoid Co-Speech Motion Generation
summary: Humanoid robots require co-speech motions that are not only expressive and speech-aligned, but also physically executable under embodiment constraints. Existing co-speech generation pipelines are predominantly human-centric: motions are first generated in human-body representations such as SMPL-X and subsequently retargeted to humanoid robots. In this work, we identify a fundamental embodiment gap in this paradigm, where the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints disrupts embodiment consistency during motion transfer and physical execution. Through extensive analysis, we show that although retargeting can preserve coarse motion semantics, it significantly compresses motion diversity and weakens prosody-motion synchronization, limiting expressive humanoid behaviors. To address this problem, we first propose IK-EER, a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting. Building upon the curated robot-native motion dataset, we further introduce PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech without relying on intermediate human-body representations. Unlike conventional human-centric pipelines, PhysDrift maintains embodiment consistency throughout both training and inference while incorporating physical regularization to stabilize robot motion dynamics. Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that embodiment-aware robot-native generation substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability.

AI.tldr: Existing co-speech motion generation relies on human-centric representations (SMPL-X) and retargeting, causing an "embodiment gap" that degrades motion diversity and prosody alignment. The authors propose IK-EER for curated robot-native data and PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech, improving alignment, physical plausibility, and real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Current co-speech motion generation pipelines generate motions in human-body representations (e.g., SMPL-X) and retarget them to humanoid robots. This introduces an embodiment gap: the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints disrupts consistency, compresses motion diversity, and weakens prosody-motion synchronization during physical execution.
AI.method: (1) IK-EER: a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting to build a robot-native dataset. (2) PhysDrift: an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech, bypassing intermediate human-body representations, with physical regularization for motion stability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that embodiment-aware robot-native generation substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability compared to human-centric pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Direct robot-native co-speech motion generation (PhysDrift) with curated robot-native data (IK-EER) effectively bridges the embodiment gap, yielding more expressive, physically executable, and prosody-aligned motions for humanoid robots compared to conventional retargeting-based approaches.

title: Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery
summary: Causal abstractions formalize when a high-level structural causal model (SCM) captures the interventional behavior of a lower-level SCM. Existing applications of this notion largely follow a hypothesis-testing paradigm: an expert proposes a candidate high-level model and then evaluates if the low-level system implements it. We study the complementary problem of learning a high-level model directly from low-level measurements. Our contributions leverage hypotheses from low-rank causal discovery, and can be summarized as follows: (1) we show that observations generated by a low-rank graph induce latents that form a causal abstraction, (2) we provide identifiability results about these latents, and (3) we propose a practical objective to learn this high-level SCM.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of automatically learning a high-level structural causal model (SCM) from low-level data, showing that low-rank causal structures naturally induce latent variables that form a causal abstraction, with accompanying identifiability results and a practical learning objective.
AI.motivation: Existing work on causal abstraction follows a top-down, hypothesis-testing paradigm where a human expert proposes a candidate high-level model and then tests whether the low-level system conforms to it. The reverse problem — learning the high-level abstraction directly from low-level measurements — remains unexplored. This paper aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: The authors leverage insights from low-rank causal discovery. They demonstrate that when observations are generated by a low-rank causal graph (i.e., the connectivity matrix has reduced rank), the resulting latent structure automatically satisfies the conditions of a causal abstraction. They then derive identifiability results for these latents and propose a practical optimization objective for learning the high-level SCM from data.
AI.result: Three main contributions: (1) a proof that observations from a low-rank graph induce latents that constitute a valid causal abstraction, (2) formal identifiability guarantees regarding these latent variables, and (3) a tractable learning objective to recover the high-level SCM in practice.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank structure in causal systems provides a principled pathway for automatically discovering high-level causal abstractions from low-level data, moving beyond the expert-driven hypothesis-testing paradigm toward data-driven abstraction learning.

title: GEMS: Geometric Constraints Enable Multi-Semantic Superposition in LLMs
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code and logs are available at: https://github.com/LuLu663939/gems-multi-semantic-steering
summary: Activation steering controls model behavior by modifying intermediate hidden states at inference time without retraining. Existing methods handle only single-direction injection; when multiple semantic directions are superposed without constraints, the model collapses. We show that this collapse decomposes into two independently acting sources: distributional deviation, where additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers and drive activations outside the training distribution, and directional interference, where non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen when superposed. These two sources define the design constraints that any training-free multi-directional intervention must address. As one instantiation of these principles, we propose GEMS, a training-free method that maps each source to a corresponding geometric constraint: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted attention-pathway injection for distributional deviation, and real-time orthogonalization for directional interference. On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserves accuracy at 98% (baseline 92%), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%; on Wikitext-2, the same injection incurs only 2.2% PPL increase. Component ablation isolates the causal role of each constraint, and layer-level probes confirm that orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Qualitative steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B.

AI.tldr: Activation steering fails when multiple semantic directions are injected simultaneously due to two independent issues: distributional deviation (norm accumulation) and directional interference (non-orthogonal vectors dampening each other). The authors propose GEMS, which solves these via norm-preserving weighted superposition, targeted attention-pathway injection, and real-time orthogonalization, enabling multi-directional steering without model collapse.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods are limited to single-direction injection. When multiple semantic directions are superposed without constraints, model performance collapses entirely. The authors aim to understand why this collapse occurs and develop a training-free solution for concurrent multi-directional steering.
AI.method: The authors first decompose the multi-direction steering collapse into two independent causal sources: (1) distributional deviation, where additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers and push activations outside the training distribution; (2) directional interference, where non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen when superposed. Based on this analysis, they propose GEMS, which applies geometric constraints corresponding to each source: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted attention-pathway injection address distributional deviation, while real-time orthogonalization mitigates directional interference.
AI.result: On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserves accuracy at 98% (vs. 92% baseline), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%. On Wikitext-2, the same multi-direction injection incurs only a 2.2% perplexity increase. Ablation studies isolate each constraint's causal role, and layer-level probes confirm orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B parameters.
AI.conclusion: The two identified failure modes (distributional deviation and directional interference) define necessary design constraints for any training-free multi-directional intervention. GEMS demonstrates that satisfying these constraints enables robust multi-directional steering without retraining, preserving model utility across tasks and scales.

title: Advancing DialNav through Automatic Embodied Dialog Augmentation
summary: For embodied agents capable of physical interaction, the capability to create and understand dialog is crucial to ensure both safety and effectiveness. While DialNav~\cite{han2025dialnav} provides a framework for holistic evaluation of the dialog--execution loop in photorealistic indoor navigation, its performance remains limited by a critical scarcity of training data (2K episodes). To address this, we propose an automatic generation pipeline, and construct the \textbf{RAINbow} dataset, a large-scale training dataset with 238K episodes for DialNav. Our pipeline converts existing VLN datasets into multi-turn dialog and creates cost-efficient and high-quality dataset. Then, we introduce two additional complementary advances to unlock the data's full potential: (1) Dual-Strategy Training, a navigation training scheme to align the navigation training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop, and (2) a localization model that leverages VLN knowledge. By combining these complementary solutions, our model substantially outperforms the baseline in success rate on both \textbf{Val Seen} (58.24, \textbf{+89\%}) and \textbf{Val Unseen} (29.05, \textbf{+100\%}) splits, establishing a new state of the art.

AI.tldr: RAINbow is a large-scale (238K episodes) automatically generated training dataset for dialog-based navigation, created by converting existing VLN datasets. Combined with Dual-Strategy Training and a VLN-knowledge-enhanced localization model, it achieves SOTA on DialNav, with +89% on Val Seen and +100% on Val Unseen success rate.
AI.motivation: DialNav provides a benchmark for evaluating dialog–execution loops in embodied navigation, but its performance is severely limited by a scarcity of training data (only 2K episodes). This data bottleneck prevents models from effectively learning the interplay between dialog understanding and physical navigation.
AI.method: Three complementary contributions: (1) An automatic generation pipeline that converts existing VLN datasets into multi-turn dialog, producing the RAINbow dataset (238K episodes). (2) Dual-Strategy Training, which aligns navigation training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop. (3) A localization model that leverages pre-existing VLN knowledge to improve spatial reasoning within dialog-based navigation.
AI.result: The combined approach substantially outperforms the DialNav baseline: Val Seen success rate reaches 58.24 (+89%), Val Unseen reaches 29.05 (+100%), establishing a new state of the art.
AI.conclusion: Scaling training data via automatic dialog generation from existing VLN datasets, paired with training strategies tailored to the dialog-navigation loop and VLN-pretrained localization, effectively unlocks dialog-based embodied navigation performance.

title: IHBench: Evaluating Post-Interruption Recovery in Voice Agents with Structured Workflows
summary:
Voice agents deployed in structured workflows (customer service, healthcare scheduling, account management) must handle frequent user interruptions while maintaining progress through multi-step procedures. Existing benchmarks for speech-capable models focus on the timing of interruptions: barge-in detection, endpointing, and turn-taking dynamics. They leave unmeasured what happens after the interruption: does the agent resume the workflow at the correct step? Does it address the user's interjection? Does it avoid re-delivering content the user already heard?
  We introduce IHBench (Interruption Handling Benchmark), a benchmark that evaluates post-interruption recovery in voice agents executing state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected at controlled points mid-utterance, with per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. Each interruption is scored on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality.
  We evaluate 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and the open-weight community. Models vary widely, and recovery quality depends strongly on the interruption type. Across our experiments, closed-weight models are consistently more robust to interruptions than open-weight ones: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade roughly 3.3x more slowly as conversations grow longer, and show no audio-versus-text modality gap, whereas the open-weight models lose ground on all three. A human study validates the LLM judge against human annotators, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge indicates that recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis.

AI.tldr: IHBench evaluates how voice agents recover after user interruptions in multi-step workflows, testing 27 audio-language models across 10 domains. Closed-weight models significantly outperform open-weight ones on task fulfillment, degrade more slowly with conversation length, and show no audio-text modality gap. Recovery quality emerges as a distinct capability axis from existing interruption-timing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for speech-capable models focus narrowly on interruption timing (barge-in detection, endpointing, turn-taking) but neglect what happens after the interruption: whether the agent correctly resumes the workflow, addresses the user's interjection, and avoids repeating already-heard content. This gap is critical for deployed voice agents in structured domains like customer service and healthcare scheduling.
AI.method: IHBench evaluates post-interruption recovery using state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected at controlled points mid-utterance. Each instance is scored on two axes — task fulfillment and recovery quality — using per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. 27 audio-language model configurations (OpenAI, Google, open-weight) are tested. A human study validates the LLM judge, and cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge assesses whether recovery quality is a distinct capability.
AI.result: Closed-weight models consistently outperform open-weight models: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade ~3.3x more slowly as conversations lengthen, and exhibit no audio-versus-text modality gap. Open-weight models lose ground on all three metrics. Human annotation validates the LLM judge, and cross-benchmark analysis shows recovery quality is largely orthogonal to capabilities measured by AudioMultiChallenge.
AI.conclusion: Post-interruption recovery is a distinct and underexplored capability axis for voice agents. Closed-weight models currently hold a substantial advantage, but the benchmark provides a framework for improving open-weight models and advancing robust, interruption-resilient voice agents in structured enterprise workflows.

title: Source-Grounded Data Generation for Text-to-JSON Learning
summary: From financial filings to clinical records, legacy industries rely heavily on long, unstructured documents to store high-value information. Reliably extracting this information into structured, machine-readable representations is a key prerequisite to making the contents accessible to automated systems. JSON is a natural target for such structured extraction, yet constructing reliable and scalable text-to-JSON training data remains challenging.
