To address this gap, we propose STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration), a source-grounded data generation pipeline that constructs reports and JSON schema by using LLMs for scalable synthesis while validating ground-truth values against the underlying spreadsheet. Evaluations on STAGE-Eval, our source-grounded benchmark with an 851-example test set, show that STAGE produces stronger training data than existing approaches. This improves Qwen3-4B exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.

AI.tldr: STAGE is a data generation pipeline that creates text-to-JSON training data grounded in spreadsheet data, using LLMs for synthesis while validating outputs against source spreadsheets. It significantly improves structured extraction performance, boosting Qwen3-4B's exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.
AI.motivation: Legacy industries rely on long, unstructured documents storing high-value information. Extracting this into structured JSON is critical for downstream automation, but constructing reliable, scalable text-to-JSON training data is difficult. Existing methods lack source-grounding, leading to hallucinated or inaccurate training examples.
AI.method: STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration) is a source-grounded pipeline that uses LLMs to synthesize paired reports and JSON schemas, while validating all ground-truth values against an underlying spreadsheet to ensure factual correctness and eliminate hallucination.
AI.result: On STAGE-Eval (an 851-example source-grounded benchmark), STAGE-generated training data outperforms existing approaches. Fine-tuning Qwen3-4B with STAGE data raises exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.
AI.conclusion: Source-grounded data generation via STAGE produces substantially higher-quality text-to-JSON training data than prior methods, enabling much more reliable structured extraction from unstructured documents.

title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
summary: Achieving dexterous robotic manipulation in the real world heavily relies on human supervision and algorithm engineering, which becomes a central bottleneck in the pursuit of general physical intelligence. Although emerging coding agents can generate code to automate algorithm search, their successes remain largely confined in digital environments. We conjecture that the missing abstraction to automate robotics research is a repeatable feedback loop for real-world policy improvement: reset the scene, execute a policy, verify the outcome, and refine the next iteration. To bridge this gap, we introduce ENPIRE, a harness framework for coding agents that instantiates this physical feedback routine with four core modules: an Environment module (EN) for automatic reset and verification, a Policy Improvement module (PI) that launches policy refinement, a Rollout module (R) to evaluate policies with one or multiple physical robots operating in parallel, and an Evolution module (E) in which coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This closed-loop system transforms real-world manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure, minimizing human effort while allowing fair ablations across training recipe and agent variants. Powered by ENPIRE, frontier coding agents can autonomously train a policy to achieve a 99% success rate on challenging, dexterous manipulation tasks, such as organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use, a process that further accelerates when we dispatch an agent team on a robot fleet. Our results suggest a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advancing robotics in the physical world.

AI.tldr: ENPIRE is a closed-loop harness framework that enables coding agents to autonomously improve real-world robotic manipulation policies through a repeatable physical feedback loop (reset, execute, verify, refine), achieving 99% success on dexterous tasks like pin box organization, zip tie fastening, and tool use.
AI.motivation: Real-world dexterous robotic manipulation currently demands heavy human supervision and algorithm engineering, creating a bottleneck for general physical intelligence. While coding agents can automate algorithm search in digital domains, they lack the physical-world feedback loop needed for robotics research automation.
AI.method: ENPIRE consists of four integrated modules: (1) Environment (EN) for automatic scene reset and outcome verification, (2) Policy Improvement (PI) for launching policy refinement, (3) Rollout (R) for parallel policy evaluation across multiple physical robots, and (4) Evolution (E) where coding agents analyze execution logs, consult literature, and iteratively improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. The system supports multi-agent teams across robot fleets.
AI.result: Frontier coding agents powered by ENPIRE autonomously trained policies achieving 99% success rates on challenging dexterous manipulation tasks: organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use. Performance further accelerates when deploying agent teams across a robot fleet.
AI.conclusion: ENPIRE demonstrates a practical and scalable pathway for deploying coding agents to autonomously advance real-world physical robotics, transforming manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure with minimal human intervention.

title: Comparing Linear Probes with Mahalanobis Cosine Similarity
summary: Linear probes are widely used in interpretability research and often compared by cosine similarity. The Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between two directions, which reweights the inner product by test data covariance, is a natural task-aware refinement. Ying et al. (2026) report that a probe's MCS to a reference probe trained on the out-of-distribution (OOD) data near-perfectly linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC (R^2 = 0.98). Here, we extend this empirical finding across models, layers, and concept domains, and prove this general phenomenon in closed form: For balanced classes whose projections are Gaussian, OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are linear because both are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data. The theory also predicts when this linearity fails, which we verify empirically. MCS offers a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between a probe and a reference probe linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC because both are sigmoid functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio on test data. The authors extend prior empirical findings and provide theoretical grounding for MCS as a superior alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.
AI.motivation: Linear probes are commonly compared via Euclidean cosine similarity, which is task-agnostic. Ying et al. (2026) empirically showed that MCS—which reweights by test data covariance—near-perfectly predicts OOD AUROC. This paper aims to provide theoretical justification for this phenomenon and determine its generality across models, layers, and domains.
AI.method: The authors assume balanced classes with Gaussian-distributed projections and derive closed-form expressions showing that both OOD AUROC and MCS to a reference probe are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on test data, establishing their linear relationship. They validate the theory by testing conditions where the linearity holds and where it fails (e.g., when Gaussian or class-balance assumptions break).
AI.result: The linear relationship between MCS and OOD AUROC generalizes across different models, layers, and concept domains. The closed-form derivation confirms that linearity arises because both metrics depend on SNR via sigmoid functions. Empirical tests confirm the theory's predictions about when the linear relationship breaks down.
AI.conclusion: MCS provides a theoretically grounded, task-aware alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes. Its linear relationship to OOD AUROC is explained by both metrics' dependence on the probe's SNR, and the theory successfully predicts failure modes.

title: IHUBERT: Vector-Based Semantic Deduplication and Domain-Balanced Pretraining for Persian Resources
summary: Persian pretrained language models (PLMs) are still limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality pretraining corpora and by insufficient evaluation beyond standard classification and NER tasks. We present IHUBERT, a monolingual Persian PLM trained from scratch with the RoBERTa-base encoder (125M parameters) on a 45 GB curated subset of the Sepahr-Danesh collection (about 7-8B tokens). To improve corpus quality and reduce redundancy, we employ a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline that includes normalization, exact and near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for distribution balancing control across domains and registers. We additionally train a 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer on the full pretraining corpus to better capture Persian morphology and orthographic variation. IHUBERT is evaluated on seven Persian NLU benchmarks covering NER, sentiment analysis, topic classification, NLI, extractive question answering, and relation extraction, using task-standard metrics (entity-level F1, Macro-F1, EM/F1). IHUBERT achieves its strongest gains on extractive QA, ranking first on both PQuAD (F1 88.3542) and ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.0987), and attains the best result on FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). On NER and topic classification, it remains competitive (e.g., 0.8308 F1 on ParsTwiNER; 0.7953 Macro-F1 on DigiMag), while relation extraction remains the main remaining gap (0.6684 Macro-F1 on PERLEX). A controlled tokenizer ablation on the IHUBERT pretraining corpus shows that BPE yields slightly lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size, supporting our tokenization design. Overall, IHUBERT advances Persian language modeling through semantically curated large-scale pretraining and broad evaluation across both classification and comprehension-oriented tasks.

AI.tldr: IHUBERT is a monolingual Persian RoBERTa-base model trained from scratch on a 45 GB semantically deduplicated corpus. It achieves state-of-the-art results on extractive QA and textual entailment benchmarks, with competitive performance on NER and topic classification, while relation extraction remains a challenge.
AI.motivation: Persian PLMs suffer from scarce high-quality pretraining corpora and narrow evaluation limited to classification and NER. There is a need for both better data curation and broader downstream assessment, including comprehension-oriented tasks.
AI.method: The authors pretrain a RoBERTa-base (125M parameters) from scratch on a 45 GB curated subset of Sepahr-Danesh (~7–8B tokens). A multi-stage preprocessing pipeline applies normalization, exact/near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for domain/register balance. A 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer is trained on the full corpus. Evaluation spans seven NLU benchmarks: NER, sentiment analysis, topic classification, NLI, extractive QA, and relation extraction.
AI.result: IHUBERT ranks first on PQuAD (F1 88.35), ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.10), and FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). It achieves competitive results on ParsTwiNER (F1 0.8308), DigiMag (Macro-F1 0.7953), and PERLEX (Macro-F1 0.6684). A tokenizer ablation shows BPE yields lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size.
AI.conclusion: Semantically curated large-scale pretraining combined with a BPE tokenizer tailored to Persian morphology advances Persian language modeling. Broad evaluation across both classification and comprehension tasks demonstrates IHUBERT's effectiveness, though relation extraction remains the primary remaining gap.

title: Reward as An Agent for Embodied World Models
summary: While RL has become a promising tool for refining world models, existing methods largely rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, limiting exploration, behavioral diversity, and richer dynamic discovery. In this work, we challenge this conservative paradigm. We argue that the core limitation is not exploration itself, but the lack of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration. Without reliable verification, expanded exploration becomes highly susceptible to reward hacking, where policies exploit imperfect rewards without achieving genuine improvement. To evaluate this motivation, we instantiate our method in embodied world models, where physical plausibility, and task completion provide a rigorous testbed for scalable RL under complex dynamics. On the verification side, we introduce Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts. On the exploration side, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification through DynDiff-GRPO, which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors beyond conservative rollout regimes. By unifying Reward as an Agent with DynDiff-GRPO, we enable RL on a more reliable reward foundation with substantially diversified sampling, effectively mitigating reward hacking while yielding significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, thereby demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges conservative exploration in RL for world model refinement, arguing the real bottleneck is lack of reliable verification. It proposes Reward as an Agent (agentic reward verification) and DynDiff-GRPO (dynamic-aware rollout diversification), which together enable broader, safer exploration, mitigate reward hacking, and achieve significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for refining world models rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, which limits exploration, behavioral diversity, and discovery of richer dynamics. The authors argue the core limitation is not exploration per se but the absence of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration. Without such verification, expanded exploration leads to reward hacking — policies exploit imperfect rewards without genuine improvement.
AI.method: Two complementary components are introduced: (1) **Reward as an Agent** — an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals, mitigating reward hacking under distribution shifts. (2) **DynDiff-GRPO** (Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification) — an exploration strategy that explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors. These are unified and instantiated in embodied world models, where physical plausibility and task completion serve as rigorous evaluation criteria.
AI.result: The unified approach yields significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.
AI.conclusion: Broader exploration in RL-based world model refinement is viable and beneficial when paired with reliable verification. The Reward as an Agent + DynDiff-GRPO framework effectively mitigates reward hacking while enabling richer dynamic discovery, challenging the conservative rollout paradigm.

title: Latent Confounded Causal Discovery via Lie Bracket Geometry
summary: Recent work on Kan-Do-Calculus (KDC) has established that the boundary between passive observation and active intervention in causal inference is a category-theoretic bi-adjunction, with interventions modeled by left Kan extensions and conditioning by right Kan extensions. This paper introduces two causal discovery algorithms under latent confounding, building on the information-geometric and categorical consequences of KDC. In smooth statistical settings, Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures induce local causal vector fields; failures of these fields to close under Lie brackets become computable Frobenius residuals, which we interpret as witnesses of failed visible integrability and possible latent or unmodeled structure. Our first algorithm, BRIDGE (Bracket Residuals for Interventional Discovery and Geometric Estimation), combines an interventional density or Radon-Nikodym-ratio engine with a geometric screen that proposes a high-recall family of admissible arrows, identifies non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and passes the reduced family to downstream score-based or differentiable discovery routines. The second algorithmic contribution, Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching (SKFM), learns amortized intervention fields and factors latent curvature spectrally, exposing the direct Lie-space endpoint toward which BRIDGE points. A detailed set of experiments show that both algorithms are capable of discovering causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential space of possible DAGs by many orders of magnitude. This paper introduces a new paradigm in causal discovery, where latent structure is inferred directly from the geometry of intervention-induced flows.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two causal discovery algorithms (BRIDGE and SKFM) that detect latent confounders by analyzing the geometric properties of intervention-induced flows in statistical manifolds. The key insight is that failures of Lie bracket closure in causal vector fields—quantified as Frobenius residuals—serve as witnesses of latent structure, dramatically reducing the search space of possible DAGs.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery with latent confounders suffers from a super-exponential explosion in the space of possible DAGs. The authors leverage the category-theoretic bi-adjunction established in Kan-Do-Calculus—where interventions are left Kan extensions and conditioning are right Kan extensions—to provide a geometric, principled alternative: rather than searching over graph structures, infer latent confounders directly from failures of integrability in intervention-induced vector fields.
AI.method: Two algorithms are proposed. (1) BRIDGE: uses an interventional density engine to estimate Radon-Nikodym derivatives, constructs local causal vector fields, computes Lie bracket closure failures as Frobenius residuals, screens for non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and passes a reduced arrow family to downstream score-based or differentiable discovery. (2) SKFM: learns amortized intervention fields and performs spectral decomposition of latent curvature to directly identify the Lie-space structure toward which BRIDGE points.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that both algorithms successfully discover causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential DAG search space by many orders of magnitude. The Frobenius residuals reliably signal the presence of unmodeled latent structure.
AI.conclusion: A new paradigm for causal discovery is established where latent structure is inferred directly from the differential geometry of intervention-induced flows, rather than through combinatorial graph search. The category-theoretic foundations of KDC provide the formal scaffolding for this geometric approach.

title: Self-Preference Is Weak or Absent in Verifiable Instruction-Following Revision: A Four-Model Test Under Genuine Authorship
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly review and revise text, including their own. A documented self-preference bias (models favoring their own generations when acting as judges) raises the question of whether models also resist valid corrections to their own writing. We test this in a setting where "valid" is decided not by another model but by a deterministic verifier: instruction-following revision on IFEval. A model writes a draft; the official IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it; the model then accepts or rejects that edit either as the genuine in-context author or as a fresh model that sees the draft neutrally. Across four mid-tier model families and 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons, we find no detectable self-preference: authors reject verified-good fixes to their own drafts at essentially the same rate as fresh models judging the same drafts (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). A self-skepticism hint from a smaller pilot did not replicate at scale. The one robust observation is qualitative: when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of their stated reasons are flaw-catching rather than preference, that is, about the character of rejections, not an elevated rate. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded at this sample size.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit self-preference bias by resisting valid corrections to their own writing. Using IFEval's deterministic verifier across 85 author-vs-fresh comparisons in four model families, the results show no detectable self-preference: authors reject verified-good fixes at similar rates to fresh models. Qualitative analysis reveals that when authors do reject valid corrections, 97% of stated reasons involve flaw-catching rather than preference.
AI.motivation: Prior work has documented a self-preference bias where LLMs favor their own generations when acting as judges. This raises the concern that models might also resist valid corrections to their own writing, undermining their reliability in self-revision tasks. The authors aim to test this in a rigorous setting where "validity" is objectively determined by a deterministic verifier rather than another model's judgment.
AI.method: The experiment uses instruction-following revision on IFEval. A model writes a draft; the official IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it; the model then either accepts or rejects that edit. Two conditions are compared: (1) the model as the genuine in-context author of the draft, and (2) a fresh model instance that sees the draft neutrally. The study spans four mid-tier model families with 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons. A self-skepticism hint condition from a smaller pilot was also tested.
AI.result: No detectable self-preference was found: authors reject verified-good fixes at essentially the same rate as fresh models judging the same drafts (gap -5.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). The self-skepticism hint from a smaller pilot did not replicate at scale. Qualitatively, when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of their stated reasons involve flaw-catching (e.g., claiming the edit introduces new errors) rather than mere preference for their own version. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded at this sample size.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to concerns raised by the broader self-preference literature, LLMs do not appear to systematically resist valid, verifiably correct edits to their own writing. The primary distinction between author and fresh-model behavior lies not in rejection rates but in the qualitative character of rejections. However, the confidence intervals leave open the possibility of small but non-zero effects below ~13 percentage points.

title: Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale
summary: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

AI.tldr: Evaluates DAG Plan & Execute vs. ReAct architectures across 208 enterprise scenarios at three scales (Persona, Department, Enterprise). Finds scale dominates performance degradation, with agent discovery noise as primary bottleneck. Introduces a Task Manager that improves priority latency by 14–75% and related-event correctness by 20+ percentage points.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI needs continuous, event-driven multi-agent orchestration, but existing systems assume discrete request-response workflows and lack evaluation at realistic enterprise scales (200+ agents). The gap between current architectures and production enterprise requirements motivates this work.
AI.method: Benchmarked two orchestration architectures (DAG Plan & Execute, ReAct) across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20–80 agents), and Enterprise (200 agents). Introduced a Task Manager module providing priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption for continuous operation. Measured orchestration performance, degradation patterns, and Task Manager impact.
AI.result: Scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance. Both architectures degrade at enterprise scale due to agent discovery noise. Simple tasks surprisingly degrade more sharply than complex ones. DAG offers higher precision and parallelization at small scale but overhead worsens at scale; ReAct proves more robust via incremental failure handling. Task Manager reduces high-priority latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by >20 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Agent discovery noise is the primary bottleneck at enterprise scale. ReAct is preferable for large-scale continuous operation due to robustness. The Task Manager effectively addresses continuous monitoring challenges, enabling priority-aware, merged-event handling in production multi-agent systems.

title: SEAGAN: domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a flexible framework for learning from scientific data linked through physical, biological, or functional relationships. One promising domain is plant physiology, where measured responses often arise from multiple interacting processes whose exact separation remains difficult even with manual intervention. In plant physiology, a key example is the A-Ci curve, which relates net CO2 assimilation rate (Anet) to leaf intercellular CO2 concentration (Ci) and is used to estimate photosynthetic parameters in leaf and crop-canopy models. However, reliable estimation requires identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each curve point, which remains a major source of uncertainty. Here, we formulate limitation-state identification along A-Ci curves as a graph-based node classification problem, with curve points as nodes. Domain-specific graph representations are created using distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The framework was evaluated against conventional learning baselines, graph-based architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark. Results on a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states show that graph-based models improve classification, particularly near biochemical transition regions. The best-performing configuration, SEAGAN (domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes), integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss, achieving an F1-score of 0.857 and an accuracy of 0.882. The results show that representing A-Ci curves as graphs improves biochemical limitation-state analysis, with edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods providing the most effective strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates biochemical limitation-state identification along photosynthetic A-Ci curves as a graph node classification problem. A domain-specific GNN architecture (SEAGAN) combining process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss achieves F1=0.857 and accuracy=0.882, outperforming conventional baselines, especially near biochemical transition regions.
AI.motivation: Accurate estimation of photosynthetic parameters from A-Ci curves requires correctly identifying the active biochemical limitation state (e.g., Rubisco-limited, RuBP-regeneration-limited, TPU-limited) at each measured point. This identification remains a major source of uncertainty, and manual intervention is often insufficient due to multiple interacting processes. An automated, reliable approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors frame limitation-state identification as a graph-based node classification problem where A-Ci curve points are nodes. Two graph construction strategies are explored: distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relationships. The proposed SEAGAN model integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention layers, trained with a weighted cross-entropy loss to handle class imbalance. The framework is evaluated against conventional ML baselines, other graph architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark using a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states.
AI.result: Graph-based models consistently outperform conventional learning baselines and the fitting-based benchmark, with the greatest gains near biochemical transition regions where limitation states change. SEAGAN achieves the best performance: F1-score of 0.857 and accuracy of 0.882. Edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods proves to be the most effective modeling strategy.
AI.conclusion: Representing A-Ci curves as graphs significantly improves biochemical limitation-state analysis. The SEAGAN architecture demonstrates that incorporating domain-specific graph structure, edge attributes, and graph attention provides a robust solution to this long-standing classification challenge in plant physiology, with potential applicability to other dynamic plant processes.

title: HydraHead: From Head-Level Functional Heterogeneity to Specialized Attention Hybridization
summary: The quadratic complexity of attention poses a critical bottleneck for long-context processing, spurring interest in hybrid attention designs. Most open-source hybrid models adopt a layer-wise strategy. Yet, prior work has noted the inherent difficulty of integrating Linear Attention (LA) with Full Attention (FA), suggesting that the design space of attention hybridization remains underexplored. To probe this space, we conduct interpretability analysis and observe that layers exhibit block-wise functional similarity, while individual heads within the same layer display distinct functional specialization despite sharing input features. This head-level heterogeneity suggests that the head dimension provides a natural and principled granularity for fusing heterogeneous attention signals. Building on this insight, we introduce HydraHead, a novel architecture that hybridizes FA and LA along the head axis. HydraHead features two key innovations: (1) an interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and preserves FA only for them, and (2) a scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs. By leveraging a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and distillation, we achieve high-performance hybrid models with minimal training overhead. Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs in long-context tasks while maintaining strong general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Crucially, trained on only 15B tokens, HydraHead achieves over 69% improvement over the baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5, a leading model of comparable size with a native context length of 256K. This highlights the significant scaling potential of head-level hybridization.

AI.tldr: HydraHead proposes hybridizing Full Attention and Linear Attention at the head level (rather than the layer level), using interpretability-driven selection to preserve Full Attention only for retrieval-critical heads and a scale-normalized fusion module to reconcile distributional gaps, achieving strong long-context performance with minimal training overhead.
AI.motivation: The quadratic complexity of Full Attention bottlenecks long-context processing. Existing layer-wise hybrid attention models struggle to integrate Linear Attention with Full Attention effectively, and the design space of attention hybridization remains underexplored. The authors aim to find a finer, more principled granularity for fusing heterogeneous attention mechanisms.
AI.method: (1) Interpretability analysis revealing block-wise functional similarity across layers and head-level functional specialization within layers, motivating head-level hybridization. (2) An interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and retains Full Attention only for them, converting the rest to Linear Attention. (3) A scale-normalized fusion module to bridge the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs. (4) A three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and distillation for efficient training on only 15B tokens.
AI.result: Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs on long-context tasks while maintaining strong general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Trained on only 15B tokens, it achieves over 69% improvement over baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5 (a comparable model with native 256K context).
AI.conclusion: Head-level hybridization is a principled and effective design choice for attention fusion. The strong scaling potential of HydraHead, demonstrated by its ability to approach leading long-context models with minimal training, suggests that the head dimension is the natural granularity for combining heterogeneous attention signals.

title: Process-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Theorem Proving via Lean
summary: While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically has relied on a single binary verification signal, symbolic proof assistants in formal reasoning offer rich, fine-grained structured feedback. This gap between structured processes and unstructured rewards highlights the importance of feedback that is both dense and sound. In this work, we demonstrate that the Lean proof assistant itself can serve as a symbolic process oracle, supplying both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level verified feedback during training. Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration marks both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, yielding dense, verifier-grounded credit signals rooted in type theory. We incorporate these structured rewards into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods that balances outcome- and process-level advantages. Experiments with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 show that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on benchmarks such as MiniF2F and ProofNet. Beyond empirical gains, our study highlights a broader perspective: symbolic proof assistants are not only verifiers at evaluation time, but can also act as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward reinforcement learning frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Lean's symbolic elaboration as a dense, process-level reward oracle for RLVR in formal theorem proving, replacing binary outcome signals with fine-grained tactic-level feedback. The method yields improvements over outcome-only baselines on MiniF2F and ProofNet.
AI.motivation: Current RLVR for formal reasoning relies on coarse binary verification signals (proved/not-proved), but proof assistants like Lean produce rich structured feedback during elaboration — marking locally sound steps and the earliest failure. The gap between this structured process information and the sparse reward signals used in training motivates the need for dense, verifier-grounded credit assignment.
AI.method: Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaborator serves as a symbolic process oracle: it identifies locally sound tactics and pinpoints the earliest failing step. This structured feedback is integrated into a GRPO-style RL objective using two credit-assignment strategies — first-error propagation (reward propagates up to the failure point) and first-token credit (reward is assigned to the first token of each tactic). The approach combines outcome- and process-level advantages. Experiments use STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5.
AI.result: Tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, with measurable improvements on the MiniF2F and ProofNet benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic proof assistants can serve not only as evaluation-time verifiers but also as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward RL frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

title: MassSpecGym in the Wild: Uncovering and Correcting Evaluation Pitfalls in AI-Driven Molecule Discovery
summary: Reliable benchmarking is critical for developing machine learning models for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) based molecule discovery. Subtle issues in experimental design and model evaluation procedures can degrade the trustworthiness of such benchmarks and lead to erroneous conclusions. We conduct a thorough review of model evaluation issues in the recent MS/MS machine learning literature, using the standard MassSpecGym benchmark suite as a case study to illustrate the impact of these issues. We find evaluation issues in at least 17 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in the first year of its adoption. We isolate three classes of failures: (i) data leakage, (ii) shortcut learning, and (iii) implementation bugs and metric divergence. Through extensive experimentation and code replication, we quantify the impact of these issues and show how they corrupt the evaluation standards MassSpecGym was designed to enforce. We distill our findings into recommendations generalizable to MS/MS challenges, benchmarks, and custom evaluation setups. We also release MassSpecGym v1.5, an implementation of our recommendations in the MassSpecGym benchmarking suite which addresses the failure modes identified in this audit. MassSpecGym v1.5 is publicly available at https://github.com/pluskal-lab/MassSpecGym.

AI.tldr: An audit of MS/MS machine learning benchmarks reveals pervasive evaluation issues — data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs — in 17 of 26 papers. The authors quantify their impact and release MassSpecGym v1.5 to fix these failure modes.
AI.motivation: Reliable benchmarking is essential for progress in ML-driven molecule discovery from tandem mass spectrometry, but subtle flaws in experimental design and evaluation can undermine trustworthiness and lead to incorrect conclusions.
AI.method: The authors systematically reviewed 26 papers that reported MassSpecGym benchmark results within its first year of adoption. They categorized evaluation failures into three classes — data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs/metric divergence — then reproduced code and conducted extensive experiments to quantify the impact of each issue.
AI.result: At least 17 of 26 papers (≈65%) exhibited one or more evaluation issues. These failures demonstrably corrupted the evaluation standards MassSpecGym was designed to enforce, inflating reported performance and undermining cross-study comparability.
AI.conclusion: The authors distill their findings into generalizable recommendations for MS/MS benchmarks and release MassSpecGym v1.5, a hardened version of the benchmark suite that directly addresses the identified failure modes.

title: Residual-Space Evolutionary Optimization via Flow-based Generative Models
comment: Accepted by ICML 2026 Workshop SPIGM, 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Data editing with generative methods typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search. However, these assumptions break down in flow-based settings, where edits are performed through forward and backward integration and often involve non-differentiable or black-box objectives. We introduce residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework that addresses this gap by combining flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. Building on the observation that conditional flow matching (CFM) can disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals, our framework directly operates in residual space and separates two complementary search regimes: self-pollination performs local exploitation through feature-preserving residual refinement, and cross-pollination promotes broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. As a proof of concept, we validate on MorphoMNIST, a benchmark dataset for counterfactual generation, and on crystal data, demonstrating that this exploration--exploitation decomposition provides a useful mechanism for balancing target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains.

AI.tldr: Proposes residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework combining flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. By operating in the residual space of conditional flow matching (CFM) models, it separates local exploitation (self-pollination) from global exploration (cross-pollination), enabling effective editing with non-differentiable objectives. Validated on MorphoMNIST and crystal data.
AI.motivation: Generative data editing typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search, but flow-based generative models—which perform edits via forward/backward integration—often encounter non-differentiable or black-box objectives where gradient methods fail. The gap between flow-based generation and gradient-free editing needs to be bridged.
AI.method: The framework leverages the property that conditional flow matching (CFM) disentangles condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals. It operates directly in this residual space with two evolutionary search mechanisms: (1) self-pollination — local exploitation via feature-preserving residual refinement, and (2) cross-pollination — broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. This decomposition balances target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity without requiring differentiable objectives.
AI.result: Validated on MorphoMNIST (counterfactual generation benchmark) and crystal data. The exploration-exploitation decomposition effectively balances target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity. The approach extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains (crystallography).
AI.conclusion: Residual-space evolutionary optimization provides a viable, model-agnostic mechanism for editing with flow-based generative models under non-differentiable objectives. The self-pollination / cross-pollination dichotomy offers an effective way to balance multiple editing desiderata, with applicability spanning from vision to scientific data.

title: Hard or Just Unreached? Diagnosing the Sampling Blind Spot in Math-Reasoning Difficulty Estimation
comment: 9 pages of main paper, 4 figures and 5 tables in the main paper, with more in the appendix
summary: Math and science reasoning benchmarks rely on pass@k, the fraction of sampled chains that reach gold, as the canonical per-example difficulty signal. The same signal drives RL with verifiable rewards, math data curation, synthetic curricula, and verifier training. We show this proxy has a persistent blind spot on its hardest stratum: on the eight free-form math cells we test (GSM8K and MATH across four open-weight models), 10.3-22.9% of the examples that no sampling seed solves in six tries are instead solved at matched compute by a six-chain deterministic regime. These are greedy decoding plus five cheap residual-stream perturbations applied via activation grafting, while greedy alone solves at most 6% on these math cells. Recovery scales with the additional budget, across perturbations whose mechanistic distinctness we verify across all twelve cells (cross-kind fix-set Jaccard <= 0.47 in every setup). Activation grafting is used as an intervention on internal representations, not a decoding method; we use it purely as a diagnostic and diversification tool, and our recovered items show that the pass@k= 0 % stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream rather than that the unmodified model reaches them under ordinary inference.

AI.tldr: Pass@k, the standard difficulty metric in math/science reasoning, misses a significant fraction of solvable problems: 10–23% of examples that fail under six independent sampling attempts are solved by a deterministic six-chain regime combining greedy decoding with five cheap activation-grafting perturbations. This reveals that the pass@k=0% stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream, not inherently unsolvable.
AI.motivation: Pass@k is the canonical per-example difficulty signal used across RL with verifiable rewards, data curation, synthetic curricula, and verifier training. The authors argue this proxy systematically underestimates solvability on the hardest examples, creating a blind spot that may distort downstream training and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors compare standard pass@k sampling against a deterministic six-chain regime: greedy decoding plus five residual-stream perturbations applied via activation grafting. Activation grafting is used not as a decoding method but as a diagnostic/diversification tool to probe whether the residual stream structurally encodes solutions that random sampling fails to surface. They evaluate on eight free-form math cells (GSM8K and MATH) across four open-weight models, verifying mechanistic distinctness of perturbations across all twelve cells via cross-kind fix-set Jaccard ≤ 0.47.
AI.result: Across all eight math cells, 10.3–22.9% of examples with pass@k=0 under six-trial sampling are recovered by the six-chain deterministic regime. Greedy decoding alone solves at most 6%. Recovery scales with additional perturbation budget, and the perturbations are confirmed mechanistically distinct.
AI.conclusion: The pass@k=0% stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream, not evidence that the unmodified model cannot reach those solutions under ordinary inference. This exposes a blind spot in pass@k as a difficulty proxy, with implications for RL, data curation, and verifier training pipelines.

title: From Texts to Scores: Tracing the Emergence of Essay Quality Representations in Large Language Models
comment: This is a preprint of a manuscript currently under peer review
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have substantially transformed Automated Essay Scoring (AES), yet the internal mechanisms underlying LLM-based scoring remain poorly understood. In this work, we systematically analyze the hidden representations of eight LLMs across two English essay datasets (ASAP++, CSEE) and one Portuguese dataset (ENEM). Using linear probing, cross-prompt generalization, dimensionality reduction, and neuron-level analyses, we find consistent evidence that essay quality information is encoded in a linearly accessible form within LLM representations. These representations emerge progressively across layers, remain robust across prompting strategies, and partially transfer across essay prompts despite differences in scoring rubrics. In addition, nonlinear probes provide only marginal and inconsistent improvements over linear probes, suggesting that most essay quality information is already linearly decodable. We further identify individual ``essay scoring neurons'' whose activations strongly correlate with essay scores and whose behavior is sensitive to targeted intervention. Moreover, the layer-wise distribution of these neurons systematically shifts with essay length, with longer essays relying more heavily on deeper layers. Overall, our findings provide evidence that LLMs encode structured representations related to essay quality and offer new insights into the interpretability of LLM-based AES systems.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates the internal representations of eight LLMs on essay scoring tasks across three datasets (two English, one Portuguese). Using linear probing, dimensionality reduction, and neuron-level analysis, the authors find that essay quality information is encoded in a linearly accessible form, emerges progressively across layers, is robust to prompting strategies, and partially transfers across prompts. They also identify individual "essay scoring neurons" whose activations correlate with scores and respond to targeted intervention.
AI.motivation: Despite significant advances in using LLMs for Automated Essay Scoring (AES), the internal mechanisms by which LLMs encode and process essay quality remain poorly understood. The authors aim to open the "black box" of LLM-based AES to uncover how these models represent scoring-relevant information.
AI.method: The authors analyze hidden representations of eight LLMs (including both open-source and proprietary models) on the ASAP++, CSEE (English), and ENEM (Portuguese) datasets. Methods include: (1) linear probing to assess linear decodability of essay scores from hidden states; (2) cross-prompt generalization to test transferability of scoring representations; (3) dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA) to visualize representation structure; and (4) neuron-level analyses to identify individual "essay scoring neurons" and conduct targeted interventions.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Essay quality is encoded in a linearly accessible form — nonlinear probes provide only marginal, inconsistent improvements. (2) Quality representations emerge progressively across layers. (3) Representations are robust across different prompting strategies. (4) Scoring-relevant information partially transfers across essay prompts despite rubric differences. (5) Individual "essay scoring neurons" are identified whose activations strongly correlate with scores and are sensitive to intervention. (6) The layer-wise distribution of these neurons shifts with essay length — longer essays rely more on deeper layers.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode structured, linearly decodable representations of essay quality, with identifiable neurons and layer-wise organization that adapts to essay length. These findings advance the interpretability of LLM-based AES systems and provide evidence that scoring-relevant information is not merely superficial but is systematically embedded in model representations.

title: Multi-Head Attention-Based Feature Extractor Integration with Soft Actor-Critic for Porosity Prediction and Process Parameter Optimization in Additive Manufacturing
summary: Additive manufacturing process optimization requires precise parameter control to minimize defects such as porosity. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) approaches using discrete action spaces suffer from slow convergence and susceptibility to local optima, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision manufacturing tasks. This study addresses these limitations by employing a continuous action space combined with a novel architecture that integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. The attention-based feature extractor enhances the agent's ability to capture subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, enabling more effective exploration-exploitation balance for navigating value spaces with local minima. We validate our approach on porosity prediction and process parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward values compared to standard RL methods including DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC. The proposed methodology achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining stability throughout training.

AI.tldr: A novel Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) variant with multi-head attention enables continuous action space optimization for laser powder bed fusion, achieving faster convergence (322.79 in 14 episodes) and outperforming DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC on porosity minimization.
AI.motivation: Traditional RL approaches using discrete action spaces converge slowly and get trapped in local optima, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision additive manufacturing tasks that require fine-grained parameter control to minimize defects like porosity.
AI.method: The authors propose integrating a multi-head attention mechanism as a feature extractor into the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm operating in a continuous action space. The attention module enhances the agent's sensitivity to subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, improving exploration-exploitation balance when navigating value landscapes with local minima.
AI.result: The proposed attention-augmented SAC achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward compared to DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC, while maintaining training stability.
AI.conclusion: Continuous action spaces paired with attention-enhanced SAC provide a superior framework for process parameter optimization in additive manufacturing, effectively overcoming the convergence and local optima limitations inherent to discrete-action RL baselines.

title: Convex training of Lipschitz-regularized shallow neural networks
summary: In this work, we introduce a training procedure for shallow neural networks that promotes robustness against adversarial attacks. We solve a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program by introducing a convex restriction that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. Our approach can be employed as a post-processing step by taking a pre-trained network as an initial solution to then solving the convex program whose optimal network is guaranteed to be no worse than the initial one. We illustrate the improvements of our training procedure with experiments using real world datasets for regression tasks under an adversarial setting. We show numerically that solving our proposed convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. Additionally, we show that on certain datasets, networks obtained using our convex training program are both more accurate and robust with respect to adversarial attacks.

AI.tldr: A convex restriction approach is proposed for training shallow neural networks with Lipschitz regularization, promoting adversarial robustness. The method can be used as a post-processing step on pre-trained networks, guaranteeing no degradation in performance, and demonstrates improved accuracy and robustness on real-world regression tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard training of neural networks yields models vulnerable to adversarial attacks. While Lipschitz regularization can promote robustness, the resulting training program is non-convex and difficult to solve optimally. The authors aim to develop a tractable method that guarantees global optimality for Lipschitz-regularized training of shallow networks.
AI.method: The authors formulate a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program and then derive a convex restriction of this program that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. Their approach functions as a post-processing step: taking a pre-trained network as initialization, the convex program is solved, with the guarantee that the resulting optimal network is at least as good as the initial one.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world regression datasets under adversarial settings show that the proposed convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. On certain datasets, networks trained this way exhibit both higher accuracy and greater robustness against adversarial attacks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convex restriction framework provides an effective and theoretically grounded post-processing procedure for improving adversarial robustness in shallow neural networks, with guarantees of global optimality and monotonic improvement over pre-trained networks.

title: MedRLM: Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence for Long-Context Clinical Reasoning, Sensor-Guided Screening, Evidence-Grounded Decision Support, and Community-to-Tertiary Referral Optimization
summary: Real-world clinical decision support requires reasoning over heterogeneous and longitudinal patient information rather than answering isolated medical questions. However, current medical large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems often rely on single-step prompting or retrieval, which can be fragile when clinical evidence is distributed across long electronic health records, medical images, sensor streams, guidelines, and referral constraints. This paper proposes MedRLM, a Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence framework for long-context clinical reasoning, sensor-guided screening, and community-to-tertiary referral support. Instead of compressing all patient information into one prompt, MedRLM treats the patient case as an external clinical environment that can be recursively inspected, decomposed, retrieved, verified, and synthesized. The framework coordinates specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, medical imaging, physiological sensor signals, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning. It further introduces a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory to connect patient-specific observations with retrieved evidence, standardized definitions, sensor-derived biomarkers, and referral criteria. A sensor-guided recursive triggering mechanism activates deeper reasoning when abnormal physiological or behavioral patterns are detected, while uncertainty-gated refinement supports clinician review for high-risk or low-confidence cases. We also outline a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. MedRLM aims to move medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, and workflow-aware clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: MedRLM is a recursive multimodal AI framework that treats patient cases as external environments to be iteratively inspected, integrating EHR, imaging, sensors, and guidelines for auditable clinical decision support from screening to referral.
AI.motivation: Current medical LLMs and RAG systems rely on single-step prompting/retrieval, which fails when clinical evidence is fragmented across long EHRs, images, sensor streams, and guidelines. Real clinical decision support requires reasoning over heterogeneous, longitudinal data rather than answering isolated questions.
AI.method: MedRLM uses a recursive inspection-decomposition-retrieval-verification-synthesis loop. It coordinates specialized agents (clinical text, EHR, imaging, sensors, guidelines, uncertainty auditing, referral planning), introduces a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory linking patient observations to evidence and criteria, and employs sensor-guided recursive triggering for abnormal patterns plus uncertainty-gated refinement for high-risk/low-confidence cases.
AI.result: The paper outlines an evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. No empirical results are reported in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: MedRLM aims to shift medical AI from static question answering to auditable, multimodal, workflow-aware clinical decision support that mirrors real-world clinical reasoning across the care continuum.

title: LOKI: Memory-Free Null-Space Constrained Lifelong Knowledge Editing
summary: Lifelong knowledge editing aims to efficiently and sequentially update language models over time, as new knowledge becomes available or when the model makes mistakes, while preserving acceptable performance on past knowledge. One unresolved challenge is that existing methods modify a fixed set of layers for all new knowledge samples, reducing flexibility and increasing catastrophic forgetting. Another is requiring access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing to obtain data statistics. To address these challenges, we introduce LOKI, a novel approach that uses dynamic layer selection based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of the model weights, bypassing the requirement for previous knowledge access. We show that LOKI achieves superior performance to existing approaches across a wide variety of experiments, achieving up to a 14\% improvement in average accuracy.

AI.tldr: LOKI is a lifelong knowledge editing method that dynamically selects layers using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and projects gradient updates onto the weight null-space, eliminating the need for prior knowledge access while improving average accuracy by up to 14%.
AI.motivation: Existing lifelong knowledge editing methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) they modify a fixed set of layers for all knowledge updates, which is inflexible and exacerbates catastrophic forgetting; (2) they require access to previous knowledge and extensive preprocessing to obtain data statistics, which is impractical in many real-world sequential update scenarios.
AI.method: LOKI introduces two core innovations: (1) dynamic layer selection guided by the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), which adaptively chooses which layers to modify per knowledge sample; (2) projecting gradient updates onto the null-space of model weights, which constrains updates to directions that minimally interfere with previously learned knowledge, all without requiring access to past data.
AI.result: LOKI achieves superior performance compared to existing lifelong knowledge editing approaches across diverse experimental settings, with up to a 14% improvement in average accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic layer selection via HSIC and null-space projection together provide an effective and practical solution for lifelong knowledge editing, overcoming the rigidity and data-dependency limitations of prior methods.

title: ReNikud: Audio-Supervised Hebrew Grapheme-to-Phoneme Conversion
summary: Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion for Modern Hebrew is needed for applications like text-to-speech (TTS), but is challenging due to the language's abjad writing system, which leaves vowels largely unwritten, creating substantial ambiguity. Standard approaches first predict vowel diacritics (nikud) to produce International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcriptions, but this is limited: vocalization data is scarce and laborious to produce, it does not specify features such as lexical stress, and it reflects formal grammatical rules rather than everyday spoken pronunciation. Direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction, meanwhile, struggles on limited data and fails to exploit the character-level alignment characteristic of abjads. Our method, ReNikud, overcomes these limitations with two key insights: (1) Weak audio supervision via a phoneme-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) pseudo-labeling pipeline on thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio, yielding phonemic transcriptions that reflect natural spoken norms without manual annotation. (2) A pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias. Results on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and the new targeted MILIM benchmark for spoken Hebrew show that ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods. We will release our code and trained models to support further work on Hebrew TTS and speech technologies.

AI.tldr: ReNikud introduces a novel G2P method for Modern Hebrew that combines weak audio supervision via ASR pseudo-labeling with a pseudo-vocalization architecture enforcing character-level alignment, surpassing prior SOTA on Hebrew G2P benchmarks including the new spoken-Hebrew MILIM benchmark.
AI.motivation: Modern Hebrew G2P is challenging due to its abjad writing system (vowels largely unwritten). Existing approaches either rely on scarce, labor-intensive vocalization (nikud) data that misses lexical stress and reflects formal rather than spoken norms, or use direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction that struggles with limited data and fails to leverage character-level alignment inherent to abjads.
AI.method: ReNikud employs two key innovations: (1) Weak audio supervision — a phoneme-based ASR pseudo-labeling pipeline applied to thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio to generate phonemic transcriptions reflecting natural spoken pronunciation without manual annotation. (2) A pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias rather than using unconstrained seq2seq.
AI.result: ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and on the newly introduced MILIM benchmark, which is specifically targeted at spoken (rather than formal) Hebrew.
AI.conclusion: The combination of weak audio supervision and the pseudo-vocalization architecture effectively addresses data scarcity and alignment challenges in Hebrew G2P. The authors plan to release code and models to facilitate further work on Hebrew TTS and speech technologies.

title: Multi-Granular Attention-Driven Reinforcement Learning Framework for Web Intelligent Enhancement Systems
comment: 2026 3rd International Conference on Integrated Intelligence and Communication Systems (ICIICS), 6 Pages
summary: From the past few years, web intelligent enhancement systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous and dynamic web data to deliver personalized, context-aware services. However, traditional machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning models often struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in continuously evolving web environments. In this research, a Multi-Granular Attention-based Reinforcement Web Intelligent Enhancement System (MGAR-WIES) is proposed to address the challenges by integrating semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Initially, heterogeneous web data comprising structured, semi-structured and unstructured sources are collected and preprocessed for generating unified feature representations. These representations are transformed into a dynamic semantic graph, where entities and their relationships are modeled by using graph embeddings enhanced by attention mechanisms for capturing both local relevance and global contextual dependencies. Subsequently, an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy leverages the attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized web actions like content recommendation, navigation optimization, and service adaptation. Finally, the continuous online feedback is further integrated to update graph representations and learning policies in real time by ensuring sustained adaptability and performance. The proposed MGAR-WIES acheived better results in terms of accuracy (80%) when compared with existing approaches.

AI.tldr: A Multi-Granular Attention-based Reinforcement Web Intelligent Enhancement System (MGAR-WIES) is proposed, combining semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning to optimize personalized web services, achieving 80% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional ML, DL, and RL models struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in dynamic, heterogeneous web environments. There is a need for a system that can effectively handle continuously evolving web data for personalized, context-aware services.
AI.method: MGAR-WIES first collects and preprocesses heterogeneous web data (structured, semi-structured, unstructured) into unified feature representations. These are transformed into a dynamic semantic graph using attention-enhanced graph embeddings to capture local relevance and global contextual dependencies. An adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy then leverages attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized web actions (content recommendation, navigation optimization, service adaptation). Continuous online feedback updates graph representations and learning policies in real time.
AI.result: The proposed MGAR-WIES achieved better results in terms of accuracy (80%) when compared with existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: MGAR-WIES effectively addresses the limitations of traditional models in dynamic web environments by integrating semantic graphs, attention mechanisms, and adaptive RL, demonstrating superior accuracy and sustained adaptability through real-time online feedback integration.

title: Pitch Spelling Jazz Lead Sheets, Solo Transcriptions, Classical Piano and Monophonic Scores
summary: We present an algorithm for pitch spelling and key estimation. Given an input in MIDI-like format, containing information on note pitches (expressed in semitones relative to the lowest reference note) and bar boundaries, it estimates the appropriate note names, a global Key Signature, and a local scale for each bar. This related information elements are evaluated jointly during two stages of optimisation. During an initial 'modal' stage, a probable scale is proposed for each bar, minimising the number of accidentals to be printed in the printed score with a shortest-path search. Then, during a second stage called 'tonal', these local scales are used to estimate the Key Signature and note names that would result in the best musical notation for the entire piece. We present evaluations conducted on datasets comprising a variety of digital musical scores: jazz lead sheets taken from the Real Book, transcriptions of recordings of jazz soli and bass lines, traditional tunes, as well as classical scores for piano and monophonic instruments. Our procedure was originally designed for use in music transcription, specifically for building digital collections of jazz solos transcribed from audio recordings, for the purposes of music analysis, teaching and the preservation of cultural heritage. This method should also prove useful for other tasks related to the processing of musical notation. Furthermore, to this end, we have defined new distances between various common jazz scales, which may be of some interest to musicological studies.

AI.tldr: A two-stage optimization algorithm for joint pitch spelling and key estimation from MIDI input: a "modal" stage assigns local scales per bar via shortest-path search to minimize accidentals, followed by a "tonal" stage that infers global key signature and note names. Evaluated on jazz lead sheets, transcriptions, traditional tunes, and classical scores. Novel jazz scale distances are defined.
AI.motivation: Designed for music transcription pipelines—specifically building digital collections of jazz solos transcribed from audio—to support music analysis, teaching, and cultural heritage preservation. Existing systems lacked robust joint inference of local scales, global key signatures, and note spellings.
AI.method: A two-stage optimization: (1) Modal stage — for each bar, a probable local scale is proposed by minimizing accidentals via shortest-path search over scale candidates. (2) Tonal stage — local scales are aggregated to estimate a global Key Signature and final note names that optimize notation quality for the entire piece. New distance metrics between common jazz scales are defined to support the optimization.
AI.result: Evaluated on diverse datasets: Real Book jazz lead sheets, transcriptions of recorded jazz solos and bass lines, traditional tunes, and classical scores (piano and monophonic). The method performs effectively across these varied musical styles and formats.
AI.conclusion: The jointly optimized two-stage approach successfully handles pitch spelling and key estimation across heterogeneous musical material. The defined jazz-scale distance metrics may have independent value for musicological research. The method is broadly applicable to music notation processing tasks beyond transcription.

title: Efficiently Representing Algorithms With Chain-of-Thought Transformers
summary: The increasing popularity of \emph{reasoning} models -- language models that output a series of reasoning or thought tokens before producing an answer -- is justified, in part, by theoretical results showing that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can simulate Turing machines, and thus perform arbitrary computation. However, the Turing machine, while suitable for complexity-theoretic analysis, is not convenient, intuitive, or efficient for discussing algorithms. Algorithms are typically designed and analyzed at a higher level of abstraction, captured by the \emph{Word RAM} model with random-access memory and unit-cost operations on $\bigO(\log n)$-bit words. As a result, Word RAM algorithms can be substantially more efficient than their Turing machine counterparts, raising the question: \emph{Can CoT transformers efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms?} For instance, can they sort $n$ items in $\bigO(n \log n)$ steps or run Dijkstra's algorithm in $\bigO(E + V \log V)$ steps? We answer affirmatively, up to poly-logarithmic overhead. We first establish this for finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, then strengthen the result to two more practical settings with finite width and log-precision: \emph{continuous} CoT, where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than tokens, and a \emph{hybrid} architecture in which transformer layers sit atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In all three cases, we find that CoT \emph{can} efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only a poly-logarithmic overhead in $n$. This overhead reduces to log-square when the Word RAM has a ``flat'' instruction set, and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions -- in stark contrast to known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms (e.g., sorting in O(n log n), Dijkstra's algorithm) with only poly-logarithmic overhead, in contrast to prior Turing machine simulations that incur quadratic overhead. Results hold for three settings: finite-precision transformers with hard attention, continuous CoT with vectors, and a hybrid transformer-RNN architecture.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical results show CoT transformers can simulate Turing machines, establishing Turing-completeness. However, Turing machines are a low-level, inconvenient model for reasoning about algorithms. Real algorithms are designed for the Word RAM model (random-access memory, unit-cost operations on O(log n)-bit words), which can be exponentially faster than Turing machines. The authors ask whether CoT transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms, closing the gap between theory and practical algorithm design.
AI.method: The authors construct CoT transformer simulations of Word RAM computations across three architectures: (1) finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, (2) continuous CoT where reasoning uses vectors instead of discrete tokens, and (3) a hybrid architecture with transformer layers atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. The constructions show that Word RAM operations (memory access, arithmetic, control flow) can be implemented with only poly-logarithmic overhead, which further reduces to O(log² n) for flat instruction sets and O(log n) for multiplication-free flat instructions.
AI.result: CoT transformers can simulate any Word RAM algorithm with poly-logarithmic overhead in n. For flat instruction sets, overhead is O(log² n); for multiplication-free flat instructions, only O(log n). This sharply contrasts with known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.
AI.conclusion: CoT transformers are not merely Turing-complete in principle; they can efficiently simulate the Word RAM model that underlies practical algorithm design, with near-optimal overhead. This provides stronger theoretical justification for the empirical success of reasoning models and suggests that transformer-based architectures can match the efficiency of standard algorithmic computation.

title: CzechDocs: A Multiway Parallel Dataset of Formatted Documents for Minority Languages in Czechia
summary: We present CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, and PDF) covering Czech and minority languages used in Czechia-primarily Ukrainian and English, with smaller portions of Vietnamese, Russian and other languages. The dataset is designed to support the evaluation of machine translation systems that aim to preserve document formatting during translation. We provide a comparison of the most common approaches to format-preserving machine translation on a validation subset of the dataset. This validation split, together with the evaluation toolkit, is publicly released for further research. A held-out test split will be reserved for a future shared task focused on document-level translation with formatting preservation.
