AI.tldr: CzechDocs is a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, PDF) covering Czech and minority languages, designed to evaluate format-preserving machine translation systems. A validation split and toolkit are publicly released; a held-out test split is reserved for a future shared task.
AI.motivation: Current machine translation evaluation lacks adequate resources for assessing how well systems preserve document formatting (HTML, DOCX, PDF) during translation, particularly for Czech and minority languages spoken in Czechia. There is a need for a standardized dataset and benchmark to drive progress in format-preserving document-level translation.
AI.method: The authors construct CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset comprising formatted documents in three formats (HTML, DOCX, PDF) across Czech and multiple minority languages (Ukrainian, English, Vietnamese, Russian, etc.). They then benchmark common format-preserving machine translation approaches on a validation subset and release this split along with an evaluation toolkit.
AI.result: A comparative evaluation of common format-preserving MT approaches is provided on the validation subset. The validation split and evaluation toolkit are publicly released to facilitate further research.
AI.conclusion: CzechDocs fills a gap in evaluation resources for format-preserving document-level machine translation. By publicly releasing the validation data and toolkit while reserving a test split for a future shared task, the authors aim to stimulate and standardize research in this under-explored area.

title: BIM-Edit: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IFC-Based Building Information Modeling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to computer-aided design (CAD) to generate design artifacts from textual instructions. In engineering practice, this requires more than creating new geometry, models must also understand existing scenes, edit them correctly, and preserve semantics and relations. However, many CAD benchmarks focus on creating new models rather than editing existing ones, and mostly evaluate geometric correctness. We introduce BIM-Edit, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (BIM) represented in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format. BIM provides a challenging testbed because building models encode geometry together with semantic and relational structure. BIM-Edit contains 324 editing tasks spanning 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes. Tasks are expressed using three instruction categories - direct, spatial, and topological - covering both explicit and scene-grounded edits. We evaluate outputs along three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Across evaluated LLMs, the best-performing model achieves only 49.5% average score across the three metrics, and no model fully solves more than 3.4% of tasks. These results demonstrate a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the requirements of structured engineering design workflows.

AI.tldr: BIM-Edit is a benchmark evaluating LLMs on editing Building Information Models (IFC format). It comprises 324 tasks across 47 scenes with three instruction types (direct, spatial, topological) and evaluates geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Best models achieve only 49.5% average score, with no model fully solving >3.4% of tasks, highlighting a major gap between LLM capabilities and structured CAD editing requirements.
AI.motivation: Current CAD benchmarks focus predominantly on generating new geometry from scratch, neglecting the practical engineering need to edit existing models while preserving semantic and relational structure. BIM presents a uniquely challenging testbed because it intertwines geometry with rich semantic and topological information, making it ideal for stress-testing LLM editing capabilities beyond simple geometric correctness.
AI.method: The authors construct BIM-Edit with 324 editing tasks derived from 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes in IFC format. Tasks span three instruction categories: direct (explicit edits), spatial (position-aware edits), and topological (connectivity/relation-aware edits). Outputs are evaluated along three orthogonal dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency, yielding a composite score per task.
AI.result: The best-performing LLM achieves only 49.5% average across all three metrics. No model fully solves more than 3.4% of the 324 tasks, indicating that current LLMs struggle substantially with structured BIM editing, particularly when tasks require maintaining semantic and topological constraints alongside geometric modifications.
AI.conclusion: There exists a substantial capability gap between current LLMs and the demands of real-world structured engineering design workflows. BIM-Edit reveals that while LLMs show some aptitude for geometric generation, they fall short on the holistic editing required in practice — preserving semantics, relations, and producing fully correct outputs — and the benchmark serves as a rigorous testbed to drive future progress.

title: Efficient Neural Network Model Selection for Few-Class Application Datasets
summary: While much effort has focused on developing and benchmarking high-performance neural networks, less attention has been given to how dataset properties, known to practitioners, can guide efficient model selection. Neural models are typically evaluated on datasets with thousands of classes, yet many real-world applications involve fewer than ten. To address this understudied but common setting, we develop a measure of classification difficulty based on data-side properties and show how it enables more efficient model selection for few-class datasets, where traditional approaches are less effective. We term this phenomenon "few-class distinctiveness". Our metric allows comparison of models and datasets 6 to 29$\times$ faster than repeated training and testing. Leveraging this insight, we extend scaled model families below the smallest published models, achieving greater efficiency at similar accuracy, for example models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano for a mobile robot task. Targeting resource-constrained applications, we demonstrate few-class model selection across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios, highlighting practical gains in efficiency without sacrificing performance.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the understudied problem of efficient neural model selection for datasets with few classes (typically <10). The authors propose a data-side measure of classification difficulty called "few-class distinctiveness" that enables 6–29× faster model selection compared to repeated training/testing. Using this metric, they extend model families below the smallest published architectures, achieving models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano with similar accuracy, and demonstrate practical gains across mobile robot, drone, and IoT applications.
AI.motivation: Most neural network benchmarking and design focuses on datasets with thousands of classes, yet many real-world applications involve fewer than ten classes. Existing model selection approaches (repeated training and testing) are computationally expensive and poorly suited to this few-class regime. There is a gap in understanding how dataset properties can guide efficient model selection for resource-constrained, few-class scenarios.
AI.method: The authors develop a classification difficulty measure grounded in data-side properties (capturing "few-class distinctiveness"). This metric quantifies how separable classes are within a given dataset, allowing direct comparison of model suitability without repeated training. They then leverage this metric to extend scaled model families downward beyond the smallest published models, systematically identifying architectures that achieve target accuracy with minimal computational cost.
AI.result: The proposed metric enables model selection 6 to 29 times faster than traditional repeated training and testing. Using the approach, the authors produce models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano while maintaining comparable accuracy on a mobile robot task. The method is validated across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios, demonstrating consistent efficiency gains without performance degradation.
AI.conclusion: Data-side properties, formalized as few-class distinctiveness, provide a powerful and efficient alternative to brute-force model selection for few-class problems. This approach is particularly impactful for resource-constrained edge deployments, where it enables significant model size reduction and faster selection without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Actionable Activation Directions for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Misalignment Across Language Model Families
summary: Fine-tuning language models on insecure code induces emergent misalignment with poorly understood internal structure. We investigate whether this misalignment corresponds to a causally actionable activation-space direction shared across architectures. Across four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) finetuned identically, a difference-in-means direction achieves 99.6% separation of aligned and misaligned activations at each model's final layer. Causal steering by subtracting this direction reduces code spillover by 21-51 points, while a secure-code control confirms content specificity. Cross-architecture transfer via ridge regression maps yields large behavioral suppression (up to 46 points) but fails specificity controls as random and orthogonal directions perform comparably. We identify a two-tier specificity structure: within-model directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. An asymmetric transfer topology emerges, with Gemma and Qwen acting as geometric donors and Llama as a receiver. These findings define the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for auditing.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LMs on insecure code creates misalignment with a shared activation-space direction within models (99.6% separation). Causal steering by subtracting this direction reduces code spillover. Cross-architecture transfer works behaviorally but fails specificity controls, revealing a two-tier structure: within-model directions are causally specific, while cross-model directions are real but non-specific. An asymmetric transfer topology (Gemma/Qwen as donors, Llama as receiver) defines limits of linear cross-architecture correction.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether emergent misalignment from fine-tuning LMs on insecure code corresponds to a causally actionable activation-space direction that is shared across architectures, and to understand the internal structure and specificity of such directions.
AI.method: Four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) were identically fine-tuned on insecure code. Difference-in-means was used to extract alignment directions from final-layer activations. Causal steering subtracted these directions to measure code spillover reduction, with a secure-code control for content specificity. Cross-architecture transfer used ridge regression for mapping; random and orthogonal directions served as baselines.
AI.result: Difference-in-means achieved 99.6% separation of aligned/misaligned activations. Within-model steering reduced code spillover by 21-51 points with content specificity confirmed by the secure-code control. Cross-architecture transfer produced large behavioral suppression (up to 46 points) but failed specificity controls — random and orthogonal directions performed comparably. A two-tier specificity structure emerged. An asymmetric transfer topology showed Gemma and Qwen as geometric donors and Llama as a receiver.
AI.conclusion: Within-model misalignment directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. These findings define the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for auditing misaligned models.

title: Modularity-Free Conflict-Averse Training for Generalized PINNs
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a powerful framework for solving PDEs by embedding physical laws into differentiable objectives. Despite their advances, training PINNs remains fragile: recent conflict-averse optimization schemes alleviate gradient interference between residual and boundary losses, but we show that their effectiveness deteriorates as model capacity increases. In this paper, we identify a capacity-induced failure mode, where overparameterized networks undergo functional modularity, self-partitioning into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and hinder convergence toward Pareto-stationary points. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework, Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks demonstrate that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/heejokong/ModSync}.

AI.tldr: Overparameterized PINNs suffer from functional modularity, where networks self-partition into task-exclusive modules that hinder convergence. The authors propose ModSync, which penalizes task-exclusive connections while preserving cross-objective interaction pathways, preventing capacity-driven failure and achieving state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing conflict-averse optimization schemes for PINNs (which address gradient interference between residual and boundary losses) lose effectiveness as model capacity increases. The authors aim to understand and resolve this capacity-induced failure mode.
AI.method: The authors first identify functional modularity as the capacity-induced failure mechanism, where overparameterized networks self-partition into modules specialized exclusively to individual loss terms, suppressing cross-objective interaction. To counter this, they propose Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), a framework that integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections (via sparsity-inducing regularization) while preserving interaction-promoting pathways, thereby maintaining cross-objective coupling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks show that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy compared to baseline conflict-averse training methods.
AI.conclusion: Functional modularity is the root cause of capacity-induced training failure in PINNs, and structural optimization via ModSync effectively resolves this issue by maintaining necessary cross-objective interactions, enabling robust scaling of PINNs to larger network capacities.

title: OnDeFog: Online Decision Transformer under Frame Dropping
summary: In challenging real-world reinforcement learning applications, communication delays or sensor failures often cause frame dropping, in which the agent cannot receive the dropped states and associated rewards. To address the performance degradation caused by frame dropping, the Decision Transformer under Random Frame Dropping (DeFog) was developed by incorporating additional mechanisms into the decision transformer to tackle frame dropping. Although DeFog can mitigate performance degradation in frame-dropping environments, since DeFog is an offline learning method, it struggles to effectively generalize to novel states not adequately represented in the training dataset. In this study, we propose OnDeFog, which integrates the mechanisms in DeFog with the online decision transformer (ODT), an online reinforcement learning method that learns policies through direct environmental interaction. Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates that our proposed OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments characterized by high dropping frame rate and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing a large amount of low-reward data.

AI.tldr: OnDeFog extends DeFog by integrating its frame-dropping mechanisms into the online decision transformer (ODT), enabling superior performance in high frame-drop environments and better generalization to low-reward data compared to offline-only DeFog.
AI.motivation: Frame dropping caused by communication delays or sensor failures degrades reinforcement learning performance. While DeFog mitigates this via offline learning, it struggles to generalize to novel states absent from the training dataset. An online learning approach is needed to overcome this limitation.
AI.method: OnDeFog integrates the frame-dropping countermeasures from DeFog into the online decision transformer (ODT) framework, enabling the agent to learn policies through direct environmental interaction while handling missing states and rewards.
AI.result: OnDeFog outperforms ODT in environments with high frame-dropping rates and surpasses DeFog on datasets containing substantial amounts of low-reward data.
AI.conclusion: Combining DeFog's frame-dropping mechanisms with online learning via ODT yields a more robust and generalizable policy for real-world RL applications subject to frame dropping.

title: The Register Gap: A Meaning Intelligence Framework for Nigerian Public Discourse
comment: Preprint. 12 pages, 2 tables. Supplementary materials: MIF Master Specification v2.0, Annotation Guidelines v1.0, and 30-item public calibration set with gold labels available from the author
summary: We introduce the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation and evaluation schema for Nigerian public discourse that separates surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Existing benchmarks for Nigerian languages, including NaijaSenti and AfriSenti, treat sentiment classification as a three-way polarity task (positive, negative, neutral). We argue that the dominant failure mode of AI systems on Nigerian discourse is not translation failure but context failure: the same utterance carries opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situation. The MIF operationalises this insight across nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. We construct a 30-item calibration dataset spanning Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers, and evaluate a frontier language model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) under zero-shot and schema-informed prompting conditions. The headline finding is the Register Gap: zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) when the model receives the MIF schema in-context. The composite Meaning Intelligence Score increases by 5.4 points (73.2 to 78.6) under schema-informed prompting, with the largest practical gains in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points). We release the framework specification, annotation guidelines, and the 30-item public calibration set to support reproducibility, while retaining a private holdout corpus for contamination-protected evaluation.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation schema for Nigerian public discourse that distinguishes surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Evaluates Gemini 2.5 Flash on a 30-item calibration dataset, demonstrating a "Register Gap" where schema-informed prompting improves register classification by 40 points and composite meaning intelligence scores by 5.4 points.
AI.motivation: Existing Nigerian-language sentiment benchmarks (NaijaSenti, AfriSenti) reduce classification to three-way polarity, overlooking the critical failure mode of AI systems: context failure rather than translation failure. The same utterance can carry opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situation — a nuance lost in polarity-only approaches.
AI.method: Proposes MIF with nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. Constructs a 30-item calibration dataset across Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers. Evaluates Gemini 2.5 Flash under zero-shot vs. schema-informed prompting conditions, measuring performance on each dimension and a composite Meaning Intelligence Score.
AI.result: The "Register Gap": zero-shot register classification achieves 33.3% accuracy, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) with MIF schema in-context. Composite Meaning Intelligence Score improves from 73.2 to 78.6 (+5.4 points). Largest practical gains occur in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points).
AI.conclusion: Context-aware, multi-dimensional annotation frameworks like MIF substantially improve LLM performance on pragmatically complex Nigerian discourse compared to polarity-only sentiment classification. The framework, annotation guidelines, and public calibration set are released for reproducibility, with a private holdout corpus retained for contamination-protected future evaluation.

title: Implicit Semantic-Aware Communication Based on Hypergraph Reasoning
comment: This work is accepted at IEEE Transactions on Communications
summary: Semantic-aware communication has emerged as a transformative paradigm for next-generation communication systems, shifting the fundamental goal from transmitting bit-level symbols to reliably recovering and understanding the semantic meaning of information. Previous studies have demonstrated that representing the semantic content of source messages as graph-based structures can significantly improve communication efficiency and the accuracy of semantic inference at the receiver. However, existing solutions typically employ graphs that capture only pairwise relationships, thereby neglecting higher-order implicit correlations commonly observed in real-world scenarios, such as group interactions, multi-entity associations, and complex relational contexts. This limitation reduces semantic expressiveness and makes semantic inference susceptible to ambiguity and performance degradation, particularly under noisy or corrupted channel conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework, HISR, which leverages hypergraphs to represent complex multi-entity relationships among semantic knowledge entities. In HISR, entities and their associated higher-order relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This design not only disentangles diverse semantic interactions to mitigate the over-smoothing effects commonly found in traditional graph embedding methods but also enables robust semantic inference even when partial information loss occurs during transmission. Numerical results show that the proposed HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over the state-of-the-art benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A hypergraph-based semantic communication framework (HISR) that captures higher-order multi-entity relationships for robust implicit semantic reasoning, achieving up to 36.6% improvement in interpretation accuracy over existing graph-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic communication systems use graph-based representations that only capture pairwise relationships, neglecting higher-order implicit correlations (group interactions, multi-entity associations, complex relational contexts). This limits semantic expressiveness and degrades inference accuracy under noisy channel conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose HISR, a hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework. Semantic knowledge entities and their higher-order relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts, disentangling diverse semantic interactions and mitigating over-smoothing effects.
AI.result: HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over state-of-the-art benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph-based semantic representations significantly outperform traditional pairwise graph approaches in semantic communication, particularly for complex multi-entity relationships and under lossy transmission conditions.

title: Federated Bilevel Performative Prediction
summary: Federated bilevel optimization is widely used for nested learning problems across distributed clients, such as federated hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning under privacy and communication constraints. Most existing formulations assume fixed client data distributions, which can be violated by performativity, where deployed decisions reshape client behavior and data collection, inducing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shift. We study federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper-level (UL) and lower-level (LL) objectives are evaluated under client-dependent, decision-dependent distributions. We formalize the federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective and provide sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. We then develop two federated methods to compute the FBPS solution: FBi-RRM, which converges linearly under a contraction condition, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method based on federated hypergradient estimation with convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when sensitivities are sufficiently small. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate the predicted stability thresholds and demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines, and CNN-based classification further demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods in nonconvex neural network settings.

AI.tldr: This paper studies federated bilevel optimization under performative distribution shifts, where deployed models alter client data distributions. The authors formalize the Federated Bilevel Performatively Stable (FBPS) point, provide existence/uniqueness conditions, and propose two algorithms: FBi-RRM (linear convergence under contraction) and FBi-SGD (communication-efficient stochastic method). Experiments on strategic regression, meta strategic classification, and CNN-based tasks validate theoretical findings and show improved meta-generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing federated bilevel optimization assumes fixed client data distributions, but real-world deployments cause performativity—where decisions reshape data collection, inducing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shifts. This gap motivates the study of federated bilevel performative prediction to jointly address nested optimization across distributed clients under performative feedback.
AI.method: The authors formalize the FBPS point using a decoupled-risk perspective with existence/uniqueness conditions. They develop FBi-RRM (Federated Bilevel Repeated Risk Minimization), which converges linearly under contraction, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method using federated hypergradient estimation with diminishing step sizes and small sensitivity requirements.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees include linear convergence for FBi-RRM under contraction conditions and convergence for FBi-SGD under diminishing step sizes with sufficiently small sensitivities. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate predicted stability thresholds and demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines. CNN-based classification confirms practical effectiveness in nonconvex neural network settings.
AI.conclusion: Federated bilevel performative prediction is both theoretically tractable and practically effective. The proposed FBPS framework and algorithms successfully handle client-dependent performative distribution shifts in nested optimization, with strong convergence guarantees and empirical validation across diverse tasks including deep neural networks.

title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
summary: Effective Automated Essay Scoring (AES) are expected to support both reliable assessment and actionable instructional feedback. However, existing approaches often treat scoring and feedback as separate components: neural scoring models provide limited interpretability, while Large Language Model (LLM)-based feedback is typically insensitive to learners proficiency levels. To address this fragmentation, this work proposes PsyScore, a psychometrically-aware framework that integrates diagnostic assessment with instructional scaffolding through a shared latent ability representation. PsyScore comprises three key modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer that incorporates the Graded Partial Credit Model (GPCM) into a neural architecture, enabling the precise estimation of student ability while maintaining psychometric interpretability, a ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator, which conditions multi-agent feedback strategies on the diagnosed ability parameter to adapt instructional focus across different proficiency levels, and a Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy that assesses feedback quality via pairwise preference judgements and student revision simulations. Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset demonstrate that PsyScore achieves competitive scoring performance while providing more pedagogically aligned feedback.

AI.tldr: PsyScore integrates psychometric modeling with LLM-based feedback for AES, using a neural IRT scorer to estimate student ability, then conditioning multi-agent feedback on ability levels within Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, evaluated through preference judgments and revision simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing AES systems suffer from fragmentation: neural scoring models lack interpretability and actionable feedback, while LLM-based feedback generation ignores learner proficiency levels, providing one-size-fits-all responses. A unified framework that diagnoses ability and adapts instruction accordingly is missing.
AI.method: PsyScore has three modules: (1) A Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer embedding the Graded Partial Credit Model into a neural network for psychometrically interpretable ability estimation; (2) A ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator that uses the diagnosed ability parameter to adapt multi-agent feedback strategies across proficiency levels; (3) A Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy using pairwise preference judgments and student revision simulations.
AI.result: Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset show PsyScore achieves competitive scoring accuracy while producing feedback that is more pedagogically aligned with student proficiency levels compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Integrating psychometric measurement with LLM-based feedback generation bridges the gap between reliable assessment and adaptive instruction, enabling feedback that is sensitive to learners' diagnosed ability levels and aligned with instructional scaffolding principles.

title: Manifold Bandits: Bayesian Curriculum Learning over the Latent Geometry of Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a central approach for improving reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), where training efficiency depends critically on how problems are sampled during optimization. Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods typically prioritize prompts of intermediate difficulty, treating problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms and overlooking the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space. In this work, we frame problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity: problems are related through the model's latent representation space, and sampling decisions can steer how learning signals evolve across that space. To operationalize this perspective, we introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a structure-aware framework that organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree and applies Bayesian learning to guide sampling. Empirically, we find that different sampling strategies induce non-trivial tradeoffs between productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). These results show that prioritizing difficulty alone is insufficient for strong downstream performance, highlighting the importance of incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling.

AI.tldr: The paper frames RL problem sampling for LLMs as a manifold-structured bandit problem, introducing Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC) — a hierarchical, structure-aware framework that organizes tasks into a tree and uses Bayesian learning to guide sampling. Experiments reveal tradeoffs between productivity, diversity, and utility, showing that difficulty-based sampling alone is insufficient.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods for RL-based LLM reasoning treat problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms, ignoring the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space. The authors argue that problems are related through the model's latent representation space, and that sampling decisions can influence how learning signals propagate across that space. This motivates a structured, manifold-aware sampling approach.
AI.method: The authors propose Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), which: (1) models problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity, (2) organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree capturing structural relationships, and (3) applies Bayesian learning to guide exploration across the task manifold, balancing productivity, diversity, and utility.
AI.result: Different sampling strategies exhibit non-trivial tradeoffs across three axes: productivity (learning signal strength), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (relevance to evaluation). Prioritizing difficulty alone proves insufficient for strong downstream performance; structure and type-awareness are critical.
AI.conclusion: Effective problem sampling for RL-based LLM reasoning requires moving beyond independent-arm bandit formulations toward structure-aware approaches that account for the manifold organization of the task space. BMC demonstrates that incorporating hierarchical task structure and type-awareness yields better downstream outcomes than difficulty-centric curricula alone.

title: CATCH-ME if you RAG: a dataset of Contextually Annotated multi-Turn Counterspeech against Hate and Misinformation Exchanges
summary: Online hate speech and misinformation frequently overlap, yet NLP research has mainly treated them in isolation. While LLMs represent a scalable solution for assisting humans in the generation of counterspeech for both threats, zero-shot models frequently generate repetitive and vague responses, underscoring the need for high-quality examples to steer model generation. However, existing counterspeech datasets against the overlap of hate and misinformation are scarce and limited to single-turn English dialogues, while real-life interactions span across multiple turns and languages. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dataset of dialogues tackling the intersection of hate and misinformation. To ensure factual grounding, the dialogues are also anchored in verified external knowledge (i.e., fact-checking articles and NGO reports) and include document- and chunk-level span annotations, making it directly applicable for RAG systems. Covering five languages and targeting hate directed at seven marginalized groups, this novel resource enables the training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the first large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dialogue dataset addressing the intersection of hate speech and misinformation, featuring fact-checking anchors and span annotations for RAG-based counterspeech generation.
AI.motivation: Existing NLP research treats hate speech and misinformation separately, despite their frequent co-occurrence. Counterspeech datasets are scarce, limited to single-turn English dialogues, and fail to capture real-world multi-turn, multilingual interactions. LLMs also generate repetitive, vague responses without high-quality exemplars.
AI.method: The authors construct a large-scale, expert-curated multilingual dialogue dataset spanning five languages and targeting seven marginalized groups. Dialogues are grounded in verified external knowledge (fact-checking articles, NGO reports) with document- and chunk-level span annotations, making it directly usable for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems.
AI.result: The resulting resource enables training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models that address the joint problem of hate speech and misinformation across multiple languages and dialogue turns.
AI.conclusion: This novel dataset bridges a critical gap by providing multi-turn, multilingual, knowledge-grounded training data for counterspeech at the hate-misinformation intersection, paving the way for more effective and scalable counterspeech systems.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
summary: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

AI.tldr: Introduces Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies how well predictive models respect logical rules, independent of predictive accuracy. RVS handles both hard and soft rules, works on any relational model, and can be computed via auto-generated SQL queries. Experiments on knowledge graphs and relational regression show models with similar accuracy can differ significantly in logical compliance.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation metrics (ranking quality, error, accuracy) only measure fidelity to ground truth but ignore whether model outputs obey logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance, logical consistency is critical, yet no standard metric exists to capture this dimension.
AI.method: RVS quantifies rule violations by treating hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently. It is defined over a relational vocabulary, applicable to any predictive model and dataset, and computable via automatically generated SQL queries for Horn rules. RVS can also evaluate dataset consistency and identify poorly defined rules.
AI.result: Evaluated on three benchmarks including knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, covering rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic models. Results show models with comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing behavioral differences invisible to standard metrics.
AI.conclusion: RVS fills a critical gap in model evaluation by measuring logical consistency as a dimension orthogonal to predictive accuracy. It enables practitioners to differentiate models that standard metrics would deem equivalent, and can also diagnose issues in training data and rule definitions.

title: Learning universal approximations for partial differential equations with Physics-Informed Broad Learning System
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a central role in modeling complex physical, biological, and engineering systems. While traditional numerical solvers are robust, they often incur prohibitive computational costs due to mesh dependencies, whereas recent Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative but frequently suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. To bridge this gap, this article proposes the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a novel backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization. We improved an algorithm within this framework to handle nonlinear PDEs efficiently and provide a rigorous mathematical proof establishing the universal approximation property of PIBLS for these equations. Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy. This framework provides a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, offering a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

AI.tldr: Proposes Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as direct least-squares optimization, achieving 1–3 orders of magnitude speedup over PINNs with higher accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical PDE solvers incur prohibitive computational costs due to mesh dependencies; Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer mesh-free alternatives but suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. There is a need for a method that combines the mesh-free advantages of PINNs with faster, more stable training.
AI.method: The authors propose PIBLS, which reformulates PDE solving as direct least-squares optimization without backpropagation. An improved algorithm within this framework handles nonlinear PDEs. A rigorous mathematical proof establishes the universal approximation property of PIBLS for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.result: Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs show PIBLS achieves 1–3 orders of magnitude speedup over conventional PINNs while delivering significantly higher solution accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PIBLS provides a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, offering a practical high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

title: Augmenting Game AI with Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Vision paper, published in Conference on Games 2026
summary: Immersion in video games depends not only on graphics, audio, and game mechanics, but also on the quality of in-game characters. Producing believable characters, or game AI, remains a significant challenge as behavioral complexity is hard to capture with hand-coded systems. Game AI is a source of immersion and engagement; however, the limitations stemming from the challenges of creating game AI often lead to frustration and the breaking of the illusion of realism within the game. The introduction of machine learning models opens the door to creating more believable, authentic, and relatable characters in games. The promise is that they either learn from interacting with the game, or from player data, to develop true human-like behavior. In this paper, we envision more applications of reinforcement learning for game AI in the future. For this to materialize, current research limitations are prohibitive to broad deployment across game genres. Therefore, we propose a framework for training reinforcement learning models with a set of requirements in mind that are suited towards game AI and game development. We present examples of games with reinforcement learning-augmented game AI and describe the practicalities of deploying player-facing machine learning agents in modern games. Furthermore, we identify bottlenecks and hard problems in these areas, which we believe offer promising research directions to accelerate the adoption of machine learning in game AI for the video game industry.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that machine learning, particularly reinforcement learning (RL), can create more believable game AI than hand-coded systems, but current research limitations hinder broad deployment. It proposes a training framework with game-development-oriented requirements, presents examples of RL-augmented game AI, and identifies key bottlenecks and research directions to accelerate ML adoption in the video game industry.
AI.motivation: Hand-coded game AI limits behavioral complexity, leading to player frustration and broken immersion. Machine learning models promise more believable, authentic, and relatable characters by learning from gameplay or player data, but practical barriers prevent widespread adoption across game genres.
AI.method: The paper takes a vision/position approach: it proposes a framework for training RL models tailored to game AI requirements (suited to game development constraints), presents case examples of games already using RL-augmented AI, and systematically identifies bottlenecks and hard problems that currently impede deployment.
AI.result: The paper identifies several key bottlenecks: current RL research limitations that prevent deployment across diverse game genres, practical deployment challenges for player-facing ML agents in modern games, and hard problems whose solutions would accelerate industry adoption.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning holds significant promise for next-generation game AI, but targeted research addressing the identified bottlenecks is needed. Solving these hard problems will accelerate ML adoption in the video game industry and enable more immersive, believable character behavior across game genres.

title: An Information Theoretic Framework for Graph Novelty Generation via Latent Mixture Modeling
summary: We propose an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation, which aims to generate data that are distinct from existing patterns while preserving global structural consistency. Our approach embeds data into a latent space, models the latent distribution using finite mixture models, and generates novel samples by imposing explicit novelty and reliability conditions formulated in terms of description length. Specifically, novelty is enforced by requiring generated samples to be poorly explained by all existing mixture components, while reliability constrains their impact on the overall mixture structure under the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, with appropriate threshold choices, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero with explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enables principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.

AI.tldr: Proposes an MDL-based framework for generating novel graphs that are distinct from training data yet globally consistent, using finite mixture models in latent space with theoretical guarantees on misclassification rates.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models lack principled mechanisms to explicitly control and quantify the novelty of generated samples. The authors aim to fill this gap by formalizing novelty generation through information-theoretic criteria.
AI.method: Data embedded into latent space; latent distribution modeled via finite mixture models. Novelty condition: generated sample must have high description length under all existing components. Reliability condition: sample must not distort overall mixture structure under MDL principle. Theoretical convergence rates derived for misclassification probabilities.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves that with proper threshold selection, probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero at explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets validate the framework's ability to generate principled novelty with quantifiable risk.
AI.conclusion: The MDL-based information-theoretic framework provides a theoretically grounded approach to novelty generation in graphs, offering explicit control over novelty and reliability with formal risk guarantees.

title: Beyond Global Replanning: Hierarchical Recovery for Cross-Device Agent Systems
summary: Real-world computer-use tasks often span multiple applications and devices, requiring agents to coordinate heterogeneous environments under dynamic runtime failures. Existing multi-device agent systems support task decomposition and cross-device assignment, but recovery remains largely coarse-grained: when execution fails, they typically retry the same strategy, reassign the subtask, or revise the global plan, without systematically modeling the device-local strategy space. This limits their ability to distinguish failures that can be repaired within the current device from those that require cross-device replanning. We propose \textbf{H-RePlan}, a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents with unified API--CLI--GUI execution. H-RePlan equips each device with interchangeable execution strategies and separates device-local strategy recovery from orchestrator-level global replanning through a compact cross-layer failure abstraction. To evaluate this capability, we introduce \textbf{HeraBench}, a fault-injected benchmark that constructs cross-device workflows over Linux and Android devices and injects strategy- and device-level failures. Experiments show that H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines, achieving higher completion, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rates while reducing the token cost required for reliable end-to-end success. These results demonstrate that scope-aware hierarchical recovery is essential for robust multi-device agent execution.

AI.tldr: H-RePlan introduces a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents that separates device-local strategy recovery from global replanning, evaluated on a new fault-injected benchmark (HeraBench) spanning Linux and Android, demonstrating superior robustness and efficiency over coarse-grained baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-device agent systems handle execution failures in coarse-grained ways — retrying, reassigning subtasks, or revising global plans — without modeling the device-local strategy space. This prevents distinguishing failures repairable within a device from those requiring cross-device replanning, limiting robustness in heterogeneous, failure-prone environments.
AI.method: H-RePlan is a hierarchical replanning framework with unified API–CLI–GUI execution. Each device is equipped with interchangeable execution strategies. A compact cross-layer failure abstraction decouples device-local strategy recovery (handled at the device level) from orchestrator-level global replanning, enabling scope-aware recovery. HeraBench is introduced as a fault-injected benchmark constructing cross-device workflows over Linux and Android with injected strategy- and device-level failures.
AI.result: H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines on HeraBench, achieving higher task completion rates, better instruction adherence, and more perfect-pass outcomes, while simultaneously reducing the token cost needed for reliable end-to-end success.
AI.conclusion: Scope-aware hierarchical recovery, which distinguishes between local and global failure scopes, is essential for robust multi-device agent execution in heterogeneous computing environments.

title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems
summary: Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA ($128\times 128$) and AFHQ ($256\times 256$) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings.

AI.tldr: Flow map models implicitly define a continuous family of denoisers parameterized by a lookahead parameter t, which smoothly traverses the distortion-perception tradeoff without retraining, auxiliary models, or sampler tuning.
AI.motivation: Image restoration methods face a fundamental distortion-perception (DP) tradeoff: low-distortion reconstructions are blurry, while perceptually sharp images are less faithful. Existing methods require committing to a single operating point or need paired supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning to access different points on the frontier. A unified, tuning-free mechanism to span the entire DP frontier with a single model is lacking.
AI.method: The authors leverage flow map models — a few-step sampling extension of flow matching that learns an average velocity field. They show that the lookahead parameter t in flow maps implicitly defines a one-parameter family of denoisers. By varying t, one can traverse from the MMSE (minimum mean squared error) regime to the perceptual-quality regime. They provide a theoretical proof that for Gaussian targets, varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier. For natural images, they embed the flow map denoiser within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) solver to handle general linear and nonlinear inverse problems, where t controls the tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency.
AI.result: A single trained flow map model spans the entire DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA (128×128) and AFHQ (256×256) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks (e.g., super-resolution, inpainting, deblurring, JPEG decompression) validate the findings.
AI.conclusion: Flow map models offer a simple, unified mechanism for controlling the distortion-perception tradeoff in image restoration. The lookahead parameter t serves as an effective control knob without requiring retraining, auxiliary networks, or sampler hyperparameter tuning, and the approach extends naturally to general inverse problems via Plug-and-Play frameworks.

title: StylisticBias: A Few Human Visual Cues Drive Most Social Biases in MLLMs
comment: Accepted to the non-archival workshops AI4Good and Culture x AI at ICML 2026
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in personally and societally consequential settings, yet the visual cues that shape how these models judge people remain poorly understood. Prior work often compares different (groups of) individuals, making it difficult to separate appearance effects from identity differences. We introduce StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute-level social bias in MLLMs. We generate 500 photorealistic base faces and create about 50 single-attribute variations per face, producing about 25K images. This design keeps identity fixed and changes one visual attribute at a time. It lets us measure how specific cues shift model judgments. We evaluate six MLLMs across 25 binary social judgment scenarios. We find that age and body type dominate identity-level effects, while fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. We further find that about 15 attributes account for nearly 80\% of the total variation, showing that bias is concentrated in a small set of visual cues. Sensitivity is strongest in judgments that are semantically aligned with appearance, especially socioeconomic and style-related judgments. We release StylisticBias as a benchmark for fine-grained bias evaluation in multimodal models. Code and dataset: https://github.com/timo-cavelius/StylisticBias and https://hf.co/datasets/shaghayegh/stylistic-bias-dataset.

AI.tldr: StylisticBias is a controlled benchmark using ~25K images of photorealistic faces with single-attribute variations to isolate how specific visual cues (e.g., age, body type, fashion) bias MLLM social judgments, finding that ~15 attributes account for 80% of bias variance.
AI.motivation: Prior work on social bias in MLLMs compares different individuals, confounding appearance effects with identity differences. A controlled method is needed to isolate how individual visual attributes—independent of identity—shape model judgments in socially consequential settings.
AI.method: The authors generate 500 photorealistic base faces and produce ~50 single-attribute variations per face (~25K images total), keeping identity fixed while changing one visual cue at a time. Six MLLMs are evaluated across 25 binary social judgment scenarios, measuring how specific attributes shift judgments at both identity and attribute levels.
AI.result: Age and body type dominate identity-level effects; fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. About 15 attributes account for nearly 80% of total variation, indicating bias concentration. Sensitivity is strongest in semantically aligned judgments, especially socioeconomic and style-related ones.
AI.conclusion: MLLM social bias is concentrated in a small set of visual attributes and is most pronounced when the judgment domain semantically aligns with the appearance cue. StylisticBias is released as a benchmark for fine-grained, attribute-level bias evaluation in multimodal models.

title: Thermodynamic Measure of Intelligence
summary: Can intelligence be measured? We propose that intelligence can be defined as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures: a system increases the probability of outcomes that would be unlikely under passive dynamics but remain admissible under the constraints of the domain. We start with the premise that an intelligent system must model the world and its own place within it. Because the system is part of the world it models, this leads naturally to recursive self-simulation: the system represents futures in which its own actions are part of the trajectory. Our central results give a necessity statement and a conditional near-sufficiency statement connecting this architecture to a precise thermodynamic measure of lawful amplification of rare-valid futures: high rare-valid lift is impossible unless the internal simulation identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity; conversely, when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, the achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Thus recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The resulting framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale, from passive matter and feedback controllers, large language models, and humans as text generators to Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a thermodynamic definition of intelligence as "lawful amplification of rare but valid futures" and proves that recursive self-simulation is both necessary and nearly sufficient for achieving high intelligence under this measure, enabling universal measurement from passive matter to language models.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous, measurable, and universal definition of intelligence grounded in thermodynamics, addressing the longstanding question "Can intelligence be measured?" by connecting intelligent behavior to the amplification of low-probability, domain-valid outcomes.
AI.method: The authors formalize intelligence thermodynamically as "rare-valid lift" — a system's ability to increase the probability of outcomes that are unlikely under passive dynamics yet admissible under domain constraints. They analyze recursive self-simulation architectures where a system models the world and its own actions within it, then prove a necessity theorem (high lift requires high-fidelity simulation of rare-valid futures) and a conditional near-sufficiency theorem (high fidelity plus an effective policy yields near-optimal lift bounded by actuation limits).
AI.result: The central results are two theorems: (1) High rare-valid lift is impossible without internal simulation that identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity (necessity); (2) When rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum (near-sufficiency). These establish recursive self-simulation as necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Intelligence can be universally measured as thermodynamic rare-valid lift. Recursive self-simulation emerges as a fundamental architectural requirement for intelligence, applying across scales from passive matter and feedback controllers to LLMs and Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling for Stable RLHF
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns large language models by training reward models on preference data and optimizing policies to maximize predicted rewards. However, this pipeline faces two fundamental challenges: (1) reward models cannot signal when their predictions are unreliable, since they usually act as deterministic point estimators; and (2) modern group-based policy optimization can amplify unreliable reward signals, as exemplified by GRPO's uniform treatment of rewards during advantage computation. As policies explore increasingly diverse responses, these two limitations create a critical vulnerability: unreliable reward estimates may be granted disproportionate influence, triggering severe reward hacking. We propose Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM), which equips reward models with calibrated uncertainty via quantile-based conformal prediction and reweights GRPO advantages through heteroscedastic variance decomposition. Experiments across HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF demonstrate that UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality compared to standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.

AI.tldr: UARM introduces calibrated uncertainty estimation into reward models via quantile-based conformal prediction and uses heteroscedastic variance decomposition to reweight GRPO advantages, mitigating reward hacking and improving alignment in RLHF pipelines.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF suffers from two issues: (1) reward models act as deterministic point estimators without signaling prediction unreliability; (2) group-based policy optimization like GRPO treats all rewards uniformly during advantage computation, amplifying unreliable signals. As policy exploration diversifies, unreliable reward estimates gain disproportionate influence, causing severe reward hacking.
AI.method: UARM equips reward models with calibrated uncertainty via quantile-based conformal prediction and reweights GRPO advantages through heteroscedastic variance decomposition. The uncertainty estimates are used to down-weight unreliable reward signals during policy optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF show UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality compared to standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating calibrated uncertainty into reward modeling and advantage weighting effectively addresses the vulnerability of RLHF to unreliable reward signals, leading to more robust and higher-quality alignment.

title: Gender Bias in LLM Hiring Decisions: Evidence from a Japanese Context and Evaluation of Mitigation Strategies
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in hiring workflows, yet most research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions has focused on English-language, Western-format resumes. This study examines whether pro-female gender bias extends to a Japanese corporate context and evaluates two practical mitigation strategies. Using a counterfactual resume design with 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes, 12 name pairs selected on linguistically grounded gender-signal criteria, and five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B), we conducted 43,200 API calls across baseline, prompt instruction, and privacy filter conditions. A crossed random-effects linear mixed model confirms a significant pro-female bias across all five models, replicating Western findings in a non-Western context. A prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produces no meaningful reduction in bias. A name-reliance analysis formally identifies the candidate name as the primary gender channel: removing the name from the prompt reduces the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. An unexpected incompatibility between the privacy filter and GPT-4o's content safety filter, resulting in a 42% refusal rate, highlights a practical deployment challenge for name anonymization in LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

AI.tldr: The study investigates whether pro-female gender bias in LLM hiring decisions extends to Japanese corporate contexts using rirekisho-format resumes. Testing five LLMs across 43,200 API calls, it confirms significant pro-female bias exists, finds that prompt-based gender-neutrality instructions are ineffective, and identifies candidate name as the primary gender signal. A critical deployment issue emerged where name anonymization via privacy filters triggered a 42% refusal rate with GPT-4o's content safety filter.
AI.motivation: Most LLM hiring bias research is limited to English-language, Western-format resumes, leaving a gap in understanding whether known pro-female biases generalize to non-Western linguistic and cultural contexts like Japan. Additionally, there is a practical need to evaluate real-world mitigation strategies such as prompt instructions and name anonymization.
AI.method: A counterfactual resume experiment using 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes paired with 12 linguistically-grounded gender-signaling name pairs. Five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B) were tested across baseline, prompt instruction (gender-neutrality directive), and privacy filter (name removal) conditions, totaling 43,200 API calls. Analysis employed a crossed random-effects linear mixed model and name-reliance analysis.
AI.result: A significant pro-female bias was confirmed across all five models in the Japanese context, replicating Western findings. Prompt-level gender-neutrality instructions produced negligible bias reduction. Name-reliance analysis demonstrated that candidate name is the primary gender channel, with name removal reducing the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. Critically, the privacy filter condition caused GPT-4o's content safety filter to reject 42% of requests, revealing a serious deployment incompatibility.
AI.conclusion: Pro-female gender bias in LLM hiring decisions is not culturally or linguistically bounded — it replicates robustly in a Japanese corporate setting. Simple prompt-based debiasing is ineffective, while name anonymization, though effective at reducing bias, introduces practical risks (such as safety filter interference) that undermine real-world deployment. The findings underscore the need for more robust, context-aware mitigation strategies in LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

title: Enhancing Graph Neural Networks Using Proximity Graphs for Dust Source Emission Forecasting
summary:
Accurate prediction of dust source emissions is critical for mitigating the significant environmental and health hazards posed by dust storms. Traditional forecasting methods often struggle to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of these phenomena.
  In this paper, we demonstrate that proximity graphs enable Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to effectively model the intricate spatial and temporal relationships between data points. Specifically, we use proximity graphs--such as Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph--as the input for GNNs (including GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Networks, and Graph Attention Networks) to perform message passing.
  Our approach highlights the effectiveness of integrating proximity graphs with GNNs for robust and accurate dust source forecasting. To emphasize the importance of proximity graph representations, we compare our method against GNNs using random graphs for message passing. The results show that GNNs with proximity graphs significantly outperform those with random graphs and are also far superior to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model in dust source emission forecasting.

AI.tldr: Proximity graphs (Delaunay, Gabriel, k-NN, Yao) combined with GNNs (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) significantly outperform random-graph GNNs and LSTM baselines for dust source emission forecasting by capturing complex spatiotemporal dynamics.
AI.motivation: Traditional dust storm forecasting methods fail to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of dust source emissions. There is a need for models that can effectively represent spatial and temporal relationships between data points to improve prediction accuracy and mitigate environmental and health hazards.
AI.method: The authors propose using proximity graphs (Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph) as input structures for Graph Neural Networks (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) to perform message passing. They benchmark this approach against (1) GNNs using random graphs and (2) LSTM models.
AI.result: GNNs with proximity graphs significantly outperform GNNs with random graphs and are far superior to LSTM models in dust source emission forecasting tasks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating proximity graphs with GNNs provides a robust and accurate framework for dust source forecasting, demonstrating that appropriate graph construction (proximity-based rather than random) is critical for capturing meaningful spatiotemporal relationships.

title: Navigating Unreliable Parametric and Contextual Knowledge: Explicit Knowledge Conflict Resolution for LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of language-based tasks by leveraging both extensive parametric knowledge and in-context learning ability, enabling them to incorporate external information provided in the input prompt. However, the integration of external knowledge can introduce conflicts, not only between the model's internal parametric knowledge and the external information, but also among multiple pieces of external contexts. Existing approaches typically assume that either the model or the provided context is reliable, overlooking the possibility that both sources may contain errors, and avoid conflicts by privileging one source over the other, rather than actively resolving inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework MACR for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond the conventional binary choice paradigm and incorporates an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism based on a multi-agent reasoning approach. Specifically, we first propose an adaptive knowledge assessment and retrieval approach that employs a modified semantic entropy measure to quantify an LLM's confidence in its answer to a given query. Based on this confidence estimation, MACR either externalizes the model's internal knowledge as textual representations or retrieves relevant external knowledge when internal knowledge is insufficient, generating basic contexts for subsequent reasoning. Then we introduce an inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three specialized agents that, respectively, induce explicit rules, analyze potential conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across all available contexts. Empirical results demonstrate that MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks, while also providing interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.

AI.tldr: MACR is a multi-agent framework for resolving knowledge conflicts in LLMs that uses semantic entropy to assess model confidence, retrieves external knowledge adaptively, and employs three specialized agents to induce rules, detect conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across both parametric and contextual knowledge sources.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to LLM knowledge conflict resolution assume either the model or external context is reliable, adopting a binary choice paradigm that privileges one source over the other. They overlook that both sources can contain errors and that multiple external contexts can conflict with each other. There is a need for a framework that actively resolves inconsistencies rather than simply choosing sides.
AI.method: MACR operates in two stages: (1) Adaptive knowledge assessment and retrieval using a modified semantic entropy measure to estimate LLM confidence in its answers. If confidence is high, internal knowledge is externalized as text; otherwise, external knowledge is retrieved. (2) An inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three agents: one induces explicit rules, one analyzes potential conflicts, and one resolves inconsistencies across all available contexts.
AI.result: MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks and provides interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.
AI.conclusion: MACR demonstrates that moving beyond binary choice paradigms toward explicit, multi-agent conflict resolution with adaptive knowledge sourcing yields both better performance and greater interpretability in handling knowledge conflicts for LLMs.

title: When, Where, and How: Adaptive Binning for Tabular Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Medical tabular data are ubiquitous in clinical research, but deep learning for tables remains underexplored because reliable labels often require costly expert adjudication, even though structured clinical variables are routinely available in tabular form. Self-supervised learning can leverage these unlabeled tables, and recent binning-based pretexts offer a promising inductive bias, but existing objectives fix a single global quantile discretization and apply feature-agnostic supervision. We propose Adaptive Binning, a training-adaptive discretization pretext for tabular SSL that couples discretization to learning through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Motivated by the spectral bias of neural networks and the principles of curriculum learning, our method progressively refines discretization per feature upon plateau detection and selects representation-aware splits to jointly improve value-space concentration and representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective unifies categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features, and experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for linear probing and fine-tuning without dataset-specific discretization tuning. We further introduce a medical tabular SSL benchmark with standardized protocols to support reproducible progress in this underexplored domain. Our code is available at https://github.com/labhai/Adaptive-Binning.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Binning proposes a self-supervised learning method for medical tabular data that uses a feature-wise, coarse-to-fine discretization curriculum. The approach dynamically refines bin boundaries per feature based on representation learning progress, combining categorical reconstruction and ordinal supervision. It achieves consistent improvements on public medical tabular datasets and introduces a standardized benchmark for the domain.
AI.motivation: Medical tabular data is abundant but deep learning for tables remains underexplored due to the cost of expert labeling. Self-supervised learning can exploit unlabeled tabular data, but existing binning-based pretext tasks use a fixed global quantile discretization with feature-agnostic supervision, limiting their effectiveness. The authors are motivated by the spectral bias of neural networks (which learn low-frequency patterns first) and curriculum learning principles to design a more adaptive discretization strategy.
AI.method: Adaptive Binning introduces a training-adaptive discretization pretext that couples binning to representation learning through three key components: (1) A feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum that progressively refines discretization per feature upon plateau detection, starting from coarse bins and gradually increasing granularity. (2) Representation-aware split selection that chooses bin boundaries to jointly optimize value-space concentration and representation-space coherence.
