(3) A heterogeneity-aware objective that unifies categorical reconstruction (cross-entropy) for categorical features with ordinal-aware supervision for numerical features, respecting their distinct statistical properties.
AI.result: Experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for both linear probing and fine-tuning compared to existing methods, without requiring dataset-specific discretization tuning. The method outperforms baselines that use fixed global quantile discretization and feature-agnostic supervision.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive Binning demonstrates that coupling discretization to the learning process via a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum is an effective inductive bias for tabular SSL. The authors also contribute a standardized medical tabular SSL benchmark to facilitate reproducible research in this underexplored domain.

title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
summary: Student-generated drawings are widely used in science education to assess learners' conceptual understanding in modeling-based tasks aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). However, scoring such drawings requires expert human judgment to interpret complex visual representations, making large-scale assessment costly to implement and sustain in classroom settings. In this work, we study automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings using a vision-based model. We evaluate a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation and propose a confidence-aware scoring framework that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions. This confidence signal enables selective automation by scoring high-confidence responses automatically while deferring uncertain cases for human review. Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed approach improves scoring reliability while supporting a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk, highlighting the value of confidence-aware methods for trustworthy educational assessment.

AI.tldr: A Vision Transformer with parameter-efficient adaptation and confidence-aware scoring automates grading of student scientific drawings, deferring uncertain cases to humans for reliable, cost-effective assessment aligned with NGSS.
AI.motivation: Scoring student-generated scientific drawings for NGSS modeling-based tasks requires costly expert human judgment. Large-scale automated scoring is needed but must be trustworthy, as fully automated systems risk misinterpreting complex visual representations.
AI.method: A Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation is trained for automated scoring. A confidence-aware framework derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions, enabling selective automation: high-confidence responses are scored automatically while low-confidence (uncertain) cases are deferred for human review.
AI.result: Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items demonstrate that the approach improves scoring reliability and enables a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-aware methods are valuable for trustworthy educational assessment, enabling selective automation that balances efficiency gains with the reliability demands of high-stakes science education evaluation.

title: Neural Additive and Basis Models with Feature Selection and Interactions
comment: Accepted at PAKDD 2024. Code is available at https://github.com/shiralab/NAM-FS
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit attractive performance in various fields but often suffer from low interpretability. The neural additive model (NAM) and its variant called the neural basis model (NBM) use neural networks (NNs) as nonlinear shape functions in generalized additive models (GAMs). Both models are highly interpretable and exhibit good performance and flexibility for NN training. NAM and NBM can provide and visualize the contribution of each feature to the prediction owing to GAM-based architectures. However, when using two-input NNs to consider feature interactions or when applying them to high-dimensional datasets, training NAM and NBM becomes intractable due to the increase in the computational resources required. This paper proposes incorporating the feature selection mechanism into NAM and NBM to resolve computational bottlenecks. We introduce the feature selection layer in both models and update the selection weights during training. Our method is simple and can reduce computational costs and model sizes compared to vanilla NAM and NBM. In addition, it enables us to use two-input NNs even in high-dimensional datasets and capture feature interactions. We demonstrate that the proposed models are computationally efficient compared to vanilla NAM and NBM, and they exhibit better or comparable performance with state-of-the-art GAMs.

AI.tldr: To address the computational intractability of Neural Additive Models (NAM) and Neural Basis Models (NBM) when handling feature interactions or high-dimensional data, the authors propose integrating a feature selection layer that learns selection weights during training, reducing computational cost and model size while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: NAM and NBM provide high interpretability via GAM-based architectures and can visualize per-feature contributions. However, they become computationally intractable when using two-input neural networks to capture feature interactions or when applied to high-dimensional datasets, due to the explosion in required computational resources.
AI.method: The authors introduce a feature selection layer into both NAM and NBM architectures. This layer learns and updates selection weights during training, enabling the model to automatically identify and retain only the most relevant features. This simple mechanism reduces the number of active NN shape functions, cutting computational costs and model size, and makes it feasible to use two-input NNs for capturing feature interactions even on high-dimensional data.
AI.result: The proposed models demonstrate significantly improved computational efficiency compared to vanilla NAM and NBM. They achieve better or comparable predictive performance relative to state-of-the-art Generalized Additive Models (GAMs).
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a feature selection layer into NAM and NBM is a simple yet effective approach to overcome their computational bottlenecks. This enables scalable training on high-dimensional datasets and facilitates the use of two-input NNs for interaction modeling, all while preserving the interpretability inherent to GAM-based architectures.

title: Lagrange: An Open-Vocabulary, Energy-Based Sparse Framework for Generalized End-to-End Driving
summary: Scaling end-to-end autonomous driving to complex, open-world environments requires perceptual models that generalize to anomalous scenarios and planners that produce kinematically valid trajectories. Existing paradigms face a distinct dichotomy between representational efficiency and generalization capacity. Dense models (e.g., occupancy networks), while geometrically robust, incur critical computational bottlenecks and struggle with high-level semantic reasoning. Conversely, sparse, query-based planners are efficient but reliant on closed-set definitions, rendering them vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) events. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer open-vocabulary reasoning, their autoregressive, discrete token generation fundamentally conflicts with the continuous, high-frequency control requirements of vehicle dynamics. To address this, we propose Lagrange, an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework based on Masked Latent Fields (MLF). Rather than relying on dense volumetric reconstructions or closed-set query mechanisms, Lagrange exploits Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. We introduce an intent-driven masked cross-attention module that temporally filters irrelevant entities, decoding the attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field defined over spatial coordinates. By framing decision-making as a Lagrangian action minimization problem spanning this energy field, we enforce strict compliance with vehicle kinematics while executing collision avoidance. Extensive offline evaluations on both standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange establishes a promising framework for robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.

AI.tldr: Lagrange is an open-vocabulary autonomous driving framework that uses Masked Latent Fields (MLF) to combine the efficiency of sparse query-based methods with the generalization of vision-language models, framing planning as Lagrangian action minimization over a learned continuous energy field to produce kinematically feasible trajectories.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous driving paradigms suffer from a dichotomy: dense occupancy networks are geometrically robust but computationally expensive and semantically limited, while sparse query-based planners are efficient but fail on out-of-distribution events due to closed-set definitions. Vision-Language-Action models offer open-vocabulary reasoning but their autoregressive discrete token generation conflicts with continuous vehicle control requirements.
AI.method: Lagrange uses Masked Latent Fields (MLF) built on three components: (1) VLMs encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens; (2) an intent-driven masked cross-attention module temporally filters irrelevant entities; (3) the attended tokens are decoded into an implicit continuous energy field over spatial coordinates. Decision-making is then cast as a Lagrangian action minimization problem over this energy field, enforcing kinematic constraints during collision avoidance.
AI.result: Extensive offline evaluations on standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange achieves robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomous driving performance.
AI.conclusion: Lagrange establishes a promising framework for open-world autonomy by unifying open-vocabulary semantic understanding with continuous, kinematically constrained planning through the Masked Latent Fields formulation.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Squeeze-Excitation-like Attention
summary: We introduce SEA-PINN, a novel architecture that incorporates a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks to dynamically recalibrate the importance of neurons across layers. A key feature of SEA-PINN is its highly stable initialization. On 17 out of 20 benchmark problems, SEA-PINN exhibit nearly negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss, establishing a quasi-deterministic and favorable starting point for optimization. Notably, without employing Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activation functions, SEA-PINN attained competitive accuracy (83\% vs. 90\% improvement relative to FNN-PINN on the high-frequency case 7) as compared with TSA-PINN-a model specifically engineered for high-frequency problems via learnable frequencies in sinusoidal activations. Furthermore, integrating SEA-PINN into TSA-PINN boosted performance by 42.49\%. These results underscore SEA-PINN as a lightweight plug-in module that enhances nonlinear representation power, promotes more robust and efficient convergence, and strengthens the overall reliability of physics-informed learning.

AI.tldr: SEA-PINN introduces a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks, achieving near-deterministic stable initialization with negligible variance on 17/20 benchmarks, competitive accuracy on high-frequency problems without Fourier features, and a 42.49% boost when integrated with TSA-PINN.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from poor initialization, unstable training dynamics, and difficulty modeling high-frequency components. Existing solutions like Fourier feature embeddings or learnable periodic activations add complexity. The authors seek a lightweight, plug-in architectural enhancement that improves nonlinear representation capacity, stabilizes initialization, and promotes robust convergence without relying on specialized input encodings or activation functions.
AI.method: The proposed SEA-PINN architecture embeds a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) style channel-wise attention mechanism into PINN layers. The SE block adaptively recalibrates neuron-wise importance by learning per-channel scaling factors derived from global spatial information, applied as a lightweight gating mechanism after each hidden layer. Critically, this design yields a highly stable, quasi-deterministic initialization. The method is evaluated both standalone and as a plug-in module integrated into TSA-PINN (which uses learnable sinusoidal activation frequencies).
AI.result: On 17 of 20 benchmark problems, SEA-PINN exhibited nearly negligible variance and substantially reduced initial loss, providing a quasi-deterministic starting point. Without Fourier features or periodic activations, SEA-PINN achieved 83% improvement over FNN-PINN on the high-frequency case 7, versus 90% for the specialized TSA-PINN. When SEA-PINN was integrated into TSA-PINN, performance improved by an additional 42.49%, demonstrating complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: SEA-PINN is a lightweight, plug-and-play attention module that enhances nonlinear representation power in PINNs. Its stable initialization properties yield quasi-deterministic behavior with minimal variance, while its integration with specialized architectures like TSA-PINN yields compounding performance gains. The work establishes channel-wise attention as an effective, low-overhead strategy for improving reliability and convergence in physics-informed deep learning.

title: Leveraging systems' non-linearity to tackle the scarcity of data in the design of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems
summary: Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) allows for the efficient building of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems (IFDS). On the other hand, DTL methods still heavily rely on large amounts of labelled data. Obtaining such an amount of data can be challenging when dealing with machines or structures faults. This document proposes a novel approach to the design of vibration-based IFDS using DTL in condition of strong data scarcity. A periodic multi-excitation level procedure leveraging intrinsic non-linearities of real-world systems is used to produce images that can be conveniently analysed by pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to diagnose faults. A new data visualization method and its augmentation technique are proposed in this paper to tackle the typical lack of data encountered during the design of IFDS. Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure provides effective support for the proposed method.

AI.tldr: Proposes a novel vibration-based Intelligent Fault Diagnosis System using Deep Transfer Learning under strong data scarcity, employing periodic multi-excitation signals to leverage system nonlinearities, combined with a new data visualization and augmentation method, validated on a railway pantograph.
AI.motivation: Deep Transfer Learning methods for fault diagnosis still require large amounts of labelled data, which is difficult to obtain for machine or structural faults. There is a need for effective IFDS design under conditions of strong data scarcity.
AI.method: A periodic multi-excitation level procedure that exploits intrinsic nonlinearities of real-world systems to produce images. These images are analyzed by pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks via transfer learning. A new data visualization method and corresponding augmentation technique are introduced to address data scarcity.
AI.result: Experimental validation conducted on a railway pantograph structure demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully enables vibration-based intelligent fault diagnosis using deep transfer learning even under conditions of strong data scarcity, with the railway pantograph case study providing effective experimental support.

title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Score Matching in Gaussian Mixtures via Reverse Fisher Divergence
summary: The score matching problem is a central training objective in modern generative modeling, diffusion models, fitting unnormalized statistical models, and inverse problems. A standard approach is to minimize the forward Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the teacher distribution. However, recent results show that even in simple Gaussian mixture model settings, this objective can lead to undesirable and initialization-dependent convergence behavior. In this paper, we study an alternative objective: the reverse Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the student distribution. We analyze gradient descent (GD) for fitting Gaussian mixture models and show that this change in the objective leads to significantly better optimization properties. First, when the teacher distribution is a single Gaussian and the student is a Gaussian mixture model with fixed weights and identity covariances, we prove the global convergence of GD from arbitrary initializations. Second, we extend the analysis to the case where the teacher is also a Gaussian mixture model and prove global convergence guarantees under a global random initialization scheme and a $\widetildeΩ(1)$-separation assumption on the target means. In particular, with high probability, each student component converges near its closest teacher component, and we provide conditions under which the student distribution converges in total variation distance. Our proofs rely on a new Lyapunov-based analysis of the gradient descent dynamics, showing that the reverse Fisher divergence has a much more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that minimizing reverse Fisher divergence (student expectation) instead of forward Fisher divergence (teacher expectation) for score matching in Gaussian mixture models yields dramatically better optimization properties, proving global convergence of gradient descent under mild conditions, in contrast to the known poor behavior of the forward objective.
AI.motivation: Standard score matching minimizes the forward Fisher divergence, which recent work shows suffers from undesirable, initialization-dependent convergence behavior even in simple Gaussian mixture models. This motivates studying the reverse Fisher divergence as an alternative training objective with potentially superior optimization properties.
AI.method: The authors analyze gradient descent dynamics on the reverse Fisher divergence for Gaussian mixture models. They employ a novel Lyapunov-based analysis to prove global convergence. Two settings are studied: (1) a single-Gaussian teacher with a Gaussian mixture student (fixed weights, identity covariances), and (2) a Gaussian mixture teacher with a Gaussian mixture student, under a global random initialization scheme and a Ω̃(1)-separation assumption on target means.
AI.result: (1) For a single-Gaussian teacher, GD converges globally from arbitrary initializations. (2) For a Gaussian mixture teacher, under a global random initialization and Ω̃(1)-separation of means, each student component converges near its closest teacher component with high probability, and conditions are given for convergence in total variation distance.
AI.conclusion: The reverse Fisher divergence offers a substantially more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence for score matching, enabling global convergence guarantees that are unavailable for the forward objective. The Lyapunov-based analysis technique developed may be of independent interest.

title: SoftSkill: Behavioral Compression for Contextual Adaptation
summary: Agent skills are commonly deployed as natural-language Markdown files that encode answer policies, evidence-use habits, and task procedures. These files are readable and portable, but they are consumed indirectly: for each task instance, a frozen language model must translate a long textual artifact into generation-time behavior. This paper asks whether a natural-language skill can instead initialize a compact continuous context object, refined by a trainable soft delta while the base model remains frozen. We propose SoftSkill, a frozen-backbone method that tunes such soft skills with next-token prediction and deploys them as latent behavioral priors at inference time. In our main single-round setting, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 points on LiveMath, and 1.3 points on DocVQA. Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 points on LiveMath, while replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown skill tokens with a few virtual tokens. We further study agentic execution as a harder boundary case, where sparse trajectory imitation provides useful signal but does not yet robustly compress long-horizon procedural behavior. More broadly, the results suggest that some task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown to be reinterpreted at inference time, but as compact latent controls over how a frozen model enters the task.

AI.tldr: SoftSkill proposes replacing verbose natural-language Markdown skill files with compact, trainable continuous prefixes (soft prompts) that condition a frozen LLM's behavior. A length-32 prefix tuned via next-token prediction outperforms explicit skill prompting and prior soft-skill methods on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, while using far fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Agent skills are typically encoded as long Markdown files that a frozen LLM must re-interpret afresh for each task instance, which is indirect and token-inefficient. The authors ask whether a skill can instead be stored as a compact latent context object — trained once and deployed as a behavioral prior — circumventing the need for repeated textual reinterpretation.
AI.method: SoftSkill freezes the entire backbone LLM and trains only a short sequence (e.g., length 32) of virtual token embeddings — the "soft skill" — that are prepended as a prefix. Training uses standard next-token prediction on task demonstrations. At inference, this learned prefix is deployed as a latent behavioral prior. The approach is also tested on agentic trajectory imitation, where sparse trajectory data provides signal for compressing procedural behavior.
AI.result: On Qwen3.5-4B, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points (SearchQA), 42.1 points (LiveMath), and 1.3 points (DocVQA). Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill yields +5.2 points on SearchQA and +12.5 points on LiveMath, while compressing hundreds to thousands of Markdown tokens into ~32 virtual tokens. For long-horizon agentic execution, trajectory imitation provides useful but not yet robust compression.
AI.conclusion: Some task skills are better represented as compact latent controls over a frozen model's behavior rather than as long-form Markdown needing repeated inference-time reinterpretation. SoftSkill demonstrates that lightweight prefix tuning can serve as an effective, efficient alternative for encoding reusable agent skills.

title: On the Oracle Complexity of Interpolation-Based Gradient Descent
summary: Recent work on first-order optimizers for empirical risk minimization (ERM) has suggested that smoothness of ERM loss functions in the training data, rather than in the optimization parameters, can be leveraged to improve the oracle complexity of gradient descent (GD) methods. In this paper, we propose an inexact gradient method, piecewise polynomial interpolation-based gradient descent (PPI-GD), which approximates the full gradient in each iteration by querying the first-order oracle at equidistant points in the data domain to construct polynomial interpolants of the resulting gradient samples over appropriately sized patches of the data domain. We analyze the oracle complexity of PPI-GD for strongly convex and non-convex loss functions when the data space dimension is bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples, and find it to outperform several GD variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth. Furthermore, our analysis extends several techniques from the error analysis of bicubic spline interpolants to the setting of $d$-variate tensor product polynomial interpolants which may be of independent interest in interpolation analysis.

AI.tldr: PPI-GD approximates full gradients by polynomial interpolation over equidistant data-domain samples, achieving oracle complexity improvements over standard GD variants for sufficiently smooth, strongly convex and non-convex ERM losses when data dimension is polylogarithmic in sample size.
AI.motivation: Leverage smoothness of ERM loss functions in the training data (rather than in optimization parameters) to improve oracle complexity of gradient-based methods. Existing work suggests this data-space smoothness can be exploited, but practical methods with strong theoretical guarantees remain underdeveloped.
AI.method: PPI-GD (Piecewise Polynomial Interpolation-based Gradient Descent): in each iteration, queries the first-order oracle at equidistant points across the data domain, constructs tensor-product polynomial interpolants of gradient samples over data-domain patches, and uses the interpolated approximation as an inexact gradient. Extends bicubic spline interpolation error analysis to general d-variate tensor-product polynomial interpolants.
AI.result: PPI-GD outperforms several GD variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth. Oracle complexity bounds are established for both strongly convex and non-convex settings, with the data dimension bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples. The interpolation error analysis for d-variate tensor-product polynomials is a standalone contribution.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting data-space smoothness via polynomial interpolation yields a practical inexact gradient method with provably improved oracle complexity. The d-variate interpolation analysis extends beyond optimization to broader numerical analysis contexts.

title: Automating SKILL.md Generation for Computer-Using Agents via Interaction Trajectory Mining
summary: Explicit skill libraries make computer-using agents easier to inspect, but it remains unclear whether such libraries can be mined from interaction data in a way that improves downstream policies. We study this question through a three-stage pipeline that segments GUI trajectories, clusters segments into candidate skills, and trains a skill-aware policy from the resulting annotations. The mined clusters are readable on the source benchmark: five of eight clusters have at least 0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels. However, readability does not imply transfer. GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5\% to 20.5\%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics. We therefore present the method as a diagnostic study: trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether explicit skill libraries mined from GUI interaction trajectories can improve downstream policies. While the clustering approach produces highly readable skills (0.95+ purity), the mined skills fail to meaningfully transfer: GRPO improves skill-step accuracy only marginally (18.5%→20.5%) and underperforms simple frequency baselines. The work is framed as a diagnostic study exposing the gap between skill readability and policy improvement.
AI.motivation: Explicit skill libraries promise inspectability for computer-using agents, but it is unknown whether such libraries can be automatically mined from interaction data and whether they actually benefit downstream policy learning. The authors aim to test this assumption end-to-end.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) segment GUI interaction trajectories into sub-sequences using a boundary detector, (2) cluster the segments into candidate skills, and (3) train a skill-aware policy (via GRPO) using the resulting skill annotations. Clusters are evaluated for purity against InteraSkill Workflows ground-truth labels. Transfer is measured on source-domain metrics and on BrowseComp+.
AI.result: Five of eight clusters achieve ≥0.95 purity against InteraSkill labels, demonstrating strong readability. However, GRPO with mined skills improves InteraSkill Workflows accuracy only from 18.5% to 20.5%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency-based priors on key source-domain metrics.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but this readability does not imply transferable policy improvement. The boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are identified as insufficient components, framing the work as a diagnostic contribution to guide future research on skill-aware agent training.

title: Matching Markets meet Cumulative Prospect Theory: Towards Optimal and Adversarially Robust Learning
summary: We study a multi-agent multi-armed bandit problem in the competitive setup with two-sided matching markets under a human centric decision making model. To capture human preferences, we use cumulative prospect theory (CPT) that weighs the actions of the agent in a nonlinear fashion using a ($α$-Hölder continuous) weight function. CPT has been widely used in behavioral economics and risk sensitive machine learning to emulate human preferences. We analyze the state-of-the-art learning algorithm with CPT weight distorted rewards and obtain a player optimal regret of $\mathcal{O}(K\log T \left(\frac{1}Δ\right)^{2/α})$, where $K$ denotes the number of arms, $T$ is the learning horizon, and $Δ$ represents (suitably defined) players' minimum preference gap. Noticing the dependence on $Δ$ to be sub-optimal, we further improve this regret by judiciously selecting the active set of arms during exploration, which removes the dependence on $K$ in the dominant term and achieves an improved (optimal) regret guarantees in the setting where the number of arms $K$ is significantly larger than the number of players $N$. In addition, we consider adversarial markets where the observed rewards of the agents may be corrupted. We propose and analyze algorithms for robust markets with CPT as risk sensitive measure in both settings where the total corruption budget is known and where it is unknown, and establish logarithmic player-optimal regret guarantees in both cases.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes multi-agent multi-armed bandit problems in competitive two-sided matching markets under Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT), which models human-centric decision-making with nonlinear probability weighting. The authors establish player-optimal regret bounds, improve them via active arm set selection when arms outnumber players, and extend their analysis to adversarial markets with reward corruption (both known and unknown corruption budgets).
AI.motivation: Traditional bandit algorithms assume rational agents with risk-neutral preferences. However, real human decision-making exhibits nonlinear probability weighting and risk sensitivity, captured by CPT. The paper aims to bridge this gap by designing and analyzing learning algorithms that account for CPT-distorted rewards in competitive matching markets, including robustness to adversarial reward corruption.
AI.method: The authors model the problem as a multi-agent multi-armed bandit with two-sided matching, where agents' rewards are distorted by a CPT weight function (α-Hölder continuous). They analyze a state-of-the-art learning algorithm under CPT distortion, then improve regret by judiciously selecting an active set of arms during exploration to remove dependence on K in the dominant term. For adversarial settings, they propose robust algorithms for both known and unknown total corruption budgets.
AI.result: The initial analysis yields a player-optimal regret of O(K log T (1/Δ)^{2/α}). The improved algorithm removes the K-dependence in the dominant term, achieving optimal regret when K ≫ N. For adversarial markets with CPT, logarithmic player-optimal regret guarantees are established under both known and unknown corruption budget settings.
AI.conclusion: CPT-based modeling provides a more realistic framework for human-centric multi-agent bandit problems in matching markets. The active-set exploration strategy achieves optimal regret when arms vastly outnumber players, and robust algorithms successfully handle adversarial reward corruption while maintaining logarithmic regret guarantees.

title: Rethinking Shrinkage Bias in LLM FP4 Pretraining: Geometric Origin, Systemic Impact, and UFP4 Recipe
summary: FP4 training promises substantial reductions in memory and computation cost for LLM pretraining, yet current FP4 hardware paths and recipes, including NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin-class systems and AMD MI350-series GPUs, remain centered on E2M1 data elements. In this study, we identify a fundamental limitation of that choice: non-uniform formats such as E2M1 inherently suffer from Shrinkage Bias, a systematic negative rounding error caused by the geometric asymmetry of their representable bins. We show that this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT), providing a unified explanation for the training instability observed in existing E2M1-based FP4 recipes. In contrast, uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) bypass this grid-geometry error and better convert the improved bucket utilization from RHT into higher quantization quality. Based on this finding, we propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe that applies RHT to all three training GEMMs while restricting stochastic rounding to dY alone. On Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining, UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than strong E2M1-based baselines, supported by scaling-law analysis and ablation studies. Our results suggest that future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "Shrinkage Bias" in non-uniform E2M1 FP4 formats—a systematic negative rounding error from geometric bin asymmetry—as the root cause of training instability in FP4 LLM pretraining. The authors propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe using RHT on all three GEMMs with stochastic rounding only on dY, achieving superior BF16-relative loss on models up to 124B parameters.
AI.motivation: Current FP4 hardware (NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin, AMD MI350) and training recipes are built around the E2M1 format, but existing FP4 training methods suffer from instability. The authors seek to explain why E2M1-based FP4 training underperforms and to propose a practical alternative that better leverages uniform 4-bit grids (E1M2/INT4).
AI.method: The authors (1) theoretically analyze "Shrinkage Bias"—a systematic negative rounding error inherent to non-uniform formats like E2M1 due to geometric bin asymmetry; (2) show this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT); (3) propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit recipe applying RHT to all three training GEMMs (forward, backward w.r.t. input, backward w.r.t. weight) with stochastic rounding restricted to dY alone; and (4) validate via scaling-law analysis and ablation on Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining.
AI.result: UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation compared to strong E2M1-based baselines across all model scales (1.5B–124B). The uniform-grid approach with RHT better converts improved bucket utilization into higher quantization quality, and scaling-law analysis supports the findings.
AI.conclusion: Future AI accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1, as uniform formats avoid the Shrinkage Bias problem and enable stable, high-quality FP4 pretraining at scale.

title: SL-S4Wave: Self-Supervised Learning of Physiological Waveforms with Structured State Space Models
summary: Modeling long-sequence medical time series data, such as electrocardiograms (ECG), poses significant challenges due to high sampling rates, multichannel signal complexity, inherent noise, and limited labeled data. While recent self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, based on various encoder architectures such as convolutional neural networks, have been proposed to learn representations from unlabeled data, they often fall short in capturing long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. Structured state space models (S4) excel at long-sequence modeling, but existing S4 architectures fail to capture the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms. In this work, we propose SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised learning framework that combines contrastive learning with a tailored encoder built on structured state space models. The encoder incorporates multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels, enabling the capture of both fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SL-S4Wave (1) consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines in a challenging arrhythmia detection task, (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples, showcasing strong label efficiency, and (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments, highlighting its capacity to model complex temporal dynamics in long sequences that most existing approaches fail to efficiently model, and (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types, underscoring its robust cross-domain generalization. We additionally evaluate SL-S4Wave on multiple EEG tasks, achieving superior performance over strong baselines, demonstrating generalizability of our approach beyond cardiac waveforms.

AI.tldr: SL-S4Wave proposes a self-supervised learning framework combining contrastive learning with a custom S4-based encoder featuring multi-layer global convolution with multiscale subkernels. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on ECG arrhythmia detection and EEG tasks, demonstrating strong label efficiency, long-sequence modeling, and cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing SSL methods for medical time series (e.g., ECG) using CNNs fail to capture long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. While S4 models excel at long-sequence modeling, current S4 architectures are not designed for the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms. There is a need for a framework that jointly addresses long-range dependency modeling, noise robustness, label efficiency, and multichannel signal complexity.
AI.method: The authors propose SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised contrastive learning framework with a tailored encoder built on structured state space models (S4). The encoder incorporates multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels to capture both fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms.
AI.result: SL-S4Wave (1) consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and SSL baselines on arrhythmia detection; (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples (strong label efficiency); (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments; and (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types (cross-domain generalization). It also achieves superior performance on multiple EEG tasks, demonstrating generalizability beyond cardiac signals.
AI.conclusion: SL-S4Wave effectively combines contrastive SSL with a multiscale S4 encoder to address key challenges in medical time series modeling. Its strong performance across ECG and EEG tasks, label efficiency, and long-sequence robustness position it as a versatile and powerful framework for physiological waveform representation learning.

title: Interpretable Sperm Morphology Classification via Attention-Guided Deep Learning
summary: Male infertility is a major cause of couple infertility, often linked to abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning models offer automated analysis, most lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. This study proposes an attention-guided deep learning framework for sperm morphology classification. We combine a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to focus on key areas of the sperm head, improving both accuracy and interpretability. Evaluated on the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets, our model achieves accuracies of 90.2% and 93.9% (macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948), outperforming SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0. Furthermore, we use Grad-CAM++ visualizations to highlight features influencing the model's decisions. The results demonstrate that this accurate and transparent framework is a practical tool for automated sperm analysis in fertility clinics.

AI.tldr: An attention-guided deep learning framework combining EfficientNet-B0 with CBAM achieves high accuracy (90.2%–93.9%) and interpretability for sperm morphology classification, validated on two public datasets using Grad-CAM++ visualizations.
AI.motivation: Male infertility is a major contributor to couple infertility, frequently associated with abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning enables automated sperm analysis, most existing models lack interpretability, hindering clinical adoption.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that integrates a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 backbone with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to enhance focus on diagnostically relevant regions of the sperm head. Interpretability is achieved via Grad-CAM++ visualizations, which highlight features driving classification decisions.
AI.result: On the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets, the model attains accuracies of 90.2% and 93.9%, with macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948, respectively, outperforming both SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0 baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework is both accurate and transparent, demonstrating practical utility as an automated sperm analysis tool suitable for deployment in fertility clinics.

title: Adversarial Bandit Optimization with Globally Bounded Perturbations to Convex Losses
summary:
We study adversarial bandit optimization in which the loss functions may be non-convex and non-smooth. In each round, the learner selects an action and observes only the loss incurred at that action. The loss consists of an underlying convex and $β$-smooth component and an adversarial perturbation that may be chosen after observing the learner's action. The perturbations are subject to a global budget controlling their cumulative magnitude over time.
  This framework extends the globally budgeted, post-action perturbation model from underlying linear losses to general convex and $β$-smooth losses. For this broader class, we establish expected regret guarantees that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget.
  To establish these guarantees, we modify a standard bandit optimization algorithm and develop an analysis that controls the additional regret caused by the perturbations. In the absence of perturbations, our results reduce to regret guarantees for the standard bandit convex optimization setting with $β$-smooth losses.

AI.tldr: This paper studies adversarial bandit optimization with non-convex, non-smooth loss functions composed of a convex β-smooth base component plus adversarial perturbations. The perturbations are globally budgeted and can be chosen post-action. The authors adapt a standard bandit algorithm and provide expected regret bounds that explicitly depend on the perturbation budget, generalizing prior work from linear to general convex-smooth losses.
AI.motivation: Prior work on post-action adversarial perturbations in bandit optimization was limited to underlying linear loss functions. The authors aim to extend this framework to the broader and more practically relevant class of general convex and β-smooth losses, providing a unified analysis that bridges standard bandit convex optimization and adversarially perturbed settings.
AI.method: The authors modify a standard bandit convex optimization algorithm to handle post-action adversarial perturbations. They develop a new analysis technique that decomposes and bounds the additional regret attributable to the perturbations. The perturbations are constrained by a global cumulative budget, and the analysis explicitly tracks how this budget affects the overall expected regret.
AI.result: The paper establishes expected regret guarantees that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget for general convex β-smooth losses. In the absence of perturbations (budget = 0), the results recover standard regret bounds for bandit convex optimization with β-smooth losses, demonstrating consistency with the existing literature.
AI.conclusion: The work successfully generalizes the globally budgeted, post-action perturbation model from linear losses to convex β-smooth losses. The derived regret bounds reveal how adversarial perturbation budgets degrade learning performance, and the analysis framework provides a foundation for studying robustness in broader bandit optimization settings.

title: Context-Aware Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling of IVF Laboratory Environmental Conditions
summary: IVF pregnancy rates are routinely modeled using patient-level variables, while high-resolution laboratory environmental data remain underutilized. We show that this is a missed opportunity. Rather than relying on raw sensor averages, we engineer 55 context-aware temporal features, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed, that capture the dynamics of incubator microenvironments. On 61 weeks of data from an Asian IVF clinic, these features reduce cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% for raw averages. We then train a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model that shares environmental effects across an Asian and a Northern European clinic via partial pooling, while preserving site-specific baselines. On held-out data from the Northern European clinic, the model achieves R2 = 0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline, demonstrating that structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful, transferable signal.

AI.tldr: Engineering 55 context-aware temporal features from IVF incubator microenvironments (e.g., thermal stability, humidity adherence, stress duration/recovery) reduces prediction error to 1.27% vs. 3–5% for raw averages. A hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model with partial pooling across an Asian and a Northern European clinic achieves R²=0.86 and 64% error reduction for the 35–39 age group on held-out data, demonstrating clinically transferable signal from structured environmental monitoring.
AI.motivation: IVF clinical pregnancy rate modeling has focused almost exclusively on patient-level covariates while high-resolution laboratory environmental data (incubator temperature, humidity, gas concentrations) are underutilized. The authors argue this is a missed opportunity: incubator microenvironment dynamics likely affect embryo development and implantation potential, but raw sensor averages fail to capture physiologically relevant temporal patterns.
AI.method: (1) Feature engineering: 55 context-aware temporal features derived from incubator sensor time series, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence windows, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed. (2) Hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression with partial pooling — environmental effects are shared across an Asian and a Northern European IVF clinic while preserving site-specific baselines. Cross-validation on 61 weeks of Asian clinic data; held-out validation on the Northern European clinic.
AI.result: The engineered features reduced cross-validated prediction error to 1.27% (versus 3–5% for raw sensor averages) on 61 weeks of Asian clinic data. The hierarchical Bayesian model achieved R² = 0.86 on held-out Northern European data, with a 64% error reduction over a naive baseline specifically for the 35–39 age group.
AI.conclusion: Structured, temporally-aware environmental monitoring of IVF incubators captures clinically meaningful and transferable signal across clinics and geographies. Feature engineering of microenvironment dynamics — not just raw averages — is essential, and hierarchical Bayesian partial pooling enables robust cross-clinic generalization.

title: Score Approximation for Diffusion Models on Arbitrary Low-Dimensional Structures
summary: The remarkable success of score-based diffusion models has spurred significant efforts to establish their theoretical foundations. However, existing complexity bounds for score approximation rely heavily on restrictive assumptions like Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports, which are routinely violated by the singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters inherent to real-world perceptual data. This work establishes a universal score approximation theorem that works for any distribution supported on any compact set of upper Minkowski dimension $d$. Using a novel discrete-mixture formulation, we prove that the score function can be approximated with a ReLU network whose complexity grows exponentially only with $d$, thus breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality. Combined with existing theories on accurately solving the backward diffusion SDE for arbitrary compact distributions, our work shows that diffusion models readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, explaining their competence in real-world generative tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a universal score approximation theorem showing that score functions for any distribution supported on a compact set of upper Minkowski dimension d can be approximated by ReLU networks with complexity exponential only in d, not the ambient dimension, thereby breaking the curse of dimensionality and explaining diffusion models' success on irregular real-world data.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical bounds for score-based diffusion models rely on restrictive assumptions (Lipschitz continuous densities, smooth manifolds) that are routinely violated by real-world perceptual data exhibiting singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters. The gap between theory and practice motivates a more general approximation theory.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel discrete-mixture formulation and prove that the score function can be approximated by a ReLU network whose complexity scales exponentially only with the upper Minkowski dimension d of the support, rather than the ambient dimension. This result is then combined with existing SDE discretization theories for backward diffusion.
AI.result: The paper establishes a universal score approximation theorem valid for any distribution on any compact set of upper Minkowski dimension d. The ReLU network complexity grows exponentially with d alone, breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality that plagued prior bounds.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models can provably adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures without requiring Lipschitz densities or manifold assumptions. This provides theoretical justification for their strong empirical performance on complex real-world generative tasks involving highly irregular data distributions.

title: What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?
summary: Prior work has shown that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak language models, but it remains unclear how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations. We study this by mixing benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and testing three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Across four models, we find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. We further show that preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, that demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias, and that models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal. Taken together, this work moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works: what models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different types of in-context compliance demonstrations (benign vs. harmful) influence jailbreaking behavior in language models. Key findings: benign and harmful demos are not interchangeable; preference optimization prevents benign demos from increasing harmful compliance; recency bias governs demonstration ordering effects; and models diverge in how refusal interacts with in-context signals.
AI.motivation: Prior work demonstrated that in-context examples can jailbreak LMs, but the mechanisms remain poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize *how* models interpret different compliance demonstrations rather than merely showing *that* demonstration-based jailbreaking works.
AI.method: The authors mix benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request + helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request + helpful response) and test three hypotheses about demonstration composition. Experiments span four models, manipulating demonstration content, ordering, and analyzing interactions with refusal behavior and training stages (specifically preference optimization).
AI.result: Benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable — benign demos can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. Preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demos from increasing harmful compliance. Demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias. Models differ in refusal–ICL interaction: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal.
AI.conclusion: What models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology. The work shifts the paradigm from demonstrating that in-context jailbreaking works to characterizing the underlying mechanisms.

title: ADaPT: Token-Level Decoupling for Efficient Large Reasoning Models
summary: Large reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought to achieve strong performance, but applying such reasoning uniformly incurs high computational cost. Existing efficiency-oriented methods attempt to shorten or mix reasoning strategies, yet often degrade reasoning capability. We identify the root cause as sequence-level coupling between efficiency incentives and correctness optimization, which implicitly penalizes long but correct reasoning trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Adaptive Dual-Process Thinking (ADaPT), a token-level dual-process framework that explicitly decouples efficiency and correctness signals during training. ADaPT introduces a mode-selection token to control fast and slow reasoning, applying efficiency-related rewards exclusively to this token to avoid penalizing correct long reasoning while encouraging efficiency when appropriate. Moreover, ADaPT enables precise and continuous control over the efficiency-performance trade-off at inference time: by adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token, a single trained model can smoothly move along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ADaPT decouples efficiency and correctness signals at the token level via a mode-selection token, enabling a single model to smoothly traverse the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier without penalizing correct long reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing efficiency-oriented methods for large reasoning models couple efficiency incentives with correctness optimization at the sequence level, inadvertently penalizing long but correct reasoning trajectories. This degrades reasoning capability when shortening or mixing strategies.
AI.method: ADaPT is a token-level dual-process framework. It introduces a mode-selection token to gate between fast and slow reasoning. During training, efficiency rewards are applied exclusively to this token, decoupling them from correctness optimization. At inference, adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token enables continuous control along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier from a single trained model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Token-level decoupling of efficiency and correctness via a mode-selection token effectively resolves the trade-off problem, enabling adaptive, controllable reasoning without sacrificing performance.

title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
summary:
LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
  We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across twelve programming languages, including Python. Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in other languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol. Because it is fully compatible with the original LCB format, Multi-LCB will automatically track future LCB updates, enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence and requiring models to sustain performance well beyond Python.
  We evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB, uncovering evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual performance. Our results establish Multi-LCB as a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities.

AI.tldr: Multi-LCB extends the Python-only LiveCodeBench to 12 programming languages while preserving contamination controls, enabling cross-language code generation evaluation. Testing 24 LLMs reveals Python overfitting and significant multilingual performance gaps.
AI.motivation: LiveCodeBench is widely adopted but limited to Python, leaving unaddressed the question of whether LLMs generalize across diverse programming languages essential for real-world software engineering.
AI.method: The authors transform Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in 11 additional languages (12 total including Python), preserving LCB's contamination-aware filtering (release-date-based), evaluation protocol, and format compatibility. Multi-LCB is designed to automatically track future LCB updates.
AI.result: Evaluation of 24 LLMs across instruction-following and reasoning tasks uncovered: (1) evidence of Python overfitting, (2) language-specific contamination, and (3) substantial disparities in multilingual code generation performance.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LCB establishes a rigorous benchmark for multi-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM multilingual coding capabilities.

title: Compositionality Emerges in a Narrow Depth-Connectivity Regime: Architecture Constraints and Solution Manifolds
summary: Compositionality is believed to be the foundation for generalization, enabling models to reuse meaningful primitives in novel combinations. Yet, models trained with standard gradient-based optimization rarely, and often only weakly, exhibit compositional internal structure, and it remains unclear how or why such compositionality forms. In this work, we show that compositionality emerges in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot. Along the connectivity axis, compositionality only appears in some specifically sparse networks, heavily depends on which connections remain rather than on weights' sparsity alone. Along the depth axis, compositionality emerges within a narrow, target-dependent regime, peaking at specific depths, while both shallower and deeper networks fail. When either the depth or connectivity condition is violated, gradient descent silently converges to fractured solutions rather than compositional ones. To discover and exploit this emergence, we introduce (i) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity and (ii) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate where compositionality is most likely to appear. Finally, we support these empirical findings with a theoretical framework based on compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds, explaining why compositional solutions are reachable only in a narrow depth-connectivity regime.

AI.tldr: Compositionality—the reuse of primitives in novel combinations—emerges only in a narrow "sweet spot" of network depth and connectivity sparsity. The authors introduce similarity-based pruning and a depth predictor to discover this regime, and provide theoretical justification via compositional sparsity and feature-interference bounds.
AI.motivation: Compositionality is thought to underpin generalization, yet standard gradient-based training rarely yields models with compositional internal structure. It is unknown how or why compositionality forms, motivating an investigation into the conditions under which it emerges.
AI.method: The authors systematically probe two axes: (1) connectivity, by varying network sparsity patterns—demonstrating compositionality depends on *which* connections remain, not sparsity alone; and (2) depth, by evaluating models across a range of layer counts. They propose similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity and a heuristic depth predictor to identify where compositionality appears. A theoretical framework using compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds is developed to explain the narrow regime.
AI.result: Compositionality emerges only in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot: specifically sparse connectivity patterns at a target-dependent intermediate depth. Outside this regime, gradient descent converges to fractured (non-compositional) solutions. Similarity-based pruning recovers compositional connectivity, and the depth predictor estimates the optimal depth.
AI.conclusion: Compositionality is not a generic byproduct of gradient-based learning; it requires specific architectural conditions—namely, sparse, properly structured connectivity and an appropriate depth. The proposed pruning method and depth heuristic enable practitioners to discover and exploit this emergent property, with theoretical grounding explaining why the regime is so narrow.

title: FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS
summary: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit enables frozen flow-matching TTS models to correct pronunciation errors on proper nouns via latent token-level edits stored in a Modern Hopfield Network, achieving 92.7% relative PER reduction without retraining.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching TTS systems produce high-quality zero-shot speech but are static post-deployment — out-of-vocabulary proper nouns cause persistent pronunciation errors that currently require full model retraining to fix. A lightweight, on-the-fly correction mechanism is needed for lifelong adaptation.
AI.method: FlowEdit introduces two core components: (1) Upon receiving corrective feedback, it optimizes a token-level perturbation vector in the text embedding space to steer pronunciation. (2) Corrections are stored in a Modern Hopfield Network functioning as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, stored corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching so that similar unseen names benefit from prior corrections.
AI.result: Evaluated on a curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns spanning 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline. General speech quality remains identical to the frozen base model. Each correction completes in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit offers a practical, efficient lifelong adaptation strategy for flow-matching TTS, eliminating the need for retraining while preserving synthesis quality. The episodic memory with fuzzy retrieval generalizes corrections to morphologically similar names, making it suitable for real-world deployment.

title: Towards Graph-Based Deep Learning for Map Generalization: Insights from Building Footprints Simplification and Aggregation
summary: Map generalization remains one of the fundamental tasks in cartography, especially for the simplification and aggregation of complex building footprints. This study presents the first exploratory application of graph-based deep learning to both tasks, reformulating simplification as node movement prediction and aggregation as link prediction within a unified graph learning framework. We evaluate representative graph neural network architectures (GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE) on multi-scale building datasets, showing that GraphSAGE demonstrates relative strengths in link prediction accuracy, while also revealing persistent challenges in precise node movement prediction. Beyond quantitative performance, the results highlight that aggregation poses greater complexity and challenges than simplification, underscoring the difficulty of capturing higher-level spatial relationships in map generalization with current deep learning approaches. Although limitations such as data imbalance and the need for post-processing remain, the study provides valuable insights and methodological directions for advancing automated map generalization with deep learning approaches.

AI.tldr: First application of graph neural networks to building footprint simplification (node movement) and aggregation (link prediction), finding GraphSAGE performs best on aggregation but both tasks remain challenging, with aggregation proving harder than simplification.
AI.motivation: Automated map generalization — simplifying and aggregating complex building footprints — remains a fundamental yet unresolved challenge in cartography. Existing approaches have not explored graph-based deep learning for these tasks, despite the inherently relational and structural nature of building data.
AI.method: The authors reformulate building simplification as node movement prediction and building aggregation as link prediction within a unified graph learning framework. Three representative graph neural network architectures — GCN (Graph Convolutional Network), GAT (Graph Attention Network), and GraphSAGE — are evaluated on multi-scale building datasets.
AI.result: GraphSAGE demonstrates relative strengths in link prediction accuracy for aggregation. However, all architectures struggle with precise node movement prediction for simplification. Quantitatively, aggregation proves more complex and challenging than simplification, indicating current GNNs have difficulty capturing higher-level spatial relationships.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based deep learning shows promise for automated map generalization but faces significant hurdles, including data imbalance, post-processing requirements, and limited ability to model higher-level spatial semantics. The study provides methodological groundwork and directions for future research.

title: DeepSWIP: Quotient-WMC Counterfactuals for Neural Probabilistic Logic Programs
summary: Neurosymbolic systems such as DeepProbLog combine neural perception with probabilistic logic, but standard inference is associational. Counterfactual reasoning additionally requires a causal semantics for interventions and evidence. We introduce DeepSWIP, a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog programs. Using neural materialization, we reduce fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, apply Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs), and compute counterfactuals by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program. Under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, DeepSWIP is exact relative to the learned materialized FCM. The standard quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals identifies active neural probabilities and explains intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. Experiments on MPI3D confirm the transformation against a DeepTwin construction against 12,000 queries, as predicted and a 2.14$\times$ inference speedup from avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment shows that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands. Code is at https://github.com/saibib/deep_SWIP.

AI.tldr: DeepSWIP introduces a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog, enabling exact counterfactual reasoning in neurosymbolic systems by materializing neural predicates into probabilistic choices, applying Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs), and computing counterfactuals via weighted model counting (WMC). Experiments confirm correctness against DeepTwin constructions and reveal insights about inference speedup and bias correction.
AI.motivation: Standard inference in neurosymbolic systems like DeepProbLog is purely associational, lacking the causal semantics required for counterfactual reasoning — answering "what would have happened if..." queries involving interventions and evidence. Existing approaches (e.g., DeepTwin) suffer from endogenous duplication overhead and fail to address calibration sensitivity and rare-evidence instability.
AI.method: The authors introduce DeepSWIP with four key components: (1) neural materialization that reduces fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, (2) application of Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs) for counterfactual semantics, (3) computation of counterfactuals by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program, and (4) the standard quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals to identify active neural probabilities. Under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, the method is exact relative to the learned materialized functional causal model (FCM).
AI.result: Experiments on MPI3D validate the transformation against DeepTwin across 12,000 queries, achieving a 2.14× inference speedup by avoiding endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment demonstrates that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW (Augmented Inverse Propensity Weighting) estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands.
AI.conclusion: DeepSWIP provides a principled, exact, and efficient framework for counterfactual reasoning in neurosymbolic systems. The approach not only matches DeepTwin's correctness while improving speed but also reveals critical insights about calibration sensitivity, rare-evidence instability, and the importance of proper estimator scoping for debiasing in learned causal models.

title: Low-Energy Reduced RISC-V Instruction Subset Processor for Tsetlin Machine Inference at the Edge
comment: 6 pages, 6 Figures, Accepted in IEEE ISVLSI Conference 2026
summary: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a logic-based machine learning approach that relies on simple bitwise operations and finite-state automata, which makes it attractive for edge AI deployments. Recent work has focused on co-processor and accelerator designs based on Tsetlin Machines (TMs). Although these designs achieve high performance, they typically depend on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, limiting flexibility and ease of programming. In this work, we present a domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor architecture and design flow tailored for TM inference. Leveraging the modular structure of RISC-V, we design a reduced instruction subset processor that retains programmability while targeting improved performance and lower energy consumption for TM workloads. Instruction profiling is employed to guide instruction reduction, followed by datapath and control path simplifications tailored to TM inference. Both the baseline RV32IM core and the proposed reduced core are evaluated across multiple datasets and compared with Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs), which serve as a hardware-efficient baseline due to their reliance on bitwise operations during inference. Results show that TM achieves comparable or higher accuracy (e.g., up to 88.18% on CIFAR-2 compared to 60.0% for BNN) while reducing execution time by up to 98% across multiple datasets. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves an average $29.7\times$ reduction in energy consumption, demonstrating its effectiveness for programmable and efficient edge AI systems.

AI.tldr: A domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor tailored for Tsetlin Machine inference is proposed, achieving up to 98% execution time reduction and 29.7× average energy savings compared to a baseline RV32IM core, while outperforming Binarized Neural Networks in accuracy on edge AI tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing TM accelerator designs rely on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, which limit flexibility and ease of programming. There is a need for a programmable yet efficient architecture for TM inference at the edge.
AI.method: The authors design a reduced instruction subset RISC-V microprocessor by profiling TM inference workloads to guide instruction reduction, then simplifying the datapath and control paths accordingly. Both the baseline RV32IM and the proposed reduced core are evaluated against Binarized Neural Networks across multiple datasets.
AI.result: TM achieves up to 88.18% accuracy on CIFAR-2 vs. 60.0% for BNNs. The proposed core reduces execution time by up to 98% and achieves an average 29.7× reduction in energy consumption compared to the baseline RV32IM core.
AI.conclusion: The domain-specific RISC-V approach effectively balances programmability with performance and energy efficiency for TM inference, making it well-suited for programmable edge AI systems.

title: LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents
summary: Policy-adherent tool-calling agents in customer-service domains must maintain task states across turns while calling tools and obeying domain policies. Task states consist of relevant facts, identifiers, constraints, and conditions observed through user interaction and tool calls. In standard agents, task states are not represented separately. Observations, tool returns, and policy instructions are placed in the prompt, leaving agents to reconstruct the relevant states from the prompt each time they decide what to do next. This design makes state management implicit, creating two common failure modes. An agent may retrieve the right facts but later ground its decision in stale, missing, or incorrect information; and a syntactically valid tool call may still violate a domain policy that depends on the current task state. We introduce \textsc{LedgerAgent}, an inference-time method for tool-calling agents that maintains observed task states in a separate ledger and renders the states into the prompt. The ledger is also used to check state-dependent policy constraints before environment-changing tool calls are executed, blocking policy violations. Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, \textsc{LedgerAgent} improves average pass\textasciicircum{}k over a standard prompt-based tool-calling approach, with the largest gains under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.

AI.tldr: LedgerAgent introduces a dedicated state ledger for tool-calling agents to explicitly track task states across turns, using it both to render relevant state into prompts and to enforce policy constraints before executing tool calls, reducing state-management failures.
AI.motivation: Standard tool-calling agents embed all observations and policy instructions directly in the prompt, forcing implicit state reconstruction at each decision step.
