This causes two failure modes: (1) grounding decisions in stale or incorrect information despite retrieving relevant facts, and (2) making syntactically valid tool calls that violate domain policies dependent on current task state.
AI.method: LedgerAgent maintains an explicit, separate ledger of observed task states (facts, identifiers, constraints, conditions) during inference. The ledger is used in two ways: (1) it renders relevant states into the prompt so the agent does not need to reconstruct them from raw conversation history, and (2) it checks state-dependent policy constraints before executing any environment-changing tool call, blocking those that would violate domain policies.
AI.result: Across four customer-service domains and a panel of both open- and closed-weight models, LedgerAgent improves average pass^k over standard prompt-based tool-calling approaches, with the largest gains observed under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicit state management via a dedicated ledger significantly improves the reliability and policy adherence of tool-calling agents, particularly when evaluated under stringent consistency requirements.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing
summary: Reservoir computing offers a lightweight framework for forecasting dynamical systems but may struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to limited representational capacity. Conventional reservoir computing recurrently uses trainable reservoirs with hyperparameter sensitivity, while the next-generation reservoir computing removes recurrence at the cost of rapidly growing feature dimensions. Here, we develop Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing (KARC), which replaces reservoirs with explicit basis-function expansions inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. We rigorously show that KARC is a lightweight design of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs), preserving the potential expressive capacity of KANs while admitting efficient closed-form training of reservoir computing. At comparable cost, KARC outperforms existing reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks including partial differential equations. It can also be integrated with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation. This work thus establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and KANs, enabling efficient and high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting.

AI.tldr: KARC replaces reservoir computing's trainable reservoirs with explicit basis-function expansions from the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, creating a lightweight KAN variant that enables closed-form training while outperforming existing reservoir methods on PDE forecasting and text-to-image generation.
AI.motivation: Reservoir computing struggles with long-range dependencies due to limited representational capacity. Conventional RC has hyperparameter sensitivity, while next-generation RC suffers from rapidly growing feature dimensions. There is a need for a method that balances expressive capacity with efficient, stable training.
AI.method: KARC replaces recurrent reservoirs with explicit basis-function expansions inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. It is formally derived as a lightweight design of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) that preserves KANs' expressive capacity while admitting the efficient closed-form training characteristic of reservoir computing.
AI.result: At comparable computational cost, KARC outperforms existing reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks including partial differential equations. It also successfully integrates with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and KANs, demonstrating that replacing reservoirs with basis-function expansions yields efficient, high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting with closed-form training.

title: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
summary: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeech-TTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models

AI.tldr: First application of cross-attention attribution (DAAM) to speech diffusion TTS, analyzing 3,600 caption-transcript pairs to reveal how style caption tokens influence acoustic output across layers and ODE steps, uncovering key findings about global conditioning, F0/energy correlation, and peak selectivity at layer 17.
AI.motivation: Style-captioned TTS systems lack interpretability: it is unknown how individual words in natural language style captions influence acoustic output. This opacity hinders failure diagnosis and controllability improvements in expressive TTS.
AI.method: The authors adapt DAAM (Diffusion Attentive Attribution Maps) from the image domain to speech diffusion models for the first time, applying it to CapSpeech-TTS. They extract per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps, analyzing 3,600 combinations (120 style captions × 30 text transcripts) using cross-attention attribution.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Style tokens exhibit lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning behavior. (2) Style attention correlates with F0 and energy. (3) Style conditioning peaks in early ODE steps and deep layers. (4) Attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, which co-occurs with the style importance peak — indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models, providing crucial interpretability insights for diagnosing failure modes and guiding future improvements in controllable, expressive TTS.

title: Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR): Function-Preserving SVD Compression for LLMs
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Resource-Adaptive Foundation Model Inference (AdaptFM), Seoul, South Korea (non-archival)
summary: We present Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR), an SVD-based LLM compression framework that guides each weight matrix's low-rank approximation with a backward-signal influence metric. Starting from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM(W), AIR runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates influence element-wise under a monotone-descent guarantee. AIR is layer-local and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods: alone it exceeds ACIP, and AIR+LoRA outperforms it further. AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at <=60% parameter retention, matches its quality with ~90% less calibration data, and turns parameter savings into FLOP, peak-memory, and per-token latency gains.

AI.tldr: AIR is an SVD-based LLM compression method that uses a backward-signal influence metric to guide low-rank approximation, improving perplexity by >18% over SVD-LLM(W) at ≤60% parameter retention while reducing calibration data needs by ~90%.
AI.motivation: Existing SVD-based LLM compression methods (e.g., SVD-LLM) rely on activation-aware weighting to preserve forward-pass fidelity, but they neglect backward-signal influence — how errors in each weight element propagate through training dynamics. AIR addresses this gap by incorporating an influence metric derived from the backward pass to better guide low-rank approximation.
AI.method: AIR starts from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM(W) and applies a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates an element-wise backward-signal influence metric into the low-rank factorization. The method is layer-local (no end-to-end pipeline required) and guarantees monotonic descent. It also composes orthogonally with downstream methods like LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.result: AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at ≤60% parameter retention. It matches SVD-LLM(W) quality while using ~90% less calibration data. Alone it exceeds ACIP; combined with LoRA, performance improves further. Gains translate into FLOP reduction, peak-memory savings, and per-token latency improvements.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating backward-signal influence into SVD-based compression yields significant quality improvements at aggressive compression ratios. AIR's layer-local design and orthogonal composability with fine-tuning methods make it a practical, plug-and-play component for LLM deployment optimization.

title: Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift
summary: Calibration aligns a model's predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how MoE models behave under distribution shift, focusing on how routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration. We show that expert calibration is sufficient to ensure calibration of the overall model under a broad class of distribution shifts in hard-routed models, but is insufficient for calibrating soft-routed models. To address this, we propose an adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift, and we demonstrate that it improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult subsets of the data, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: The paper studies calibration in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models under distribution shift. It shows expert-level calibration is sufficient for hard-routed but not soft-routed MoE. The authors propose adversarial reweighting to penalize routing-level calibration errors, improving the accuracy-calibration tradeoff across diverse settings.
AI.motivation: While calibration at the individual predictor level has been shown to improve ensemble and MoE performance, the theoretical conditions under which calibration benefits MoE models—particularly under distribution shift—remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze how routing mechanisms (hard vs. soft) interact with expert-level calibration under distribution shift. They prove sufficiency results for hard-routed models and identify failure modes in soft-routed models. They then propose an adversarial reweighting objective that directly penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate, designed to be robust to distribution shift.
AI.result: Expert calibration guarantees overall model calibration under broad distribution shifts for hard-routed MoE, but not for soft-routed MoE. The proposed adversarial reweighting method improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult data subsets, across different model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Expert calibration alone is insufficient for soft-routed MoE under distribution shift; explicitly optimizing for calibration of the routed aggregate via adversarial reweighting resolves this, yielding better-calibrated and more accurate models robustly.

title: Connect the Dots: Training LLMs for Long-Lifecycle Agents with Cross-Domain Generalization Via Reinforcement Learning
comment: Work in progress; we will continuously update the codebase and arXiv version
summary: This work presents a general framework for training large language models (LLMs) to "Connect the Dots" (CoD), a meta-capability required by long-lifecycle agents: as an LLM-based AI agent gets deployed in an environment, it solves a long sequence of tasks while continuously exploring the environment, learning from its own experiences, and iteratively self-updating its context about the environment, thereby achieving progressively better performance on future tasks conditioned on the updated context. Major components of the CoD framework include: (1) algorithm design and infrastructure for end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) with long rollout sequences interleaving solve-task and update-context episodes; (2) tasks and environments for incentivizing and eliciting the targeted meta-capability in LLMs during training, as well as for faithfully measuring progress during evaluation. We present proof-of-concept implementations of the CoD framework, including a GRPO-style RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment, as well as tasks and environments tailored to the targeted meta-capability (rather than domain-specific LLM capabilities or standard task-by-task RL). Empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting, and demonstrate the potential for out-of-distribution generalization -- within the training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings -- of the elicited meta-capability. Our investigation of CoD connects several lines of prior works, and opens up new opportunities for advancing LLMs and AI agents. To facilitate further research and applications, we release our implementations at \url{https://github.com/agentscope-ai/Trinity-RFT/tree/research/cod/examples/research_cod}.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CoD (Connect the Dots), a reinforcement learning framework for training LLMs as long-lifecycle agents that continuously explore, learn from experience, and self-update environmental context to improve performance on sequential tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based AI agents deployed over long lifecycles must chain together exploration, learning from past experiences, and context updating — a meta-capability not addressed by standard RL paradigms that treat tasks in isolation.
AI.method: The CoD framework combines (1) end-to-end RL with GRPO-style credit assignment over long rollout sequences interleaving solve-task and update-context episodes, and (2) custom tasks/environments specifically designed to incentivize and measure the targeted meta-capability rather than domain-specific skills.
AI.result: Empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL training under CoD, demonstrating out-of-distribution generalization of the elicited meta-capability across domains within training, to different domains, and to Ralph-loop settings.
AI.conclusion: CoD connects multiple prior research threads and opens new directions for advancing LLM-based agents. The authors release their implementation publicly to facilitate further research.

title: Human-AI Agent Interaction in a Business Context
comment: 9 pages, 5 tables, 1 figure, submitted to Springer Nature
summary: As AI agents are increasingly integrated into core business processes, understanding and designing effective interaction patterns between humans and AI agents becomes crucial for value creation. This study identifies and evaluates principles and criteria for a positive User Experience (UX) with AI agents, along with methods for its measurement. We identify user expectations and needs to facilitate adoption, build trust, and support user-centered decision-making by development teams. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative techniques, we explore interaction patterns between humans and AI agents. The findings from this exploratory research serve as the basis to develop a survey experiment which evaluates the effectiveness of specific design elements on a larger scale. This foundational research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings.

AI.tldr: This study investigates design principles and evaluation criteria for positive user experience (UX) with AI agents in business contexts, using a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative techniques. The exploratory research aims to identify user expectations, build trust, and support user-centered decision-making, with findings informing a subsequent large-scale survey experiment.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become embedded in core business processes, there is a pressing need to understand and design effective human-AI interaction patterns. Without clear principles and measurement methods, adoption may be hindered by poor UX, lack of trust, and misalignment with user expectations.
AI.method: The study employs a mixed-methods approach integrating qualitative and quantitative techniques. It begins with exploratory research to identify interaction patterns, user expectations, and needs. These findings then serve as the foundation for developing a survey experiment to evaluate specific design elements at scale.
AI.result: The paper reports that exploratory research yielded foundational insights into human-AI agent interaction patterns, user expectations, and needs. These results provide the basis for a larger-scale survey experiment (not yet reported in this abstract), which will evaluate the effectiveness of specific UX design elements.
AI.conclusion: This foundational research contributes to developing more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings by providing empirically grounded principles and criteria for UX design and measurement, thereby facilitating adoption, trust, and user-centered development.

title: StreamKL: Fast and Memory-Efficient KL Divergence for Boosting Attention Distillation
summary: Attention distillation, which trains one attention distribution to match another by minimizing their Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, is widely used in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training. However, existing approaches materialize both attention distributions before computing the KL reduction, incurring $O(N_QN_K)$ memory and IO costs that become prohibitive at long context lengths. We present StreamKL, the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates this quadratic materialization. StreamKL derives a novel online formulation for the coupled two-distribution KL reduction, enabling a single one-pass forward kernel that streams query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM. For the backward pass, StreamKL recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile, avoiding storage of quadratic intermediates. We further design and implement efficient GPU kernels with dedicated optimizations. Experiments show StreamKL delivers up to $43\times$ and $14\times$ speedups over baseline methods in the forward and backward passes, respectively. Most importantly, StreamKL reduces the extra HBM footprint of attention distillation from $O(N_QN_K)$ to $O(1)$, enabling long-context distillation on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: StreamKL is a fused GPU primitive that computes the KL divergence between two attention distributions in a single streaming pass, eliminating the $O(N_Q N_K)$ memory materialization overhead. It achieves up to 43× forward and 14× backward speedups and reduces HBM footprint to $O(1)$, enabling long-context attention distillation on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Attention distillation via KL divergence is widely used but requires materializing both attention matrices, incurring $O(N_Q N_K)$ memory and IO costs. This quadratic overhead becomes prohibitive at long context lengths, severely limiting the applicability of attention distillation in large-scale LLMs.
AI.method: StreamKL introduces a novel online formulation that decomposes the coupled two-distribution KL reduction into a single fused forward kernel, streaming query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM. For the backward pass, attention probabilities are recomputed tile-by-tile to avoid storing quadratic intermediates. Dedicated GPU kernel optimizations are designed for both passes.
AI.result: StreamKL achieves up to 43× speedup in the forward pass and 14× in the backward pass over baseline methods. Critically, it reduces the extra HBM footprint from $O(N_Q N_K)$ to $O(1)$, enabling attention distillation at long context lengths that were previously infeasible on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: StreamKL fundamentally solves the memory bottleneck of attention distillation, making it practical for long-context scenarios on resource-constrained hardware. The streaming, fusion-based approach demonstrates that quadratic materialization is unnecessary for KL-based attention distillation.

title: VIMPO: Value-Implicit Policy Optimization for LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a central tool for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but current methods face a trade-off between simplicity and credit assignment. Group-relative methods such as GRPO avoid training a critic, but typically assign a trajectory-level advantage to every token. Actor-critic methods provide denser learning signals, but require a learned value function with its own training instability. We introduce VIMPO, a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized reinforcement learning. For autoregressive generation, the resulting value recurrence can be written in terms of policy-reference log-ratios and anchored by the terminal condition that no future reward remains at the end of a trajectory. This gives a simple value loss that incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards without training a critic. The same derivation also yields a critic-free actor advantage, allowing VIMPO to separate reward incorporation through the value loss from policy improvement through a PPO-style actor update. On mathematical RLVR benchmarks, VIMPO improves over GRPO across MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with especially larger gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO retains a consistent advantage over GRPO, suggesting that policy-implied value optimization can provide finer credit assignment while preserving the practical simplicity of critic-free training.

AI.tldr: VIMPO is a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a value function from the policy itself using KL-regularized RL optimality conditions. It separates reward incorporation (via a simple value loss) from policy improvement (via PPO-style updates), achieving finer credit assignment than GRPO without the instability of actor-critic methods. It outperforms GRPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, especially under noisy rewards.
AI.motivation: Current reinforcement learning for verifiable rewards (RLVR) faces a trade-off: GRPO is simple but assigns only trajectory-level advantages to every token (poor credit assignment), while actor-critic methods provide token-level signals but require a learned critic with training instability. The authors aim to achieve fine-grained credit assignment while preserving critic-free simplicity.
AI.method: VIMPO derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL. For autoregressive generation, this yields a value recurrence expressed in terms of policy-reference log-ratios, anchored by a terminal condition of zero future reward. This produces a critic-free value loss that incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards. A critic-free actor advantage is also derived, enabling a PPO-style actor update decoupled from reward incorporation.
AI.result: VIMPO outperforms GRPO on MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with particularly large gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy reward conditions, VIMPO maintains a consistent advantage over GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Policy-implied value optimization (VIMPO) provides finer credit assignment than group-relative methods like GRPO while retaining the practical simplicity of critic-free training, offering an effective middle ground in the RLVR design space.

title: Self-Adaptive Scale Handling for Forecasting Time Series with Scale Heterogeneity
comment: This is the full version of the paper accepted by the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP). The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF
summary: Current time series forecasting (TSF) research predominantly focuses on scale-homogeneous data, where different time series share similar numerical magnitude ranges. However, in real-world industrial scenarios such as financial product sales, different time series often differ by orders of magnitude (scale heterogeneity). Since these series share similar temporal patterns, joint modeling is desirable for better data utilization, yet existing scaling methods either compress low-scale signals (global normalization) or destroy semantic discriminability and amplify inverse-scaling errors (window-based scaling). This paper proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module that learns adaptive scale factors tailored to each input, preserving semantic discriminability while reducing inverse-scaling errors. AS consists of Scale Calibrating (SC), which calibrates prior mean scaling factors through neural networks, and Scaling Selection (SS), which decides whether to apply calibration or retain the original factor, avoiding over-calibration. Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay show that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their performance. The code and dataset are available at the link https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AS (self-Adaptive Scale-handling), a module that learns per-input adaptive scaling factors for time series forecasting under scale heterogeneity, using Scale Calibrating and Scaling Selection components; it consistently improves TSF model performance on real-world financial sales data.
AI.motivation: Real-world industrial time series (e.g., financial product sales) exhibit scale heterogeneity — different series differ by orders of magnitude but share similar temporal patterns. Joint modeling is desirable for data efficiency, but existing scaling approaches fail: global normalization compresses low-scale signals, while window-based scaling destroys semantic discriminability and amplifies inverse-scaling errors.
AI.method: The proposed AS module has two components: (1) Scale Calibrating (SC), which uses neural networks to calibrate prior mean scaling factors, and (2) Scaling Selection (SS), which adaptively decides whether to apply the calibrated factor or retain the original, preventing over-calibration. The module is model-agnostic and integrates into existing TSF architectures.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay demonstrate that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their forecasting performance.
AI.conclusion: The AS module effectively addresses scale heterogeneity in time series forecasting, enabling better joint modeling of multi-scale series without the drawbacks of existing normalization methods, and has practical value in industrial financial applications.

title: Hierarchical Control in Multi-Agent Games: LLM-based Planning and RL Execution
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong performance in sequential decision-making, yet scaling to complex multi-agent environments remains challenging due to sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the difficulty of learning coordinated strategies. We propose a hierarchical architecture where a pretrained large language model (LLM) acts as a centralized strategic controller that selects among specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents, while RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. We evaluate this hybrid system in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) and \emph{``Flat''} RL (end-to-end training without skill decomposition) baselines. The LLM+RL system achieves task performance statistically equivalent to hand-crafted BT (46.4\% vs 51.5\% win rate, $p=0.103$) while both significantly outperform Flat RL trained without skill decomposition. A user study ($n=15$) reveals that 60\% of participants perceive LLM+RL agents as the most human-like ($p=0.027$), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability. These results demonstrate that pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills, achieving competitive multi-agent coordination and superior perceived believability without manual rule engineering.

AI.tldr: A hybrid LLM+RL system uses a pretrained LLM as a strategic controller selecting from specialized RL skill policies, achieving competitive performance against hand-crafted behavior trees in a 2v2 game and superior human-likeness ratings, without manual rule engineering.
AI.motivation: Scaling RL to complex multi-agent environments is difficult due to sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the challenge of learning coordinated strategies. The authors aim to leverage LLM reasoning to overcome these limitations by providing high-level strategic orchestration of low-level RL skills.
AI.method: A hierarchical architecture where a pretrained LLM serves as a centralized strategic controller that selects among specialized, pretrained RL skill policies for a team of agents. RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. Evaluated in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) baselines and "Flat" RL (end-to-end training without skill decomposition). A user study (n=15) assessed perceived human-likeness.
AI.result: LLM+RL achieved a 46.4% win rate vs. BT's 51.5% (statistically equivalent, p=0.103), both significantly outperforming Flat RL. In the user study, 60% of participants rated LLM+RL agents as most human-like (p=0.027), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills for multi-agent coordination, achieving competitive performance and superior perceived believability without manual rule engineering.

title: Adaptive Distance-Aware Trunk Deep Operator Learning for Long-Span Roadway Bridges
summary: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated FE analysis computationally expensive for applications such as influence surface generation and structural digital twins. Existing SciML approaches struggle to accurately capture these localized responses. To address this challenge, this study proposes an adaptive-trunk DeepONet for localized structural response prediction in large-scale bridge systems. The framework dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain using a KNN strategy, allowing the network to focus on structural influence zones. The trunk network is further enhanced using distance-aware features that encode the geometric relationship between the load and structural nodes. A physics-based full-field reconstruction is incorporated through a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation, enabling predictions at adaptive nodes to be extended to the entire structural domain. To enable scalable training, response data are generated using a reduced-order equivalent shell model that preserves the dominant global behavior while significantly reducing computational cost. The proposed framework is validated on both a benchmark bridge model and the real-world Mussafah Bridge. Results show that the method achieves FEM-level accuracy with relative errors below 5%, while reducing the total response evaluation time (including full-field reconstruction) by approximately 60x; excluding the post-processing reconstruction step, the AD-DeepONet inference is up to four orders of magnitude faster than FEM. In addition, the framework enables rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading configurations, demonstrating strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive-trunk DeepONet that uses KNN-based dynamic domain construction, distance-aware features, and a Schur complement reconstruction to predict localized structural responses in long-span bridges up to 4 orders of magnitude faster than FEM with <5% error.
AI.motivation: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated full FEM analysis computationally prohibitive for influence surface generation and digital twin applications. Existing SciML methods fail to accurately capture these localized responses.
AI.method: An adaptive-trunk DeepONet is proposed with: (1) a KNN strategy that dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain focused on structural influence zones; (2) distance-aware features in the trunk network encoding geometric relationships between load and structural nodes; (3) a physics-based full-field reconstruction via a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation to extend predictions from adaptive nodes to the entire domain; and (4) a reduced-order equivalent shell model for scalable training data generation.
AI.result: Validated on a benchmark bridge and the real-world Mussafah Bridge: FEM-level accuracy with relative errors below 5%; total response evaluation time reduced by ~60x (including full-field reconstruction); AD-DeepONet inference alone is up to four orders of magnitude faster than FEM.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading, demonstrating strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

title: What Makes Effective Supervision in Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Information-Theoretic Analysis
summary: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) internalizes reasoning within continuous hidden states, offering a promising alternative to verbose discrete reasoning traces. However, robust latent reasoning remains difficult because outcome supervision provides weak learning signals and leaves latent trajectories prone to semantic drift. In this work, we analyze Latent CoT from an information-theoretic perspective and identify this failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in the latent space. We further decompose process supervision into two complementary dimensions: Trajectory Supervision, which injects dense stepwise reasoning signals, and Space Supervision, which preserves the semantic structure of the latent manifold. Our analysis shows that rigid geometric compression can collapse the reasoning space, whereas generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity. To measure these effects, we introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), which quantifies the mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments reveal a clear Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy depends on the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. These findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision and suggest shifting from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Supervision-in-Latent-CoT}{this repository}.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses failures in Latent Chain-of-Thought as a dual collapse (gradient attenuation and representational drift) and proposes two-dimensional process supervision—Trajectory Supervision and Space Supervision—finding that generative reconstruction outperforms rigid geometric compression for preserving reasoning fidelity.
AI.motivation: Latent CoT internalizes reasoning in continuous hidden states, but outcome supervision alone provides weak learning signals, causing semantic drift and unreliable reasoning. The authors aim to understand why this occurs and how to fix it through principled supervision.
AI.method: From an information-theoretic perspective, the authors diagnose Latent CoT failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in the latent space. They decompose process supervision into Trajectory Supervision (dense stepwise reasoning signals) and Space Supervision (preserving semantic structure of the latent manifold). They introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP) to measure mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps, comparing geometric compression against generative reconstruction as semantic anchors.
AI.result: Experiments reveal an "Information-Performance Binding": reasoning accuracy depends on the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. Generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor than rigid geometric compression, better preserving information capacity. The ULP effectively quantifies this relationship.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision, suggesting a shift from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization as the guiding objective for training latent CoT models.

title: Exploring the potential of AlphaEarth and TESSERA embeddings for Fine-scale Local Climate Zone Mapping: A case study across five cities in Switzerland
summary: Understanding urban spatial morphology is critical for climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable urban design, and Local Climate Zone (LCZ) mapping provides the basic framework for this. However, many cities still use coarse ~100-m resolution LCZ records, which are unsuitable for fine-scale urban research. In this study, precomputed embeddings from TESSERA (Feng et al., 2025) and AlphaEarth (Brown et al., 2025) are compared to traditional Sentinel-1/2 (S1S2) composites in five Swiss cities to see if they can upscale coarse LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net. Three experiments assess multi-city transferability, the impact of higher-resolution reference data, and temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. We find that all datasets achieve strong performance with test data Intersection-over-Union (IoU) ranging from 0.59-0.69 and 0.77-0.82 in the first two experiments. TESSERA consistently outperforms both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings As expected, we find that the transfer of embedding-based models from one year to another remains an open challenge. Overall, however, our results demonstrate the promising potential of embeddings derived from EO foundation models to reduce time consuming preprocessing, respectively, manual feature engineering tasks and to guide a universal deep learning-based LCZ mapping workflow. When combined with a simple location-aware attention U-Net architecture, the embeddings enhance regional transferability and scalability, supporting the development of comprehensive and reproducible fine-scale LCZ maps for global urban climate applications Improving reference data quality remains the strongest lever for further accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: This study compares foundation model embeddings (TESSERA, AlphaEarth) against traditional Sentinel-1/2 composites for upscaling coarse (~100 m) LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net across five Swiss cities. TESSERA consistently outperforms baselines (IoU: 0.59–0.82), but temporal transfer across years remains challenging. Reference data quality is identified as the key limiting factor.
AI.motivation: Many cities rely on ~100-m resolution Local Climate Zone (LCZ) maps, which are too coarse for fine-scale urban research (e.g., microclimate modeling, building-level risk assessment). The authors seek to leverage Earth observation foundation model embeddings to automate and improve the upscaling of coarse LCZ maps to 10-m resolution, reducing reliance on manual feature engineering and Sentinel-1/2 preprocessing.
AI.method: The authors employ an attention-based U-Net architecture to upscale LCZ maps from ~100 m to 10 m resolution. Three experiments are conducted: (1) multi-city transferability — training on some Swiss cities and testing on held-out ones; (2) impact of higher-resolution reference data; and (3) temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. Three input feature sets are compared: traditional Sentinel-1/2 composites, TESSERA embeddings (Feng et al., 2025), and AlphaEarth embeddings (Brown et al., 2025). Performance is evaluated using Intersection-over-Union (IoU).
AI.result: All datasets achieve strong performance: IoU of 0.59–0.69 for multi-city transfer and 0.77–0.82 when using higher-resolution reference data. TESSERA consistently outperforms both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings. Temporal transfer of embedding-based models across different years remains an open challenge, with performance degradation observed. Reference data quality is identified as the strongest lever for further accuracy improvements.
AI.conclusion: EO foundation model embeddings (especially TESSERA) demonstrate strong potential to streamline the LCZ mapping pipeline by reducing manual preprocessing and feature engineering. Combined with a simple location-aware attention U-Net, they enhance regional transferability and scalability toward global fine-scale LCZ mapping. However, temporal robustness across years remains unresolved, and improving reference data quality offers the greatest potential for future accuracy gains.

title: Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis using a Multimodal Approach with 3D MRI and PET
comment: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible neurodegenerative disorder and a leading cause of death worldwide. Early diagnosis plays an important part especially at the Mild Cognitive Impairment stage, where timely intervention can help slow its progression before it advances to AD. Neuroimaging data, like Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans, can help detect brain changes early by providing structural and functional brain changes related to the disease. Yet, many multimodal models still fuse MRI and PET with static concatenation and apply identical computation to all subjects, which limits robustness to patient/site heterogeneity and can waste computation. To address these limitations, we present the first study of combining 3D convolutional feature extractors with three fusion strategies - concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and gated self-attention - and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier that performs input-adaptive routing, activating only the most informative experts per case. Finally, we utilize Grad-CAM to visualize disease-related regions, ensuring model interpretability. Experiments are performed across three binary classification tasks (NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD). Results show that GMU achieves accuracies of 80.46 % (NC vs. MCI) and 95.47 % (NC vs. AD), while gated self-attention attains 82.08 % on MCI vs. AD. Ablations show that removing the MoE consistently degrades accuracy across all tasks. These findings underscore the value of input-adaptive, multimodal modeling for AD diagnosis by leveraging the complementary nature of MRI and PET.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multimodal Alzheimer's disease diagnosis framework combining 3D convolutional feature extractors with three fusion strategies (concatenation, GMU, gated self-attention) and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts classifier for input-adaptive routing. Evaluated on three binary classification tasks (NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, NC vs. AD), GMU achieves 80.46% and 95.47% accuracy, while gated self-attention attains 82.08% on MCI vs. AD. Ablations confirm MoE consistently improves performance.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal models for AD diagnosis typically fuse MRI and PET via static concatenation and apply uniform computation across all subjects, which limits robustness to patient and site heterogeneity and wastes computational resources. There is a need for input-adaptive mechanisms that tailor computation per subject.
AI.method: The authors propose using 3D convolutional feature extractors for MRI and PET, combined with three fusion strategies: (1) standard concatenation, (2) Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and (3) gated self-attention. A sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier performs input-adaptive routing, selectively activating only the most relevant experts per case. Grad-CAM is employed for visualizing disease-related brain regions to ensure interpretability.
AI.result: On three binary classification tasks: GMU achieves 80.46% (NC vs. MCI) and 95.47% (NC vs. AD); gated self-attention achieves 82.08% (MCI vs. AD). Ablation studies demonstrate that removing the MoE classifier consistently degrades accuracy across all tasks.
AI.conclusion: Input-adaptive, multimodal modeling leveraging complementary MRI and PET data, particularly with gated fusion mechanisms and MoE routing, significantly improves AD diagnosis performance. The work underscores the importance of tailoring computation to individual subjects for robustness and efficiency.

title: Comparative Study of Neural Surrogate Architectures for Autoregressive Prediction of Internal Battery States
summary: The Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model resolves internal electrochemical states in lithium-ion batteries with high fidelity. However, the numerical solution of its governing equations is computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment, limiting scalability from individual cells to pack and fleet-scale applications. While machine learning surrogates can substantially reduce inference latency through GPU acceleration, most existing approaches learn solution approximations tied to specific operating conditions rather than learning generalizable state-evolution dynamics. This work presents a systematic comparison of four neural network architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators that predict full DFN internal states across a wide range of operating conditions. To ensure a controlled architectural comparison, all models are trained under a unified framework using multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning, isolating the impact of spatial inductive bias. Results demonstrate that the U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% averaged across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, while providing a 5.38x speed-up over the numerical solver. These findings highlight spatial inductive bias as a critical determinant of surrogate performance, advancing the development of surrogates for internal state observability for next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

AI.tldr: Four neural architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) are compared as autoregressive state-transition surrogates for the Doyle-Fuller-Newman battery model; U-Net achieves 3% nRMSE after 300-step rollouts with 5.38× speedup, highlighting spatial inductive bias as critical for surrogate performance.
AI.motivation: The DFN model provides high-fidelity internal electrochemical state resolution for Li-ion batteries but is computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment. Existing ML surrogates learn approximations tied to specific operating conditions rather than generalizable state-evolution dynamics, limiting scalability to pack- and fleet-level applications.
AI.method: Four neural architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, Fourier Neural Operator) are formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators predicting full DFN internal states. All models are trained under a unified framework with multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning to isolate the effect of spatial inductive bias in a controlled comparison.
AI.result: U-Net achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts and provides a 5.38× speed-up over the numerical solver. Spatial inductive bias emerges as a critical determinant of surrogate performance.
AI.conclusion: Spatial inductive bias is critical for developing performant DFN surrogates. U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy makes it the most effective architecture among those tested, advancing internal state observability for next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

title: PaAno+: Multiscale Encoding and Cross-Variable Attention for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Time-series anomaly detection has significant practical value for industrial and medical monitoring, as well as other critical domains. Current Transformer- and large-model-based detection approaches incur excessive computational overhead, while existing lightweight alternatives are constrained by insufficient feature extraction and inadequate modeling of dependencies across multivariate variables. To mitigate the above drawbacks, this study develops a lightweight, efficient anomaly detection model, dubbed PaAno, within the patch-oriented representation learning paradigm. In the encoder module, a multiscale feature-extraction backbone is constructed using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields to capture hierarchical temporal characteristics; subsequent cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation, combined with residual connection optimization, further stabilizes feature representation learning. A cross-variable fusion attention module is embedded to explicitly characterize inter-variable correlations, empowering the model to identify anomalous patterns amid intricate operational conditions. Moreover, a novel pretext task based on temporal patch-window sorting is customized to uncover intrinsic structural properties of time series, and triplet loss is leveraged to optimize the patch embedding space for enhanced feature discrimination. Extensive experiments on the TSB-AD benchmark demonstrate that the proposed PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate tasks, yielding significant performance gains across evaluation metrics, including VUS-PR, relative to the original PaAno. Leveraging a compact network design, the presented model achieves favorable computational efficiency, enabling deployment on resource-limited terminals for real-time anomaly inference.

AI.tldr: PaAno is a lightweight, patch-oriented anomaly detection model for time-series that uses multiscale convolutional encoders, cross-variable fusion attention, and a novel temporal patch-window sorting pretext task with triplet loss to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on TSB-AD while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for resource-limited deployment.
AI.motivation: Current Transformer- and large-model-based time-series anomaly detectors are computationally prohibitive, while existing lightweight methods suffer from insufficient feature extraction and weak modeling of inter-variable dependencies in multivariate settings. There is a need for a model that balances high detection accuracy with low computational cost for real-time deployment on resource-constrained terminals.
AI.method: The paper proposes PaAno, built on patch-oriented representation learning. Key components: (1) A multiscale feature-extraction encoder using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields for hierarchical temporal features, augmented with cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation and residual connections. (2) A cross-variable fusion attention module that explicitly models inter-variable correlations. (3) A novel pretext task — temporal patch-window sorting — that reveals intrinsic structural properties of time series, combined with triplet loss to optimize the patch embedding space for enhanced feature discrimination.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the TSB-AD benchmark show PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate anomaly detection tasks. It yields significant performance gains across evaluation metrics including VUS-PR relative to the original baseline, while maintaining favorable computational efficiency due to its compact network design.
AI.conclusion: PaAno successfully bridges the gap between lightweight efficiency and high detection performance in time-series anomaly detection. Its compact architecture enables deployment on resource-limited terminals for real-time anomaly inference, making it practically viable for industrial and medical monitoring applications.

title: Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics
summary: Perception for action suggests that representations of the world should be shaped not by visual fidelity alone, but by their relevance for actions. At the same time, latent JEPA-style world models advocate learning compact predictive states from high-dimensional observations to facilitate the prediction of future states, but end-to-end training of these models is nontrivial because representations may collapse if our only goal is to construct a latent state that is easy to predict. We introduce a sensorimotor world model (SMWM): a latent world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization. This single regularizer addresses both issues: it prevents representation collapse and induces action-aligned representations. By forcing latent states to preserve information about the action underlying a transition, it biases the model toward the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment while discarding uncontrollable distractors. This yields stable latent world models trained from offline, reward-free trajectories, without frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers. Empirically, SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and enables competitive planning performance across simple 2D and 3D control tasks.

AI.tldr: SMWM introduces a sensorimotor world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization, which simultaneously prevents representational collapse and induces action-aligned latent representations for planning and control.
AI.motivation: Two key challenges in world model learning are addressed: (1) representations should be shaped by action relevance, not just visual fidelity (perception for action); (2) end-to-end training of latent predictive models (e.g., JEPA-style) suffers from representational collapse when the sole objective is easy predictability of future states.
AI.method: The Sensorimotor World Model (SMWM) is a latent world model trained end-to-end with a single regularizer: inverse dynamics prediction. At each transition, the latent states must preserve information about the action that caused the transition. This forces the representation to align with controllable degrees of freedom while discarding uncontrollable distractors. Training uses offline, reward-free trajectories and requires no frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers.
AI.result: SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and achieves competitive planning performance on simple 2D and 3D control tasks. The inverse dynamics regularizer alone is sufficient to prevent collapse and produce stable, action-aligned representations.
AI.conclusion: A single inverse dynamics regularization term elegantly solves both representation collapse and action-alignment in end-to-end latent world model training, yielding a parsimonious architecture that matches competitive methods while being simpler to implement.

title: Quantile of Means: A Bonus-Free Ensemble Method for Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning
summary: Optimal Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms typically rely on carefully constructed count-based uncertainty estimates to drive exploration. Although theoretically sound, such estimates are hard to compute in practical settings and therefore offer limited insight for designing exploration heuristics. Meanwhile, ensembling has emerged as a practical approach, but remains without theoretical justification. Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, we propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Our simple count-free approach achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, providing theoretical grounding for ensemble-based exploration in RL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon MDPs that achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds without using count-based uncertainty estimates, providing theoretical justification for ensemble-based exploration in RL.
AI.motivation: Optimal RL algorithms rely on count-based uncertainty estimates that are theoretically sound but impractical to compute. Ensembling is a practical heuristic for exploration but lacks theoretical grounding. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a theoretically justified ensemble-based method.
AI.method: The authors propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon MDPs, building on a recent ensemble-based approach for Multi-Armed Bandits. The method is count-free and leverages quantile statistics from an ensemble of value estimates to drive exploration.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, matching the theoretical guarantees of count-based methods while using a simpler ensemble-based mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based exploration can be theoretically grounded and achieve optimal performance in RL. The quantile-based ensemble approach provides a principled alternative to count-based uncertainty estimation for finite-horizon MDPs.

title: When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital: Federated Conformal Risk Control via Risk-Curve Shrinkage
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the DeCaF Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees on segmentation quality by calibrating a prediction-set threshold on held-out data. In federated deployments, the standard approach pools calibration scores across sites into a single threshold. We provide the first quantification, on real multi-institutional brain tumor data (FeTS-2022, 1,251 subjects, 20 institutions), showing that this naive pooled CRC protects the average hospital but violates coverage at 40% of individual institutions, with the worst site exceeding the target false-negative rate by 7.8 percentage points. The naive alternative, per-site local CRC, largely restores coverage but inflates prediction sets by 83x, rendering them clinically useless. We propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol: each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. A single hyperparameter n0 smoothly trades worst-case coverage for prediction-set efficiency; leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis identifies n0=19, achieving 2.7/20 violations at 2.0x stretch. We further show that direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets fails, concentrating risk on vulnerable hospitals, and that the finite-sample correction term is essential: removing it triples violations. The marginal CRC guarantee is preserved by construction under the stated site-mixture assumption; per-site coverage is validated across four targets with three seeds. No patient-level images, masks, or per-volume scores leave any site.

AI.tldr: Federated conformal risk control (CRC) with standard pooled calibration fails to provide per-institution coverage guarantees, violating coverage at 40% of sites. The authors propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol that transmits only empirical risk curves (G scalars) per site, using a single hyperparameter to trade worst-case coverage against prediction-set efficiency, while preserving privacy by never sharing patient-level data.
AI.motivation: Standard pooled CRC in federated settings only protects the average hospital, leaving individual institutions vulnerable to coverage violations. Per-site local CRC restores coverage but inflates prediction sets by 83x, making them clinically useless. There is a need for a federated approach that balances per-site coverage guarantees with clinically usable prediction-set sizes.
AI.method: Each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a central server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. A single hyperparameter n0 controls the trade-off between worst-case coverage and prediction-set efficiency, with regularization shrinking site-specific thresholds toward a global value. The method includes a finite-sample correction term and preserves the marginal CRC guarantee under a site-mixture assumption. Leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis is used to select n0.
AI.result: On FeTS-2022 data (1,251 subjects, 20 institutions): naive pooled CRC violates coverage at 40% of institutions (worst site exceeds target FNR by 7.8 pp); per-site local CRC inflates sets 83x. The proposed method with n0=19 achieves only 2.7/20 violations at 2.0x stretch. Direct Lagrangian optimization fails, concentrating risk on vulnerable hospitals. Removing the finite-sample correction triples violations. Per-site coverage validated across four targets with three seeds.
AI.conclusion: The shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol effectively balances per-institution coverage guarantees with prediction-set efficiency, outperforming both naive pooled CRC and per-site local CRC. The method maintains strict privacy (no patient-level data leaves any site), and the marginal CRC guarantee is preserved by construction.

title: Multi-Modal Contrastive Learning for Implicit Earth Embeddings via Location Tying
summary: Spatial prediction tasks are often limited by a lack of high-quality labelled ground-truth observations. To overcome this challenge, self-supervised pre-training is a possible solution, with contrastive learning dominant for location encoders. Those approaches usually align geographic coordinates with just one additional modality. We propose two multimodal contrastive learning architectures: Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying (MELT) and Sequential Alternating Location Training (SALT). These architectures expand this framework beyond two modalities by utilising unpaired geospatial data. Both methods are technically viable and match the performance of the strongest two-modality baseline (SATCLIP) across four downstream tasks. However, increasing the number of modalities does not consistently improve performance, suggesting that the chosen location encoder is the main limitation - the contrastive objective reaches its peak early, regardless of modality diversity or pre-training volume. MELT provides more stable training than SALT and presents a stronger foundation for future scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two multimodal contrastive learning architectures (MELT and SALT) for self-supervised location encoder pre-training using unpaired geospatial data. Both match the best two-modality baseline but adding more modalities does not consistently improve performance, suggesting the location encoder is the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Spatial prediction tasks suffer from scarce high-quality labelled ground-truth data. While self-supervised contrastive learning has emerged as a solution for pre-training location encoders, existing approaches are limited to aligning coordinates with only one additional modality. The authors aim to extend this to multiple modalities using unpaired geospatial data.
AI.method: Two architectures are proposed: MELT (Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying), which ties all modality embeddings through a shared location encoder in a joint contrastive objective; and SALT (Sequential Alternating Location Training), which alternates training between different modality pairs sequentially. Both leverage unpaired geospatial data and are benchmarked against SATCLIP across four downstream tasks.
AI.result: Both MELT and SALT match SATCLIP's performance across four downstream tasks. However, increasing the number of modalities beyond two does not yield consistent performance gains. The contrastive objective saturates early regardless of modality diversity or pre-training data volume, indicating the location encoder architecture is the primary limiting factor. MELT exhibits more stable training than SALT.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal contrastive pre-training with unpaired geospatial data is technically viable, but simply adding modalities yields diminishing returns. Future work should focus on improving the location encoder rather than scaling modalities or data. MELT is recommended over SALT as a more stable foundation for future scaling efforts.

title: Predicting gestational age at birth in the context of preterm birth from multi-modal fetal MRI
comment: Accepted for publication at the Journal of Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging (MELBA) https://melba-journal.org/2026:013
summary: Preterm birth is associated with significant mortality and a risk for lifelong morbidity. The complex multifactorial aetiology hampers accurate prediction and thus optimal care. A pipeline consisting of bespoke machine learning methods for data imputation, feature selection, and regression models to predict gestational age (GA) at birth was developed and evaluated from comprehensive multi-modal morphological and functional fetal MRI data from 333 control cases and 93 preterm birth cases. The GA at birth predictions were classified into term and preterm categories and their accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were reported. An ablation study was performed to further validate the design of the pipeline. Performance was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The pipeline achieves an R2 score of 0.13 and a mean absolute error of 2.74 weeks. It also achieves a 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity across folds. The predominant features selected by the pipeline include cervical length and statistics derived from placental T2* values. The confluence of fast, motion-robust and multi-modal fetal MRI techniques and machine learning prediction allowed the prediction of the gestation at birth. This information is essential for any pregnancy. To the best of our knowledge, preterm birth had only been addressed as a classification problem in the literature. Therefore, this work provides a proof of concept. Future work will increase the cohort size to allow for finer stratification within the preterm birth cohort. Our code is available at https://github.com/dfajardorojas/ml-for-preterm-birth-.

AI.tldr: A machine learning pipeline using multi-modal fetal MRI data (333 controls, 93 preterm cases) predicts gestational age at birth with 0.77 accuracy for term/preterm classification. Key predictive features include cervical length and placental T2* statistics.
AI.motivation: Preterm birth carries high mortality and lifelong morbidity risk, yet its complex multifactorial etiology impairs accurate prediction. Better prediction would enable optimal clinical care.
AI.method: A bespoke ML pipeline combining data imputation, feature selection, and regression models was developed using comprehensive multi-modal morphological and functional fetal MRI from 333 controls and 93 preterm cases. Performance was evaluated via stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with an ablation study to validate pipeline design. Output was a continuous GA prediction subsequently dichotomized into term/preterm categories.
AI.result: The pipeline achieved R²=0.13, MAE=2.74 weeks for regression; classification yielded 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity. Dominant selected features were cervical length and placental T2* statistics.
AI.conclusion: This is the first work framing preterm birth prediction as a GA regression problem rather than solely classification, providing proof of concept. Future work requires larger cohorts for finer preterm stratification. Code is publicly available.

title: Computational Methods and Challenges in Cell-Free DNA Analysis for Multi-Cancer Early Detection
summary: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a promising avenue for non-invasive multicancer early detection (MCED), in that, it can enable multiple cancer detection simultaneously from a single blood draw, with particular sensitivity to cancers that currently lack established screening programs. Here we review the computational methods developed between 2022 and 2025 for cfDNA-based MCED. We focus on how fragmentomics and epigenetic features are extracted and analyzed to detect cancer at early stages. We first briefly outline the biological basis of cfDNA signals, then review classical statistical and machine learning approaches alongside deep learning frameworks including autoencoder-based models. For each method we discuss biological interpretability, validation strategy, and readiness for clinical integration. Furthermore, we categorize the current challenges into technical, computational, and methodological while outlining open problems in the field. This review shows that multimodal ensemble approaches have the strongest promise for clinical integration and the highest readiness. However, for better assessment of future work and side-by-side comparison, standardization of evaluation protocols and reporting results will be crucial.

AI.tldr: Review of computational methods (2022–2025) for cfDNA-based multicancer early detection (MCED), covering fragmentomic and epigenetic feature extraction, classical ML and deep learning approaches, with emphasis on biological interpretability, validation, clinical readiness, and standardization challenges.
AI.motivation: cfDNA enables non-invasive, simultaneous multi-cancer early detection from a single blood draw, especially for cancers lacking established screening programs. The rapid development of computational methods between 2022–2025 necessitates a systematic review to assess their maturity, interpretability, and readiness for clinical translation.
AI.method: The authors conducted a targeted literature review of computational methods for cfDNA-based MCED published between 2022 and 2025. They categorized approaches by feature type (fragmentomics, epigenetic signals), algorithmic paradigm (classical statistics, machine learning, deep learning including autoencoders), and evaluated each method along axes of biological interpretability, validation strategy, and clinical integration readiness.
AI.result: Multimodal ensemble approaches demonstrate the highest promise and readiness for clinical integration. The review also identifies persistent challenges across technical, computational, and methodological domains, and highlights the critical need for standardized evaluation protocols and reporting to enable fair comparison of future work.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal ensemble methods are currently best positioned for clinical deployment in cfDNA-based MCED. However, progress in the field hinges on establishing standardized benchmarks and transparent reporting practices to rigorously compare emerging computational strategies.

title: Effective Dimension Governs Generalization in Quantum Kernel Vision Models
summary: Recent quantum vision models-quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks-report two striking but unexplained empirical phenomena: (i) ansatze with more, or more uniformly distributed, entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve test accuracy rather than degrade it. These observations are currently treated as curiosities, discovered by grid search and explained, if at all, by hand. We show that both are manifestations of a single, measurable quantity: the \emph{effective dimension} $d_{\rm eff}$ of the (noise-shaped) quantum feature kernel. Working primarily with quantum-kernel vision models-a quantum feature map read out by a kernel classifier-we give a spectral account in which entanglement structure and quantum noise are two knobs that move $d_{\rm eff}$; in an overfitting regime, contracting $d_{\rm eff}$ acts as ridge-like regularization. We analyze the mechanism: an \emph{exact} decomposition of the depolarized kernel $K_p=(1-p)^2K+\tfrac{p(2-p)}{D}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ with $d_{\rm eff}(K_p)\to1$, a contraction result (and its boundary) for amplitude damping, a kernel-machine capacity bound, and a capacity/alignment risk decomposition; the monotone contraction operative in our entangled experiments is verified empirically, not proven in general. Along the one-parameter depolarizing family the collapse is instead exact by construction; we use it only to confirm the kernel decomposition to machine precision and at up to $12$ qubits, not as evidence for $d_{\rm eff}$. Amplitude damping contracts $d_{\rm eff}$ and lifts test accuracy by up to $+13\%$ along an inverted-U sweet spot; the effect's sign flips between the over- and under-fitting regimes; noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier. Our results organize two reported anecdotes into a single measurable principle for designing quantum-vision models.

AI.tldr: Two unexplained empirical phenomena in quantum vision models—more/uniform entanglement improves generalization, and quantum noise can boost test accuracy—are unified as manifestations of the effective dimension of the noise-shaped quantum feature kernel. Controlling entanglement structure and noise levels tunes effective dimension, which acts as ridge-like regularization in overfitting regimes.
AI.motivation: Two striking but unexplained empirical observations in quantum vision models (quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks) lack a unifying theoretical framework: (i) ansätze with more or more uniformly distributed entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve rather than degrade test accuracy. The authors aim to provide a single measurable principle explaining both phenomena.
AI.method: The authors work primarily with quantum-kernel vision models (quantum feature map plus kernel classifier) and provide a spectral analysis centered on the effective dimension d_eff of the quantum feature kernel. Key technical contributions include: (1) an exact decomposition of the depolarized kernel, (2) a contraction result for amplitude damping, (3) a kernel-machine capacity bound with a capacity/alignment risk decomposition, (4) empirical verification of monotone contraction under entangled experiments, and (5) demonstration that noise injection traces an explicit spectral-filtering frontier with an inverted-U sweet spot.
AI.result: Both entanglement structure and quantum noise are shown to be two knobs controlling effective dimension. In overfitting regimes, contracting d_eff acts as ridge-like regularization. Amplitude damping contracts d_eff and lifts test accuracy by up to +13% along an inverted-U curve; the effect's sign flips between over- and under-fitting regimes. The depolarizing family provides exact collapse to d_eff→1, confirmed to machine precision at up to 12 qubits.
AI.conclusion: The two previously anecdotal observations are organized into a single measurable principle: effective dimension of the noise-shaped quantum feature kernel governs generalization in quantum vision models, providing a design principle for tuning entanglement and noise.

title: Learner-based Concept Drift Detection: Analysis and Evaluation
summary: Machine learning algorithms deployed for evolving streaming environments must handle the non-stationary data distributions, commonly referred to as concept drift. The presence of concept drift poses a major challenge for many real-world applications because it can severely degrade their predictive performance, hindering their ability to support robust decision-making. Consequently, the timely and efficient detection of drift events is critical for sustaining high accuracy over time. This study examines theoretically the concept drift characteristics and numerous drift detection algorithms across several categories. Furthermore, we evaluate their performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets exhibiting diverse streaming scenarios and drift characteristics, such as abrupt and gradual changes. This study aims to enhance understanding of the complex notion of concept drift characteristics and behavior of drift detectors, along with their applicability to diverse contexts.

AI.tldr: A theoretical and empirical examination of concept drift characteristics and detection algorithms across multiple categories, evaluated on synthetic and real-world streaming datasets with abrupt and gradual drift patterns.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models in streaming environments suffer performance degradation from concept drift (non-stationary data distributions), and timely, efficient drift detection is critical for maintaining predictive accuracy in real-world decision-making applications.
AI.method: The authors conduct a theoretical analysis of concept drift characteristics and categorize numerous drift detection algorithms. They then perform empirical evaluation on both synthetic and real-world streaming datasets covering diverse drift scenarios, including abrupt and gradual changes.
AI.result: The study provides a comparative performance assessment of drift detectors across varying streaming contexts and drift types, offering insights into the behavior and suitability of different detection approaches under distinct conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work enhances understanding of concept drift characteristics and drift detector behavior, clarifying the applicability of different algorithms to diverse streaming contexts and drift patterns.

title: Boundary Embedding Shaping with Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Graph Structural Disentanglement
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at aggregating neighbor information for classification, yet their performance is hindered by graph structural entanglement, where spurious correlations from semantically irrelevant neighbors contaminate node embeddings. This challenge is most acute for nodes near class boundaries in the embedding space, where amplified structural noise blurs decision boundaries and destabilizes predictions. Existing robust GNN methods largely treat all nodes uniformly, ignoring boundary vulnerabilities.
