In this paper, to improve classification performance, we tackle graph structural disentanglement by identifying boundary-region entanglement as the primary bottleneck and propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning GNN plug-in module that selectively suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries with minimal model parameter perturbation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms existing leading methods. Notably, BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction.

AI.tldr: BES is a plug-in contrastive learning module that identifies and mitigates spurious neighbor correlations specifically at class decision boundaries, improving GNN node classification (avg +3.3%) and link prediction without substantial parameter changes.
AI.motivation: GNNs suffer from graph structural entanglement — semantically irrelevant neighbors introduce spurious correlations that contaminate node embeddings. This problem is most severe for nodes near class boundaries, where structural noise blurs decision boundaries. Existing robust GNN methods treat all nodes uniformly, neglecting these boundary-specific vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning plug-in module for GNNs. BES first identifies boundary-region nodes, then applies selective suppression of spurious structural noise at those decision boundaries through contrastive learning, all while minimally perturbing model parameters.
AI.result: BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms leading methods. It boosts GCN node classification by an average of 3.3%, with up to 5.0% improvement on WikiCS, and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-region structural entanglement is the primary bottleneck in GNN classification. BES effectively addresses this by adaptively shaping embeddings at decision boundaries, yielding significant and consistent performance gains as a lightweight plug-in module.

title: Integrating national forest inventory, airborne lidar, and satellite imagery for wall-to-wall mapping of forest structure with computer vision
summary: Remote sensing is increasingly relied upon to deliver actionable science for forest and wildfire risk management across large landscapes. Wall-to-wall, annually updated maps are a persistent need for effective forest management. Many planning systems and data collections combine disparate data sources with different purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, which leads to confounding behavior in operational planning systems. We introduce the VibrantForests framework, developed and applied to map forest attributes and provide a coherent foundation for effective forest and wildfire planning. VibrantForests includes a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived samples and applied across the contiguous United States to concurrently generate estimates of canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter at 10-meter resolution. We demonstrate predictive capability spanning the full spectrum of forest conditions ranging from sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass. Results show that our model extends the range at which saturation is commonly encountered in comparable passive-sensor models, and reduces regression-to-mean behavior that commonly produces overestimation of forest attributes in small/sparse conditions and underestimation in large/dense conditions. The VibrantForests framework addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent wall-to-wall estimates of management-relevant attributes at annual cadence and 10m resolution.

AI.tldr: VibrantForests is a satellite-based framework that produces wall-to-wall, 10m resolution, annually updated maps of five key forest attributes (canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter) across the contiguous US, overcoming common saturation and regression-to-mean biases in passive-sensor models to support wildfire and forest management planning.
AI.motivation: Current operational forest and wildfire planning systems integrate disparate data sources with mismatched purposes, vintages, and quality, creating confounding behavior. There is a persistent need for coherent, annually updated, wall-to-wall forest attribute maps that deliver actionable science across large landscapes.
AI.method: The VibrantForests framework uses a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived reference samples. The model ingests passive optical satellite imagery and is applied across the contiguous United States at 10-meter spatial resolution to concurrently estimate five forest attributes: canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter.
AI.result: The model demonstrates predictive capability across the full spectrum of forest conditions (sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass). It extends the saturation range typically encountered in comparable passive-sensor models and reduces regression-to-mean behavior — mitigating overestimation in sparse/small conditions and underestimation in dense/large conditions.
AI.conclusion: VibrantForests addresses a critical gap in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent, wall-to-wall, management-relevant forest attribute estimates at annual cadence and 10m resolution, providing a unified foundation for operational decision-making.

title: Shifting-based Optimizable Linear Relaxations for General Activation Functions
summary: The use of neural networks (NNs) is rapidly increasing, including in safety- and security-critical domains. To provide formal guarantees about NN behavior, many verification methods rely on optimizable linear relaxations of activation functions. However, existing techniques depend on hand-crafted relaxations for each activation function. Extension to state-of-the-art activation functions therefore requires substantial manual effort. In contrast, our approach SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) is broadly applicable, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points. SLiR parameterizes relaxations by their slope and computes the corresponding offset via a shifting procedure that ensures sound upper and lower bounds over the input domain, enabling efficient optimization while maintaining correctness. Our experiments show that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions and enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: SLiR is a general framework for generating sound linear relaxations of activation functions for neural network verification, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or critical points. It parameterizes relaxations by slope and computes offsets via a shifting procedure, achieving tighter bounds and enabling verification of up to 7.8× more properties than prior hand-crafted methods.
AI.motivation: Existing neural network verification methods rely on hand-crafted linear relaxations tailored to each specific activation function. As novel activation functions (e.g., GELU, Swish, Mish) become prevalent, manually deriving relaxations for each one is labor-intensive and error-prone. A general, automated approach is needed to provide sound relaxations for arbitrary activation functions with minimal manual effort.
AI.method: SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) takes as input only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points of the activation function. It parameterizes linear relaxations by their slope and derives the corresponding offset (intercept) through a shifting procedure: the linear bounds are shifted vertically until they become sound (i.e., guarantee upper and lower enclosure) over the entire input domain. This shifting is computed to ensure tightness while maintaining formal correctness, enabling efficient optimization over the relaxation parameters.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that SLiR produces tight linear relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions. When integrated into neural network verification, SLiR enables verifying up to 7.8× more properties compared to state-of-the-art verification methods that rely on hand-crafted relaxations.
AI.conclusion: SLiR provides a general, automated, and sound approach for generating linear relaxations of activation functions, significantly reducing the manual effort required for neural network verification and substantially improving verification scalability across diverse activation functions.

title: Recurrent neural networks approximate continuous functions
summary: Classical approximation theorems ask for a new neural network whenever the target accuracy is improved. This paper studies the opposite possibility: can the network be chosen once and for all, and can accuracy be bought only by letting it run longer? We prove that this is possible for every continuous function on [-1,1]. More precisely, each such function is uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension. The mechanism behind the construction is a new intermediate model, the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU). This model retains the algorithmic freedom needed to implement polynomial approximation schemes, while remaining rigid enough to be simulated by RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitude. The resulting convergence rates reflect the underlying polynomial approximation rates. We complement the construction with minimax lower bounds showing that runtime is not merely a proof artifact, but an unavoidable resource in this fixed-network approximation paradigm.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that a single, fixed-weight ReLU recurrent neural network (RNN) can uniformly approximate any continuous function on [-1,1] simply by running longer, eliminating the need for retraining or redesigning the network when higher accuracy is required. This is achieved via a new intermediate model called the Turing Machine with Neural Units (TMNU), and the construction is complemented by lower bounds showing runtime is a necessary resource.
AI.motivation: Classical neural network approximation theory requires designing a new network (different architecture, more parameters) each time better accuracy is sought. The authors flip this question: can a single, fixed-architecture, fixed-weight network achieve arbitrary accuracy merely through extended runtime? This explores whether computation time can substitute for network complexity in function approximation.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Turing Machine with Neural Units (TMNU), an intermediate computational model that balances algorithmic expressiveness (to implement polynomial approximation schemes) with sufficient rigidity (to be simulated by RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weights). A single ReLU RNN with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension is constructed to simulate the TMNU, whose time evolution uniformly approximates any continuous function on [-1,1]. Convergence rates mirror those of underlying polynomial approximations. Minimax lower bounds are also derived to demonstrate that runtime is an unavoidable resource.
AI.result: Every continuous function on [-1,1] can be uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU RNN with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension. The approximation rates inherit the rates of the polynomial approximation scheme used. Lower bounds establish that runtime must grow as accuracy improves—runtime is not a mere artifact of the proof technique but a fundamental necessity in the fixed-network paradigm.
AI.conclusion: The fixed-network, runtime-as-resource paradigm is viable: a single ReLU RNN can universally approximate all continuous functions on a compact interval, with accuracy controlled solely by runtime. However, runtime is provably necessary, not eliminable. This reframes the classical approximation theory trade-off between network size and accuracy into a trade-off between runtime and accuracy.

title: Quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for PDEs
summary: We develop QCPIKAN, the first quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network designed to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). Built upon Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers and parameterized quantum circuits, this hybrid framework embeds physical constraints into the training loss to enforce physical consistency. Our theoretical investigations grounded in approximation theory prove that this design accelerates high-frequency error convergence to an exponential rate and effectively mitigates numerical dispersion. We validate the framework across three typical seepage scenarios in porous media, including single-phase flow, component transport and two-phase flow. Compared with existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks, QCPIKAN achieves superior performance in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking and displacement front localization. This work provides a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs.

AI.tldr: QCPIKAN introduces a hybrid quantum-classical physics-informed KAN (Kolmogorov-Arnold Network) using Chebyshev polynomials and parameterized quantum circuits to solve PDEs, achieving exponential high-frequency error convergence and superior performance in porous media seepage scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) struggle with high-frequency error convergence and numerical dispersion when solving complex PDEs. This motivates a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that leverages KAN's approximation power and quantum circuits to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: QCPIKAN combines Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers with parameterized quantum circuits in a physics-informed framework, embedding PDE constraints into the loss function. Theoretical analysis uses approximation theory to prove exponential convergence rates for high-frequency errors and mitigation of numerical dispersion.
AI.result: Validated on three porous-media seepage problems (single-phase flow, component transport, two-phase flow), QCPIKAN outperforms existing quantum-classical PINNs in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking, and displacement front localization.
AI.conclusion: QCPIKAN provides a robust, efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs, with theoretical guarantees and empirical superiority over existing quantum-classical physics-informed approaches.

title: Constrained hybrid modelling to predict microbial dynamics and organic matter turnover in soil systems
summary: Soil microorganisms control organic matter cycling and largely determine how soil systems can cope with and mitigate climate change and environmental threats. Representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is therefore critical to predict carbon cycling in soils, albeit highly challenging to inform from data. One promising approach to improve their parametrisation is the integration of genomic data, yet modelling the complex and unknown relationship between genomes and the processes the microbes are driving is an unsolved problem. In this work, we present the first hybrid modeling framework for deriving biokinetic parameter values of a process-based soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-inferred functional traits based on DNA sequencing data. Our model predicts biokinetic parameters of the process-based model from genomic trait data with a neural network and integrates constraints from ecological theory and literature to ensure realistic behavior, even of non-observed state variables. We evaluate our method on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data, showing that our approach improves performance over multiple baselines and learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model effectively, even for small training datasets.

AI.tldr: A hybrid modeling framework uses neural networks to predict biokinetic parameters of a soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-derived functional traits, integrating ecological constraints for realistic dynamics, and demonstrates improved performance on both synthetic and real genomic data.
AI.motivation: Soil microorganisms drive organic matter cycling and carbon dynamics, but representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is data-limited and challenging. Integrating genomic data offers promise, yet the relationship between genomes and microbial processes remains unknown and unsolved.
AI.method: The authors develop a hybrid modeling framework combining a process-based soil organic matter turnover model with a neural network. The neural network predicts biokinetic parameters from metagenome-inferred functional traits (DNA sequencing data). Ecological theory and literature-derived constraints are integrated to ensure realistic behavior, including for unobserved state variables. The approach is evaluated on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real metagenomic data.
AI.result: The hybrid framework outperforms multiple baselines on both synthetic and real datasets. It effectively learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model, even with small training datasets.
AI.conclusion: Integrating genomic data into process-based soil carbon models via hybrid neural network approaches is feasible and effective, enabling improved prediction of microbial-driven carbon cycling while respecting ecological constraints, even under data-scarce conditions.

title: Critical Percolation as a Synthetic Data Model for Interpretability
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Neural networks learn features that reflect the hierarchical, multi-scale structure of natural data. Synthetic datasets used to evaluate interpretability methods typically lack this structure, limiting their value as realistic toy models. To close this gap, we introduce a family of synthetic datasets consisting of hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in a high-dimensional data space. The percolation data consists of sparse, low-dimensional fractal clusters with a power-law size distribution. Latent variables modeling a taxonomic hierarchy generate each data point's target value. The data model is analytically tractable with known critical exponents that fix its properties without requiring hyperparameter tuning. We leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to propose an almost linear-time algorithm to jointly sample a random tree and its hierarchical latent decomposition, enabling data generation at arbitrary scale. Using probing experiments, we find that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations. Together, sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability make critical percolation a principled testbed for interpretability research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a synthetic dataset family based on hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters, providing a principled, analytically tractable testbed for neural network interpretability research with realistic multi-scale structure.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic datasets for evaluating interpretability methods lack the hierarchical, multi-scale structure characteristic of natural data. The authors aim to close this gap with a realistic yet analytically tractable toy model that captures sparsity, self-similarity, and power-law statistics.
AI.method: The authors construct datasets using hierarchical functions on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in high-dimensional space. They leverage the established mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to design an almost linear-time algorithm for jointly sampling random trees and their hierarchical latent decompositions, enabling scalable data generation. Critical exponents analytically fix the model's properties without hyperparameter tuning.
AI.result: Probing experiments demonstrate that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations, confirming the dataset's utility as a testbed for interpretability methods.
AI.conclusion: Critical percolation offers a principled testbed for interpretability research due to its combination of sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability, making it superior to prior synthetic datasets lacking hierarchical structure.

title: On the Variance of Temporal Difference Learning and its Reduction Using Control Variates
summary: We analyze the variance of temporal difference (TD) learning using the phased setting with tabular representation, and show that one of the mechanisms behind its ability to reduce variance is by effectively aggregating over a larger number of independent trajectories. Based on this insight, we demonstrate that (1) the variance of TD is asymptotically bounded from above by Monte Carlo (MC) estimators, and (2) shorter horizon updates incurs less variance for a fixed number of samples. Beyond TD, we show that Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE), a method for estimating the advantage function, can be seen as a type of regression-adjusted control variate, which achieves a tighter bound on the variance compared to TD in the large-sample limit. Finally, we numerically illustrate the behaviors of these estimators with carefully designed environments.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the variance properties of temporal difference (TD) learning in the tabular, phased setting, showing that TD reduces variance by implicitly aggregating over more independent trajectories. It proves TD's variance is asymptotically upper-bounded by Monte Carlo estimators and that shorter horizons yield lower variance. The paper further shows Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) acts as a regression-adjusted control variate, achieving tighter variance bounds than TD.
AI.motivation: Understand the variance reduction mechanisms of TD learning compared to MC methods, and characterize how update horizon length affects variance in policy evaluation. Additionally, to provide a theoretical framework for understanding DAE's variance properties relative to TD.
AI.method: Variance analysis in the phased, tabular setting using asymptotic expansions. The authors decompose TD's variance, relate it to MC variance, and employ control variate theory to analyze DAE as a regression-adjusted estimator.
AI.result: TD variance is asymptotically upper-bounded by MC variance. Shorter-horizon TD updates incur strictly less variance for a fixed sample budget. DAE is shown to be a regression-adjusted control variate with a tighter variance bound than TD in the large-sample limit. Numerical experiments in designed environments corroborate the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: TD's variance reduction stems from effectively leveraging more independent trajectories through bootstrapping. DAE further improves upon TD by incorporating regression adjustment, yielding even lower variance. These insights clarify the bias-variance trade-off in policy evaluation and advantage estimation.

title: Train, Retrieve, or Both? A Four-Arm Head-to-Head for Correct Statutory Citation on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act
summary: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need to be pointed at the provision of law that actually governs a question, with a correct statutory citation. We study this task on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) and its core regulation, asking the operator's question empirically: is fine-tuning enough, or is hybrid retrieval needed? We run a four-arm head-to-head on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (base zero-shot, LoRA SFT-only, RAG-only, and an SFT+RAG hybrid), scored on citation exact-match (section+subsection) over a small, human-verification-pending real eval set. The base model cannot cite the RTA and SFT-only mis-recalls sections; retrieval is essential and drives hallucination to zero by construction; and the SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. Its edge comes from SFT making provision selection more robust to the higher-recall candidate sets that hurt zero-shot RAG. Notably, this cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats a pipeline built on bigger, specialized retrieval models (a larger embedder and a cross-encoder reranker), and a larger/improved training set does not help either: strong statutory-citation performance here does not require specialized retrieval models or more data. The artifact zeroes hallucination and clears the lift-over-base bar but does not reach the aspirational 0.70 exact-match target. All results are on a small, human-verification-pending real eval set and are reported as preliminary.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning + retrieval (SFT+RAG) outperforms pure SFT or pure RAG for statutory citation on Ontario's RTA, achieving 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucination; SFT improves robustness to high-recall retrieval sets, and a cheap bge-small hybrid matches larger specialized retrieval pipelines.
AI.motivation: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need accurate statutory citations to the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act (RTA). The authors empirically investigate whether fine-tuning alone suffices or whether hybrid retrieval is necessary for correct citation generation.
AI.method: A four-arm head-to-head experiment using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: (1) base zero-shot, (2) LoRA SFT-only, (3) RAG-only, and (4) SFT+RAG hybrid. Evaluation uses exact-match on section+subsection over a small human-verification-pending real eval set. The hybrid uses bge-small for retrieval and is compared against pipelines with larger embedders and cross-encoder rerankers.
AI.result: Base model cannot cite the RTA; SFT-only mis-recalls sections. Retrieval drives hallucination to zero by construction. SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. SFT makes provision selection more robust to higher-recall candidate sets that degrade zero-shot RAG. The cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats pipelines using larger specialized retrieval models. A larger training set does not improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Strong statutory-citation performance does not require specialized retrieval models or more data; the SFT+RAG hybrid using bge-small suffices to eliminate hallucination. However, the 0.481 exact-match score falls short of the aspirational 0.70 target. All results are preliminary and pending human verification.

title: Judging to Improve: A De-biased VLM-as-3D-Judge Protocol for Single-Image 3D Generation
summary: A companion study established a de-biased, cross-model VLM-as-3D-judge that reliably ranks single-image-to-3D mesh quality where cheap geometry and CLIP proxies fall short. This paper asks: can that judge's preferences specialize a strong open generator, TRELLIS, on one asset class (furniture), cheaply and without human labels? Taking the judge from ranking to optimization is where the work lives. Pushing a VLM judge into the training and evaluation loop exposes failure modes ranking never triggered, so our contribution is an optimization-grade hardening of the judge: a training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) held distinct from an evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to break circularity; position-bias correction; and fixes for three failure modes (image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs), with calibration evidence (clear-gap win-rate 0.83-1.0; base-vs-base ~0.5). Using this protocol as an independent evaluator, and working only from public models and data with lightweight parameter-efficient adaptation, we find our methods match the strong base rather than exceed it. Independent base samples carry essentially no learnable preference (0.94 order-flip rate), so signal must be engineered by quality-contrastive construction. Across six adaptation methods, two input regimes, and a severity sweep, the most targeted - conditioner repair under severe degradation - reaches parity (0.50) with the base, while no method clears the >=65% win-rate target. The result is mechanistic: clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DIT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is the locus that moves geometry. Win-rates are directional at n=8 objects. Matching a strong public-data base with cheap adaptation is itself informative: exceeding it needs more than lightweight PEFT on public data, and the judge protocol is reusable.

AI.tldr: A hardened VLM-as-3D-judge protocol is developed to specialize the TRELLIS 3D generator on furniture via lightweight adaptation without human labels. Despite extensive engineering to prevent feedback loops and failure modes, no method exceeds the strong base model; only conditioner repair under severe degradation reaches parity (0.50 win-rate), revealing mechanistic limits of cheap PEFT-based optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing single-image-to-3D evaluation relies on cheap geometry/CLIP proxies that fall short. A prior companion study produced a reliable VLM judge for ranking, but repurposing that judge for optimization (training feedback) introduces new failure modes. The goal is to cheaply specialize a strong open generator on a specific asset class (furniture) without human labels, using only the judge's preferences as signal.
AI.method: The core contribution is an optimization-grade hardening of the VLM judge protocol: (1) separate training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to break circularity; (2) position-bias correction; (3) fixes for three failure modes: image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs. Using this protocol, six PEFT adaptation methods are tested across two input regimes and a severity sweep on TRELLIS, with quality-contrastive construction providing the learnable signal since independent base samples carry negligible preference (0.94 order-flip rate).
AI.result: No adaptation method clears the ≥65% win-rate target over the base model. Only conditioner repair under severe degradation reaches parity (0.50 win-rate). Flow-DiT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and clean inputs saturate the judge. The mechanistic locus for moving geometry is conditioning repair. Win-rates are computed directionally at n=8 objects. Independent base samples show a 0.94 order-flip rate, confirming signal must be engineered. Calibration evidence shows clear-gap win-rate of 0.83–1.0 and base-vs-base ~0.5.
AI.conclusion: Matching a strong public-data base with cheap adaptation is informative: exceeding it requires more than lightweight PEFT on public data. The reusable judge protocol is a contribution in itself for future optimization-grade VLM judging in 3D generation.

title: CRAX: Fast Safe Reinforcement Learning Benchmarking
summary: Safety is a core concern for deploying reinforcement learning (RL) agents in real-world domains such as robotics and autonomous driving. While benchmarks have been central to progress in RL, existing safety benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics remain computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. To address this gap, we propose CRAX (Constrained RL Accelerated with JAX). Built on top of the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine with realistic 3D dynamics, CRAX leverages vectorized operations and hardware acceleration, yielding up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. The benchmark features six environment suites and three agent-specific tasks, each spanning three difficulty levels. Evaluating six popular safe RL methods shows that no single approach dominates across all tasks, and reveals the trade-offs between performance and safety. We find that curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer can improve performance over direct training in harder settings.

AI.tldr: CRAX is a JAX-accelerated safe RL benchmark built on MuJoCo XLA, achieving ~100x speedups over CPU-based alternatives. It provides six environment suites with three difficulty levels each, and benchmarking six safe RL methods reveals no single dominant approach, while curriculum learning and safety transfer improve performance.
AI.motivation: Existing safe RL benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics are computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. There is a need for a fast, hardware-accelerated benchmark that maintains realistic dynamics while enabling extensive evaluation of safe RL algorithms.
AI.method: CRAX is built on the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine, leveraging JAX-based vectorized operations and hardware acceleration (GPU/TPU). It provides six environment suites with three agent-specific tasks, each at three difficulty levels. The authors benchmark six popular safe RL methods across these environments.
AI.result: CRAX achieves up to ~100x speedup over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. Evaluation of six safe RL methods shows no single algorithm dominates across all tasks, revealing performance-safety trade-offs. Curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer both improve performance over direct training on harder settings.
AI.conclusion: CRAX enables rapid, large-scale experimentation in safe RL with realistic 3D physics. The benchmark highlights that algorithm selection must be task-dependent, and that curriculum-based training strategies offer a promising path for improving both performance and safety in constrained RL settings.

title: Towards Modality-imbalanced Federated Graph Learning: A Data Synthesis-based Approach
summary: MultiModal Federated Graph Learning (MM-FGL) offers a natural collaborative training paradigm, but its practical deployment is challenged by two granularities of modality imbalance. Client-level imbalance occurs when certain clients lack entire modalities, while node-level imbalance occurs when individual nodes exhibit missing visual or textual attributes. While several relevant studies exist, our investigation reveals that they predominantly target graph-agnostic or centralized scenarios, rendering them difficult to adapt directly. To address these challenges, we formalize modality-imbalanced MM-FGL as an implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis problem. This paradigm recovers missing modal semantics directly within the representation space, thereby maximizing alignment with the original data's semantic distribution and mitigating the high variance induced by missing modalities. To this end, we propose FedMGS (Federated Modality-aware Graph Synthesis), which integrates three core components. The availability-aware graph encoder prevents missing modalities from contaminating local structural propagation. The prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities. The reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism regulates the impact of recovered latent representations prior to predictive readout. Extensive experiments on four tasks show that FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines with gains up to 17.41% with best efficiency-performance tradeoff.

AI.tldr: FedMGS is a federated graph learning framework that addresses client-level and node-level modality imbalance by synthesizing missing modal semantics in latent representation space via prototype-guided synthesis and reliability-calibrated fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal federated graph learning methods fail under two granularities of modality imbalance: client-level (entire modalities missing per client) and node-level (missing visual/textual attributes per node). Current solutions are graph-agnostic or centralized, unfit for federated graph settings.
AI.method: FedMGS comprises three components: (1) an availability-aware graph encoder that gates out missing modalities during local message passing; (2) a prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer that uses cross-client semantic prototypes to reconstruct missing modality representations; (3) a reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism that weights recovered latents before readout.
AI.result: FedMGS outperforms competitive baselines by up to 17.41% across four tasks, achieving the best efficiency-performance tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: Synthesizing missing modalities implicitly in latent representation space, guided by cross-client prototypes and calibrated fusion, effectively mitigates modality imbalance in federated graph learning.

title: The Significance of Style Diversity in Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Generating high-utility synthetic data for intent classification typically requires human-annotated seed data, which is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings. In this paper, we propose a framework for synthetic dialogue generation that works entirely without human-annotated data, relying solely on intent definitions. Our proposed dialogue generation framework utilizes two different types of topic and style attributes to improve data diversity. Also, we propose two novel post-hoc stylization models called Univ and Exam to transform synthetic LLM-generated utterances into more varied, human-like linguistic styles. To enhance data quality, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge filtering process. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained using human-annotated training data. Crucially, the findings reveal that style diversity is more critical than topic diversity for synthetic data utility, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Furthermore, the study shows that incorporating style attributes during the generation process is more effective than post-hoc style adaptation.

AI.tldr: A fully unsupervised framework for synthetic dialogue generation for intent classification that relies only on intent definitions, uses topic/style attributes for diversity, introduces two post-hoc stylization models, and employs LLM-as-a-judge filtering, achieving 93.3% of human-annotated performance while demonstrating that style diversity matters more than topic diversity.
AI.motivation: Industrial intent classification systems depend on human-annotated seed data, which is often unavailable in fast-paced settings. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency entirely by generating synthetic training data using only intent definitions.
AI.method: The framework uses intent definitions as the sole input. It generates synthetic dialogues with two types of topic and style attributes to boost diversity. Two novel post-hoc stylization models, Univ and Exam, transform LLM-generated utterances into more human-like styles. An LLM-as-a-judge filtering step improves data quality by discarding low-quality examples.
AI.result: On industrial and public datasets, the approach reaches up to 93.3% of the performance achieved with human-annotated training data. Style diversity proves more critical than topic diversity, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Incorporating style attributes during generation outperforms post-hoc style adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data for intent classification can be effectively generated without any human annotation. Style diversity is the key driver of utility, and style control should be integrated during generation rather than applied post-hoc.

title: Direct Advantage Estimation for Scalable and Sample-efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) has been shown to improve the sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning algorithms. However, its reliance on full environment observability limits its applicability in realistic settings, and its requirement to model transition probabilities incurs substantial computational overhead for high-dimensional observations. In the present work, we address both limitations. First, we extend the theoretical framework of DAE to partially observable domains with minimal modifications. Second, we reduce its computational complexity by introducing discrete latent dynamics models that efficiently approximate transition probabilities. We evaluate our approach on the Arcade Learning Environment and find that DAE scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) to partially observable environments and reduces its computational cost via discrete latent dynamics models, demonstrating effective scaling and high sample efficiency on the Arcade Learning Environment.
AI.motivation: DAE improves sample efficiency in deep RL but suffers from two key limitations: (1) it requires full environment observability, making it unsuitable for realistic partially observable settings; (2) modeling transition probabilities imposes significant computational overhead for high-dimensional observations. The authors aim to address both issues.
AI.method: The authors (1) extend the DAE theoretical framework to partially observable domains with minimal modifications, and (2) introduce discrete latent dynamics models to efficiently approximate transition probabilities, reducing computational complexity.
AI.result: Evaluated on the Arcade Learning Environment, the proposed approach demonstrates that DAE scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: DAE can be successfully adapted to partially observable environments and made computationally tractable for high-dimensional observations through discrete latent dynamics, without sacrificing its sample efficiency benefits.

title: Pseudo-Feature Padding: A Lightweight Defense Against False Data Injection in Power Grids
summary: Deep Neural Networks DNNs have achieved remarkable accuracy in various tasks including their application in CyberPhysical Systems CPS for detecting False Data Injection Attacks FDIA during critical operations However the unique infrastructure of CPS makes DNNs vulnerable to exploitation by attackers aiming to evade detection Additionally the distinct nature of CPS presents challenges for conventional defense mechanisms against FDIA This paper proposes an innovative defense framework that strengthens DNNs against such attacks by introducing an additional input layer that performs padding in the input samples using pseudofeature values derived from the inputs statistical distribution This padding increases the input dimensionality in a randomized and dataaware manner making adversarial attacks computationally infeasible due to the nontransferable nature of crafted perturbations and the unpredictability of the padded structure Our method is lightweight modelagnostic and requires no modifications to the core architecture making it highly deployable in realworld CPS settings We evaluated our framework on critical power grid applications such as state estimation using the IEEE 14bus 30bus 118bus and 300bus systems Experiments under adversarial settings demonstrate that our padding strategy significantly improves model robustness with negligible impact on performance and effectively mitigates attacks that would otherwise bypass conventional defenses

AI.tldr: A defense framework for DNNs in CPS against FDIA evasion attacks, using randomized, data-aware pseudo-feature padding to increase input dimensionality, making adversarial perturbations non-transferable and computationally infeasible, while remaining lightweight and model-agnostic.
AI.motivation: DNNs are effective for FDIA detection in CPS, but CPS's unique infrastructure exposes DNNs to adversarial evasion attacks. Conventional defense mechanisms are ill-suited to the distinct characteristics of CPS environments.
AI.method: An additional input layer performs randomized, data-aware padding using pseudo-feature values sampled from the input's statistical distribution. This increases input dimensionality unpredictably, making crafted adversarial perturbations non-transferable and attacks computationally infeasible, without modifying the core DNN architecture.
AI.result: Evaluated on IEEE 14-bus, 30-bus, 118-bus, and 300-bus power grid state estimation systems. The padding strategy significantly improved model robustness against adversarial attacks with negligible performance impact, mitigating attacks that bypass conventional defenses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pseudo-feature padding framework is a lightweight, model-agnostic, and highly deployable defense that effectively hardens DNN-based FDIA detectors in CPS against adversarial evasion, validated across multiple power grid benchmarks.

title: On the Redundancy of Timestep Embeddings in Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models rely heavily on explicit timestep embeddings to modulate the denoising process across various noise scales. In this work, we challenge the necessity of these temporal signals by analyzing their impact on U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures. Beyond empirical evidence, we provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be achieved without explicit timestep conditioning. Our findings reveal a surprising robustness when timestep embeddings are completely removed. Extensive ablation studies on the CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets show that these time-agnostic models can maintain high structural fidelity and even surpass their conditioned counterparts in competitive metrics, including FID, precision, and recall. Our analysis suggests these architectures can implicitly infer noise scales from the corrupted input under specific assumptions, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant. This study challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms and paves the way for more efficient and structurally focused generative architectures.

AI.tldr: Paper challenges the necessity of explicit timestep embeddings in diffusion models, showing both theoretically and empirically that U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures can achieve competitive or superior performance without temporal conditioning, suggesting noise scale can be implicitly inferred from corrupted inputs.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models universally rely on explicit timestep embeddings to condition the denoising process at each noise level. The authors question whether this design is truly necessary, aiming to simplify generative architectures by eliminating temporal signals that have long been considered indispensable.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical framework proving that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective is attainable without explicit timestep conditioning. Empirically, they conduct extensive ablation studies on CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets, completely removing timestep embeddings from both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures and evaluating performance via FID, precision, and recall.
AI.result: Time-agnostic models (without timestep embeddings) maintain high structural fidelity and can even surpass their conditioned counterparts on competitive metrics including FID, precision, and recall. The architectures exhibit surprising robustness, implicitly inferring noise scales from the corrupted input alone.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal conditioning in diffusion models is redundant under specific assumptions, as architectures can implicitly infer noise scales from inputs. This challenges long-standing paradigms and opens the door to more efficient, structurally focused generative architectures.

title: Neural network surrogates with uncertainty quantification for inverse problems in partial differential equations
summary: Inverse problems for differential equations arise throughout science and engineering, where one seeks to infer unknown model parameters from noisy or incomplete observations. Traditional numerical methods for these problems are often computationally expensive, particularly in Bayesian settings where evaluating the likelihood becomes costly for complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces. To address this challenge, we introduce DeepGaLA, a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions, reducing overconfident inference when training data are limited. To evaluate the fidelity of the surrogate-induced posterior approximations in practice, we show that a short run of delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo can serve as an effective diagnostic. Across a range of numerical experiments, DeepGaLA delivers forward-model approximations with accuracy comparable to established Gaussian-process surrogates, while better maintaining efficiency as parameter dimension grows. Moreover, it can incorporate differential-equation constraints, including in nonlinear settings. Overall, these results indicate that uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems.

AI.tldr: DeepGaLA is a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions for Bayesian inverse problems, enabling scalable inference with accuracy comparable to Gaussian processes but better efficiency in high dimensions, and can incorporate differential-equation constraints including nonlinear settings.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical methods for inverse problems in differential equations are computationally expensive in Bayesian settings, especially with complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces. Existing surrogates either lack uncertainty quantification or scale poorly with parameter dimension.
AI.method: The authors propose DeepGaLA, a neural-network surrogate that provides uncertainty-aware predictions. They use delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) as a diagnostic tool to evaluate the fidelity of surrogate-induced posterior approximations.
AI.result: DeepGaLA achieves forward-model approximation accuracy comparable to Gaussian-process surrogates while maintaining better efficiency as parameter dimension grows. It successfully incorporates differential-equation constraints, even in nonlinear settings.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates like DeepGaLA can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems, offering a practical alternative to traditional computationally expensive methods.

title: Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting: A Mechanistic Study of Representation Retention in Continual Learning
summary: Continual learning (CL) systems often forget previously acquired knowledge, yet the mechanisms driving forgetting remain hard to isolate in practice because real datasets entangle many factors. We present a controlled, toy-world framework that makes these mechanisms observable and testable. Using a synthetic generator-separator pipeline, we define ground-truth latent features, build tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap, and introduce measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition (directional overlap among features). We then study retention dynamics-the temporal change of representation strength by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) between retention, superposition, and exposure history. A complementary task-level analysis based on effective rank characterizes how representational capacity is allocated across tasks. Our controlled experiments yield three takeaways. (1) Superposition tends to increase over time with transient dips at task boundaries, suggesting boundary-specific interference rather than steady drift. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition yet does not inevitably cause forgetting; when representations remain strong, forgetting can be reduced despite overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, indicating broader capacity usage under sparse regimes. Together, these results nuance the common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting by showing that overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation. Our toy analysis provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for CL.

AI.tldr: A controlled synthetic framework is introduced to study forgetting in continual learning by tracking representation strength, superposition, and capacity allocation, revealing that increased superposition does not necessarily cause forgetting when representations remain strong and that sparsity shapes capacity dynamics.
AI.motivation: Forgetting in continual learning is hard to isolate in real datasets because many factors are entangled. The authors aim to create a controlled, observable environment where mechanisms driving forgetting can be directly tested.
AI.method: A synthetic generator-separator pipeline is used to define ground-truth latent features, construct tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap, and measure representation strength and superposition. SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) is applied to fit sparse dynamical relations among retention, superposition, and exposure history. Effective rank analysis is used at the task level to characterize representational capacity allocation.
AI.result: (1) Superposition increases over time with transient dips at task boundaries, indicating boundary-specific interference. (2) Higher sparsity induces more superposition but does not inevitably cause forgetting; strong representations can mitigate forgetting despite overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, suggesting broader capacity usage under sparse regimes.
AI.conclusion: The common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting is incomplete; overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation. The framework provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for continual learning research.

title: Evolutionary Two-Stage Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: Equal advising: Daria Pugacheva and Fedor Ratnikov. Accepted to the ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI and PDEs
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into neural network training. However, their performance suffers from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and strong sensitivity to architectural and optimization hyperparameters due to the highly non-convex and multi-term structure of the physics-informed loss. In this setting, the outer-loop hyperparameter search is a noisy and black-box optimization problem over heterogeneous parameters, where classical local or gradient-based strategies are easily trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms, with their population-based exploration and ability to handle mixed, non-differentiable search spaces, provide a more robust mechanism for discovering promising configurations. We propose and investigate a two-stage approach based on evolutionary algorithms that combines exploration and exploitation parts of PINNs training to improve solution accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets. In the first stage, we perform low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate configurations, treating hyperparameter selection as a black-box outer-loop problem. In the second stage, only the most promising candidates are fully trained with standard gradient-based optimizers to refine the solution. Evaluated on three popular problems, namely Advection, Klein-Gordon and Helmholtz equations, our method consistently outperforms standard training and achieves significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage evolutionary algorithm approach for hyperparameter optimization in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). Stage 1 uses low-fidelity truncated training to rapidly screen configurations via black-box evolutionary search; Stage 2 fully trains only the most promising candidates. The method outperforms standard PINN training on Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations under fixed computational budgets.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and high sensitivity to hyperparameters due to the non-convex, multi-term physics-informed loss. Classical local or gradient-based hyperparameter search strategies easily get trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms offer robust, population-based exploration suited to this noisy, heterogeneous, black-box optimization problem, but applying them naively to full PINN training is computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: A two-stage evolutionary hyperparameter optimization framework. Stage 1: low-fidelity training with truncated epochs to rapidly evaluate and screen candidate configurations using evolutionary algorithms on the black-box outer-loop problem. Stage 2: only the top-performing candidates from Stage 1 are fully trained using standard gradient-based optimizers (e.g., Adam/L-BFGS) to refine solutions. This decouples exploration (Stage 1) from exploitation (Stage 2) under a fixed computational budget.
AI.result: The proposed method consistently outperforms standard PINN training across three benchmark PDEs — Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations — achieving significantly lower mean error while operating within constrained computational resources.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary algorithms, when structured as a two-stage exploration-exploitation pipeline with low-fidelity screening, provide a practical and effective solution to the hyperparameter sensitivity problem in PINNs, enabling robust and accurate PDE solutions without exceeding typical computational budgets.

title: Data Bias Mitigation under Coverage Constraints & The Price of Fairness
summary: Machine learning models have been shown to exhibit discriminatory outcomes or degraded performance for individuals at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes, such as race and gender. This stems in part from two interrelated challenges: the lack of principled measures for quantifying bias (potentially intersectional), and insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. We extend a recent bias mitigation framework to incorporate coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. Since achieving exactly zero bias for all groups may not be data efficient (meaning it may require large amounts of data), our solution trades small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency while satisfying coverage constraints. We also formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, and characterize the price of fairness, the minimum data modification cost, as a function of fairness tolerance. This is essential both for legal compliance, where regulations may mandate specific fairness thresholds, and for data governance, enabling practitioners to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data modification (particularly, data purchasing) costs. We evaluate our techniques on publicly available datasets, demonstrating that bias mitigation via our framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers, and that coverage constraints, while motivated by statistical considerations, are essential for preserving downstream ML performance.

AI.tldr: The paper extends a bias mitigation framework with coverage constraints to ensure sufficient representation of intersectional subgroups, trades small bias approximation errors for data efficiency, and formulates bias mitigation as an integer linear program to characterize the price of fairness as a function of fairness tolerance.
AI.motivation: ML models exhibit discriminatory outcomes for intersectional subgroups (e.g., race × gender) due to two challenges: lack of principled bias quantification measures and insufficient representation of these subgroups in training data. Existing fairness approaches often ignore intersectionality or require prohibitive amounts of data to achieve zero bias across all groups.
AI.method: The authors extend a prior bias mitigation framework by incorporating coverage constraints that enforce minimum representation thresholds across intersectional subgroups. They formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program (ILP) that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, trading small ε-approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency. They characterize the "price of fairness" — the minimum data modification cost as a function of fairness tolerance ε — enabling principled cost-fairness trade-offs for legal compliance and data purchasing decisions.
AI.result: Evaluations on public datasets show that the coverage-constrained framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers, and that coverage constraints are essential for maintaining downstream ML performance, not merely a statistical nicety.
AI.conclusion: Coverage constraints are necessary for effective intersectional bias mitigation; the ε-approximation approach enables practical, data-efficient fairness interventions; and the price-of-fairness characterization empowers practitioners to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data acquisition costs.

title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Characterizing PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks
summary: Mathematicians understand a PDE solution through mathematical structures rather than tables of computed values. Historically, this has been the product of mathematical analysis, carried out by hand for each problem individually. Neither numerical simulation nor neural networks produce those structures directly. We propose Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), a prior-guided framework in which an agent translates PDE theory, public problem constraints, and accumulated search experience into testable differentiable symbolic programs. The mathematical forms are refined under evolutionary search, while their continuous parameters are fit by gradient-based optimization. This makes the search an automated form of inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression. For problems with known analytical forms, ASYS recovers these forms naturally; for other problems, ASYS constructs analytical approximations which can guide mathematicians toward further analysis. In our experiments, across five problems spanning bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing, ASYS produces interpretable representations, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up, in settings where no closed-form description was previously available. ASYS shows the possibility of a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions, beyond handcrafted analytical solutions, mesh-based numerical solutions, and neural network approximations.

AI.tldr: ASYS is a prior-guided evolutionary framework that combines agentic translation of PDE theory with differentiable symbolic programs to automatically discover interpretable analytical forms for PDE solutions, recovering known solutions and producing novel approximations where none previously existed.
AI.motivation: Traditional mathematical analysis of PDEs relies on manual, problem-specific derivations, while numerical simulations and neural networks produce opaque representations. There is a need for automated methods that yield interpretable, structurally meaningful analytical forms — bridging the gap between human-like mathematical insight and computational scale.
AI.method: ASYS uses an agent to translate PDE theory, problem constraints, and search experience into testable differentiable symbolic programs. These symbolic forms are refined via evolutionary search (structure-level), while continuous parameters are optimized through gradient descent. This constitutes automated inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression.
AI.result: Across five problems — bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing — ASYS recovered known analytical forms where they exist and discovered novel interpretable approximations otherwise. Key findings include a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up.
AI.conclusion: ASYS demonstrates a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions that goes beyond handcrafted analysis, mesh-based numerics, and neural network surrogates, offering interpretable symbolic forms that can guide further mathematical analysis.

title: Fisher-Geometric Sharpness and the Implicit Bias of SGD toward Flat Minima
summary: A widely held intuition in deep learning is that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) implicitly favors flat minima and that flat minima generalize better, but standard Euclidean measures of flatness such as the trace or maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, which undermines the theoretical foundations of this narrative. In this study we resolve this issue by grounding flatness in the Riemannian geometry of the statistical manifold induced by the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We define Riemannian sharpness mathematically and prove that it is invariant under smooth, function-preserving reparametrizations, which directly addresses the critique of Dinh et al. in the paper ``Sharp minima can generalize for deep nets''.We note that this invariance is a property of the true FIM; the diagonal empirical estimator used in practice (and in all experiments below) inherits invariance only approximately, and exact invariance under arbitrary reparametrizations would require structured estimators such as K-FAC. We formalize the gradient noise of mini-batch SGD as having a covariance structure proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the resulting stochastic differential equation, and then show that the probability mass is exponentially concentrated at Riemannian-flat minima. A PAC-Bayes generalization bound controlled explicitly by SR formally links this geometric bias to test performance. Our experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm that SR reliably tracks generalization in ways that Euclidean sharpness does not, and that its scaling with $η/B$ matches the theoretical predictions. Together these results provide a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the long-standing critique that Euclidean flatness measures are not invariant under function-preserving reparametrizations by grounding flatness in Riemannian geometry via the Fisher Information Matrix. The authors define Riemannian sharpness, prove its invariance, derive theoretical connections to SGD dynamics and PAC-Bayes generalization bounds, and validate empirically on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: The narrative that SGD favors flat minima and that flat minima generalize better is undermined by Dinh et al.'s observation that Euclidean flatness measures (e.g., Hessian trace or max eigenvalue) are not invariant under reparametrizations preserving the network function. This paper aims to restore the theoretical foundation by formulating a geometrically principled, invariant notion of flatness.
AI.method: The authors define Riemannian sharpness (S_R) using the Riemannian geometry of the statistical manifold induced by the Fisher Information Matrix. They prove invariance under smooth function-preserving reparametrizations. They model mini-batch SGD gradient noise as having covariance proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the corresponding SDE, and show probability mass concentrates exponentially at low-S_R minima. A PAC-Bayes bound controlled by S_R links this geometric bias to generalization. Empirically, they compare S_R against Euclidean sharpness on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and verify scaling with η/B.
AI.result: Riemannian sharpness is proven invariant under function-preserving reparametrizations, directly addressing Dinh et al.'s critique. The stationary distribution of SGD exponentially favors Riemannian-flat minima. The PAC-Bayes bound formally ties S_R to test error. Experiments confirm S_R reliably tracks generalization where Euclidean sharpness fails, and its scaling with η/B matches theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant framework explaining why flat minima generalize, resolving a key theoretical weakness in the flatness-generalization narrative. The Riemannian perspective successfully links optimization geometry, SGD dynamics, and generalization via PAC-Bayes theory, validated by experiments.

title: UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents
summary: Context-heavy agents place unusual pressure on the key-value (KV) cache: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, while concurrency determines whether the serving system can keep GPUs utilized. We study 4-bit KV-cache compression for this setting, using TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. We report three contributions. First, we frame 4-bit KV caching around multi-round agent workloads where task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput must be measured jointly. Second, we describe the practical design choices needed to make the 4-bit path robust, including asymmetric K/V treatment, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, QJL removal, and block-scale variants. Third, we present serving optimizations on AMD GPUs, including optimized decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant, an FP4 approximation path that uses FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA support on CDNA4. On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant cuts P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47x in the cache-pressured late rounds (2.3x across all rounds) and raises output throughput by 1.63x over the FP8 KV baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper studies 4-bit KV-cache compression for multi-round agent workloads, presenting design choices (asymmetric K/V treatment, rotations, block-scaling) and an AMD GPU-optimized FP4 scheme called UltraQuant that achieves 3.47x faster TTFT under cache pressure and 1.63x higher throughput vs. FP8 KV caching.
AI.motivation: Long-context, multi-turn agent workloads create extreme KV-cache pressure: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, and concurrency dictates GPU utilization. Existing 4-bit quantization methods lack robustness for this setting, and deployment-quality systems like vLLM FP8 KV caching leave throughput on the table.
AI.method: The authors use TurboQuant-style rotation plus codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as a deployment baseline. They introduce practical design choices: asymmetric precision for keys vs. values, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, removal of QJL projections, and block-scale quantization variants. On AMD CDNA4 GPUs, they implement optimized decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant — an FP4 approximation using FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA instructions.
AI.result: On a long-context multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant reduces P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47× in late cache-pressured rounds (2.3× across all rounds) and increases output throughput by 1.63× over the vLLM FP8 KV baseline.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput makes 4-bit KV caching viable and highly effective for agent workloads. Hardware-aware FP4 approximations with native GPU instruction support can substantially outperform FP8 baselines in latency and throughput.

title: Marginal Advantage Accumulation for Memory-Driven Agent Self-Evolution
summary: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation may receive contradictory feedback across different batches. Existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism, making it impossible to distinguish stably effective operations from accidental hits. This paper formalizes the requirement as two structural conditions, alignability and comparability, and proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA). MAA constructs differential signals to make them comparable across batches, accumulates signed evidence per operation via EMA, and ensures cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging. As a post-processing architecture, MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.

AI.tldr: MAA introduces cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation for trace distillation, using EMA-based signed evidence and semantic identity merging to satisfy alignability and comparability conditions, achieving SOTA on 14/16 settings while cutting token usage ~75%.
AI.motivation: Batch-style trace distillation suffers from contradictory feedback for the same memory operation across batches, and existing methods lack a mechanism to accumulate evidence across batches at the operation level, preventing reliable discrimination between genuinely effective operations and spurious successes.
AI.method: MAA formalizes two structural conditions — alignability and comparability — that cross-batch evidence accumulation must satisfy. It constructs differential signals to enable cross-batch comparison, accumulates signed evidence per operation using Exponential Moving Average (EMA), and ensures cross-batch traceability via semantic identity merging of operations. MAA functions as a post-processing architecture on top of existing batch-level methods.
AI.result: MAA achieves the best results on 14 out of 16 experimental settings spanning 4 benchmarks and 4 target models. It consistently outperforms existing batch-level distillation baselines and matches or surpasses online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.
AI.conclusion: MAA effectively addresses the cross-batch contradictory feedback problem in trace distillation by introducing operation-level signed evidence accumulation with formal structural guarantees, yielding state-of-the-art performance with substantially lower computational cost.

title: Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving
summary: Mainstream LLM serving systems reuse prefix work mainly through paged or radix key-value (KV) caches. This is highly effective for high-throughput, high-concurrency serving, but it manages only one positional fragment of execution state: the KV cache. We study the opposite regime: low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive LLM agents, speech systems, and robot policies repeatedly branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. We introduce execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint and restore mechanism for the complete restorable state at a committed boundary. FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime whose evaluated NVIDIA CUDA backend runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. Because the live state is a closed set of named buffers, a capsule can snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the whole execution boundary, including KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, and metadata. This moves reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries. On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, showing that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore are sub-millisecond, and TTFT speedup over cold prefill grows from 3.9x at 2k tokens to 27x at 16k tokens. On Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, the same correctness and structural properties hold. Capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse.

AI.tldr: FlashRT introduces execution-state capsules — a graph-bound checkpoint/restore mechanism for low-latency, on-device LLM serving. Unlike paged/radix KV caches that reuse token-addressed fragments, capsules snapshot the complete execution state (KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, metadata) at committed boundaries, enabling sub-millisecond restore, fork, and rollback. On RTX 5090, TTFT speedup over cold prefill reaches 27× at 16k tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM serving systems optimize for high-throughput, high-concurrency scenarios using paged or radix KV caches, which manage only one positional fragment of execution state. These systems are ill-suited for low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive agents, speech systems, and robot policies frequently branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. There is a need for a latency-first mechanism that captures and restores the complete restorable execution state at explicit boundaries.
AI.method: FlashRT implements a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime with an NVIDIA CUDA backend that runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers without block-table indirection. The live state is maintained as a closed set of named buffers, enabling execution-state capsules to snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the entire execution boundary — including KV cache, recurrent state, convolution state, multi-token prediction (MTP) state, and metadata. This shifts reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries.
AI.result: On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, confirming that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore operations are sub-millisecond. TTFT speedup over cold prefill grows from 3.9× at 2k tokens to 27× at 16k tokens. The same correctness and structural properties hold on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark.
AI.conclusion: Execution-state capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving but define a complementary, latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse. FlashRT demonstrates that graph-bound capsules provide strong correctness guarantees and substantial latency improvements for interactive, on-device physical-AI workloads.

title: Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning
