summary: Bayesian predictive inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, data efficiency, and robust generalization. However, exact inference is often intractable, and scalable approximations may remain computationally expensive or require restrictive modeling assumptions that degrade predictive performance. Prior-Data Fitted and in-context models have recently emerged as an amortized alternative by learning to map datasets directly to predictive distributions, but existing approaches are tightly coupled to the support of the training prior and lack explicit mechanisms for adapting to new priors at test time, resulting in limited robustness under distribution shift. We introduce a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that explicitly represents prior information as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt its predictions across families of priors. On a suite of evaluations with increasing difficulty, including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures, our method matches oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. We further demonstrate its practical relevance on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/martianmartina/multi-task-bayesian-icl/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference, where prior information is explicitly represented as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt predictions across families of priors, matching oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster, even under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Bayesian predictive inference is principled but computationally intractable; existing amortized alternatives (Prior-Data Fitted and in-context models) are tightly coupled to the training prior and lack mechanisms to adapt to new priors at test time, resulting in poor robustness under distribution shift.
AI.method: A multi-task in-context learning framework where a transformer is trained on sequences that prefix prior tasks before target tasks. This explicit representation of hierarchical prior information enables the model to learn adaptation across families of priors, including out-of-meta-distribution priors and those with high-dimensional latent structures.
AI.result: The method matches oracle Bayesian predictors across evaluations of increasing difficulty (out-of-meta-distribution priors, high-dimensional latent structures) while being orders of magnitude faster. Practical relevance is demonstrated on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly representing prior information as in-context prefixes enables transformers to perform amortized hierarchical Bayesian inference that is both accurate (matching oracle performance) and computationally efficient, with strong generalization even under prior distribution shift.

title: Predictability as a Fine-Grained Measure for Privacy
summary: Differential privacy (DP) ensures rigorous individual-level privacy guarantees against even the most knowledgeable attackers, but its worst-case nature can impose a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. We introduce privacy via predictability, a fine-grained framework that explicitly incorporates the attacker's core knowledge, a compromised portion of the dataset generated by a stochastic process, and a specified family of queries. Predictability measures privacy leakage as the incremental gain in an attacker's ability to predict sensitive information about unknown individuals after observing the algorithm's output, beyond what can already be inferred from the compromised data. We show that predictability and DP are generally incomparable: each can be small while the other is large. However, in the worst-case regime where all but one individual is compromised, and all binary queries are considered sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. More generally, predictability provides a finer-grained privacy metric tailored to specific sensitive information and specific attacker models. We introduce a general framework, using the generalized method of moments (GMM), to analyze asymptotic predictability when the compromised data is generated by a stationary, ergodic, mixing process. Using this analysis, we derive a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for ERM. Our approach is complementary to DP and can be used alongside DP to provide fine-grained privacy control.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "privacy via predictability," a fine-grained privacy framework that measures leakage as an attacker's incremental predictive gain over compromised data, contrasting with worst-case DP. They show the two are generally incomparable but connect under extreme compromise; they develop asymptotic analysis via GMM for stationary mixing processes and apply it to a calibrated ERM output perturbation scheme.
AI.motivation: Differential privacy offers worst-case, attacker-agnostic guarantees that can be overly conservative, imposing a heavy privacy-accuracy tradeoff. The authors seek a more fine-grained framework that explicitly accounts for the attacker's prior knowledge (a compromised subset of data), the data-generating process, and a restricted query family, enabling more efficient privacy control when the worst-case threat model is unrealistic.
AI.method: They propose a "predictability" metric defined as the incremental gain in an attacker's predictive ability (e.g., mutual information or conditional probability gap) about unknown individuals after observing the output, beyond what the compromised data already reveals. They analyze asymptotic predictability using the generalized method of moments (GMM) under the assumption that data is generated by a stationary, ergodic, mixing stochastic process. They then derive a predictability-calibrated output perturbation mechanism for empirical risk minimization (ERM).
AI.result: Predictability and DP are shown to be generally incomparable — one can be large while the other is small. However, in the worst-case regime where all but one individual is compromised and all binary queries are sensitive, low predictability implies mutual-information DP. Asymptotic analysis via GMM yields a practical predictability-calibrated perturbation scheme for ERM.
AI.conclusion: Predictability provides a finer-grained, attacker-aware privacy metric that complements rather than replaces differential privacy. It can be deployed alongside DP to achieve more nuanced, context-specific privacy-accuracy tradeoffs, particularly when strong distributional assumptions about the data-generating process are justified.

title: The Token Is a Group Element: On Lie-Algebra Attention over Matrix Lie Groups
summary: We place the attention token on the group: a token is an element $g_i$ of a matrix Lie group $G$ -- a bare transformation, with no feature payload and no external action $ρ(g)$ carrying it. To our knowledge this is the first attention construction whose tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements: their score is the closed-form algebra norm of the relative pose rather than a learned kernel, and it reaches the affine full-frame groups that every irrep- or surjective-exp-based method must exclude. We call it Lie-Algebra Attention. Once tokens are group elements, the rest follows with none of the usual representation-theoretic machinery. The relative geometry of a pair is canonical, $g_i^{-1} g_j$, so the pairwise invariant $w_{ij} = \log(g_i^{-1} g_j)$ is intrinsic rather than designed; equivariance under the diagonal $G$-action is tautological, and the cocycle condition holds automatically. The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm, $s_{ij} = -\|\log(g_i^{-1} g_j)\|_λ^2/τ$: the canonical proximity kernel under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product, with no irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernel. The construction applies to any matrix Lie group on a chosen logarithm chart containing the relative poses, including the non-compact non-abelian affine groups with scale and shear that no vector-token attention method reaches: neither the irrep tradition nor surjective-exp methods. Three sequence-completion experiments, on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2), bear this out: the closed-form score matches a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant and outperforms it on SE(2), using 50 to 80x fewer score parameters, while a vector-token baseline breaks invariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Lie-Algebra Attention, where attention tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements. The attention score is computed as the negative squared algebra norm of the relative pose logarithm — a closed-form, canonical proximity kernel requiring no learned parameters, irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, or Clebsch-Gordan products. The method naturally handles non-compact, non-abelian affine groups (e.g., with scale and shear) that prior vector-token and surjective-exp approaches cannot. Experiments on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2) show competitive or superior performance with 50–80× fewer score parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing attention mechanisms operate on vector tokens with feature payloads and use learned kernels or representation-theoretic machinery (irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, surjective exponentials). These methods cannot reach non-compact non-abelian affine groups that include scale and shear transformations. The authors seek a simpler, intrinsic attention formulation where tokens are bare group elements — eliminating learned pairwise kernels and the need for representation theory — that naturally extends to all matrix Lie groups, including affine full-frame groups.
AI.method: Tokens are elements g_i of a matrix Lie group G. The relative geometry is canonical: g_i^{-1} g_j. The pairwise invariant is w_{ij} = log(g_i^{-1} g_j), computed on a chosen logarithm chart. The attention score is s_{ij} = -||log(g_i^{-1} g_j)||_λ^2 / τ — the negative squared algebra norm under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product. This yields a closed-form proximity kernel with no learned parameters. Equivariance under diagonal G-action and the cocycle condition hold automatically by construction. The method applies to any matrix Lie group where relative poses fall within the logarithm chart.
AI.result: Three sequence-completion experiments on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2) demonstrate that the closed-form Lie-algebra score matches or outperforms a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant. On SE(2), it surpasses the MLP kernel while using 50–80× fewer score parameters. A vector-token baseline breaks equivariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude, underscoring the necessity of the group-token approach.
AI.conclusion: Lie-Algebra Attention demonstrates that bare group elements can serve directly as attention tokens, with a canonical, closed-form score derived from the Lie algebra norm. This eliminates the need for learned kernels and representation-theoretic machinery while extending attention to affine full-frame groups previously inaccessible. The approach unifies simplicity, parameter efficiency, and formal guarantees of equivariance.

title: Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction
summary:
A model is multicalibrated on a collection of group weights $G$ if it is calibrated -- i.e. unbiased even conditional on its prediction -- not just overall, but also after reweighting contexts by each $g \in G$. It is a useful property for many downstream applications and is a basic desideratum of trustworthy machine learning. Before this work, all predictors known to attain the minimax-optimal $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity rate for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration were randomized, while deterministic predictors were known only with substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization is necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration was explicitly asked by [CLNR26] and implicitly in several prior works.
  We resolve this open problem by giving a minimax-optimal multicalibration algorithm that outputs a deterministic predictor. We then generalize the algorithm to produce optimal deterministic predictors that satisfy outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests. As an application, this also gives deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors with optimal sample complexity, resolving open problems posed by [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the open problem of whether randomization is necessary for achieving minimax-optimal sample complexity in multicalibration, presenting a deterministic algorithm that matches the optimal O(ε⁻³) rate. It further generalizes this to outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors.
AI.motivation: Prior to this work, all predictors achieving the minimax-optimal sample complexity of Õ(ε⁻³) for ε-multicalibration were randomized; deterministic predictors had substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization is strictly necessary was an explicit open problem raised by [CLNR26] and implicitly in earlier works.
AI.method: The authors construct a minimax-optimal deterministic multicalibration algorithm. They then generalize this algorithmic framework to produce optimal deterministic predictors satisfying outcome indistinguishability (OI) for finite or finitely covered test collections, and apply it to deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors.
AI.result: The paper provides the first deterministic predictor that achieves the minimax-optimal Õ(ε⁻³) sample complexity for ε-multicalibration, proving that randomization is not necessary. The generalization yields optimal deterministic OI predictors, omnipredictors, and panpredictors, resolving open problems from [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].
AI.conclusion: Randomization is not necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration or related notions like outcome indistinguishability, omniprediction, and panprediction. The deterministic construction closes a significant gap in the theoretical foundations of trustworthy machine learning.

title: How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?
comment: 20 main text pages and 6 pages of references and appendices
summary: LLM reasoning transparency is a critical affordance for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse and misalignment, and debugging surprising model behaviors. However, DiffusionGemma performs a larger fraction of its computation in a continuous latent space; does this make its reasoning less transparent? We study this question by decomposing transparency into two components: variable transparency, whether we understand intermediate snapshots of a model's computational state; and algorithmic transparency, whether we can use these snapshots to reconstruct the process by which the model arrived at its outputs. Naively, DiffusionGemma has poor variable transparency: its opaque serial depth, the amount of serial computation that occurs in between interpretable model states, seems at first 28.6X higher than the corresponding autoregressive Gemma 4 model. However, we show that we can map the information flowing between denoising steps through an interpretable token bottleneck with no decrease in downstream performance. Treating these intermediate states as interpretable reduces the opaque serial depth to just 1.1X that of Gemma 4. Algorithmic transparency is harder for diffusion models than for autoregressive models because all token predictions in the canvas can change at every denoising step, giving the model the power to implement complicated distributed algorithms during the denoising process. To begin bridging this gap, we conduct a suite of interpretability case studies, uncovering initial evidence of novel diffusion-specific phenomena such as non-chronological reasoning, token and sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Finally, we test monitorability, a key application of transparency that measures whether model outputs are useful for downstream tasks. We find that DiffusionGemma is similarly monitorable to Gemma 4.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether diffusion language models (specifically DiffusionGemma) are less transparent than autoregressive models (Gemma 4). It decomposes transparency into variable and algorithmic transparency, finding that initial opacity (28.6X higher opaque serial depth) can be reduced to 1.1X via interpretable token bottlenecks. Algorithmic transparency remains harder due to distributed denoising dynamics, with novel phenomena discovered. Monitorability is comparable between models.
AI.motivation: DiffusionGemma performs much of its computation in continuous latent space, raising the question of whether this architectural choice sacrifices reasoning transparency compared to autoregressive models. Transparency is critical for understanding decisions, mitigating misuse, and debugging, so establishing whether diffusion LMs preserve it is an urgent open problem.
AI.method: The authors decompose transparency into two axes: (1) variable transparency — whether intermediate computational states are interpretable, quantified via "opaque serial depth" (amount of serial computation between interpretable states); and (2) algorithmic transparency — whether snapshots can reconstruct the reasoning process. They map information flow through an interpretable token bottleneck between denoising steps, conduct interpretability case studies (non-chronological reasoning, token/sequence smearing, intermediate-context reasoning), and evaluate monitorability as a downstream application.
AI.result: Naive opaque serial depth for DiffusionGemma is 28.6X higher than Gemma 4, but mapping through an interpretable token bottleneck reduces this to 1.1X with no performance loss. Algorithmic transparency is fundamentally harder due to all token predictions changing at every denoising step, enabling distributed algorithms. Case studies reveal novel diffusion-specific phenomena. Monitorability is comparable between DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4.
AI.conclusion: DiffusionGemma's reasoning is not inherently less transparent than autoregressive models. While initial variable transparency appears poor, it can be largely recovered via interpretable intermediate states. Algorithmic transparency remains a challenge requiring new interpretability methods tailored to diffusion-specific reasoning patterns. Comparable monitorability suggests practical transparency for downstream applications is preserved.
